Contraindicated: Avoid colonoscopy or barium enema during the acute phase due to high risk of bowel perforation.

cards.q: What vascular GI condition is classically associated with calcific Aortic Stenosis and End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD)?
cards.a: Angiodysplasia (vascular ectasia). Associated with Heyde's Syndrome (destruction of Von Willebrand factor multimers across the stenotic aortic valve, leading to bleeding from GI angiodysplasias).

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and diagnostic workup of Gastroparesis.
cards.a:
Delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction. Associated with diabetes.

Presentation: Postprandial fullness, early satiety, nausea, vomiting of undigested food.
Diagnosis: Gastric emptying scintigraphy showing retention of > 10% of solid meal at 4 hours.
Treatment: Metoclopramide (prokinetic, dopamine antagonist) or erythromycin.

cards.q: What is the autoantibody association in Autoimmune Hepatitis?
cards.a:
• Type 1: Anti-Smooth Muscle Antibodies (ASMA) and ANA. Most common in adults.
• Type 2: Anti-liver-kidney microsomal-1 (anti-LKM-1) antibodies. More common in children.

cards.q: What is Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES), and how is it diagnosed?
cards.a:
A gastrin-producing tumor (gastrinoma), often located in the duodenum or pancreas, causing recurrent refractory peptic ulcers.

Diagnosis: Elevated fasting serum gastrin (> 1000 pg/mL) + positive Secretin stimulation test (secretin paradoxically increases gastrin levels in gastrinomas).

cards.q: Contrast Acute Mesenteric Ischemia vs. Ischemic Colitis by clinical presentation and risk factors.
cards.a:
• Acute Mesenteric Ischemia: Sudden occlusion of the SMA (often embolic from AF). Presents as severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical exam. Acidosis and elevated lactate. Emergency CT angiogram.
• Ischemic Colitis: Hypoperfusion of 'watershed' areas of the colon (e.g., splenic flexure, rectosigmoid junction) due to transient hypotension. Presents as crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed by hematochezia/bloody diarrhea. Diagnose via colonoscopy.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI)?
cards.a:
Oral Vancomycin or oral Fidaxomicin.
Note: IV metronidazole is only added in cases of fulminant C. diff (characterized by hypotension, shock, ileus, or megacolon).

cards.q: Define Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS) and its clinical diagnostic criterion.
cards.a:
Acute kidney injury in a patient with advanced cirrhosis and ascites, caused by renal vasoconstriction due to splanchnic vasodilation.

Diagnosis: Serum creatinine increase ≥ 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or ≥ 50% increase from baseline, that does not improve after 48 hours of fluid challenge (albumin infusion) and withdrawal of diuretics.

cards.q: What is the medical management for Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)?
cards.a: Combination of vasoconstrictors (Terlipressin or Midodrine + Octreotide) + IV Albumin.

cards.q: What diagnostic findings characterize Wilson's Disease?
cards.a:
Defect in biliary copper excretion (ATP7B mutation) → copper accumulation in liver, brain, cornea.

Diagnosis: Low serum ceruloplasmin, increased 24h urinary copper excretion, Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam.
Treatment: Chelators (Penicillamine, Trientine) or zinc.

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and risk factors for Budd-Chiari Syndrome.
cards.a:
Thrombosis/obstruction of the hepatic veins leading to hepatic congestion.

Presentation: Triad of hepatomegaly, ascites, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
Risk factors: Polycythemia vera (JAK2 mutation), hypercoagulable states, pregnancy, HCC.

cards.q: What is the next best step in management for a patient with suspected Achalasia after a barium swallow is performed?
cards.a: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) (endoscopy) to rule out pseudoachalasia (esophageal cancer at the GE junction mimicking achalasia) before performing manometry.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic evaluation of choice for a patient presenting with new-onset dyspepsia who is ≥ 60 years old?
cards.a: Upper endoscopy (EGD) to evaluate for gastric cancer. In patients < 60 with no alarm features (weight loss, dysphagia, anemia), use a 'test-and-treat' strategy for H. pylori.

cards.q: Name the key laboratory findings in Hepatic Osteodystrophy / Primary Biliary Cholangitis.
cards.a: Marked elevation of Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) and GGT, with normal or mildly elevated AST/ALT. Hyperbilirubinemia occurs in late-stage disease.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of toxic megacolon?
cards.a:
Life-threatening complication of UC or C. diff infection.

Presentation: Severe bloody diarrhea, systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, altered mental status), and colonic dilation > 6 cm on abdominal X-ray.
Treatment: IV fluids, IV steroids, bowel decompression, broad-spectrum antibiotics. Emergency colectomy if no improvement in 24–48 hours.

cards.q: Define Courvoisier's Law / Sign.
cards.a: A palpable, non-tender, distended gallbladder in the presence of mild jaundice. Suggests malignant obstruction of the common bile duct (e.g., pancreatic adenocarcinoma) rather than gallstones.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute ascending Cholangitis?
cards.a:
• Charcot's Triad: Fever, RUQ pain, jaundice.
• Reynold's Pentad: Charcot's triad + Hypotension/shock + altered mental status (indicates severe sepsis/pus in the biliary tree).

cards.q: What is the immediate management for acute ascending cholangitis?
cards.a: IV antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam) + urgent biliary decompression via Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).

cards.q: Describe the clinical significance of a positive antimitochondrial antibody (AMA).
cards.a: Highly specific (95%) for Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC). PBC is treated with Ursodeoxycholic Acid (UDCA) to slow disease progression.

cards.q: What is the association between Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) and Cholangiocarcinoma?
cards.a: Patients with PSC have a significantly increased lifetime risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer), requiring periodic screening with CA 19-9 and imaging.

cards.q: What is the screening recommendation for colorectal cancer in patients with a history of Ulcerative Colitis?
cards.a: Screening colonoscopy with surveillance biopsies every 1–2 years, beginning 8 years after the initial diagnosis of UC (covers the entire colon except in patients with isolated proctitis).

cards.q: What is the presentation of acute mesenteric ischemia on CT angiography?
cards.a: Focal segment of bowel wall thickening, lack of bowel wall enhancement, pneumatosis intestinalis (air in the bowel wall), or portal venous gas (indicates bowel infarction).

cards.q: What is the diagnosis and diagnostic test of choice for suspected Lactose Intolerance?
cards.a:
Malabsorption of lactose due to lactase deficiency.

Diagnostic test: Hydrogen Breath Test (demonstrates rise in breath hydrogen after oral lactose ingestion due to bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed lactose in the colon).

cards.q: Explain the difference between unconjugated (indirect) and conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia.
cards.a:
• Unconjugated: Excess production (hemolysis) or impaired conjugation (Gilbert's, Crigler-Najjar). Biliary excretion is normal; urine is normal color (bilirubin is bound to albumin and not filtered).
• Conjugated: Impaired biliary excretion (biliary obstruction, Dubin-Johnson, Rotor, hepatitis). Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and filtered by kidneys → dark, tea-colored urine.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic marker of choice for Gilbert's Syndrome, and what is its prognosis?
cards.a:
Mild, intermittent, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia triggered by stress, fasting, infection, or exercise, with completely normal liver enzymes and no hemolysis.

Prognosis: Benign autosomal recessive condition caused by reduced activity of UGT1A1. No treatment required.

cards.q: What is the best initial step in management for a patient presenting with high clinical suspicion of achalasia?
cards.a: Barium esophagram, followed by upper endoscopy to rule out pseudoachalasia (malignancy), and definitively confirmed by esophageal manometry.

cards.q: What is the medical treatment for esophageal spasm when nitrates or calcium channel blockers fail?
cards.a: Tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., imipramine) or botulinum toxin injection.

cards.q: How does the presentation of eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) classically differ from GERD in adults?
cards.a: EoE often presents with solid food dysphagia and food impaction in young men with atopic history, often unresponsive to PPI trial.

cards.q: What are the endoscopic findings pathognomonic for Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE)?
cards.a: Multiple corrugated rings (trachealization), longitudinal furrows, and white exudates. Biopsy shows >15 eosinophils/hpf.

cards.q: What is the next best step for an incidentally found Zenker's diverticulum that is asymptomatic?
cards.a: Observation. Surgery (cricopharyngeal myotomy) is reserved for symptomatic patients.

cards.q: What is the primary pathophysiology behind the formation of a Zenker's diverticulum?
cards.a: Motor dysfunction and impaired relaxation of the cricopharyngeus muscle during swallowing, leading to high intraluminal pressure above the upper esophageal sphincter.

cards.q: What diagnostic finding distinguishes Mallory-Weiss tear from Boerhaave syndrome on imaging?
cards.a: Boerhaave syndrome shows pneumomediastinum or contrast extravasation on gastrografin swallow due to transmural rupture, whereas Mallory-Weiss is mucosal and lacks extravasation.

cards.q: What is the screening recommendation for a patient with Barrett's esophagus and NO dysplasia?
cards.a: Endoscopy with biopsy every 3 to 5 years.

cards.q: What is the management of Barrett's esophagus with HIGH-grade dysplasia?
cards.a: Endoscopic eradication therapy (e.g., radiofrequency ablation or endoscopic mucosal resection).

cards.q: In a patient with suspected upper GI bleed and ongoing hematemesis, what is the initial medical therapy before endoscopy?
cards.a: IV fluid resuscitation, IV PPI, IV octreotide (if varices suspected), and prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) in cirrhotics.

cards.q: What is the optimal prophylactic antibiotic regimen for a patient with cirrhosis and an acute variceal bleed?
cards.a: IV ceftriaxone for up to 7 days.

cards.q: What is the most accurate diagnostic test for Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES)?
cards.a: Secretin stimulation test. In ZES, secretin paradoxically stimulates the release of gastrin (normal response is suppression).

cards.q: When is surgery indicated for a patient with a perforated peptic ulcer?
cards.a: Immediate surgical exploration with omental patch closure is indicated for a perforated peptic ulcer presenting with acute peritonitis and pneumoperitoneum.

cards.q: What is the preferred non-invasive test to confirm H. pylori eradication after treatment?
cards.a: Urea breath test or stool antigen test (performed at least 4 weeks after completion of therapy). Serology cannot distinguish active from past infection.

cards.q: A patient with diarrhea, flatulence, and weight loss has PAS-positive macrophages in the lamina propria on small bowel biopsy. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Whipple's disease (caused by Tropheryma whipplei).

cards.q: What is the standard treatment for Whipple's disease?
cards.a: IV ceftriaxone or penicillin for 2 weeks, followed by oral TMP-SMX for 1-2 years.

cards.q: What antibody is highly specific for Celiac disease and used for screening?
cards.a: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) antibody. Total IgA must be measured to rule out selective IgA deficiency.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Tropical Sprue and how is it treated?
cards.a: Chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and megaloblastic anemia (B<sub>12</sub>/folate deficiency) after residing in the tropics. Treated with tetracycline and folic acid for 3-6 months.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test of choice for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO)?
cards.a: Carbohydrate breath test (lactulose or glucose) showing an early rise in breath hydrogen.

cards.q: What is the medical treatment for Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)?
cards.a: Oral broad-spectrum antibiotics, commonly Rifaximin.

cards.q: What unique extraintestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease parallels bowel activity?
cards.a: Erythema nodosum (along with peripheral arthritis and episcleritis).

cards.q: What dermatologic manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease progresses independently of bowel disease activity?
cards.a: Pyoderma gangrenosum (along with primary sclerosing cholangitis and ankylosing spondylitis).

cards.q: What is the most accurate test for evaluating an acute exacerbation of Crohn's disease to check for complications?
cards.a: CT enterography or MR enterography (to evaluate for fistulas, abscesses, or strictures).

cards.q: What is the maintenance therapy of choice for moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease?
cards.a: Anti-TNF agents (e.g., Infliximab, Adalimumab), often combined with an immunomodulator (azathioprine).

cards.q: What is the initial diagnostic modality of choice for a patient suspected of having acute diverticulitis?
cards.a: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with IV and oral contrast. Colonoscopy is contraindicated during acute infection due to perforation risk.

cards.q: What are the criteria for diagnosing toxic megacolon?
cards.a: Radiographic evidence of colonic dilation (>6 cm) plus systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, anemia).

cards.q: A patient with chronic liver disease has a SAAG (Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient) of > 1.1 g/dL. What does this indicate?
cards.a: Portal hypertension (e.g., cirrhosis, right heart failure, Budd-Chiari syndrome). SAAG < 1.1 indicates non-portal hypertension causes (e.g., nephrotic syndrome, TB, malignancy).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic criteria for Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)?
cards.a: Ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count (ANC) ≥ 250 cells/mm<sup>3</sup>.

cards.q: What is the empirical treatment of Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)?
cards.a: Third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., IV Cefotaxime or Ceftriaxone). IV Albumin is also given to prevent hepatorenal syndrome.

cards.q: What is the next best step for a patient with cirrhosis and new-onset, unexplained fever, encephalopathy, or worsening renal function?
cards.a: Diagnostic paracentesis to rule out Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP).

cards.q: What is the preferred initial treatment for hepatic encephalopathy?
cards.a: Lactulose (to lower colonic pH and convert NH<sub>3</sub> to non-absorbable NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>). Rifaximin is added for refractory cases.

cards.q: What is the classic pentad of Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) presentation?
cards.a: Middle-aged woman, pruritus (often worse at night), fatigue, jaundice, and xanthelasmas. Positive for Anti-Mitochondrial Antibodies (AMA).

cards.q: What is the medical treatment of choice to slow disease progression in Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)?
cards.a: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). Liver transplantation is the only curative treatment.

cards.q: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) is strongly associated with which other condition?
cards.a: Ulcerative Colitis (UC). Most patients with PSC have UC, though the reverse is less common.

cards.q: What classic imaging finding on MRCP/ERCP is pathognomonic for Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)?
cards.a: Multifocal stricturing and dilation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts (described as a 'beaded' appearance).

cards.q: A patient presents with markedly elevated AST and ALT (>10,000 U/L). What is the most likely etiology?
cards.a: Acetaminophen toxicity, shock liver (ischemic hepatopathy), or severe acute viral hepatitis.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for acetaminophen overdose within 4 hours of ingestion?
cards.a: Activated charcoal to decrease GI absorption, followed by N-acetylcysteine (NAC) administration based on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram.

cards.q: Which hepatitis B serological marker is present during the 'window period' of acute infection?
cards.a: IgM anti-HBc (Hepatitis B core antibody). HBsAg and anti-HBs are both negative during this time.

cards.q: What constitutes the criteria for acute liver failure?
cards.a: Severe acute liver injury (elevated transaminases), hepatic encephalopathy, and synthetic liver dysfunction (INR ≥ 1.5) in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis.

cards.q: What is the triad of Hemochromatosis?
cards.a: Liver cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus (bronze diabetes), and skin hyperpigmentation. Due to autosomal recessive mutation in the HFE gene.

cards.q: Which joints are classically affected by the arthropathy seen in hemochromatosis?
cards.a: 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, characterized by calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystal deposition.

cards.q: What is the most accurate test for diagnosing Wilson disease?
cards.a: Hepatic copper concentration on liver biopsy. Non-invasive screening involves low serum ceruloplasmin and high 24-hour urinary copper excretion.

cards.q: What is the initial medical therapy for Wilson disease?
cards.a: Copper chelators like D-penicillamine or Trientine. Oral zinc can be used for maintenance as it prevents enterocyte copper absorption.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of Budd-Chiari syndrome?
cards.a: Abdominal pain, massive ascites, and hepatomegaly due to hepatic vein thrombosis.

cards.q: What is the first-line screening modality for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in cirrhotic patients?
cards.a: Ultrasound of the liver every 6 months, with or without alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) testing.

cards.q: What is the treatment for a symptomatic patient with a benign hepatic adenoma?
cards.a: Discontinue oral contraceptives (OCPs) if < 5 cm. Surgical resection is indicated if > 5 cm or symptomatic due to risk of rupture/hemorrhage and malignant transformation.

cards.q: A young female presents with a central stellate scar on liver imaging. What is the diagnosis and management?
cards.a: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia (FNH). It is a benign condition and managed conservatively with observation.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic criteria for Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)?
cards.a: Progressive renal failure in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites, lacking other causes of AKI, that is unresponsive to a fluid challenge (albumin and diuretic withdrawal).

cards.q: What is the pharmacologic bridge to liver transplantation for Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)?
cards.a: Splanchnic vasoconstrictors (e.g., Midodrine + Octreotide, or Terlipressin) along with IV Albumin.

cards.q: What vitamin deficiency is characterized by the 3 D's (Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia) and can be seen in Carcinoid Syndrome?
cards.a: Niacin (Vitamin B<sub>3</sub>) deficiency (Pellagra). Carcinoid tumors consume tryptophan to make serotonin, thereby depleting niacin synthesis.

cards.q: What is the formula for Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG), and how do SAAG values ≥ 1.1 g/dL vs. < 1.1 g/dL differentiate ascites etiologies?
cards.a:
SAAG = Serum Albumin − Ascitic Fluid Albumin.
• SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL: Indicates portal hypertension (e.g., Cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, Congestive Heart Failure).
• SAAG < 1.1 g/dL: Indicates non-portal hypertension causes (e.g., Peritoneal carcinomatosis, TB peritonitis, Nephrotic syndrome, Pancreatic ascites).

cards.q: How is Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP) diagnosed, and what are the initial treatment and prophylaxis guidelines?
cards.a:
Diagnosis: Ascitic fluid absolute PMN count ≥ 250/mm3.
Treatment: Empiric 3rd generation cephalosporin (e.g., Cefotaxime or Ceftriaxone) plus IV Albumin (to prevent hepatorenal syndrome).
Prophylaxis: Daily Fluoroquinolone (e.g., Ciprofloxacin) or TMP-SMX.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, and management of Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)?
cards.a:
Pathophysiology: Severe splanchnic vasodilation leading to renal hypoperfusion and RAAS activation.
Diagnosis: Acute kidney injury in liver failure unresponsive to volume expansion (saline trial) with low urine Na+ (< 10 mEq/L) and normal renal ultrasound.
Management: Splanchnic vasoconstrictors (Terlipressin or Octreotide + Midodrine) + IV Albumin; definitive treatment is Liver Transplantation.

cards.q: What lab parameters and initial fluid management strategies are critical in Acute Pancreatitis?
cards.a:
Diagnosis: Serum Lipase ≥ 3× upper limit of normal (more specific than Amylase).
Severity/Hydration indicator: Rising BUN or Hct indicates intravascular depletion/hemoconcentration.
Initial Management: Aggressive fluid resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's (LR) solution and enteral nutrition (if tolerated).

cards.q: What genetic mutation, diagnostic findings, and treatment options characterize Wilson Disease?
cards.a:
Mutation: AR mutation in ATP7B gene leading to impaired biliary copper secretion.
Clinical Presentation: Cirrhosis, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Labs: Low serum ceruloplasmin, increased 24-hr urinary Cu2+, increased hepatic copper content.
Treatment: Copper chelators (Penicillamine or Trientine) and oral Zinc.

cards.q: What is the key diagnostic serologic marker and first-line therapy for Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)?
cards.a:
Serology: Positive Anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA).
Pathology: Autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic interlobular bile ducts (middle-aged women).
First-line therapy: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA); liver transplantation for end-stage disease.

cards.q: What imaging finding, strong disease association, and major long-term risk are associated with Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)?
cards.a:
Imaging (MRCP/ERCP): 'Bead-on-a-string' appearance (multifocal strictures and segmentally dilated intra/extrahepatic bile ducts).
Association: Strongly associated with Ulcerative Colitis (approx. 70-80%).
Complication: High risk of Cholangiocarcinoma.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic gold standard for Achalasia, and what findings are expected on barium swallow and manometry?
cards.a:
Barium swallow: Smooth taper of lower esophagus ('Bird's-beak' sign) with proximal dilation.
Esophageal Manometry (Gold standard): Absence of esophageal peristalsis and incomplete/absent relaxation of the Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES) with elevated resting LES pressure.

cards.q: What is the anatomic defect in Zenker Diverticulum, how does it present, and what is the diagnostic test of choice?
cards.a:
Anatomic location: Herniation through Killian triangle (between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles).
Presentation: Oropharyngeal dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, and a neck mass.
Diagnostic test: Barium esophagram (Upper endoscopy is contraindicated due to risk of perforation).

cards.q: What is Boerhaave Syndrome, how is it diagnosed, and which contrast agent MUST be used?
cards.a:
Definition: Transmural esophageal perforation following severe/repetitive vomiting.
Presentation: Retrosternal chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, and Hamman sign (mediastinal crunch).
Diagnosis: Esophagram using water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin). Barium contrast must be avoided due to risk of mediastinitis.

cards.q: What is the management of early-stage gastric MALT Lymphoma associated with Helicobacter pylori?
cards.a:
Management: H. pylori eradication therapy (e.g., PPI + Amoxicillin + Clarithromycin or Quadruple therapy).
Outcome: Complete regression of early low-grade MALT lymphoma occurs in up to 75-80% of cases following bacterial eradication alone.

cards.q: What are the key serologic markers, small intestine biopsy findings, and malignancy risk associated with Celiac Disease?
cards.a:
Serology: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) and IgA anti-endomysial antibodies.
Duodenal biopsy: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis.
Malignancy complication: Increased risk of Enteropathy-Associated T-Cell Lymphoma (EATL).

cards.q: How do Crohn Disease and Ulcerative Colitis (UC) differ regarding gross/histologic distribution and transmural involvement?
cards.a:
Crohn Disease: Transmural inflammation, skip lesions, non-caseating granulomas, cobblestoning, fistulas/perianal disease, ASCA positive.
Ulcerative Colitis: Mucosal/submucosal inflammation only, continuous extension starting from rectum, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps, p-ANCA positive.

cards.q: What genetic defect causes Hereditary Hemochromatosis, what is the classic clinical triad, and what is the primary treatment?
cards.a:
Genetics: AR mutation in HFE gene (e.g., C282Y mutation) leading to excessive iron absorption.
Classic triad: Cirrhosis, Diabetes mellitus ('bronze diabetes'), and Skin hyperpigmentation.
Treatment: Therapeutic phlebotomy (target serum ferritin < 50-100 ng/mL).

cards.q: How does Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) differ from Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD) in terms of AST/ALT ratios?
cards.a:
NAFLD/NASH: AST/ALT ratio is typically < 1 (ALT > AST). Associated with metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance.
Alcoholic Liver Disease: AST/ALT ratio is typically ≥ 2:1 (AST > ALT, with AST rarely > 500 U/L).

cards.q: What are the first-line treatment regimens for initial episodes of Clostridioides difficile infection?
cards.a:
First-line oral therapy: Oral Fidaxomicin (200 mg BID for 10 days) or Oral Vancomycin (125 mg QID for 10 days).
Note: IV Vancomycin is ineffective because it is not excreted into the intestinal lumen.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation, initial best diagnostic test, and pathophysiology of Acute Mesenteric Ischemia?
cards.a:
Pathophysiology: Sudden occlusion of the Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA), commonly from cardiac emboli (e.g., AFib).
Presentation: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings.
Initial best test: CT Angiography of the abdomen.

cards.q: What is Angiodysplasia, what cardiac valvular disorder is it associated with, and how does it present?
cards.a:
Definition: Vascular ectasia / tortuous submucosal veins commonly located in the cecum/right colon.
Association: Aortic Stenosis (Heyde syndrome, due to acquired von Willebrand factor cleavage) and renal disease.
Presentation: Episodic, painless lower GI bleeding (hematochezia) in elderly patients.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Lactulose and Rifaximin in treating Hepatic Encephalopathy?
cards.a:
Lactulose: Colonic bacteria degrade lactulose into lactic acid and acetic acid → acidifies gut lumen → converts NH3 to non-absorbable NH4+ (ion trapping) + osmotic laxative effect.
Rifaximin: Non-absorbable antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria.

cards.q: What is Ogilvie Syndrome (Acute Colonic Pseudo-obstruction), how is it diagnosed, and what pharmacological agent is used when conservative therapy fails?
cards.a:
Definition: Massive dilation of the colon in the absence of mechanical obstruction, usually in severely ill/surgical patients.
Diagnosis: Abdominal CT showing marked colonic/cecal dilation without distal transition zone.
Pharmacotherapy: IV Neostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) if cecal diameter > 10-12 cm or failing conservative tx.

cards.q: What is Winter's Formula, and what does it evaluate?
cards.a:
Winter's Formula: \(P_aCO_2 = (1.5 \times [HCO_3^-]) + 8 \pm 2\).

Evaluation: Evaluates the adequacy of respiratory compensation in a patient with metabolic acidosis. If the measured \(P_aCO_2\) is higher than the calculated range, there is a co-existing respiratory acidosis. If it is lower, there is a co-existing respiratory alkalosis.

cards.q: What is the formula for the Serum Anion Gap, and what is a normal value?
cards.a:
Anion Gap = \([Na^+] - ([Cl^-] + [HCO_3^-])\).
• Normal Value: 10–12 mEq/L.
Note: A high anion gap indicates accumulation of unmeasured organic anions (e.g., lactate, ketones, toxins).

cards.q: State the mnemonic and causes of High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (HAGMA).
cards.a:
Mnemonic: MUDPILES (or GOLDMARK).
• M: Methanol
• U: Uremia (renal failure)
• D: Diabetic (or starvation/alcoholic) Ketoacidosis
• P: Propylene glycol / Paracetamol
• I: Iron / Isoniazid
• L: Lactic Acidosis
• E: Ethylene glycol (antifreeze)
• S: Salicylates (aspirin toxicity — causing mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis).

cards.q: What is the calculated serum osmolality formula, and how do you calculate the Osmolar Gap?
cards.a:
• Calculated Osmolality = \(2 \times [Na^+] + \frac{[Glucose]}{18} + \frac{[BUN]}{2.8}\)
• Osmolar Gap = Measured Osmolality − Calculated Osmolality (Normal < 10 mOsm/kg)
An elevated Osmolar Gap suggests the presence of an unmeasured osmole (e.g., methanol, ethanol, ethylene glycol).

cards.q: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with acute kidney injury whose urinalysis reveals muddy brown granular casts?
cards.a: Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)

cards.q: A patient presents with acute kidney injury after taking amoxicillin. Urinalysis shows WBC casts and eosinophiluria. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN)

cards.q: What do RBC casts on urinalysis strongly suggest?
cards.a: Glomerulonephritis

cards.q: What do fatty casts (oval fat bodies, Maltese crosses under polarized light) indicate?
cards.a: Nephrotic syndrome

cards.q: What do broad waxy casts indicate?
cards.a: Chronic renal failure (they form in dilated, hypertrophied tubules)

cards.q: What is the very first diagnostic step in a patient with unexplained new-onset Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)?
cards.a: Renal ultrasound to rule out post-renal etiology (e.g., hydronephrosis/obstruction).

cards.q: What BUN/Cr ratio and FENa+ are indicative of pre-renal azotemia?
cards.a: BUN/Cr > 20:1 and FENa < 1% (kidneys are actively reabsorbing Na+ and water).

cards.q: What are the absolute indications for urgent hemodialysis (AEIOU)?
cards.a: Acidosis (severe, refractory), Electrolyte imbalance (severe hyperkalemia), Intoxication (Li, toxic alcohols, salicylates), Overload (refractory volume overload), Uremia (pericarditis, encephalopathy).

cards.q: What is the first-line medication for a patient with severe hyperkalemia showing EKG changes (e.g., peaked T waves)?
cards.a: IV Calcium Gluconate (or Calcium Chloride) to stabilize the cardiac myocyte membrane.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in African American adults and is associated with HIV, heroin use, and sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

cards.q: What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in Caucasian adults, often associated with solid tumors (e.g., lung, colon, breast)?
cards.a: Membranous Nephropathy

cards.q: What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, typically treated with empiric corticosteroids?
cards.a: Minimal Change Disease (MCD)

cards.q: Which nephrotic syndrome is highly associated with Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C, and shows a "tram-track" appearance on electron microscopy?
cards.a: Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN)

cards.q: What pathognomonic renal biopsy finding (nodular glomerulosclerosis) is seen in Diabetic Nephropathy?
cards.a: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules

cards.q: A patient develops hematuria, edema, and hypertension 1-2 weeks after a skin infection (impetigo) or pharyngitis. Serum complement C3 is low. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Poststreptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

cards.q: A young man develops gross hematuria concurrently (within days) of an upper respiratory infection. Serum complement levels are normal. Diagnosis?
cards.a: IgA Nephropathy (Berger disease)

cards.q: A patient presents with hemoptysis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN). Renal biopsy shows linear IgG deposition on the glomerular basement membrane. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Goodpasture Syndrome (Anti-GBM antibodies)

cards.q: A patient presents with asthma, eosinophilia, purpura, and renal disease. Blood tests are positive for p-ANCA (anti-MPO). Diagnosis?
cards.a: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss)

cards.q: A patient presents with sinusitis, hemoptysis (cavitary lung lesions), and renal failure. Blood tests are positive for c-ANCA (anti-PR3). Diagnosis?
cards.a: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Wegener)

cards.q: What is the classic tetrad of Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (IgA Vasculitis)?
cards.a: Palpable purpura (lower extremities/buttocks), arthralgias, abdominal pain/intussusception, and renal disease (similar to IgA nephropathy).

cards.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with sensorineural hearing loss, anterior lenticonus (eye problems), and painless hematuria. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Alport Syndrome (Mutation in Type IV collagen)

cards.q: What is the most common composition of kidney stones?
cards.a: Calcium oxalate

cards.q: Which kidney stones are radiolucent (invisible on standard X-ray) and form in acidic urine?
cards.a: Uric acid stones

cards.q: Which kidney stones form large "staghorn" calculi, have a "coffin-lid" appearance, and are caused by urease-producing bugs (e.g., Proteus mirabilis)?
cards.a: Struvite stones (Magnesium ammonium phosphate)

cards.q: Which kidney stones are uniquely associated with a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test and have a hexagonal shape?
cards.a: Cystine stones (due to a defect in COLA amino acid transporter)

cards.q: What is the best initial pharmacological prevention for recurrent calcium oxalate stones?
cards.a: Thiazide diuretics (they increase renal calcium reabsorption, lowering urine calcium) and hydration. (Do NOT restrict dietary calcium).

cards.q: What is the pharmacological treatment to prevent uric acid stones?
cards.a: Potassium citrate (to alkalinize the urine) and Allopurinol.

cards.q: What are the 4 classic triggers for Renal Papillary Necrosis (SAAD pneumonic)?
cards.a: Sickle cell disease/trait, Analgesics (NSAIDs), Acute pyelonephritis, Diabetes mellitus.

cards.q: Which type of Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) is characterized by a defect in H<sup>+</sup> secretion in the collecting tubule, leading to urine pH > 5.5 and calcium stones?
cards.a: Type 1 (Distal) RTA

cards.q: Which type of Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) is characterized by a defect in HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> reabsorption in the proximal tubule and is associated with Fanconi syndrome?
cards.a: Type 2 (Proximal) RTA

cards.q: Which type of Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) is characterized by hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance, leading to hyperkalemia and an acidic urine (pH < 5.5)?
cards.a: Type 4 RTA

cards.q: What is the treatment for Central Diabetes Insipidus?
cards.a: Desmopressin (dDAVP)

cards.q: What are the primary treatments for Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus?
cards.a: Hydration, dietary salt restriction, Thiazide diuretics (and Amiloride if Lithium-induced).

cards.q: What is the formula for calculating the Anion Gap?
cards.a: Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-). Normal is 8-12 mEq/L.

cards.q: What are the common causes of a High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (MUDPILES)?
cards.a: Methanol, Uremia, Diabetic ketoacidosis, Propylene glycol, Iron/Isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates.

cards.q: What are the common causes of a Normal Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (HARDASS)?
cards.a: Hyperalimentation, Addison disease, RTA, Diarrhea, Acetazolamide, Spironolactone, Saline infusion.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for acute, severe hypercalcemia (> 14 mg/dL)?
cards.a: Aggressive Normal Saline hydration, plus Calcitonin. (Bisphosphonates are given for long-term control).

cards.q: What severe neurological complication occurs due to the rapid correction of hyponatremia?
cards.a: Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (Central Pontine Myelinolysis). "From low to high, your pons will die."

cards.q: What severe complication occurs due to the rapid correction of hypernatremia?
cards.a: Cerebral edema (Brain herniation). "From high to low, your brains will blow."

cards.q: How do you differentiate between psychogenic polydipsia and central diabetes insipidus using a water deprivation test?
cards.a: In psychogenic polydipsia, urine osmolality increases (concentrates) with water deprivation. In central DI, urine osmolality remains low (dilute) but increases significantly after administration of exogenous ADH (Desmopressin).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic hallmark of Fibromuscular Dysplasia on renal angiography, typically seen in young women with resistant hypertension?
cards.a: "String of beads" appearance of the renal arteries.

cards.q: What is the preferred antihypertensive class for a patient with Scleroderma Renal Crisis?
cards.a: ACE inhibitors (e.g., Captopril), even in the setting of acute kidney injury.

cards.q: What ultrasound finding is highly characteristic of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) in adults?
cards.a: Bilateral, massively enlarged kidneys with numerous cysts. (Associated with berry aneurysms and hepatic cysts).

cards.q: What is the classic pentad of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)?
cards.a: FAT RN: Fever, Anemia (microangiopathic hemolytic), Thrombocytopenia, Renal failure, Neurologic symptoms. (Due to ADAMTS13 deficiency).

cards.q: A child develops acute renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia shortly after an episode of bloody diarrhea (e.g., E. coli O157:H7). Diagnosis?
cards.a: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)

cards.q: In the treatment of severe hypercalcemia, why are loop diuretics (like furosemide) no longer routinely recommended as first-line unless the patient is volume overloaded?
cards.a: They can worsen volume depletion, which exacerbates hypercalcemia. Aggressive IV hydration with normal saline is the priority.

cards.q: A patient with long-standing Rheumatoid Arthritis develops nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy with Congo red stain shows "apple-green birefringence" under polarized light. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Secondary (AA) Amyloidosis

cards.q: What is the Winters formula used to calculate expected PCO2 in metabolic acidosis (to check for mixed acid-base disorder)?
cards.a: Expected PCO2 = (1.5 × [HCO3-]) + 8 ± 2.

cards.q: What typical EKG changes are associated with hypokalemia?
cards.a: U waves, flattened/inverted T waves, and ST-segment depression.

cards.q: In a patient with hypernatremia and hypovolemia, what is the best initial IV fluid to administer?
cards.a: Isotonic Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl) to correct the volume deficit first, before switching to hypotonic fluids (like 5% Dextrose) to correct the free water deficit.

cards.q: What are the typical urinary diagnostic markers (FENa, FEUrea, Urine Na<sup>+</sup>, Urine Osmolality, BUN/Cr ratio) that differentiate prerenal azotemia from acute tubular necrosis (ATN)?
cards.a:
Prerenal Azotemia: FENa < 1% (or FEUrea < 35% if on diuretics), Urine Na+ < 20 mEq/L, Urine Osmolality > 500 mOsm/kg, BUN/Cr ratio > 20:1.
ATN: FENa > 2% (FEUrea > 50%), Urine Na+ > 40 mEq/L, Urine Osmolality < 350 mOsm/kg, BUN/Cr ratio < 15:1.

cards.q: A patient presenting with fever, maculopapular rash, and renal failure 1–2 weeks after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or an NSAID most likely has what condition, and what is seen on urinalysis?
cards.a:
Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN).
Urinalysis demonstrates WBC casts, sterile pyuria, and urine eosinophils (eosinophiluria).

cards.q: An end-stage renal disease (ESRD) patient on hemodialysis presents with painful, violaceous subcutaneous plaques and ischemic skin necrosis on the thighs. Laboratory evaluation reveals hyperphosphatemia and an elevated Ca<sup>2+</sup> × PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> product. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy), caused by arteriolar vascular calcification and thrombosis leading to severe tissue ischemia and cutaneous necrosis.

cards.q: What are the diagnostic laboratory findings for Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH) secretion (Serum Na<sup>+</sup>, Serum Osmolality, Urine Osmolality, Urine Na<sup>+</sup>)?
cards.a: Euvolemic hyponatremia characterized by: Serum Na+ < 135 mEq/L, Serum Osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg, Urine Osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg (inappropriately concentrated), and Urine Na+ > 40 mEq/L.

cards.q: In a patient with severe hyperkalemia (K<sup>+</sup> > 6.5 mEq/L) presenting with ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS), what is the immediate first-line medication to administer and its mechanism of action?
cards.a:
Intravenous Calcium Gluconate (or Calcium Chloride).
Mechanism: Stabilizes the cardiac myocyte membrane potential to prevent fatal arrhythmias. (Note: It does not lower serum K+ levels.)

cards.q: What is the most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults, strongly associated with anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R) antibodies, solid organ malignancies, and Hepatitis B?
cards.a:
Membranous Nephropathy.
Renal biopsy demonstrates subepithelial immune complex deposition causing a 'spike and dome' appearance on electron microscopy.

cards.q: A 5-year-old child presents with sudden-onset periorbital edema, heavy proteinuria (> 3.5 g/day), and hypoalbuminemia. What is the diagnosis, light microscopy finding, and first-line treatment?
cards.a:
Minimal Change Disease.
Light microscopy is normal; electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes. First-line treatment: oral corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone).

cards.q: Which nephrotic syndrome variant is most common in Black patients and strongly associated with HIV infection, heroin use, morbid obesity, and APOL1 gene mutations?
cards.a:
Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).
Renal biopsy demonstrates sclerosis affecting segments of < 50% of glomeruli.

cards.q: How does the timing of gross hematuria following an upper respiratory infection distinguish IgA Nephropathy from Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN)?
cards.a:
IgA Nephropathy: Presents within 5 days (synpharyngitic) of URI; serum C3/C4 complement levels are normal.
PSGN: Presents 1–4 weeks post-pharyngitis/impetigo; serum C3 level is low, with positive anti-streptolysin O (ASO) or anti-DNase B titers.

cards.q: What serologic marker (c-ANCA vs. p-ANCA) and systemic clinical features distinguish Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA) from Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA)?
cards.a:
GPA: c-ANCA positive (anti-PR3); features upper respiratory involvement (nasal ulcers, sinusitis), lower respiratory (cavitary pulmonary nodules), and glomerulonephritis.
MPA: p-ANCA positive (anti-MPO); causes glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis but lacks upper airway and granulomatous lesions.

cards.q: How is the serum Anion Gap calculated, what is its normal reference range, and what is the standard mnemonic for high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA)?
cards.a:
Serum Anion Gap = [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]). Normal range: 8–12 mEq/L.
Mnemonic: MUDPILES (Methanol, Uremia, Diabetic Ketoacidosis, Propylene glycol, Isoniazid/Iron, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates).

cards.q: What are the key distinguishing features (Urine pH, Serum K<sup>+</sup> level) among Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) Type 1 (Distal), RTA Type 2 (Proximal), and RTA Type 4 (Hypoaldosteronism)?
cards.a:
Type 1 (Distal): Urine pH > 5.5, Hypokalemia (impaired H+ excretion).
Type 2 (Proximal): Urine pH < 5.5 (eventually), Hypokalemia (impaired HCO3- reabsorption).
Type 4: Urine pH < 5.5, Hyperkalemia (aldosterone deficiency or resistance).

cards.q: An adult patient presents with bilateral flank pain, hypertension, palpable abdominal masses, and hematuria. What extrarenal manifestations are strongly associated with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)?
cards.a: Intracranial berry aneurysms (risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage), hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse (MVP), and colonic diverticulosis.

cards.q: What is the primary pathophysiologic mechanism of Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS) in patients with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites, and what is the definitive treatment?
cards.a:
Splanchnic vasodilation causing severe renal vasoconstriction and hypoperfusion.
Urinalysis is bland with FENa < 1%. Definitive treatment: liver transplantation (bridged with vasoconstrictors like octreotide + midodrine or terlipressin plus IV albumin).

cards.q: A patient with severe chronic kidney disease presents with position-dependent chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) > 60 mg/dL. ECG shows low voltage without diffuse ST-segment elevations. What is the immediate treatment of choice?
cards.a:
Urgent Hemodialysis.
Uremic pericarditis is an absolute indication for dialysis. (Avoid NSAIDs or anticoagulants due to increased risk of hemorrhagic pericarditis.)

cards.q: A 62-year-old smoker with generalized atherosclerosis presents with resistant hypertension and an acute rise in serum creatinine > 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor. What is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice?
cards.a:
Renal Artery Duplex Ultrasonography (or CT/MR angiography).
Caused by renovascular atherosclerosis impairing angiotensin II-dependent efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction.

cards.q: What is the most common chemical composition of kidney stones, their appearance on abdominal X-ray, urinary crystal shape, and key dietary prevention strategies?
cards.a:
Calcium Oxalate stones.
Radiopaque on X-ray, showing envelope- or dumbbell-shaped crystals. Prevention: Increased fluid intake, low-sodium & normal-calcium diet, and Thiazide diuretics.

cards.q: A patient on long-term Lithium therapy presents with hypernatremia, polyuria, and polydipsia. Water deprivation testing shows urine osmolality < 300 mOsm/kg that does not rise after exogenous desmopressin (dDAVP). What is the diagnosis and preferred medication to manage it?
cards.a:
Lithium-induced Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus.
Treatment: Discontinue lithium if feasible; administer Amiloride to block lithium entry via ENaC channels in the collecting duct.

cards.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with microhematuria, progressive sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus. Biopsy shows irregular thinning and splitting of the glomerular basement membrane. What gene defect causes this condition?
cards.a: X-linked mutation in the COL4A5 gene encoding the type IV collagen α-5 chain (Alport Syndrome).

cards.q: Following a cardiac catheterization, a patient develops acute kidney injury, livedo reticularis, blue toes, and eosinophilia. What classic histologic finding is seen on renal biopsy?
cards.a: Biconvex, needle-shaped cholesterol clefts occluding small renal arteries and arterioles (Atheroembolic / Cholesterol Embolization Syndrome).

cards.q: What is the Delta-Delta (\(\Delta-\Delta\)) ratio, and how do you interpret it in mixed acid-base disorders?
cards.a:
Delta-Delta = \(\frac{\Delta AG}{\Delta [HCO_3^-]} = \frac{AG - 12}{24 - [HCO_3^-]}\).

Interpretation in HAGMA:
• Ratio < 1: Mixed HAGMA and normal anion gap (non-gap) metabolic acidosis (NAGMA).
• Ratio 1–2: Pure HAGMA.
• Ratio > 2: Mixed HAGMA and metabolic alkalosis (e.g., due to concurrent vomiting or diuretic use).

cards.q: Compare Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) and Intrinsic AKI (Acute Tubular Necrosis, ATN) by FENa, Urine Sodium, and BUN/Cr ratio.
cards.a:
• Prerenal AKI (volume depletion): FENa < 1%, Urine Sodium < 20 mEq/L, BUN/Cr ratio > 20 (kidney avidly reabsorbs water/urea).
• Intrinsic AKI (ATN): FENa > 2%, Urine Sodium > 40 mEq/L, BUN/Cr ratio 10–15 (damaged tubules cannot reabsorb sodium/urea).

cards.q: What urine microscopy findings are characteristic of Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) vs. Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN)?
cards.a:
• ATN: Muddy brown granular casts (sloughed tubular epithelial cells).
• AIN: WBC casts and eosinophils (allergic/inflammatory reaction).

cards.q: What is the classic clinical triad of Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN), and what are the most common offending drugs?
cards.a:
• Triad (present in < 15% of patients): Fever, maculopapular rash, and peripheral eosinophilia + sterile pyuria/eosinophiluria.
• Offending Drugs: Penicillins/cephalosporins, PPIs (omeprazole), NSAIDs, Sulfonamides, Rifampin (Mnemonic: 5 Ps — Pee, Penicillins, PPIs, Pain-killers, Rifam-Pin).

cards.q: How is Contrast-Induced Nephropathy prevented, and what is its typical clinical course?
cards.a:
• Prevention: Intravenous hydration with normal saline (or sodium bicarbonate) before and after the administration of contrast media. Avoid volume depletion.
• Course: Transient rise in creatinine peaking 3–5 days post-contrast, usually resolving within 7–10 days. Characterized by low FENa despite intrinsic injury (due to afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction).

cards.q: What are the core diagnostic features of Nephrotic Syndrome?
cards.a:
1. Nephrotic-range proteinuria (> 3.5 g/24 hours).
2. Hypoalbuminemia (< 3.0 g/dL).
3. Generalized edema.
4. Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria (fatty casts, 'maltese crosses' on microscopy).
Complication: Hypercoagulability due to loss of Antithrombin III in urine.

cards.q: Describe the clinical associations, biopsy findings, and treatment of Minimal Change Disease.
cards.a:
• Associations: Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children; associated with Hodgkin Lymphoma.
• Biopsy: Light microscopy is normal; electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes.
• Treatment: Highly responsive to Corticosteroids (prednisone).

cards.q: Identify the primary patient populations and etiologies associated with Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).
cards.a:
Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in African Americans and adults.

Etiologies: Idiopathic, HIV infection, heroin abuse, obesity, and interferon therapy.

cards.q: What autoantibody is associated with primary Membranous Nephropathy, and what secondary causes must be screened?
cards.a:
• Autoantibody: Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibody (present in 70-80% of primary cases).
• Secondary Causes: Solid tumor malignancies (lung, colon, breast), Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, NSAID use, and SLE.

cards.q: What is the earliest clinical marker of Diabetic Nephropathy, and what histological finding is pathognomonic?
cards.a:
• Earliest Marker: Microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/day). Managed by initiating an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
• Histology: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular mesangial expansion/glomerulosclerosis).

cards.q: Contrast Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) and IgA Nephropathy by timing relative to infection and serum complement levels.
cards.a:
• IgA Nephropathy (Berger's): Hematuria occurs synpharyngitically (1–2 days after upper respiratory infection). Serum complement (C3/C4) levels are normal.
• PSGN: Hematuria occurs post-pharyngitic (1–3 weeks) or post-impetigo (3–6 weeks). Serum complement (C3) levels are persistently low for 6–8 weeks.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect and clinical triad of Alport Syndrome?
cards.a:
Mutation in the COL4A5 gene encoding Type IV Collagen, causing splitting and thinning of the glomerular basement membrane ('basket-weave' appearance).

Clinical Triad:
1. Hereditary nephritis (hematuria/proteinuria)
2. Sensorineural deafness
3. Ocular abnormalities (anterior lenticonus, cataracts).

cards.q: Describe the pathophysiology and diagnostic findings of Goodpasture's Disease.
cards.a:
Autoantibodies directed against the alpha-3 chain of Type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes.

Presentation: Hemoptysis (pulmonary hemorrhage) + Hematuria (RPGN).
Renal Biopsy: Crescentic GN with linear immunofluorescence showing IgG deposition along the GBM.

cards.q: What renal biopsy class of Lupus Nephritis requires aggressive immunosuppression, and what is the treatment regimen?
cards.a:
• Class III/IV: Focal / Diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis (characterized by subendothelial deposits and 'wire-looping' on light microscopy).
• Treatment: High-dose IV corticosteroids + Mycophenolate Mofetil or Cyclophosphamide.

cards.q: Define the diagnostic criteria for SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH).
cards.a:
1. Euvolemic hyponatremia.
2. Hypo-osmolality of serum (< 275 mOsm/kg).
3. Inappropriate urine concentration (Urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg).
4. High urine sodium concentration (Urine sodium > 40 mEq/L).
5. Normal renal, adrenal, and thyroid function.

cards.q: What is the management of SIADH based on severity of symptoms?
cards.a:
• Mild/Moderate: Fluid restriction, oral salt tablets, loop diuretics, or demeclocycline (blocks ADH action in renal tubules).
• Severe (seizures, coma): Hypertonic (3%) saline + limit correction rate to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome.

cards.q: Explain the correction limit for hyponatremia and the consequence of rapid correction.
cards.a:
• Limit: Correct sodium at a rate of < 8–12 mEq/L in 24 hours (e.g., 0.5 mEq/L per hour).
• Consequence: Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia causes Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (Central Pontine Myelinolysis), presenting with dysarthria, dysphagia, paraparesis, and locked-in syndrome.
Mnemonic: From low to high, your pons will die! (From high to low, your brain will blow — refers to cerebral edema in rapid hypernatremia correction).

cards.q: What is the progression of ECG changes seen in Hyperkalemia?
cards.a:
1. Peaked T waves (earliest change).
2. Prolonged PR interval, flat/absent P waves.
3. Widening of the QRS complex.
4. Sine wave pattern (fusion of QRS and T wave).
5. Ventricular fibrillation / Asystole.

cards.q: What is the stepwise emergency treatment of severe Hyperkalemia (≥ 6.5 mEq/L or ECG changes)?
cards.a:
1. Calcium Gluconate (or Calcium Chloride): IV infusion to stabilize the cardiac membrane (does not lower potassium).
2. Insulin + Glucose (IV) and/or inhaled Albuterol: Shifts potassium intracellularly.
3. Sodium Bicarbonate: Shifts potassium intracellularly (specifically in metabolic acidosis).
4. Furosemide or Patiromer/SPS: Promotes potassium elimination via urine or GI tract.
5. Hemodialysis: Definitive treatment for refractory cases.

cards.q: What are the ECG findings of Hypokalemia?
cards.a: Flattened T waves, ST depression, prolonged QT interval, and the presence of U waves (a wave following the T wave).

cards.q: Why is hypokalemia sometimes refractory to potassium replacement, and how is this managed?
cards.a: Co-existing hypomagnesemia promotes renal potassium wasting by removing inhibition of ROMK channels in the collecting duct. Management: You must check and correct magnesium first (replete magnesium) before potassium levels can normalize.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of Renal Osteodystrophy in chronic kidney disease?
cards.a:
1. Decreased GFR leads to phosphate retention.
2. Hyperphosphatemia binds free calcium, causing hypocalcemia.
3. Damaged kidneys cannot convert Vitamin D to its active form (1,25-\(OH)_2\) Vitamin D, worsening hypocalcemia.
4. Hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia stimulate parathyroid glands → Secondary Hyperparathyroidism → high bone turnover, osteitis fibrosa cystica.

cards.q: What is the target hemoglobin for patients with anemia of CKD on Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents (ESAs), and why?
cards.a:
• Target: 10–11 g/dL.
• Why: Normalizing hemoglobin (> 11.5–12 g/dL) with ESAs (e.g., epoetin alfa) increases the risk of stroke, cardiovascular events, and thromboembolism.

cards.q: Compare the 4 major types of Nephrolithiasis (kidney stones) by urine pH, shape, and radiopacity.
cards.a:
• Calcium Oxalate: Acidic/normal pH; envelope/dumble-shaped; radiopaque (most common).
• Struvite (MAP): Alkaline pH (> 7.2); coffin-lid shape/staghorn calculi; radiopaque.
• Uric Acid: Acidic pH (< 5.5); rhomboid/rosette shape; radiolucent (invisible on plain X-ray).
• Cystine: Acidic pH; hexagonal shape; radiopaque/faint.

cards.q: What organism is associated with Struvite (staghorn) calculi, and what is its mechanism?
cards.a: Urease-producing bacteria (e.g., Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella). Urease hydrolyzes urea to ammonia and CO\(_2\), alkalinizing the urine (pH > 7.2), which precipitates magnesium ammonium phosphate.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment of choice for Uric Acid stones?
cards.a: Urine alkalinization with oral Potassium Citrate (increases urine pH to ≥ 6.5, which solubilizes uric acid) + high hydration.

cards.q: How is Cystinuria diagnosed and managed?
cards.a:
Defect in the PCT amino acid transporter for COLA (Cystine, Ornithine, Lysine, Arginine).

Diagnosis: Hexagonal crystals in acidic urine; positive sodium nitroprusside cyanide test (urine turns purple).
Management: High hydration, urine alkalinization, chelating agents (penicillamine).

cards.q: Contrast the three types of Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA 1, 2, and 4) by urine pH, serum potassium, and defect.
cards.a:
• Type 1 (Distal): Urine pH > 5.5; Hypokalemia; Defect in distal \(H^+\) secretion. Associated with nephrolithiasis.
• Type 2 (Proximal): Urine pH < 5.5 (eventually); Hypokalemia; Defect in proximal \(HCO_3^-\) reabsorption. Associated with Fanconi syndrome.
• Type 4 (Hyperkalemic): Urine pH < 5.5; Hyperkalemia; Aldosterone deficiency or resistance. Seen in diabetic nephropathy (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism).

cards.q: What is the etiology and treatment of Type 4 RTA?
cards.a:
• Etiology: Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism (diabetic nephropathy, adrenal insufficiency, drugs like ACEi, spironolactone).
• Treatment: Dietary potassium restriction, loop diuretics, and Fludrocortisone (aldosterone analog, for primary deficiency).

cards.q: What is the next best step for a patient presenting with suspected nephrolithiasis?
cards.a: Non-contrast helical CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (gold standard, detects all stone types).

cards.q: What is the conservative management strategy for a ureteral stone < 5–10 mm without complications?
cards.a: High fluid intake, pain control (NSAIDs preferred), and Tamsulosin (alpha-1 blocker to relax distal ureter/facilitate stone passage).

cards.q: Under what conditions is urgent urological intervention (decompression) indicated for a kidney stone?
cards.a: Ureteral obstruction with concurrent UTI/pyelonephritis (fever), acute kidney injury/anuria, or intractable pain/vomiting. Management includes retrograde ureteral stent placement or percutaneous nephrostomy.

cards.q: What is the formula for calculating Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa)?
cards.a:
FENa = \(\frac{U_{Na} \times P_{Cr}}{P_{Na} \times U_{Cr}} \times 100\).
Note: In patients taking diuretics, FENa is unreliable; use Fractional Excretion of Urea (FEUrea) instead (FEUrea < 35% indicates prerenal state).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Loop Diuretics (e.g., Furosemide)?
cards.a: Inhibits the \(Na^+/K^+/2Cl^-\) cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, destroying the corticomedullary osmotic gradient and preventing urine concentration.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Thiazide Diuretics (e.g., Hydrochlorothiazide)?
cards.a: Inhibits the \(Na^+/Cl^-\) cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Potassium-Sparing Diuretics?
cards.a:
• Spironolactone / Eplerenone: Aldosterone receptor antagonists in the cortical collecting duct.
• Amiloride / Triamterene: Direct blockers of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the cortical collecting duct.

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormality classically causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
cards.a: Severe hypercalcemia or chronic hypokalemia (induces ADH resistance in the collecting duct).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Lithium-induced Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus?
cards.a: Amiloride (blocks lithium entry through ENaC channels in the collecting duct) + stop lithium if possible.

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) and its high-yield extrarenal manifestations.
cards.a:
• Presentation: Bilateral flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, progressive renal failure in young adults.
• Extrarenal: Berry aneurysms (circle of Willis — risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage), hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse (MVP), diverticulosis.

cards.q: Define the diagnostic features of Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (IgA Vasculitis) nephritis.
cards.a:
Most common systemic vasculitis in children. Characterized by IgA immune complex deposition in the mesangium.

Presentation: Palpable purpura on buttocks/lower limbs, arthralgias, abdominal pain (intussusception risk), and hematuria.

cards.q: Contrast the indications for Hemodialysis in acute kidney injury (Mnemonic AEIOU).
cards.a:
• A: Refractory metabolic Acidosis (pH < 7.1–7.2).
• E: Refractory Electrolyte abnormalities (hyperkalemia > 6.5 or ECG changes).
• I: Intoxications (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylates).
• O: Volume Overload (refractory to diuretics with respiratory failure).
• U: symptomatic Uremia (uremic pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of Hypercalciuria in patients with normal serum calcium who form calcium stones, and how is it treated?
cards.a:
• Mechanism: Idiopathic hypercalciuria (most common cause of calcium stones).
• Treatment: Thiazide diuretics (promotes calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, lowering urine calcium levels) + dietary sodium restriction.

cards.q: Why is oral calcium restriction contraindicated in patients with calcium oxalate kidney stones?
cards.a: Restricting dietary calcium decreases calcium in the GI tract. Less calcium is available to bind dietary oxalate in the gut, causing increased absorption of free oxalate, leading to hyperoxaluria and increased risk of calcium oxalate stone formation.

cards.q: What nephrotoxicity is classically associated with Acyclovir, and how is it prevented?
cards.a:
• Toxicity: Crystalline nephropathy (acyclovir precipitates in renal tubules, causing obstruction and AKI).
• Prevention: Co-administration of aggressive IV fluids.

cards.q: What is the definition of severe metabolic alkalosis unresponsive to normal saline, and how do you differentiate it?
cards.a:
• Saline-Responsive (Urine Cl < 20 mEq/L): Caused by vomiting, nasogastric suction, or diuretic use. Normalizes with normal saline infusion.
• Saline-Unresponsive (Urine Cl > 20 mEq/L): Caused by mineralocorticoid excess (Conn's, Cushing's) or severe hypokalemia. Does not normalize with saline.

cards.q: Explain the difference in etiology between IgA Nephropathy and IgA Vasculitis (HSP).
cards.a: They share the same underlying pathology (IgA deposition in tissues), but IgA Nephropathy is isolated to the kidneys, while IgA Vasculitis (HSP) is a systemic vasculitis involving skin, joints, GI tract, and kidneys.

cards.q: Compare Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS) by glucose, pH, ketones, and serum osmolality.
cards.a:
• DKA (typically Type 1): Glucose usually 250–600 mg/dL, pH < 7.3 (metabolic acidosis with anion gap), positive ketones in blood/urine, mild increase in osmolality.
• HHS (typically Type 2): Glucose > 600 mg/dL (often > 1000), pH > 7.3 (no acidosis), negative/minimal ketones, serum osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg.

cards.q: What is the cornerstone management of DKA and HHS, and what are the rules for potassium management?
cards.a:
1. Aggressive IV Fluids (Normal Saline first, add 5% dextrose once glucose is < 200–250 mg/dL).
2. IV Insulin (hold if potassium is < 3.3 mEq/L).
3. Potassium Repletion:
• If \(K^+\) < 3.3 mEq/L: Hold insulin, give IV potassium until > 3.3.
• If \(K^+\) 3.3–5.3 mEq/L: Give 20–30 mEq of potassium per liter of IV fluid.
• If \(K^+\) > 5.3 mEq/L: Do not give potassium; monitor every 2 hours.

cards.q: What is the autoantibody association in Graves' Disease and Hashimoto's Thyroiditis?
cards.a:
• Graves' Disease: Thyrotropin (TSH) Receptor Antibodies (TRAb) / Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI).
• Hashimoto's Thyroiditis: Anti-Thyroid Peroxidase (anti-TPO) and Anti-Thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) antibodies.

cards.q: Name the 4 medications used in order for the treatment of Thyroid Storm and their rationales.
cards.a:
1. Beta-Blocker (Propranolol): Blocks adrenergic symptoms and inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
2. Thionamide (PTU preferred over methimazole): Blocks new hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion.
3. Iodine Solution (SSKI or Lugol's): Blocks hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect). Must be given at least 1 hour after thionamides to prevent iodine from being used as substrate.
4. Glucocorticoids (Hydrocortisone/Dexamethasone): Inhibits peripheral T4 to T3 conversion and treats potential adrenal insufficiency.

cards.q: What are the indications for treating Subclinical Hypothyroidism?
cards.a:
Subclinical Hypothyroidism = Elevated TSH with normal free T4.

Treat with Levothyroxine only if:
1. TSH ≥ 10 mU/L.
2. Patient has symptoms of hypothyroidism.
3. Positive anti-TPO antibodies.
4. Pregnancy or plans to become pregnant.

cards.q: What is the initial screening algorithm for suspected Cushing's Syndrome?
cards.a:
Perform at least 2 of the following:
1. 24-hour urine free cortisol (elevated).
2. Late-night salivary cortisol (elevated).
3. Overnight low-dose (1 mg) Dexamethasone suppression test (failure to suppress morning cortisol < 1.8 \(\mu\)g/dL).

cards.q: How do you localize the source of Cushing's Syndrome once hypercortisolism is confirmed?
cards.a:
1. Measure baseline ACTH level:
• ACTH < 5 pg/mL: ACTH-independent (adrenal tumor or exogenous steroids). Perform CT adrenals.
• ACTH > 15 pg/mL: ACTH-dependent. Proceed to next step.
2. High-dose (8 mg) Dexamethasone suppression test or CRH stimulation:
• Cortisol suppresses (> 50% drop): Cushing's Disease (pituitary ACTH adenoma). Perform MRI pituitary.
• Cortisol does not suppress: Ectopic ACTH secretion (e.g., small cell lung cancer). Perform CT chest/abdomen.

cards.q: Contrast Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's Disease) and Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency by ACTH levels, electrolyte abnormalities, and skin findings.
cards.a:
• Primary (destruction of adrenal cortex): High ACTH; hyperpigmentation (ACTH stimulates melanocytes); hypoaldosteronism (hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, non-gap metabolic acidosis).
• Secondary (pituitary dysfunction): Low ACTH; no hyperpigmentation; normal aldosterone levels (potassium is normal because aldosterone is regulated by RAAS, not ACTH).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test of choice for Adrenal Insufficiency?
cards.a: Cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH) stimulation test. Measure serum cortisol before and 30–60 minutes after administration. Cortisol level failing to rise > 18–20 \(\mu\)g/dL confirms adrenal insufficiency.

cards.q: What is the management of primary vs. secondary Adrenal Insufficiency?
cards.a:
• Primary (Addison's): Daily Glucocorticoid (Hydrocortisone or prednisone) + Mineralocorticoid (Fludrocortisone).
• Secondary: Daily Glucocorticoid only (mineralocorticoids are not needed because aldosterone is intact).

cards.q: What is the emergency management of an acute Adrenal Crisis?
cards.a: Immediate IV bolus of Hydrocortisone 100 mg (preferred due to mineralocorticoid activity) + aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (normal saline/dextrose).

cards.q: What is Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome), and how is it screened?
cards.a:
Aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.

Presentation: Treatment-resistant hypertension, hypokalemia (often mild/absent), and metabolic alkalosis.
Screening Test: Plasma Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR) > 20–30, with plasma aldosterone > 15 ng/dL.

cards.q: How is Conn's Syndrome confirmed, and what is the treatment for unilateral vs. bilateral disease?
cards.a:
• Confirmation: Oral or IV saline suppression test (aldosterone fails to suppress < 5–10 ng/dL after saline load). Perform adrenal CT and adrenal vein sampling.
• Unilateral Adenoma Treatment: Surgical resection (adrenalectomy).
• Bilateral Hyperplasia Treatment: Medical management with aldosterone antagonists (Spironolactone or Eplerenone).

cards.q: How is Pheochromocytoma diagnosed, and what is the preoperative management?
cards.a:
Catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla.

Diagnosis: 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines, or plasma free metanephrines.
Preoperative Prep (Critical): Alpha-blockade FIRST (e.g., Phenoxybenzamine) for 10–14 days, followed by Beta-blockade. Never give beta-blocker first, as unopposed alpha-1 vasoconstriction can trigger a hypertensive crisis.

cards.q: What are the components of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN 1) syndrome?
cards.a:
Mnemonic: The 3 Ps.
1. Parathyroid hyperplasia/adenoma (hypercalcemia)
2. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma/ZES, insulinoma, VIPoma)
3. Pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma).

cards.q: What are the components of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2A (MEN 2A) and 2B (MEN 2B) syndromes?
cards.a:
Both are associated with mutations in the RET proto-oncogene.
• MEN 2A: Medullary Thyroid Cancer + Pheochromocytoma + Parathyroid hyperplasia.
• MEN 2B: Medullary Thyroid Cancer + Pheochromocytoma + mucosal neuromas/marfanoid habitus.

cards.q: Compare the clinical presentation and laboratory findings of Primary Hyperparathyroidism.
cards.a:
• Presentation: Stones (nephrolithiasis), bones (osteitis fibrosa cystica/osteoporosis), groans (abdominal pain/constipation), and psychiatric overtones (depression/confusion).
• Labs: Hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and inappropriately elevated PTH. 24h urinary calcium is normal/elevated (excludes FHH).

cards.q: How do you differentiate Primary Hyperparathyroidism from Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH)?
cards.a:
Both present with elevated calcium and PTH.

Differentiating marker: 24-hour urine calcium.
• Primary Hyperparathyroidism: Urine calcium excretion is high/normal (fractional excretion of calcium > 2%).
• FHH (inactivating calcium-sensing receptor mutation): Low urine calcium (fractional excretion of calcium < 1%). Surgery is contraindicated in FHH.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic criteria for Diabetes Mellitus?
cards.a:
Requires one of the following:
1. Fasting Plasma Glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL.
2. HbA1c ≥ 6.5%.
3. Two-hour oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) ≥ 200 mg/dL.
4. Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL in a patient with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action and key side effect of Metformin?
cards.a:
• Mechanism: Inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis and increases peripheral insulin sensitivity.
• Side Effects: Diarrhea, abdominal cramps, B12 deficiency, and Lactic Acidosis (rare but serious; contraindications include eGFR < 30 mL/min).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action and key side effect of Sulfonylureas (e.g., Glipizide, Glimepiride)?
cards.a:
• Mechanism: Closes ATP-sensitive \(K^+\) channels on pancreatic beta cells, depolarizing the cell and stimulating endogenous insulin secretion.
• Side Effects: Hypoglycemia and weight gain.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action and key side effects of SGLT2 Inhibitors (e.g., Empagliflozin, Canagliflozin)?
cards.a:
• Mechanism: Inhibits the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 in the proximal tubule, promoting glycosuria.
• Side Effects: Genitourinary tract infections (vulvovaginal candidiasis), dehydration/hypotension, and euglycemic DKA.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action and key side effects of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (e.g., Semaglutide, Liraglutide)?
cards.a:
• Mechanism: Mimics incretin hormone to enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion, slow gastric emptying, and promote satiety.
• Side Effects: Nausea/vomiting, gastroparesis, and risk of acute pancreatitis. Contraindicated in patients with a history of Medullary Thyroid Cancer.

cards.q: What is the first-line medical therapy for a patient with a symptomatic Prolactinoma?
cards.a: Dopamine Agonists (e.g., Cabergoline or Bromocriptine). They decrease prolactin secretion and reduce tumor size. Surgery is only indicated if refractory to medical therapy.

cards.q: Describe the diagnostic workup for suspected Acromegaly.
cards.a:
1. Screening Test: Serum IGF-1 level (highly stable, elevated in acromegaly).
2. Confirmatory Test: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT). Fail to suppress growth hormone (GH) < 1 ng/mL after 75g oral glucose load confirms diagnosis.
3. Localization: Pituitary MRI.

cards.q: What is the screening recommendation for Osteoporosis, and how is it diagnosed?
cards.a:
• Screening: All women age ≥ 65 (or younger women with equivalent risk factors) using a DEXA scan.
• Diagnosis: T-score ≤ −2.5 at the femoral neck or spine.
Note: Osteopenia is defined as T-score between −1.0 and −2.5.

cards.q: What are the key side effects and administration instructions for Bisphosphonates (e.g., Alendronate)?
cards.a:
• Side Effects: Pill-induced esophagitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw, and atypical subtrochanteric femur fractures.
• Instructions: Take with a full glass of water first thing in the morning on an empty stomach, and remain upright for at least 30 minutes (prevents esophageal irritation).

cards.q: Contrast Central vs. Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (DI) by pathophysiology and response to desmopressin.
cards.a:
• Central DI: Lack of ADH production by the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary. Desmopressin (dDAVP) response: Urine osmolality increases by > 50%.
• Nephrogenic DI: ADH resistance in the renal collecting duct. Desmopressin response: No significant increase in urine osmolality (< 10%).

cards.q: Describe the results of the Water Deprivation Test in Diabetes Insipidus.
cards.a: Withholding water will fail to concentrate urine (urine osmolality remains low, < 300 mOsm/kg, while serum osmolality and sodium rise).

cards.q: What are the clinical and laboratory features of Primary Hypothyroidism?
cards.a:
• Clinical: Weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes ('hung-up' reflexes).
• Labs: Elevated TSH, decreased free T4.

cards.q: What is Myxedema Coma, and how is it managed?
cards.a:
Severe, life-threatening hypothyroidism presenting with altered mental status, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, and hyponatremia.

Treatment: IV Levothyroxine (T4) + IV Liothyronine (T3) + IV Glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone, must be given prior to thyroid hormone to prevent adrenal crisis if co-existing adrenal insufficiency is present).

cards.q: What is the next best step for a solitary thyroid nodule (> 1 cm) with normal/high TSH?
cards.a: Thyroid Ultrasound to assess nodule characteristics, followed by Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) if ultrasound shows high-risk features (e.g., microcalcifications, solid hypoechoic, irregular margins).

cards.q: What is the next best step for a thyroid nodule (> 1 cm) with a low TSH?
cards.a:
Perform a Thyroid Scintigraphy (Radioactive Iodine Uptake Scan):
• 'Hot' nodule (increased uptake): Benign hyperfunctioning nodule. Treat hyperthyroidism (no FNA needed).
• 'Cold' nodule (decreased uptake): Higher risk of malignancy. Proceed to thyroid ultrasound and FNA.

cards.q: Name the 4 major types of Thyroid Cancer and their key clinical characteristics.
cards.a:
1. Papillary Carcinoma: Most common (80%); excellent prognosis; histology shows Orphan Annie eyes and Psammoma bodies.
2. Follicular Carcinoma: Invades thyroid capsule and hematogenously spreads. Cannot diagnose with FNA (requires surgical lobectomy to assess capsular invasion).
3. Medullary Carcinoma: Arises from parafollicular C-cells (produces calcitonin); associated with RET mutation/MEN 2A & 2B.
4. Anaplastic Carcinoma: Highly aggressive, rapidly expanding neck mass in elderly; dismal prognosis.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test of choice for a patient suspected of having a Gastrinoma?
cards.a: Fasting serum gastrin levels. If elevated but non-diagnostic (100–1000 pg/mL), perform a Secretin Stimulation Test (gastrin rises > 120–200 pg/mL in gastrinomas).

cards.q: What is the presentation and diagnostic features of VIPoma?
cards.a:
Neuroendocrine tumor secreting Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP).

Presentation: WDHA syndrome: Watery Diarrhea (tea-colored), Hypokalemia, Achlorhydria (decreased gastric acid).
Labs: VIP level > 75 pg/mL, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, hypercalcemia.

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Glucagonoma.
cards.a:
A glucagon-secreting tumor of the pancreatic alpha cells.

Presentation: 5 Ds: Dermatitis (Necrolytic Migratory Erythema — red, painful, blistering rash in perineum/extremities), Diabetes (mild hyperglycemia), DVT, Decline (weight loss), and Depression.

cards.q: What are the diagnostic features of Primary Hyperaldosteronism due to bilateral adrenal hyperplasia vs. adrenal adenoma?
cards.a:
• Both have elevated aldosterone and low renin.
• Adrenal vein sampling (AVS) is the gold standard to differentiate: lateralized aldosterone gradient indicates unilateral adenoma, symmetric elevation indicates bilateral hyperplasia.

cards.q: Name the classic clinical triad of a Pheochromocytoma.
cards.a:
Mnemonic: 5 Ps.
Classic Triad: Episodic headache, sweating (diaphoresis), and tachycardia/palpitations (with severe hypertension).
Associated with: Anxiety, weight loss, tremor.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic criteria for Diabetic Nephropathy based on albuminuria?
cards.a: Persistent albumin excretion > 300 mg/day (severely increased albuminuria) confirmed on at least 2 readings over 3–6 months.

cards.q: What class of diabetes medications should be avoided in a patient with a history of recurrent heart failure hospitalizations?
cards.a: Thiazolidinediones (TZDs, e.g., Pioglitazone, Rosiglitazone) as they promote fluid retention and exacerbate heart failure.

cards.q: What is the screening target for Diabetes Mellitus in asymptomatic adults according to the ADA?
cards.a: All adults starting at age 35 (or younger if overweight/obese with ≥ 1 cardiovascular risk factor), repeated every 3 years.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of Primary Hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: A single benign parathyroid adenoma (~85% of cases), followed by parathyroid hyperplasia.

cards.q: Describe the clinical significance of pseudohypoparathyroidism.
cards.a:
End-organ resistance to PTH (caused by maternal transmission of GNAS1 mutation).

Labs: Hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, but inappropriately elevated PTH.
Physical features: Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (short stature, round face, short 4th/5th metacarpals).

cards.q: What is the first-line pharmacotherapy for a patient with acute severe Hypercalcemia (> 14 mg/dL)?
cards.a: Immediate aggressive IV hydration with normal saline, followed by IV loop diuretics (only once volume-repleted). Add IV Bisphosphonates (Pamidronate/Zoledronic acid) for long-term control (takes 2-4 days to work) + Calcitonin (rapid, short-term effect).

cards.q: Explain the difference in etiology between Pituitary Cushing's Disease and Ectopic ACTH syndrome.
cards.a:
• Cushing's Disease: Pituitary ACTH adenoma. Responds to high-dose dexamethasone suppression and CRH stimulation.
• Ectopic ACTH: ACTH-secreting tumor (e.g., small cell lung cancer, bronchial carcinoid). Independent of feedback control; does not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone.

cards.q: What is the association between Thyroid Peroxidase (TPO) antibodies and pregnancy?
cards.a: Women with positive anti-TPO antibodies are at increased risk of miscarriage, gestational hypothyroidism, and postpartum thyroiditis.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of De Quervain (Subacute Granulomatous) Thyroiditis?
cards.a:
