• Presentation: Painful, tender thyroid gland, fever, and transient hyperthyroidism following a viral upper respiratory infection. Very high ESR.
• Uptake scan: Low radioactive iodine uptake.
• Treatment: NSAIDs/Aspirin (first-line) or steroids if severe; self-limiting.

cards.q: Describe the mechanism and presentation of secondary hyperparathyroidism.
cards.a: Chronic hypocalcemia (e.g., CKD, severe Vitamin D deficiency) leads to chronic overstimulation of all four parathyroid glands. Presents with normal/low calcium, elevated phosphate, and elevated PTH.

cards.q: What is the diagnosis of a patient with hypercalcemia, low PTH, and a history of sarcoidosis or tuberculosis?
cards.a: Granulomatous disease-induced hypercalcemia (macrophages inside granulomas express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, causing extra-renal conversion of Vitamin D to its active form, leading to calcium hyperabsorption). Treated with glucocorticoids.

cards.q: What is the initial screening test of choice for suspected acromegaly?
cards.a: Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) level. If elevated, confirm with an oral glucose suppression test (failure to suppress growth hormone).

cards.q: A patient presents with thyrotoxicosis, a tender goiter, and a markedly decreased radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU). What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis. (Often post-viral, associated with high ESR/CRP).

cards.q: What is the preferred medical treatment for hyperthyroidism during the first trimester of pregnancy?
cards.a: Propylthiouracil (PTU). Methimazole is teratogenic in the 1st trimester (aplasia cutis) but is preferred in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters due to PTU hepatotoxicity.

cards.q: Patients with carcinoid syndrome are at risk of developing a deficiency of which vitamin?
cards.a: Niacin (Vitamin B3), leading to Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia). This occurs because tryptophan is diverted to synthesize serotonin.

cards.q: A patient with a history of bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease presents with hyperpigmentation and bitemporal hemianopsia. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Nelson syndrome. Rapid enlargement of a pre-existing pituitary corticotroph microadenoma due to the loss of negative feedback from cortisol.

cards.q: What is the correct sequence of preoperative pharmacological blockade for a patient with a pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Alpha-blockade (e.g., phenoxybenzamine) must be initiated FIRST for 10-14 days, followed by Beta-blockade (e.g., propranolol) to prevent unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation and hypertensive crisis.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for a large prolactinoma (macroprolactinoma) causing visual field deficits?
cards.a: Dopamine agonists (e.g., cabergoline or bromocriptine). Transsphenoidal surgery is reserved for patients who fail or do not tolerate medical therapy.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) in developed countries?
cards.a: Autoimmune adrenalitis (often associated with anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies).

cards.q: What is the initial management for severe, symptomatic hypercalcemia (Ca<sup>2+</sup> > 14 mg/dL)?
cards.a: Aggressive IV isotonic saline hydration and calcitonin (for rapid reduction). Bisphosphonates (e.g., zoledronic acid) are given simultaneously but take 2-4 days to work.

cards.q: In a patient being treated for Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), when should 5% dextrose be added to the intravenous fluids?
cards.a: When the serum glucose drops below 200 mg/dL, to prevent hypoglycemia while continuing insulin infusion to close the anion gap.

cards.q: What is the key pathophysiological difference distinguishing Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS) from DKA?
cards.a: In HHS, there is sufficient endogenous insulin to prevent ketogenesis and significant lipolysis, but not enough to prevent severe hyperglycemia and osmotic diuresis.

cards.q: What is the best initial screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)?
cards.a: The plasma aldosterone concentration to plasma renin activity (PAC/PRA) ratio. A ratio > 20 with a PAC > 15 ng/dL is suggestive.

cards.q: A patient in the intensive care unit for severe sepsis is found to have low T<sub>3</sub>, normal T<sub>4</sub>, and normal TSH levels. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Euthyroid sick syndrome (Low T3 syndrome). It requires no thyroid replacement therapy; observe and treat the underlying illness.

cards.q: What are the indications for parathyroidectomy in an asymptomatic patient with primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Serum Ca<sup>2+</sup> > 1.0 mg/dL above normal limit, CrCl < 60 mL/min, bone mineral density T-score < -2.5, or age < 50 years.

cards.q: What are the three classic neoplasms associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1)?
cards.a: Pituitary adenomas, Parathyroid hyperplasia/adenomas, and Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (the 3 P's).

cards.q: What features distinguish MEN 2A from MEN 2B?
cards.a: MEN 2A includes parathyroid hyperplasia, whereas MEN 2B includes mucosal neuromas and a marfanoid habitus. Both share medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

cards.q: What is the most characteristic histological finding of papillary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Optically clear, overlapping nuclei with finely dispersed chromatin (Orphan Annie eye nuclei) and calcified spheres (psammoma bodies).

cards.q: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from which type of cells, and what tumor marker does it secrete?
cards.a: It arises from parafollicular C cells and secretes calcitonin.

cards.q: What is the Chvostek sign, and what electrolyte abnormality does it indicate?
cards.a: Twitching of the facial muscles in response to tapping over the facial nerve in the preauricular area; it indicates hypocalcemia.

cards.q: What is the classic pattern of electrolyte abnormalities seen in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)?
cards.a: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hyperchloremic non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, and mild hypoglycemia (due to loss of aldosterone and cortisol).

cards.q: What is the standard confirmatory test for suspected primary adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a: The Cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH) stimulation test. A failure of serum cortisol to rise > 18 μg/dL confirms the diagnosis.

cards.q: What is Whipple's triad, used to suggest the presence of an insulinoma?
cards.a: 1) Symptoms of hypoglycemia, 2) documented low blood glucose during symptoms, and 3) resolution of symptoms with glucose administration.

cards.q: How can you chemically differentiate factitious hypoglycemia (surreptitious insulin administration) from an insulinoma?
cards.a: In factitious hypoglycemia, insulin is high but C-peptide is low. In an insulinoma, both insulin and C-peptide are elevated.

cards.q: How can you differentiate a sulfonylurea overdose from an insulinoma?
cards.a: Both present with elevated insulin and C-peptide. A plasma or urine sulfonylurea screen will be positive in an overdose.

cards.q: What effect does hypothyroidism have on the lipid profile?
cards.a: It frequently causes hypercholesterolemia due to decreased surface expression of LDL receptors and decreased lipid clearance.

cards.q: Why does primary hypothyroidism often lead to hyperprolactinemia?
cards.a: Low T3/T4 leads to an increase in Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone (TRH) from the hypothalamus, which directly stimulates lactotrophs in the anterior pituitary to secrete prolactin.

cards.q: What are the characteristic serum laboratory findings (Ca2+, PO43-, PTH, ALP) in osteomalacia?
cards.a: Low or low-normal Ca2+, low PO43-, elevated PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), and elevated ALP.

cards.q: What are the characteristic serum laboratory findings (Ca2+, PO43-, PTH, ALP) in Paget disease of bone?
cards.a: Normal Ca2+, normal PO43-, normal PTH, and highly elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP).

cards.q: What antiarrhythmic drug can cause both hypothyroidism (Wolff-Chaikoff effect) and hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow phenomenon)?
cards.a: Amiodarone, due to its very high iodine content and structural similarity to thyroid hormone.

cards.q: What are the three most acceptable screening tests for Cushing syndrome?
cards.a: 24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, and the overnight low-dose (1 mg) dexamethasone suppression test.

cards.q: In the evaluation of Cushing syndrome, how does the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test differentiate between Cushing disease (pituitary adenoma) and ectopic ACTH production?
cards.a: High-dose dexamethasone will suppress cortisol levels in Cushing disease, but fails to suppress cortisol in ectopic ACTH production (e.g., small cell lung cancer).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a female newborn with classical 21-hydroxylase deficiency?
cards.a: Ambiguous genitalia (virilization) and salt-wasting (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia) in the first 1-2 weeks of life. Lab shows elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

cards.q: What is the most serious potential adverse effect of Metformin, and in what conditions is it contraindicated?
cards.a: Lactic acidosis. It is contraindicated in severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m2), acute decompensated heart failure, and severe hepatic impairment.

cards.q: Which two classes of anti-diabetic medications are specifically recommended for patients with Type 2 Diabetes and established cardiovascular disease?
cards.a: GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., liraglutide, semaglutide) and SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin).

cards.q: What is the recommendation for statin therapy in patients with Type 2 Diabetes mellitus?
cards.a: A moderate-intensity statin is recommended for all diabetic patients aged 40 to 75 years, regardless of baseline lipid levels.

cards.q: How does the baseline serum osmolality differ between primary polydipsia and Diabetes Insipidus (DI)?
cards.a: Primary polydipsia presents with low serum osmolality (< 270 mOsm/kg), whereas DI typically presents with high-normal or high serum osmolality (> 290 mOsm/kg).

cards.q: During a water deprivation test, a patient's urine osmolality increases by more than 50% following the administration of exogenous desmopressin. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Central Diabetes Insipidus.

cards.q: What is the most feared neurological complication of correcting severe hyponatremia too rapidly?
cards.a: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (Central pontine myelinolysis), presenting as locked-in syndrome (quadriplegia and pseudobulbar palsy).

cards.q: What are the classic serum and urine laboratory findings in Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH)?
cards.a: Euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia (serum Osm < 275 mOsm/kg), inappropriately concentrated urine (urine Osm > 100 mOsm/kg), and high urine Na+ (> 40 mEq/L).

cards.q: A patient has asymptomatic hypercalcemia, high-normal PTH, and a urine calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (UCCR) of < 0.01. What is the underlying pathophysiology?
cards.a: A mutation in the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), leading to Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH).

cards.q: What is the classic clinical presentation of Sheehan syndrome?
cards.a: A postpartum woman who presents with failure to lactate, amenorrhea, and signs of secondary hypothyroidism/adrenal insufficiency following severe postpartum hemorrhage.

cards.q: A patient with a known pituitary adenoma suddenly develops a severe headache, visual field defects, and profound hypotension. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Pituitary apoplexy (acute hemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary adenoma), which can lead to acute secondary adrenal insufficiency and cardiovascular collapse.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of a toxic multinodular goiter?
cards.a: Focal patches of hyperfunctioning follicular cells that have mutated (often a TSH receptor mutation) and produce thyroid hormone autonomously, independent of TSH stimulation.

cards.q: How does bone metastasis typically affect serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels compared to multiple myeloma?
cards.a: Osteoblastic or mixed bone metastases (e.g., prostate, breast) typically cause markedly elevated ALP. Multiple myeloma typically has a normal ALP due to purely osteolytic lesions without osteoblastic response.

cards.q: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test for a newly discovered thyroid nodule with normal or elevated TSH?
cards.a: Thyroid ultrasound followed by Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) biopsy if suspicious features or size criteria are met.

cards.q: What is the best management for a pregnant patient currently taking levothyroxine for hypothyroidism?
cards.a: Increase the levothyroxine dose by approximately 30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, due to increased TBG (Thyroxine-Binding Globulin) and fetal demands.

cards.q: What ECG findings are classically associated with severe hypocalcemia?
cards.a: Prolongation of the QT interval.

cards.q: What is the initial medical therapy for a patient presenting with thyroid storm?
cards.a: Beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol), followed by PTU or methimazole, then iodine (given 1 hour AFTER antithyroid drugs to prevent the Jod-Basedow effect), and glucocorticoids.

cards.q: In a patient with hyperthyroidism, what finding on a radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) scan distinguishes Graves' disease from a toxic adenoma?
cards.a: Graves' disease shows diffuse, homogeneous increased uptake. A toxic adenoma shows a focal area of intense uptake with suppression of the surrounding gland.

cards.q: What rare but life-threatening hematologic complication can occur with the use of antithyroid medications (PTU and Methimazole)?
cards.a: Agranulocytosis. Patients should be instructed to immediately stop the drug and seek medical attention if they develop a sudden fever or sore throat.

cards.q: What is the formula for calculating the Free T4 Index (FTI), and when is it preferred over direct free T4 measurement?
cards.a:
FTI = Total T4 × T3 Resin Uptake (T3RU).
Preferred when protein binding is abnormal (e.g., pregnancy increases TBG → high total T4 but normal free T4; OCP use). FTI corrects for these binding protein fluctuations.

cards.q: A patient on amiodarone develops hypothyroidism. What is the mechanism and management?
cards.a:
Amiodarone contains 37% iodine by weight. It causes hypothyroidism via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect (excess iodine blocks thyroid hormone synthesis).
Management: Levothyroxine replacement. Stopping amiodarone is usually not necessary and may be dangerous.

cards.q: What distinguishes a functioning (toxic) thyroid nodule from Graves disease on radioiodine (<sup>123</sup>I) scan?
cards.a:
Toxic adenoma: Single 'hot' nodule with suppressed uptake in surrounding gland.
Graves disease: Diffusely increased, homogeneous uptake throughout the entire gland.
Both cause hyperthyroidism, but the mechanism and treatment approach differ.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis), and what is the correct order of medications?
cards.a:
Give in this order to block synthesis → block release → block conversion:
1. PTU (blocks synthesis AND conversion of T4→T3)
2. Potassium Iodide (SSKI) — give 1 hour after PTU to prevent iodine from being used for new hormone synthesis
3. Propranolol (controls adrenergic symptoms)
4. Hydrocortisone (prevents adrenal crisis, also blocks T4→T3 conversion)

cards.q: What urine and serum findings distinguish Cushing disease (pituitary) from ectopic ACTH syndrome?
cards.a:
Cushing disease (pituitary adenoma): ACTH mildly elevated, cortisol suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone (8 mg overnight).
Ectopic ACTH (e.g., small cell lung cancer): ACTH markedly elevated (often >200 pg/mL), cortisol does NOT suppress even with high-dose dexamethasone.
CRH stimulation test: Cushing disease → cortisol rises; ectopic → no response.

cards.q: A patient with Cushing syndrome has undetectable ACTH. What is the diagnosis and next best step?
cards.a:
Undetectable ACTH = ACTH-independent Cushing → adrenal source (adenoma, carcinoma, or bilateral hyperplasia).
Next step: CT abdomen/pelvis to visualize adrenal glands.
Mnemonic: Low ACTH = adrenal is autonomous → don't need pituitary to tell it what to do.

cards.q: What is the mechanism by which metformin causes lactic acidosis, and who is at risk?
cards.a:
Metformin inhibits mitochondrial complex I, reducing oxidative phosphorylation and increasing anaerobic glycolysis → excess lactate.
Risk factors: Renal insufficiency (GFR <30 mL/min/1.73m2) causes drug accumulation. Also: hepatic failure, heavy alcohol use, IV contrast administration (hold 48 hours).

cards.q: What is the dawn phenomenon vs. the Somogyi effect in type 1 diabetes, and how is each managed?
cards.a:
Dawn phenomenon: Early morning hyperglycemia from normal overnight GH/cortisol surges (no hypoglycemia overnight). Manage by increasing evening basal insulin.
Somogyi effect: Rebound hyperglycemia from nocturnal hypoglycemia (counter-regulatory hormone surge). Manage by reducing evening insulin dose. Distinguish with 3 AM glucose check.

cards.q: What is the target HbA1c for most non-pregnant adults with type 2 diabetes, and when is a less stringent goal (e.g., <8%) appropriate?
cards.a:
Standard target: HbA1c < 7% (corresponds to average glucose ~154 mg/dL).
Less stringent (<8%) is appropriate for: Elderly patients, limited life expectancy, severe hypoglycemia unawareness, multiple comorbidities, long-standing difficult-to-control DM.
HbA1c reflects ~3-month average glucose; each 1% change ≈ 35 mg/dL change in mean glucose.

cards.q: What is the management of hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS), and how does it differ from DKA management?
cards.a:
HHS: Extreme hyperglycemia (glucose often >600 mg/dL), hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), minimal/no ketoacidosis, profound dehydration.
Management: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (Normal Saline first) is the cornerstone — often 6-10L deficit. Insulin is secondary (start after fluids). Replace K+.
Key difference from DKA: No bicarbonate needed (no acidosis), glucose drops faster with fluids alone.

cards.q: A patient with primary hyperparathyroidism has serum Ca<sup>2+</sup> 11.8 mg/dL and is asymptomatic. What are the surgical indications?
cards.a:
Surgery (parathyroidectomy) is indicated if any of the following:
1. Serum Ca2+ > 1 mg/dL above upper normal (>11 mg/dL typically)
2. Nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis
3. eGFR < 60 mL/min
4. BMD T-score < −2.5 at any site (osteoporosis) or vertebral fracture
5. Age < 50 years
6. 24-hour urine Ca2+ > 400 mg/day

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology and treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy?
cards.a:
Two main mechanisms:
1. PTHrP (PTH-related peptide): Secreted by tumor (squamous cell, renal, breast); acts like PTH. Lab: ↑Ca2+, ↓PO43−, ↑PTHrP, suppressed PTH.
2. Osteolytic metastases: Cytokines destroy bone (myeloma).
Tx: IV Normal Saline (forced diuresis) → then IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid) to reduce bone resorption. Calcitonin for rapid, temporary effect.

cards.q: What are the classic lab findings in hypoparathyroidism vs. pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP)?
cards.a:
Hypoparathyroidism: ↓PTH, ↓Ca2+, ↑PO43− (PTH is truly absent → no phosphaturia).
PHP (type 1a): ↑PTH (gland works, but kidney is resistant), ↓Ca2+, ↑PO43−.
PHP 1a also shows: Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (short stature, short 4th metacarpal, round face, subcutaneous calcifications).

cards.q: What medication is first-line for central diabetes insipidus (CDI) and what lab values confirm DI diagnosis vs. psychogenic polydipsia?
cards.a:
CDI treatment: Desmopressin (dDAVP) — synthetic ADH analog.
Water deprivation test:
→ Urine Osm <300 mOsm/kg after dehydration = DI (can't concentrate)
→ After dDAVP: Urine Osm rises >50% = CDI (responds to exogenous ADH)
→ After dDAVP: Urine Osm rises <50% = Nephrogenic DI (kidneys don't respond)
→ Psychogenic polydipsia: Urine Osm rises with dehydration alone (>500 mOsm/kg)

cards.q: A patient has low TSH, low free T4, and inappropriately normal or low FSH/LH. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a:
Secondary (central) hypothyroidism due to pituitary or hypothalamic failure (e.g., pituitary adenoma, Sheehan syndrome, cranial irradiation).
Low TSH is inappropriately low given the low T4 — the pituitary cannot compensate.
Coexisting low FSH/LH, low cortisol (secondary adrenal insufficiency) suggests panhypopituitarism.
Treat with levothyroxine after replacing cortisol to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., semaglutide, liraglutide), and what are their non-glycemic benefits?
cards.a:
GLP-1 agonists: Mimic glucagon-like peptide-1 → ↑glucose-dependent insulin secretion, ↓glucagon, delay gastric emptying, ↑satiety.
Non-glycemic benefits:
1. Weight loss (strong)
2. Cardiovascular mortality reduction in established ASCVD or high CV risk
3. Renal protective effects
Side effects: Nausea, vomiting, pancreatitis risk; contraindicated in medullary thyroid carcinoma/MEN2 history.

cards.q: What is the next step if a urine metanephrine or plasma free metanephrine test is positive for suspected pheochromocytoma?
cards.a:
After biochemical confirmation, next step: Imaging to localize the tumor.
Best initial: CT abdomen/pelvis (90% are in adrenal gland).
If CT negative: MIBG scintigraphy (meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan) to find extra-adrenal paragangliomas.
Before any surgery: Alpha-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine for 10-14 days), then beta-blockade (never beta first — causes unopposed alpha → hypertensive crisis).

cards.q: What is Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1) vs. MEN2A, and which genetic mutation underlies each?
cards.a:
MEN1 ('3 Ps'): Parathyroid hyperplasia (most common), Pituitary adenoma, Pancreatic tumors (gastrinoma/insulinoma). Gene: MEN1 tumor suppressor.
MEN2A: Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (100%), Pheochromocytoma, Parathyroid hyperplasia. Gene: RET proto-oncogene.
MEN2B: MTC + Pheo + Marfanoid habitus + mucosal neuromas (no parathyroid).

cards.q: What is the Whipple triad, and what is the next step if all three criteria are met?
cards.a:
Whipple Triad (classic for insulinoma):
1. Symptoms of hypoglycemia (diaphoresis, tremor, confusion)
2. Documented low plasma glucose (<55 mg/dL during symptoms)
3. Relief of symptoms with glucose administration
Next step: 72-hour supervised fast with simultaneous measurement of glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin at time of hypoglycemia.
Insulinoma: ↑Insulin + ↑C-peptide + ↑Proinsulin (endogenous source).

cards.q: A patient with Addison disease requires emergency surgery. How is their perioperative steroid management handled?
cards.a:
Patients with primary adrenal insufficiency cannot mount a cortisol stress response → risk of adrenal crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia).
Stress dose steroids:
→ Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV before induction of anesthesia
→ Then 50-100 mg IV q8h during and for 24-48 hours post-op
→ Taper back to baseline maintenance dose as patient recovers
Never use dexamethasone alone (lacks mineralocorticoid activity).

cards.q: How do you differentiate Iron Deficiency Anemia from Anemia of Chronic Disease (ACD) on iron studies?
cards.a:
• Iron Deficiency Anemia: Low serum iron, low ferritin (most sensitive marker), high TIBC (transferrin), and low transferrin saturation.
• Anemia of Chronic Disease: Low serum iron, normal/high ferritin (acute phase reactant sequestering iron in macrophages), low/normal TIBC, and low/normal transferrin saturation.

cards.q: How do you differentiate Vitamin B12 deficiency from Folate deficiency on laboratory testing?
cards.a:
Both cause macrocytic megaloblastic anemia (hypersegmented neutrophils, MCV > 100).
• Vitamin B12 Deficiency: Elevated Methylmalonic Acid (MMA) and elevated Homocysteine. Associated with neurological symptoms (subacute combined degeneration).
• Folate Deficiency: Normal MMA, elevated Homocysteine. No neurological symptoms.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and diagnostic findings of G6PD Deficiency?
cards.a:
X-linked recessive disorder causing episodic hemolysis triggered by oxidative stress (fava beans, sulfa drugs, infections).

Blood Smear: Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) and Bite cells (macrophages biting out Heinz bodies in spleen).
Diagnostic Note: G6PD enzyme levels can be falsely normal during an acute hemolytic episode because older, enzyme-deficient RBCs have already lysed.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test of choice and management for Hereditary Spherocytosis?
cards.a:
Defect in RBC membrane proteins (ankyrin, spectrin).

Diagnosis: Spherocytes on blood smear, elevated MCHC, negative Direct Coombs test, and positive eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test or osmotic fragility test.
Treatment: Folic acid supplementation, splenectomy for severe/symptomatic cases (cures anemia/gallstone risk, but spherocytes remain).

cards.q: Contrast Warm vs. Cold Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (AIHA) by antibody type, site of hemolysis, and clinical associations.
cards.a:
• Warm AIHA: IgG antibodies coating RBCs. Hemolysis occurs extravascularly in the spleen. Associated with SLE, CLL, and drugs (alpha-methyldopa, penicillins). Treated with corticosteroids.
• Cold AIHA: IgM antibodies. Hemolysis is complement-mediated in cold extremities. Associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae and EBV/mononucleosis. Treated by avoiding cold; steroids are ineffective.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology and gold standard diagnosis of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
cards.a:
Acquired PIGA gene mutation leading to loss of GPI-anchor proteins that bind CD55 and CD59, which normally protect RBCs from complement destruction.

Presentation: Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis (especially hepatic/portal veins).
Diagnosis: Flow cytometry demonstrating absent CD55/CD59 on RBCs/WBCs.
Treatment: Eculizumab (monoclonal antibody against C5 complement).

cards.q: Compare Hemophilia A/B and Von Willebrand Disease (vWD) by Platelet Count, Bleeding Time, PT, and PTT.
cards.a:
• Hemophilia A/B: Normal platelet count, normal bleeding time, normal PT, and prolonged PTT (intrinsic pathway defect: Factor VIII or IX).
• vWD: Normal platelet count (usually), prolonged bleeding time (impaired platelet adhesion), normal PT, and normal or prolonged PTT (vWF stabilizes Factor VIII).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of Von Willebrand Disease (vWD)?
cards.a:
Mnemonic: bleeding from mucous membranes (nosebleeds, easy bruising, menorrhagia).
• Diagnosis: Reduced vWF antigen, reduced ristocetin cofactor activity, and decreased Factor VIII activity.
• Treatment: Desmopressin (dDAVP) (stimulates release of vWF/Factor VIII from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies) for mild/moderate type 1; vWF/Factor VIII concentrates for severe cases.

cards.q: Explain the difference in diagnostic test results between a Factor Deficiency (e.g., Hemophilia) and a Factor Inhibitor (e.g., Lupus Anticoagulant) using a Mixing Study.
cards.a:
In a patient with a prolonged PTT:
• Mixing Study (patient plasma + normal pool):
• PTT corrects to normal: Indicates a Factor Deficiency (normal plasma supplied the missing factor).
• PTT fails to correct: Indicates the presence of a Factor Inhibitor or anticoagulant.

cards.q: What are the classic clinical features and laboratory findings of Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)?
cards.a:
Systemic activation of coagulation depleting platelets and coagulation factors, leading to simultaneous thrombosis and hemorrhage.

Labs: Thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and PTT, decreased fibrinogen, and elevated D-Dimer / FDPs. Schistocytes on blood smear. Associated with sepsis, trauma, APML, and obstetrical complications.

cards.q: Describe the pathophysiology and classic clinical pentad of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP). Mnemonic: FAT RN.
cards.a:
Deficiency or inhibition of the ADAMTS13 metalloprotease, preventing cleavage of ultra-large vWF multimers, leading to microvascular platelet thrombi.

Pentad (FAT RN):
1. Fever
2. Anemia (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes)
3. Thrombocytopenia (with normal PT/PTT)
4. Renal insufficiency
5. Neurologic symptoms (headache, confusion, seizures).

cards.q: What is the emergency management of choice for Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP), and what is contraindicated?
cards.a:
• Management: Immediate therapeutic plasma exchange (plasmapheresis, PEX) + corticosteroids.
• Contraindicated: Platelet transfusions are absolutely contraindicated as they 'fuel the fire' of microvascular thrombosis.

cards.q: Describe the clinical triad and etiology of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS).
cards.a:
• Etiology: Shiga-like toxin produced by Escherichia coli O157:H7 (often after eating undercooked beef).
• Clinical Triad: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + Thrombocytopenia + Acute Kidney Injury.
• Management: Supportive. Avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents as they increase toxin release.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology and treatment of Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
cards.a:
Autoantibodies directed against platelet factor 4 (PF4)-heparin complexes leading to platelet activation and severe arterial/venous thrombosis.

Clinical: > 50% drop in platelet count 5–10 days after starting heparin.
Treatment: Stop all heparin products immediately, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant (e.g., Argatroban or Bivalirudin).

cards.q: What is Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP), and what is the treatment algorithm based on platelet count and symptoms?
cards.a:
Autoantibodies (IgG) against platelet GPIIb/IIIa receptors, causing splenic destruction of platelets.

Management:
• Platelets ≥ 30,000/\(\mu\)L and no bleeding: Observation.
• Platelets < 30,000/\(\mu\)L or bleeding: Corticosteroids first-line, IVIG (if rapid increase needed), or anti-D immunoglobulin. Splenectomy or rituximab for refractory cases.

cards.q: Define the CRAB criteria for Multiple Myeloma diagnosis.
cards.a:
• C: hyperCalcemia.
• R: Renal insufficiency (creatinine > 2 mg/dL or uremic cast nephropathy).
• A: Anemia (normocytic normochromic).
• B: Bone lytic lesions (osteolytic 'punched-out' lesions on skeletal survey).
Diagnostic markers: M-spike on serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP), monoclonal plasma cells ≥ 10% on bone marrow biopsy.

cards.q: What is Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance (MGUS), and how is it managed?
cards.a:
Asymptomatic clonal plasma cell proliferation.

Criteria: M-protein < 3 g/dL, < 10% bone marrow plasma cells, and NO CRAB symptoms.
Management: Observation/surveillance (risk of progression to multiple myeloma is 1% per year).

cards.q: What is the chromosome translocation, fusion gene, and treatment of choice for Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APML)?
cards.a:
• Translocation: t(15;17).
• Fusion Gene: PML-RARA (retinoic acid receptor alpha).
• Treatment: All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA) + arsenic trioxide. Promotes differentiation of promyelocytes. High risk of DIC at presentation.

cards.q: What histopathologic finding is diagnostic for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)?
cards.a: Bone marrow biopsy showing ≥ 20% myeloblasts, and presence of Auer rods (needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions of crystalized myeloperoxidase).

cards.q: What is the chromosome translocation, fusion gene, and first-line treatment for Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)?
cards.a:
• Translocation: t(9;22) (Philadelphia Chromosome).
• Fusion Gene: BCR-ABL (constitutively active tyrosine kinase).
• Treatment: Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (e.g., Imatinib, Dasatinib).

cards.q: How do you differentiate Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) from a leukemoid reaction on laboratory testing?
cards.a:
Both present with leukocytosis (> 50,000) with left shift.
• CML: Low Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) score, splenomegaly, and positive t(9;22) translocation.
• Leukemoid Reaction (reactive to infection): High LAP score, no splenomegaly, no t(9;22).

cards.q: What clinical and peripheral blood smear findings characterize Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Asymptomatic lymphocytosis in an elderly patient, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy.
• Smear: Mature-looking lymphocytes with fragile membranes that rupture during preparation, appearing as Smudge Cells.
• Complication: Richter Transformation (transformation of CLL into diffuse large B-cell lymphoma).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and diagnostic findings of Hodgkin Lymphoma?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Bimodal age distribution (20s and 60s); painless localized lymphadenopathy (cervical/mediastinal) that can be painful after alcohol consumption; B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss).
• Biopsy: Reed-Sternberg Cells ('owl-eye' multinucleated giant cells) which are CD15 and CD30 positive.

cards.q: State the electrolyte abnormalities that define Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS).
cards.a:
1. Hyperuricemia (nucleic acid breakdown → uric acid precipitating in renal tubules).
2. Hyperkalemia (intracellular potassium release).
3. Hyperphosphatemia (intracellular phosphate release).
4. Hypocalcemia (phosphate binds calcium → precipitation).
Prevention: Aggressive IV hydration + Allopurinol or Rasburicase.

cards.q: What is the emergency management of suspected malignant Spinal Cord Compression?
cards.a: Immediate administration of IV Dexamethasone (reduces vasogenic spinal cord edema) before obtaining an MRI of the entire spine.

cards.q: What mutation, clinical presentation, and treatment characterize Polycythemia Vera (PV)?
cards.a:
Clonal myeloproliferative disorder causing erythrocytosis.

Key Mutation: JAK2 mutation (V617F) in ≥ 95% of cases.
Presentation: Pruritus after a hot bath/shower (aquagenic pruritus due to histamine release), erythromelalgia, headache, thrombosis.
Treatment: Therapeutic phlebotomy (target hematocrit < 45%) + low-dose aspirin + Hydroxyurea for high-risk.

cards.q: How do you differentiate Polycythemia Vera from secondary polycythemia (e.g., due to hypoxia or EPO-secreting tumors)?
cards.a:
• Polycythemia Vera: Low serum Erythropoietin (EPO) level (negative feedback from high RBC mass).
• Secondary Polycythemia: High/elevated EPO level.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia Type I vs. Type II?
cards.a:
• Type I: Non-immune-mediated direct effect of heparin on platelets. Occurs within 1–2 days, mild drop in platelets (> 100,000), no thrombosis. Management: Continue heparin, monitor.
• Type II (True HIT): Immune-mediated (anti-PF4-heparin IgG). Occurs 5–10 days, severe drop (30–50k), high risk of thrombosis. Management: Stop heparin, start argatroban.

cards.q: Contrast Hemolytic, Febrile Non-Hemolytic, and Anaphylactic transfusion reactions by timing and pathophysiology.
cards.a:
• Acute Hemolytic: Within minutes. ABO incompatibility (Type II hypersensitivity) → intravascular hemolysis. Fever, flank pain, hemoglobinuria, DIC.
• Febrile Non-Hemolytic: Within 1–6 hours. Cytokines accumulated in storage of donor blood. Fever, chills, no hemolysis. Treat with acetaminophen.
• Anaphylactic: Within seconds. IgA-deficient recipient receiving IgA-containing blood. Dyspnea, bronchospasm, shock. Treat with epinephrine.

cards.q: Contrast TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury) and TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload) by pathophysiology and volume status.
cards.a:
• TRALI: Donor antibodies react against recipient neutrophils in pulmonary vasculature → non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Euvolemic status, normal PCWP, no response to diuretics.
• TACO: Fluid overload from rapid transfusion. Hypervolemic status (elevated JVP, S3, high BNP/PCWP), responds well to diuretics.

cards.q: What genetic defect, clinical features, and treatment characterize Sickle Cell Disease?
cards.a:
Autosomal recessive mutation in the beta-globin gene (glutamic acid substituted by valine at position 6).

Clinical: Vaso-occlusive pain crises, acute chest syndrome, splenic autoinfarction by age 5, risk of stroke.
Treatment: Hydroxyurea (increases production of fetal hemoglobin HbF, reducing sickling) + vaccinations against encapsulated organisms.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in patients with Sickle Cell Disease?
cards.a: Salmonella species (followed closely by Staphylococcus aureus).

cards.q: What infection classically triggers an aplastic crisis in patients with Sickle Cell Disease or Hereditary Spherocytosis?
cards.a: Parvovirus B19 (selectively infects and destroys erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow, causing a temporary halt in RBC production).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of Acute Chest Syndrome in a patient with Sickle Cell Disease?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Fever, chest pain, tachypnea, cough, hypoxemia, and a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest X-ray.
• Management: IV fluids, pain control, oxygen, empiric antibiotics (ceftriaxone + macrolide), and exchange transfusion if severe/hypoxemic.

cards.q: What screening is recommended for pediatric patients with Sickle Cell Disease to prevent stroke, and what is the prevention strategy?
cards.a:
• Screening: Annual Transcranial Doppler (TCD) ultrasound for children aged 2–16 years.
• Prevention: Chronic monthly simple or exchange blood transfusions if TCD shows high velocity (indicates stenosis/stroke risk).

cards.q: What is Aplastic Anemia, and what is the diagnostic bone marrow finding?
cards.a:
Pancytopenia caused by bone marrow failure (often autoimmune-mediated T-cell destruction of stem cells).

Bone Marrow: Severe hypocellularity with replacement of hematopoietic elements by fat cells (fatty marrow).

cards.q: Name the key laboratory findings in Lead Poisoning.
cards.a: Microcytic anemia, elevated serum lead, elevated zinc protoporphyrin, and basophilic stippling of RBCs on blood smear (due to inhibition of pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Lead Poisoning based on lead level?
cards.a:
• Mild (< 45 \(\mu\)g/dL): Remove source of exposure.
• Moderate (45–69 \(\mu\)g/dL): Oral Succimer (DMSA).
• Severe (≥ 70 \(\mu\)g/dL): IV/IM Dimercaprol (BAL) + IV EDTA (calcium disodium).

cards.q: Describe the bone marrow biopsy finding of Sideroblastic Anemia.
cards.a: Bone marrow aspirate showing ringed sideroblasts (Prussian blue stain showing iron-laden mitochondria forming a ring around the nucleus of erythroid precursors). Caused by alcohol, isoniazid (B6 antagonist), lead, or myelodysplasia.

cards.q: Compare Beta-Thalassemia Minor vs. Major by hemoglobin electrophoresis findings.
cards.a:
• Beta-Thalassemia Minor (trait): Mild asymptomatic microcytic anemia. Electrophoresis shows elevated HbA\(_2\) (> 3.5%) and mildly elevated HbF.
• Beta-Thalassemia Major: Severe transfusion-dependent anemia. Electrophoresis shows absent HbA, with almost all hemoglobin being HbF and HbA\(_2\).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) with active thrombosis vs. without thrombosis?
cards.a: Both require immediate cessation of all heparin and initiation of a non-heparin anticoagulant (Argatroban). You do not wait for antibody confirmation to switch therapy. FONDAPARINUX can be used once platelets recover.

cards.q: What is the therapeutic target and clinical indication for Erythropoietin (EPO) therapy in cancer patients?
cards.a: Indicated only for chemotherapy-induced anemia with Hb < 10 g/dL. Target is Hb 10-11 g/dL. Avoid in patients with curative-intent chemotherapy as ESAs can stimulate tumor growth and shorten survival.

cards.q: Define Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome and its management.
cards.a:
Obstruction of the SVC (most commonly due to lung cancer or lymphoma).

Presentation: Face/neck swelling, upper extremity edema, dilated collateral chest wall veins, dyspnea.
Management: Elevation of head, oxygen, urgent radiation therapy (for lung cancer/metastasis) or chemotherapy (for lymphoma), or SVC stenting.

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Spinal Cord Compression in a cancer patient.
cards.a: Localized back pain (worse when lying down, percussion tenderness over spine), followed by progressive motor weakness, sensory deficit, and late bowel/bladder dysfunction (urinary retention/incontinence).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test of choice and treatment for Hyperviscosity Syndrome in Waldenström Macroglobulinemia?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Headache, blurry vision, mucosal bleeding, retinal hemorrhages ('sausage-link' veins).
• Diagnosis: Serum viscosity measurement, IgM M-spike, ≥ 10% lymphoplasmacytic cells on bone marrow.
• Treatment: Immediate plasmapheresis.

cards.q: Describe the difference between Hemophilia A and Hemophilia B.
cards.a:
• Hemophilia A: Factor VIII deficiency. Treated with recombinant Factor VIII.
• Hemophilia B (Christmas disease): Factor IX deficiency. Treated with recombinant Factor IX.
They are clinically indistinguishable and both are X-linked recessive.

cards.q: What is the next best step for a patient presenting with an asymptomatic platelet count of 8,000/\(\mu\)L?
cards.a: Hospitalization, activity restriction (avoid trauma), and initiation of IVIG or high-dose corticosteroids to prevent spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage (risk increases dramatically when platelets < 10,000).

cards.q: What is Heparin reversal agent, and what is Warfarin reversal agent?
cards.a:
• Heparin Reversal: Protamine Sulfate.
• Warfarin Reversal: Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) + IV Vitamin K for life-threatening bleeding; Vitamin K alone for elevated INR without bleeding.

cards.q: What is the reversal agent for Dabigatran, and what is the reversal agent for Rivaroxaban/Apixaban?
cards.a:
• Dabigatran Reversal: Idarucizumab.
• Rivaroxaban/Apixaban Reversal: Andexanet Alfa.

cards.q: What is the target international normalized ratio (INR) for patients on Warfarin for atrial fibrillation vs. a mechanical mitral valve?
cards.a:
• Atrial Fibrillation / DVT: Target INR 2.0–3.0.
• Mechanical Mitral Valve: Target INR 2.5–3.5 (due to higher thrombogenicity of the mitral position compared to the aortic position).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of microcytic anemia, and what are the classic iron study findings (Ferritin, TIBC, Serum Iron)?
cards.a: Iron deficiency anemia; Low Ferritin, High TIBC, Low Serum Iron.

cards.q: How does thalassemia minor present differently from iron deficiency anemia on CBC and Mentzer index?
cards.a: Thalassemia minor has a normal or elevated RBC count and a Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) < 13, whereas iron deficiency has low RBC and Mentzer index > 13.

cards.q: What peripheral smear finding is pathognomonic for lead poisoning?
cards.a: Basophilic stippling (due to inhibition of rRNA degradation).

cards.q: A patient with microcytic anemia, elevated ferritin, and ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow likely has what condition, and what is the treatment?
cards.a: Sideroblastic anemia; treatment is Pyridoxine (Vitamin B<sub>6</sub>).

cards.q: What is the key neurologic difference between Vitamin B<sub>12</sub> and Folate deficiency?
cards.a: B<sub>12</sub> deficiency presents with subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (neurologic symptoms), while folate deficiency does not.

cards.q: A patient with sickle cell disease presents with acute drop in hemoglobin and a low reticulocyte count. What is the diagnosis and most common infectious cause?
cards.a: Aplastic crisis; caused by Parvovirus B19.

cards.q: What is the most common organism responsible for osteomyelitis in a sickle cell patient?
cards.a: Salmonella (though S. aureus is still very common).

cards.q: A patient taking TMP-SMX develops acute hemolytic anemia with bite cells and Heinz bodies. What is the diagnosis and underlying mechanism?
cards.a: G6PD deficiency; decreased NADP<sup>+</sup> to NADPH conversion leads to oxidative damage to RBCs.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of Hereditary Spherocytosis, and what is the definitive diagnostic test?
cards.a: Hemolytic anemia, Jaundice, Splenomegaly; Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test or Osmotic fragility test.

cards.q: How do you differentiate Warm vs. Cold Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia based on antibody type and treatment?
cards.a: Warm is IgG-mediated (treat with steroids/splenectomy); Cold is IgM-mediated (treat with cold avoidance/Rituximab).

cards.q: A patient presents with dark morning urine, venous thrombosis (e.g., Budd-Chiari), and pancytopenia. What is the diagnosis and missing surface proteins?
cards.a: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH); CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (MIRL) deficiency.

cards.q: What is the pentad of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)?
cards.a: FAT RN: Fever, Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia, Thrombocytopenia, Renal failure, Neurologic symptoms.

cards.q: What is the primary defect and treatment of choice for TTP?
cards.a: ADAMTS13 deficiency (cleaves vWF); treatment is Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis). NEVER give platelets.

cards.q: A child develops bloody diarrhea followed by acute renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and hemolytic anemia. What is the diagnosis and typical pathogen?
cards.a: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS); Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7).

cards.q: What is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, and what is the first-line treatment for mild bleeding?
cards.a: von Willebrand Disease; Desmopressin (DDAVP).

cards.q: How do PT, aPTT, bleeding time, and platelet count present in DIC?
cards.a: High PT, High aPTT, High bleeding time, Low platelets (with high D-dimer and low fibrinogen).

cards.q: An isolated prolonged aPTT that corrects with a mixing study suggests what type of disorder?
cards.a: Factor deficiency (e.g., Hemophilia A or B). If it does NOT correct, suspect a factor inhibitor (e.g., Lupus anticoagulant).

cards.q: What is the most common inherited hypercoagulable state, and what is its mechanism?
cards.a: Factor V Leiden; mutated Factor V is resistant to degradation by activated Protein C.

cards.q: A patient started on warfarin develops skin necrosis. What underlying deficiency did they likely have?
cards.a: Protein C deficiency (warfarin transiently drops Protein C levels, leading to a hypercoagulable state before factors II, IX, and X are depleted).

cards.q: What antibodies are diagnostic for Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)?
cards.a: Anticardiolipin, Anti-β<sub>2</sub>-glycoprotein I, and Lupus anticoagulant.

cards.q: A child with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and > 20% lymphoblasts (TdT+) in the marrow has what diagnosis?
cards.a: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL).

cards.q: A 60-year-old with pancytopenia and circulating myeloblasts containing Auer rods. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).

cards.q: Which AML subtype is associated with t(15;17), DIC, and treated with ATRA?
cards.a: Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL or M3 AML).

cards.q: An asymptomatic elderly patient has a severely elevated WBC count with smudge cells on a smear. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL).

cards.q: What translocation and gene product are characteristic of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML), and what is the targeted therapy?
cards.a: t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome; BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase; treated with Imatinib.

cards.q: How do you differentiate CML from a leukemoid reaction using the Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) score?
cards.a: LAP score is LOW in CML and HIGH in a leukemoid reaction.

cards.q: A young adult presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and systemic B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss). Biopsy shows Reed-Sternberg cells. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Hodgkin Lymphoma.

cards.q: What is the characteristic translocation of Burkitt Lymphoma, and what classic histologic pattern is seen?
cards.a: t(8;14) c-myc activation; "Starry sky" appearance.

cards.q: An older patient presents with CRAB symptoms (Calcium elevation, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions). What is the diagnosis and marrow finding?
cards.a: Multiple Myeloma; > 10% monoclonal plasma cells in the bone marrow.

cards.q: How does Waldenström Macroglobulinemia differ from Multiple Myeloma?
cards.a: Hyperviscosity syndrome (visual/neuro deficits), IgM spike, hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy, and NO lytic bone lesions.

cards.q: A patient with pruritus after hot showers, ruddy cyanosis, and a JAK2 V617F mutation has what condition, and what is the first-line treatment?
cards.a: Polycythemia Vera; Phlebotomy (and Hydroxyurea if high risk).

cards.q: Essential thrombocythemia involves a massive proliferation of which cell lineage?
cards.a: Megakaryocytes (leading to dramatically elevated platelets > 450,000/μL).

cards.q: Teardrop RBCs (dacrocytes) and a "dry tap" on bone marrow aspiration are highly suggestive of what myeloproliferative disorder?
cards.a: Primary Myelofibrosis.

cards.q: What is the management of a patient presenting with Superior Vena Cava (SVC) syndrome?
cards.a: Head elevation, O<sub>2</sub>, steroids (if airway compromised or lymphoma), and urgent radiation/chemotherapy of the underlying tumor.

cards.q: A cancer patient presents with back pain worse at night, motor weakness, and bowel/bladder dysfunction. What is the most urgent next step?
cards.a: High-dose IV Dexamethasone followed immediately by MRI of the spine to evaluate for Epidural Spinal Cord Compression.

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormalities characterize Tumor Lysis Syndrome?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia, Hyperphosphatemia, Hyperuricemia, and Hypocalcemia (due to PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> binding Ca<sup>2+</sup>).

cards.q: How is Tumor Lysis Syndrome prevented before initiating chemotherapy?
cards.a: Vigorous IV hydration and Allopurinol or Rasburicase.

cards.q: What paraneoplastic syndrome is most commonly associated with Squamous cell lung carcinoma?
cards.a: Hypercalcemia (due to PTHrP secretion).

cards.q: Which lung cancer is most strongly associated with SIADH, ectopic ACTH, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
cards.a: Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC).

cards.q: A 50-year-old female presents with a newly palpated hard, immobile, irregular breast mass. What is the best initial diagnostic step?
cards.a: Mammogram (since she is ≥ 30 years old), followed by core needle biopsy.

cards.q: What is the most common type of invasive breast cancer?
cards.a: Invasive Ductal Carcinoma.

cards.q: At what age and frequency is routine screening mammography recommended for average-risk women?
cards.a: Age 50 to 74, every 2 years (per USPSTF guidelines).

cards.q: What tumor marker is used to track colon cancer recurrence (but NOT for screening)?
cards.a: CEA (Carcinoembryonic Antigen).

cards.q: A patient with iron deficiency anemia and a history of changing bowel habits must undergo what procedure to rule out malignancy?
cards.a: Colonoscopy (to rule out right-sided colon cancer).

cards.q: What is the classic initial presentation and characteristic PSA level of prostate cancer?
cards.a: Often asymptomatic with an elevated PSA (> 4 ng/mL) or an asymmetric, nodular prostate on DRE.

cards.q: A patient has elevated unconjugated bilirubin, normal LFTs, and no anemia after a period of fasting or stress. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Gilbert Syndrome (decreased UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity).

cards.q: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) involves antibodies against what complex, and what is the treatment?
cards.a: Heparin-PF4 (Platelet Factor 4) complex; STOP all heparin and start a direct thrombin inhibitor (e.g., Argatroban, Bivalirudin).

cards.q: How do you urgently reverse the anticoagulation effect of Warfarin versus Heparin?
cards.a: Warfarin: Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) + IV Vitamin K. Heparin: Protamine sulfate.

cards.q: What is the target INR for a patient with a mechanical aortic valve vs. a mechanical mitral valve?
cards.a: Aortic valve: INR 2.0-3.0; Mitral valve: INR 2.5-3.5 (due to higher shear stress/stasis).

cards.q: What is the primary difference in the indication for direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs, e.g., Apixaban) vs. Warfarin in atrial fibrillation?
cards.a: DOACs are preferred for Non-valvular AF, whereas Warfarin is REQUIRED for Valvular AF (e.g., moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valves).

cards.q: What is the immediate next step in management when Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) is suspected?
cards.a: Stop all heparin products immediately and start a non-heparin anticoagulant (e.g., argatroban, bivalirudin, or fondaparinux). Do NOT start warfarin until platelet count recovers (>150,000/μL).

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL, t(15;17)), and what major complication does it prevent?
cards.a: Start all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) immediately to induce myeloid differentiation and prevent life-threatening disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

cards.q: What are the primary diagnostic features represented by the CRAB mnemonic in Multiple Myeloma?
cards.a: Calcium elevated (>11 mg/dL), Renal insufficiency (Cr >2 mg/dL), Anemia (Hb <10 g/dL), Bone lytic lesions / bone pain.

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic enzymatic deficiency in Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP), and what is the primary treatment?
cards.a: Deficiency of ADAMTS13 (vWF-cleaving protease) leading to uncleaved ultra-large vWF multimers. Primary treatment is emergent plasma exchange (plasmapheresis). Platelet transfusions are contraindicated.

cards.q: What specific gene mutation is present in >95% of patients with Polycythemia Vera (PV), and what is the expected erythropoietin (EPO) level?
cards.a: JAK2 V617F mutation; EPO levels are low / suppressed. Treatment includes therapeutic phlebotomy and low-dose aspirin.

cards.q: What laboratory abnormalities define Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS), and what agent is indicated for severe hyperuricemia?
cards.a: Elevated K+, elevated PO43-, elevated Uric Acid, and decreased Ca2+ leading to acute kidney injury. Treat/prevent with IV hydration and rasburicase (or allopurinol for low risk).

cards.q: Contrast the immunoglobulin type, site of hemolysis, and first-line management for Warm vs. Cold Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (AIHA).
cards.a:
Warm AIHA: IgG, extravascular (spleen), treat with corticosteroids.
Cold AIHA: IgM, intravascular/C3b-mediated, treat with avoidance of cold exposure and rituximab (steroids are ineffective).

cards.q: What genetic defect causes Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH), what is the clinical triad, and what targeted agent is used?
cards.a: Mutation in the PIGA gene leading to deficiency of CD55 & CD59 (GPI-anchor proteins). Triad: Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis (e.g., Budd-Chiari syndrome). Treat with eculizumab (C5 inhibitor).

cards.q: What laboratory pattern (PT, PTT, bleeding time, platelet count) is expected in Von Willebrand Disease (vWD), and what is the treatment for mild acute bleeding in Type 1 vWD?
cards.a: Normal PT, prolonged PTT (due to Factor VIII instability), prolonged bleeding time, normal platelets. Treat acute mild bleeding with desmopressin (DDAVP), which triggers endothelial release of stored vWF and Factor VIII.

cards.q: In adults with newly diagnosed Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP) presenting with active bleeding or platelets <30,000/μL, what is first-line therapy?
cards.a: First-line therapy is corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone). If corticosteroids are contraindicated or rapid platelet recovery is required, give IVIG or anti-D immunoglobulin.

cards.q: What classic peripheral blood smear findings are seen during an acute hemolytic episode in G6PD deficiency, and what are key triggers to avoid?
cards.a: Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin fragments) and Bite cells (degmacytes). Triggers to avoid: Fava beans, infections, sulfa drugs, primaquine, nitrofurantoin, and dapsone.

cards.q: How do you clinically differentiate Febrile Non-Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction (FNHTR) from Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction (AHTR)?
cards.a:
FNHTR: Fever/chills within 1-6 hours due to donor leukocyte cytokines; no hemolysis, negative Coombs.
AHTR: Fever, flank pain, DIC, hemoglobinuria within 1 hour due to ABO incompatibility; positive direct Coombs test.

cards.q: How do you differentiate Polycythemia Vera (primary) from Secondary Polycythemia (e.g., chronic hypoxia, renal cell carcinoma) using serum EPO levels?
cards.a: Polycythemia Vera has low / suppressed EPO; Secondary Polycythemia has elevated or inappropriately normal EPO.

cards.q: What gene mutation causes Hereditary Hemochromatosis, what is the best screening test, and what is the definitive long-term management?
cards.a: HFE gene (C282Y) mutation. Best screening test: Serum transferrin saturation (>45%) and elevated ferritin. Definitive management: Therapeutic phlebotomy.

cards.q: What is the initial best next step in management for a patient with known cancer presenting with acute back pain and lower extremity weakness suspected of epidural spinal cord compression?
cards.a: Administer high-dose IV corticosteroids (dexamethasone) immediately, followed by urgent MRI of the spine.

cards.q: What pathognomonic cell is seen on lymph node biopsy in Hodgkin Lymphoma, and what cell surface markers characterize it?
cards.a: Reed-Sternberg cell ('owl's eye' appearance), which is characteristically positive for CD15+ and CD30+.

cards.q: What chromosomal translocation, fusion gene, and targeted therapy define Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (CML)?
cards.a: t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome forming the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (constitutive tyrosine kinase). Targeted therapy: Imatinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor).

cards.q: What monoclonal immunoglobulin elevation is characteristic of Waldenström Macroglobulinemia, and what classic symptom triad indicates hyperviscosity syndrome?
cards.a: Monoclonal IgM elevation. Hyperviscosity triad: visual changes (sausage-like retinal veins), neurologic deficits (headache, dizziness), and mucosal bleeding. Treat hyperviscosity with emergent plasmapheresis.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic threshold for Neutropenic Fever (Absolute Neutrophil Count threshold), and what is the immediate empiric antibiotic therapy?
cards.a: Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) <500/μL (or expected to fall <500/μL) with temp ≥38.3°C (101.0°F). Immediate empiric antipseudomonal monotherapy: cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem.

cards.q: What are the hallmark clinical manifestations of Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome, and what is the best initial diagnostic step?
cards.a: Facial edema, neck vein distension, dyspnea, and upper extremity swelling. Best initial diagnostic step: Chest CT scan with IV contrast to evaluate the site and cause of obstruction (most commonly lung cancer).

cards.q: What autoantibodies are most sensitive and most specific for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)?
cards.a:
• Most Sensitive: ANA (Antinuclear Antibody) — positive in > 95% of cases; good screening test.
• Most Specific: Anti-dsDNA (correlated with lupus nephritis activity) and Anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibodies.

cards.q: What antibody is associated with Drug-Induced Lupus, and which organs are typically spared?
cards.a:
• Antibody: Anti-Histone Antibodies (present in > 95% of cases).
• Spared Organs: The kidneys and central nervous system (CNS) are rarely affected (unlike systemic SLE). Common drugs include hydralazine, procainamide, and isoniazid.

cards.q: What antibody is associated with neonatal lupus and congenital heart block?
cards.a: Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies (cross the placenta and can damage the fetal cardiac conduction system, leading to congenital third-degree heart block).

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) and joint distribution.
cards.a:
• Presentation: Symmetric inflammatory arthritis, morning stiffness lasting > 1 hour that improves with use, constitutional symptoms.
• Distribution: Affects MCP and PIP joints of hands, wrists, and MTP joints of feet. Spares the DIP joints (unlike osteoarthritis).

cards.q: What autoantibody is most specific for Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)?
cards.a: Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (anti-CCP) antibody (specificity > 95%). Rheumatoid Factor (RF) is sensitive but less specific.

cards.q: What is the first-line disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) of choice for RA, and what is its main toxicity?
cards.a:
• Drug: Methotrexate.
• Toxicity: Hepatotoxicity, stomatitis/oral ulcers, bone marrow suppression, and pulmonary fibrosis. Folic acid supplementation is co-administered to reduce side effects. Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.

cards.q: What screening must be performed before starting a patient on anti-TNF DMARDs (e.g., Infliximab, Adalimumab, Etanercept)?
cards.a: Screening for latent Tuberculosis (via PPD or interferon-gamma release assay [IGRA]) and Hepatitis B. Anti-TNF agents can cause reactivation of latent TB (due to breakdown of granulomas).

cards.q: Describe the classic clinical features and X-ray findings of Ankylosing Spondylitis.
cards.a:
Seronegative spondyloarthropathy associated with HLA-B27.

Clinical: Young male with chronic low back pain that is worse at rest/night and improves with exercise; enthesitis; anterior uveitis.
X-ray: Sacroiliitis (earliest finding), syndesmophytes leading to bamboo spine.

cards.q: What is the classic clinical triad of Reactive Arthritis (formerly Reiter Syndrome)?
cards.a:
Mnemonic: 'Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree.'
1. Conjunctivitis / Uveitis
2. Urethritis / Cervicitis
3. Asymmetric Oligoarthritis
Etiology: Occurs weeks after a GI (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter) or GU (Chlamydia trachomatis) infection.

cards.q: What are the X-ray findings in Psoriatic Arthritis?
cards.a: Asymmetric inflammatory arthritis in patients with psoriasis. Classic X-ray finding in fingers is the 'pencil-in-cup' deformity.

cards.q: How do you differentiate Gout from Pseudogout on joint fluid analysis under polarized light microscopy?
cards.a:
• Gout: Monosodium urate crystals; needle-shaped, negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis).
• Pseudogout (CPPD): Calcium pyrophosphate crystals; rhomboid/weekly positive birefringent (blue when parallel).

cards.q: What is the first-line pharmacotherapy for an acute Gout flare?
cards.a:
NSAIDs (e.g., Indomethacin), Colchicine, or systemic/intra-articular Corticosteroids.
Note: Do not initiate or change the dose of allopurinol during an acute flare, as shifting uric acid levels can worsen the inflammation.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action and primary indication for Allopurinol in gout?
cards.a:
• Mechanism: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor, blocking the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine, and xanthine to uric acid.
• Indication: Long-term chronic gout prevention (uratelowering therapy). Check for HLA-B*5801 allele in Asian patients before starting (high risk of SJS/DRESS).

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and risk of Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis (GCA).
cards.a:
Large-vessel vasculitis in patients aged > 50.

Presentation: Unilateral headache, jaw claudication (highly specific), scalp tenderness, high ESR (> 50–100). Strongly associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica.
Risk: Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy causing permanent blindness.

cards.q: What is the next best step in management for a patient with suspected Giant Cell Arteritis?
cards.a: Immediate initiation of high-dose systemic Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 60 mg daily). Do not wait for temporal artery biopsy results to start steroids, as delaying treatment can lead to irreversible blindness.

cards.q: What medium-vessel vasculitis is classically associated with Hepatitis B infection, and what organ system is spared?
cards.a:
• Vasculitis: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN) (necrotizing vasculitis of medium arteries, leading to microaneurysms 'string of pearls' appearance on angiography).
• Spared System: The lungs / pulmonary circulation are spared.

cards.q: Contrast Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA / Wegener's) and Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA) by antibody association and clinical involvement.
cards.a:
• GPA: Associated with c-ANCA (anti-PR3). Triad of upper respiratory tract (sinusitis, saddle nose, otitis), lower respiratory tract (cavitary nodules/hemoptysis), and renal (pauci-immune crescentic GN). Histology shows granulomas.
• MPA: Associated with p-ANCA (anti-MPO). Similar lung/renal involvement but spares the upper respiratory tract. Histology shows necrotizing vasculitis without granulomas.

cards.q: What is the antibody profile and clinical features of Diffuse Systemic Sclerosis?
cards.a:
Widespread skin involvement (trunk and proximal limbs) + early visceral organ disease (renal crisis, interstitial lung disease).

Antibody: Anti-Scl-70 (Anti-Topoisomerase I) antibody.

cards.q: What is Limited Systemic Sclerosis (CREST Syndrome), and what is its associated autoantibody?
cards.a:
Skin involvement limited to face and distal extremities.

CREST: Calcinosis cutis, Raynaud's phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias.
Antibody: Anti-Centromere antibody.
Complication: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH).

cards.q: What is Scleroderma Renal Crisis, and what is the treatment of choice?
cards.a:
Sudden onset of severe malignant hypertension, oliguric acute kidney injury, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

Treatment of Choice: ACE Inhibitors (specifically Captopril, short-acting). Steroids are avoided as they can precipitate a renal crisis.

cards.q: Compare Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis by biopsy histology and skin findings.
cards.a:
Both present with symmetric proximal muscle weakness, elevated CK/aldolase, and anti-Jo-1 antibodies.
• Polymyositis: Endomysial CD8+ T-cell infiltration. No skin findings.
• Dermatomyositis: Perimysial CD4+ T-cell infiltration (perifascicular atrophy). Skin findings include Heliotrope rash (purple eyelids), Gottron papules (scaly plaques on knuckles), and shawl sign. Strongly associated with underlying malignancy.

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) and its lab profile.
cards.a:
• Presentation: Pain and stiffness in the shoulder and pelvic girdles in a patient > 50 years. No objective muscle weakness on exam (unlike myositis).
• Labs: Significantly elevated ESR/CRP; normal CK and aldolase.
• Treatment: Rapid response to low-dose prednisone (10–20 mg/day).

cards.q: What is Fibromyalgia, and how is it diagnosed and managed?
cards.a:
Chronic widespread pain syndrome.

Diagnosis: Widespread pain for ≥ 3 months + ≥ 11 of 18 specific tender points on exam. Normal inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) and normal CK.
Management: Regular aerobic exercise, sleep hygiene, and tricyclic antidepressants (Amitriptyline) or SNRIs (Duloxetine).

cards.q: What is Sjogren's Syndrome, and what autoantibodies are associated?
cards.a:
Autoimmune destruction of exocrine glands (salivary and lacrimal).

Presentation: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes), xerostomia (dry mouth), dental cavities. Positive Schirmer test (measures tear production).
Antibodies: Anti-Ro/SSA and Anti-La/SSB.
Complication: 40-fold increased risk of B-cell non-Hodgkin Lymphoma.

cards.q: What is Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS), and what are its diagnostic criteria?
cards.a:
Hypercoagulable state requiring at least 1 clinical and 1 laboratory criterion:
• Clinical: Vascular thrombosis (arterial or venous) OR pregnancy morbidity (≥ 3 consecutive miscarriages < 10 weeks, or ≥ 1 premature birth due to preeclampsia/placental insufficiency).
• Labs: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, or anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I IgG/IgM on 2 occasions 12 weeks apart.

cards.q: Why does a patient with Antiphospholipid Syndrome paradoxically have a prolonged PTT on routine labs?
cards.a: Lupus anticoagulant antibodies bind to the phospholipid reagents used in the PTT assay, preventing clotting in vitro (prolonging PTT). This prolongation does not correct in a 1:1 mixing study, yet in vivo it causes a highly hypercoagulable state.

cards.q: What is Behçet's Disease, and what is the pathergy test?
cards.a:
Systemic vasculitis of variable-sized vessels.

Presentation: Recurrent, painful oral aphthous ulcers + genital ulcers + uveitis + erythema nodosum.
Pathergy Test: Sterile pustule formation 24–48 hours after skin puncture with a sterile needle (demonstrates hyper-reactivity).

cards.q: What antibody is highly specific for Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD)?
cards.a: Anti-U1-RNP (ribonucleoprotein) antibody.

cards.q: What is the autoantibody association in Drug-Induced Lupus vs. Systemic Lupus?
cards.a:
• Drug-Induced Lupus: Anti-histone antibodies (95%), ANA (99%), anti-dsDNA (< 5%).
• Systemic Lupus: ANA (> 95%), anti-dsDNA (70%), anti-Smith (30%), anti-histone (< 30%).

cards.q: What are the common side effects of Hydroxychloroquine, and what monitoring is required?
cards.a:
Used as baseline therapy in SLE.

Side Effect: Retinal toxicity (maculopathy / 'bull's-eye' retinopathy).
Monitoring: Baseline and annual ophthalmologic examinations (slit-lamp, visual fields, OCT) after 5 years of use.

cards.q: What is IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura) clinical presentation, and what is its histology?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Palpable purpura on lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, and hematuria (IgA nephropathy) in a child.
• Histology: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis with deposition of IgA immune complexes in vessel walls.

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and risk of Kawasaki Disease.
cards.a:
Medium-vessel vasculitis in children.

Presentation: Fever ≥ 5 days + ≥ 4 of: conjunctival injection, oral changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips), cervical lymphadenopathy, polymorphous rash, extremity changes (desquamation, erythema of palms/soles).
Risk: Coronary artery aneurysms.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Kawasaki Disease?
cards.a:
IV Immunoglobulin (IVIG) + High-dose Aspirin (reduces risk of coronary artery aneurysm).
Note: This is one of the rare indications where aspirin is given to children despite the risk of Reye syndrome.

cards.q: Describe the clinical features of Churg-Strauss Syndrome (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, EGPA).
cards.a:
Small-vessel vasculitis.

Presentation: Severe asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, transient pulmonary infiltrates, mononeuritis multiplex, and marked peripheral eosinophilia. Associated with p-ANCA.

cards.q: What is Buerger's Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans), and what is the key treatment?
cards.a:
Segmental, thrombosing vasculitis of small/medium vessels in extremities.

Presentation: Male smoker < 45 years with distal extremity ischemia, gangrene, autoamputation, and superficial migratory thrombophlebitis.
Treatment: Complete smoking cessation (only effective therapy).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test of choice for Sjögren's syndrome if serologies are negative?
cards.a: Minor salivary gland biopsy (lip biopsy) showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.

cards.q: Explain the difference in joint pain improvement between Osteoarthritis (OA) and Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA).
cards.a:
• Osteoarthritis: Pain is worse with activity/use, improves with rest. Morning stiffness is short-lived (< 30 minutes).
• Rheumatoid Arthritis: Pain and stiffness are worse in the morning / after inactivity, and improve with movement/exercise.

cards.q: What physical exam findings differentiate Osteoarthritis from Rheumatoid Arthritis in the hands?
cards.a:
• Osteoarthritis: Heberden's nodes (DIP joints) and Bouchard's nodes (PIP joints). Hard and bony.
• Rheumatoid Arthritis: Swan-neck deformity, boutonniere deformity, ulnar deviation of MCP joints. Soft, warm, and boggy.

cards.q: What is Felty Syndrome, and what is its associated risk?
cards.a:
A severe complication of long-standing Rheumatoid Arthritis.

Triad:
1. Rheumatoid Arthritis
2. Splenomegaly
3. Neutropenia
Associated with: High risk of recurrent bacterial infections.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of a patient presenting with an acute, hot, swollen joint (Monoarthritis)?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Warm, red, tender monoarticular swelling with limited range of motion. Must assume Septic Arthritis.
• Immediate Step: Arthrocentesis (joint aspiration) to obtain synovial fluid for Gram stain, culture, cell count (septic is > 50,000 WBC with > 75% PMNs), and crystal analysis.

cards.q: What is the empiric antibiotic therapy for a patient with suspected Septic Arthritis?
cards.a: IV Vancomycin (covers Gram-positives/MRSA) + IV Ceftriaxone or Ceftazidime (covers Gram-negatives/Pseudomonas).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Raynaud's Phenomenon?
cards.a:
• Non-pharmacologic: Keep hands warm, avoid smoking/caffeine.
• Pharmacologic: Dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., Nifedipine, Amlodipine) to promote vasodilation.

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD).
cards.a: Inflammatory disorder presenting with high spiking daily fevers, a salmon-pink maculopapular rash (transient, occurs during fever spikes), polyarthritis, hepatosplenomegaly, and extremely high serum ferritin levels (> 10,000 ng/mL).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of bone loss in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• Mechanism: Steroids inhibit osteoblast function, stimulate osteoclast activity, and decrease GI calcium absorption.
• Management: Initiate calcium + Vitamin D supplementation + bisphosphonates for patients on prednisone ≥ 7.5 mg/day for ≥ 3 months.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and pathophysiology of Paget's Disease of Bone?
cards.a:
Disordered bone remodeling (hyperactive osteoclasts followed by chaotic osteoblast bone deposition).

Presentation: Bone pain, increasing hat size, hearing loss (due to narrowing of auditory canal), high Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) with normal calcium/phosphate.
X-ray: Osteolytic and osteoblastic lesions, thickened cortex.
Treatment: Bisphosphonates.

cards.q: Describe the antibody association and clinical features of Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS) during pregnancy.
cards.a: Lupus anticoagulant or anticardiolipin antibodies promote thrombosis in placental vessels, leading to placental infarction and recurrent miscarriages. Treated with low-dose aspirin + prophylactic LMWH (heparin) during pregnancy.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of a positive HLA-B27?
cards.a: Associated with seronegative spondyloarthropathies: Ankylosing Spondylitis, Reactive Arthritis, Psoriatic Arthritis, Enteropathic Arthritis. HLA-B27 is present in 90% of AS patients but only 8% of the general population.

cards.q: What is the difference between inflammatory and non-inflammatory synovial fluid based on WBC count?
cards.a:
• Non-inflammatory (e.g., Osteoarthritis): WBC < 2,000 cells/mm\(^3\).
• Inflammatory (e.g., RA, Gout): WBC 2,000–50,000 cells/mm\(^3\).
• Septic: WBC > 50,000 cells/mm\(^3\).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of Fibromyalgia tender points?
cards.a: 18 specific tender points located at insertion sites of muscles (e.g., occiput, low cervical, trapezius, supraspinatus, second rib, lateral epicondyle, gluteal, greater trochanter, knee). Digital palpation with ~4 kg of pressure triggers localized pain without radiation.

cards.q: Name the key side effects of Leflunomide in RA management.
cards.a:
Inhibits pyrimidine synthesis (dihydroorotate dehydrogenase).

Side Effects: Diarrhea, hepatotoxicity, hypertension, alopecia, and severe teratogenicity (must be washed out with cholestyramine before pregnancy).

cards.q: What is the most specific autoantibody for Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies.

cards.q: What joint of the hand is classically spared in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints.

cards.q: What is the initial disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) of choice for Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Methotrexate (often given with folic acid to reduce side effects).

cards.q: A patient with RA presents with neutropenia and splenomegaly. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Felty syndrome.

cards.q: Before starting a patient on biologic DMARDs (e.g., TNF-α inhibitors) for RA, what screening must be performed?
cards.a: Screening for latent tuberculosis (e.g., PPD or IFN-γ release assay) and Hepatitis B and C.

cards.q: What is the classic radiographic finding in Osteoarthritis?
cards.a: Joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts, and osteophytes.

cards.q: What is the characteristic hand joint involvement in Osteoarthritis?
cards.a: DIP joints (Heberden nodes), PIP joints (Bouchard nodes), and the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint.

cards.q: Which autoantibodies are most specific for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)?
cards.a: Anti-dsDNA and Anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibodies.

cards.q: What is the most common cardiac manifestation in SLE?
cards.a: Pericarditis.

cards.q: What specific complement levels are characteristically low during an active SLE flare?
cards.a: C<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>4</sub>.

cards.q: Which autoantibody is associated with drug-induced lupus?
cards.a: Anti-histone antibodies.

cards.q: Which medication is recommended for all patients with SLE to reduce flares and improve survival?
cards.a: Hydroxychloroquine.

cards.q: Which antibodies are commonly associated with Sjogren's syndrome?
cards.a: Anti-Ro/SSA and Anti-La/SSB antibodies.

cards.q: Patients with Sjogren's syndrome have a significantly increased risk of developing which malignancy?
cards.a: B-cell lymphoma (especially MALT lymphoma).

cards.q: What is the specific autoantibody for diffuse cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma)?
cards.a: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-DNA topoisomerase I) antibody.

cards.q: What is the specific autoantibody for limited cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis (CREST syndrome)?
cards.a: Anti-centromere antibody.

cards.q: What medication is used to treat scleroderma renal crisis?
cards.a: ACE inhibitors (e.g., captopril), even if the creatinine is elevated.

cards.q: A patient presents with proximal muscle weakness and a heliotrope rash. What specific autoantibody is associated with interstitial lung disease in this condition?
cards.a: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase) antibodies in Dermatomyositis/Polymyositis.

cards.q: Patients with Dermatomyositis have an increased risk of what underlying condition?
cards.a: Underlying malignancy (e.g., ovarian, lung, colorectal, non-Hodgkin lymphoma).

cards.q: What autoantibody is the hallmark of Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD)?
cards.a: Anti-U1 RNP (ribonucleoprotein) antibodies.

cards.q: What is the best initial imaging test for Ankylosing Spondylitis if plain X-rays of the pelvis are normal but clinical suspicion is high?
cards.a: MRI of the sacroiliac (SI) joints (detects early sacroiliitis).

cards.q: Which genetic marker is strongly associated with the seronegative spondyloarthropathies (e.g., Ankylosing Spondylitis)?
cards.a: HLA-B27.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of Reactive Arthritis?
cards.a: Urethritis, conjunctivitis, and oligoarthritis ("can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree").

cards.q: What common infections precipitate Reactive Arthritis?
cards.a: Gastrointestinal infections (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter) or genitourinary infections (Chlamydia trachomatis).

cards.q: What is the classic radiographic finding in Psoriatic Arthritis involving the DIP joints?
cards.a: "Pencil-in-cup" deformity.

cards.q: What type of crystals are seen in Gout upon synovial fluid analysis?
