cards.a: Monosodium urate crystals, which are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of allopurinol used in chronic gout management?
cards.a: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor, which decreases uric acid production.

cards.q: In a patient with an acute gout flare who has chronic kidney disease, what is the best treatment option?
cards.a: Intra-articular or systemic glucocorticoids (NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated or require caution in severe CKD).

cards.q: What type of crystals are seen in Pseudogout (CPPD) upon synovial fluid analysis?
cards.a: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (Ca<sub>2</sub>P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) crystals, which are rhomboid-shaped and weakly positively birefringent (blue when parallel to the compensator axis).

cards.q: What radiographic finding in the knee is highly suggestive of Pseudogout?
cards.a: Chondrocalcinosis (calcification of the articular cartilage or meniscus).

cards.q: Pseudogout is often associated with which underlying metabolic conditions?
cards.a: Hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and hypothyroidism.

cards.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with bilateral shoulder and hip stiffness worse in the morning, and an elevated ESR. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR).

cards.q: What is the most serious complication of Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) if left untreated?
cards.a: Irreversible vision loss (anterior ischemic optic neuropathy).

cards.q: What is the immediate next step in management for a patient strongly suspected of having Giant Cell Arteritis with visual symptoms?
cards.a: Start high-dose IV glucocorticoids immediately (do not wait for temporal artery biopsy results).

cards.q: A young Asian woman presents with unequal arm pulses, claudication in the upper extremities, and constitutional symptoms. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Takayasu Arteritis.

cards.q: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN) is characterized by necrotizing inflammation of medium-sized arteries. Which viral infection is it strongly associated with?
cards.a: Hepatitis B virus (HBV).

cards.q: Which organs are classically spared in Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN)?
cards.a: The lungs.

cards.q: What triad of clinical manifestations characterizes Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA / Wegener's)?
cards.a: Upper respiratory tract involvement (e.g., sinusitis, saddle nose), lower respiratory tract involvement (e.g., cavitary lung nodules), and glomerulonephritis.

cards.q: Which autoantibody is highly specific for Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)?
cards.a: c-ANCA (anti-Proteinase 3 / anti-PR3 antibodies).

cards.q: What features distinguish Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss) from other vasculitides?
cards.a: Asthma, allergic rhinitis, peripheral blood eosinophilia, and p-ANCA (anti-Myeloperoxidase / anti-MPO) positivity.

cards.q: Which vasculitis presents with palpable purpura, arthritis or arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal disease, most commonly in children?
cards.a: IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein Purpura).

cards.q: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is most commonly associated with which viral infection?
cards.a: Hepatitis C virus (HCV).

cards.q: A patient presents with recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Behcet's syndrome.

cards.q: What are the classic laboratory criteria for Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)?
cards.a: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, and anti-β<sub>2</sub>-glycoprotein I antibodies.

cards.q: A patient with suspected Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS) may have what paradoxical laboratory finding?
cards.a: Prolonged PTT that does not correct with a mixing study (due to lupus anticoagulant), despite being a pro-thrombotic state.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Adult-Onset Still's Disease?
cards.a: Quotidian (daily spiking) fevers, evanescent salmon-colored maculopapular rash, inflammatory arthritis, and markedly elevated ferritin.

cards.q: What synovial fluid WBC count is generally considered diagnostic for septic arthritis?
cards.a: WBC > 50,000 cells/mm<sup>3</sup> (often > 90% PMNs).

cards.q: A sexually active young adult presents with tenosynovitis, polyarthralgia, and painless vesiculopustular skin lesions. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI).

cards.q: What is the treatment for severe Lupus Nephritis?
cards.a: High-dose glucocorticoids combined with an immunosuppressant such as Mycophenolate Mofetil or Cyclophosphamide.

cards.q: Which HLA subtype is associated with an increased risk of severe allopurinol hypersensitivity (e.g., SJS/TEN), particularly in patients of Han Chinese, Thai, or Korean descent?
What is the single most specific initial lab test for Rheumatoid Arthritis, and what DMARD should be started immediately upon diagnosis?
cards.a: Anti-CCP (Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide, > 95% specificity) antibody; Methotrexate is first-line DMARD (monitor CBC, LFTs, and chest X-ray for pulmonary toxicity).

cards.q: In a patient with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), which laboratory parameters best correlate with active lupus nephritis and overall disease flares?
cards.a: High anti-dsDNA antibody titers combined with decreased serum complement levels (C3 and C4).

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for Scleroderma Renal Crisis (SRC), and which class of medications is strictly contraindicated due to triggering SRC?
cards.a: Treatment: Immediate high-dose ACE inhibitors (e.g., captopril); Contraindication: High-dose systemic corticosteroids (precipitates/worsens SRC).

cards.q: Patients with primary Sjögren Syndrome have a > 40-fold increased risk of developing which specific long-term systemic complication?
cards.a: B-cell Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (most commonly MALT lymphoma; suspect if persistent painless parotid gland enlargement or lymphadenopathy develops).

cards.q: How do you clinically and diagnostically distinguish Dermatomyositis from Polymyositis?
cards.a: Dermatomyositis presents with skin manifestations (Gottron papules, heliotrope rash, shawl sign) and has a strong association with underlying occult malignancy (requires age-appropriate cancer screening). Both feature elevated CK/aldolase and proximal muscle weakness.

cards.q: What is the immediate initial management for a patient suspected of having Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis with visual symptoms?
cards.a: Immediate high-dose systemic corticosteroids (e.g., IV methylprednisolone or oral prednisone 60 mg/day) BEFORE obtaining a temporal artery biopsy to prevent irreversible blindness.

cards.q: What is the most common extra-articular manifestation of Ankylosing Spondylitis, and what is the first-line pharmacotherapy?
cards.a: Extra-articular: Acute anterior uveitis (unilateral painful red eye and photophobia); First-line tx: NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin, naproxen) combined with continuous physical therapy/exercise.

cards.q: What clinical triad defines Reactive Arthritis, and what HLA association is present in > 80% of affected patients?
cards.a: Triad: Urethritis, Conjunctivitis, and asymmetric Oligoarthritis ("can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree"); Associated with HLA-B27 following GI (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or GU (Chlamydia trachomatis) infection.

cards.q: Which characteristic radiographic feature and physical exam findings are pathognomonic for Psoriatic Arthritis?
cards.a: Radiography: "Pencil-in-cup" deformity of the DIP joints; Exam: Dactylitis ("sausage digits"), nail pitting, and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint arthritis.

cards.q: Describe the synovial fluid crystal findings in acute Gout vs. Pseudogout (CPPD) under polarized light microscopy.
cards.a: Gout: Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals (yellow when parallel to axis); Pseudogout: Rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (Ca2P2O7) crystals (blue when parallel).

cards.q: What is the first-line pharmacotherapy for Fibromyalgia, and what baseline lab abnormalities are expected?
cards.a: First-line tx: Non-pharmacologic therapy (aerobic exercise, sleep hygiene); FDA-approved meds include Duloxetine, Pregabalin, or Milnacipran; Labs: All baseline inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, CK) and labs are completely normal.

cards.q: A patient presents with chronic recurrent sinusitis, cavitary lung nodules with hemoptysis, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. What is the diagnosis and target autoantibody?
cards.a: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA / Wegener's); Associated with PR3-ANCA / c-ANCA (anti-proteinase 3).

cards.q: What clinical features and lab finding differentiate Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA) from Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA)?
cards.a: EGPA presents with severe refractory asthma, allergic rhinitis/nasal polyps, and peripheral eosinophilia (> 10%); Associated with MPO-ANCA / p-ANCA.

cards.q: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN) characteristically affects medium-sized arteries. Which organ system is classically spared, and which viral infection is strongly associated?
cards.a: Lungs are classically spared (no pulmonary involvement); Strongly associated with chronic Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) (and Hepatitis C) infection.

cards.q: What is the classic clinical tetrad of IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura)?
cards.a: Tetrad: Palpable purpura (buttocks/lower extremities without thrombocytopenia), Arthralgias, Abdominal pain (risk of intussusception), and Renal disease (IgA mesangial deposition).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic hallmark autoantibody for Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD), and what three diseases overlap in MCTD?
cards.a: Antibody: Anti-U1 RNP (ribonucleoprotein); Overlap features of: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Systemic Sclerosis, and Polymyositis.

cards.q: What autoantibodies and coagulation lab finding are characteristic of Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APLS)?
cards.a: Autoantibodies: Anti-β2-glycoprotein I, Anti-cardiolipin, and Lupus Anticoagulant; Lab finding: Paradoxically prolonged aPTT that fails to correct on a 1:1 mixing study.

cards.q: What synovial fluid white blood cell (WBC) count threshold confirms Septic Arthritis, and what is the empiric antibiotic coverage for a native joint?
cards.a: Synovial fluid WBC: > 50,000/mm3 with > 75-90% PMNs; Empiric tx: IV Vancomycin (covers MRSA) plus 3rd generation cephalosporin (e.g., Ceftriaxone, covers Gram-negative rods/Neisseria).

cards.q: What is the classic symptom triad of Behçet Disease, and what office test supports the diagnosis?
cards.a: Triad: Recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis; Positive Pathergy test (sterile pustule forms 24-48 hours after needle prick).

cards.q: How do you clinically differentiate Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) from Polymyositis regarding muscle strength and muscle enzymes?
cards.a: PMR presents with proximal muscle stiffness/pain with NORMAL muscle strength and NORMAL muscle enzymes (CK, aldolase) but markedly elevated ESR/CRP; Polymyositis presents with TRUE proximal muscle weakness and ELEVATED muscle enzymes (CK/aldolase).

cards.q: What is the empiric antibiotic regimen for bacterial meningitis in adults aged 1 month to 50 years?
cards.a:
IV Ceftriaxone (or Cefotaxime) + IV Vancomycin + IV Dexamethasone.
Note: Dexamethasone is administered before or with the first dose of antibiotics to reduce risk of hearing loss/neurological sequelae from Streptococcus pneumoniae.

cards.q: What is the empiric antibiotic regimen for bacterial meningitis in adults aged > 50 years or immunocompromised patients?
cards.a: IV Ceftriaxone + IV Vancomycin + IV Ampicillin (covers Listeria monocytogenes) + IV Dexamethasone.

cards.q: Compare the CSF findings of Bacterial, Viral, and Fungal/Tubercular Meningitis.
cards.a:
• Bacterial: WBC > 1,000 (mostly PMNs), elevated protein (> 250), low glucose (< 40, or ratio < 0.4), elevated opening pressure.
• Viral: WBC 10–500 (mostly lymphocytes), normal/mild protein, normal glucose, normal/mild opening pressure.
• Fungal/TB: WBC 100–500 (mostly lymphocytes), elevated protein, low glucose, elevated opening pressure.

cards.q: State the CD4 threshold and prophylaxis of choice for Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) in HIV.
cards.a:
• CD4 Threshold: < 200 cells/\(\mu\)L.
• Prophylaxis of Choice: Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) (daily or 3x/week).
Alternative: Dapsone or inhaled pentamidine (if sulfa-allergic).

cards.q: State the CD4 threshold, clinical presentation, and prophylaxis of choice for Toxoplasma gondii in HIV.
cards.a:
• CD4 Threshold: < 100 cells/\(\mu\)L (in patients with positive Toxoplasma IgG serology).
• Prophylaxis: TMP-SMX (daily).
• Presentation: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions on MRI with focal deficits. Treated with pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine.

cards.q: State the CD4 threshold, clinical presentation, and prophylaxis of choice for Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) in HIV.
cards.a:
• CD4 Threshold: < 50 cells/\(\mu\)L.
• Prophylaxis: Azithromycin (weekly).
Note: MAC prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended in patients who immediately start antiretroviral therapy (ART), but remains highly tested.
• Presentation: Fever, night sweats, weight loss, diarrhea, splenomegaly, elevated alkaline phosphatase.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and treatment of choice for Lyme Disease stages?
cards.a:
Caused by Borrelia burgdorferi transmitted by Ixodes ticks.

Stages & Treatment:
• Early Localized: Erythema migrans ('bull's-eye' rash). Treatment: Oral Doxycycline (Amoxicillin or cefuroxime in pregnant women or children < 8 years).
• Early Disseminated: Bilateral Bell's palsy, AV heart block. Treatment: IV Ceftriaxone (for carditis or meningitis).
• Late: Lyme arthritis. Treatment: Oral doxycycline.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic algorithm for screening and confirming Syphilis?
cards.a:
1. Screening (Nontreponemal): VDRL or RPR (sensitive but non-specific; titers used to monitor treatment response).
2. Confirmation (Treponemal): FTA-ABS or TP-PA (specific for Treponema pallidum; remains positive for life regardless of treatment).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Syphilis by stage?
cards.a:
• Primary, Secondary, or Early Latent: A single IM dose of Benzathine Penicillin G (2.4 million units).
• Late Latent or Unknown Duration: Three doses of IM Benzathine Penicillin G (weekly intervals).
• Neurosyphilis: IV Aqueous Penicillin G for 10–14 days.
Note: Pregnant patients with penicillin allergy must be desensitized and treated with penicillin.

cards.q: What is the Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction, and how is it managed?
cards.a:
Acute febrile reaction (fever, chills, headache, myalgias, worsening rash) occurring within 24 hours of starting penicillin therapy for syphilis, caused by rapid lysis of spirochetes releasing endotoxins.

Management: Supportive (NSAIDs, fluids, rest); self-limiting.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic criteria and treatment of choice for uncomplicated acute Cystitis?
cards.a:
• Diagnosis: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, absence of vaginal discharge, positive nitrite/leukocyte esterase on urinalysis.
• First-line Treatment: Nitrofurantoin (5 days), TMP-SMX (3 days), or Fosfomycin (1 dose). Avoid nitrofurantoin if eGFR < 30.

cards.q: What are the indications for screening and treating Asymptomatic Bacteriuria?
cards.a:
Only indicated for:
1. Pregnant women (at 12–16 weeks gestation; untreated bacteriuria leads to pyelonephritis and low birth weight).
2. Patients undergoing invasive urological procedures involving mucosal bleeding.

cards.q: What is the outpatient and inpatient treatment of choice for acute Pyelonephritis?
cards.a:
• Outpatient (mild/moderate, hemodynamically stable): Oral Ciprofloxacin or Levofloxacin for 7 days.
• Inpatient (severe, vomiting, pregnant, hemodynamically unstable): IV Ceftriaxone, Cefepime, or Piperacillin-tazobactam, transitioned to oral therapy once afebrile for 24–48 hours.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic gold standard for confirming Osteomyelitis?
cards.a: Bone biopsy with histopathology and culture. Superficial wound cultures are unreliable.

cards.q: Name the key toxicities of the RIPE antitubercular regimen.
cards.a:
• R: Rifampin → Hepatotoxicity, red-orange discoloration of bodily fluids, potent CYP450 inducer.
• I: Isoniazid → Hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy (prevented by co-administering Pyridoxine / Vitamin B6), drug-induced lupus.
• P: Pyrazinamide → Hepatotoxicity, hyperuricemia (can trigger gout).
• E: Ethambutol → Optic Neuritis (reversible loss of red-green color vision, blurry vision).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test of choice and treatment for Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI)?
cards.a:
• Diagnostic Test: C. diff toxin PCR or enzyme immunoassay (EIA) in stool.
• Treatment: Oral Vancomycin 125 mg QID or oral Fidaxomicin 200 mg BID for 10 days.

cards.q: Define Neutropenic Fever and its immediate management.
cards.a:
• Definition: A single oral temperature ≥ 38.3°C (101°F) or ≥ 38.0°C (100.4°F) sustained for 1 hour, in a patient with absolute neutrophil count (ANC) < 500 cells/\(\mu\)L.
• Immediate Management: Obtain blood cultures and start empiric IV antipseudomonal monotherapy (e.g., Cefepime, Piperacillin-tazobactam, or Meropenem) within 1 hour. Do not wait for labs/cultures.

cards.q: What is the definition of SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) criteria?
cards.a:
Requires ≥ 2 of the following:
1. Temp > 38°C (100.4°F) or < 36°C (96.8°F).
2. HR > 90 bpm.
3. RR > 20/min or \(P_aCO_2\) < 32 mmHg.
4. WBC > 12,000, < 4,000, or > 10% bands.

cards.q: What are the components of the quick SOFA (qSOFA) score used to identify patients at risk of poor sepsis outcomes?
cards.a:
Requires ≥ 2 of the following:
1. Altered mental status (GCS < 15).
2. Tachypnea (RR ≥ 22/min).
3. Hypotension (Systolic BP ≤ 100 mmHg).

cards.q: How is Septic Shock defined clinical-hemodynamically?
cards.a: Sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥ 65 mmHg, and a serum lactate level > 2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation.

cards.q: How do you clinically differentiate Cellulitis from Erysipelas?
cards.a:
• Erysipelas: Involves the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics (most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes). Presents as a bright-red, raised, indurated rash with sharp, well-demarcated borders.
• Cellulitis: Involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous fat (caused by S. pyogenes or S. aureus). Presents as warm, flat, erythematous swelling with poorly-demarcated, diffuse borders.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of Necrotizing Fasciitis?
cards.a:
Severe, deep tissue infection involving muscle fascia.

Presentation: Pain out of proportion to physical exam, rapid progression of swelling/erythema, crepitus, purple bullae, and gas on imaging.
Management: Immediate surgical debridement (priority) + empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (Vancomycin + Piperacillin-tazobactam + Clindamycin — clindamycin inhibits toxin production).

cards.q: What is Infectious Mononucleosis, and what counseling is critical?
cards.a:
Caused by Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV).

Presentation: Fever, pharyngitis with tonsillar exudates, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytes, positive monospot test (heterophile antibodies).
Counseling: Avoid contact sports for ≥ 3–4 weeks due to the risk of splenic rupture.

cards.q: Why does a patient with mononucleosis develop a diffuse maculopapular rash after receiving Ampicillin or Amoxicillin?
cards.a: A benign, immune-mediated drug reaction (not a true allergy) that occurs in ≥ 80% of patients with EBV infection who are treated with aminopenicillins.

cards.q: What is the treatment window and drug of choice for uncomplicated Influenza?
cards.a:
• Drug: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) — neuraminidase inhibitor.
• Window: Initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset. Patients with severe disease (hospitalized) or high-risk factors (elderly, pregnant, comorbid) receive treatment even after 48 hours.

cards.q: Contrast the treatment of Plasmodium falciparum vs. Plasmodium vivax/ovale malaria.
cards.a:
• P. falciparum (uncomplicated): Artemether-lumefantrine or Atovaquone-proguanil.
• P. vivax / P. ovale: Chloroquine + Primaquine. Primaquine is required to eradicate the dormant liver form (hypnozoites) to prevent relapses. You must screen for G6PD deficiency before giving primaquine (causes severe hemolysis).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for severe malaria?
cards.a: IV Artesunate (preferred over IV quinidine).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Cat-Scratch Disease?
cards.a:
Caused by Bartonella henselae.

Presentation: Painful, unilateral lymphadenopathy near a scratch site.
Treatment: Oral Azithromycin (shortens duration of lymphadenopathy).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for animal/human bites, and what organism are we targeting?
cards.a:
• First-line Treatment: Oral Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (Augmentin).
• Pathogens: Pasteurella multocida (dog/cat bites), Eikenella corrodens (human bites), and oral anaerobes.

cards.q: What is the prophylaxis strategy for suspected Rabies exposure in an unvaccinated patient?
cards.a:
Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP):
1. Immediate wound cleansing.
2. Rabies Immune Globulin (RIG): Infiltrated around the wound site.
3. Rabies Vaccine: 4-dose series (days 0, 3, 7, 14) administered IM in the deltoid.

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and risk factors for secondary/reactivation Tuberculosis.
cards.a:
Reactivation of latent TB (usually in upper lobes of lungs).

Presentation: Productive cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, low-grade fever.
Risk factors: TNF-alpha inhibitor use, HIV, immunosuppressive therapy, silicosis.

cards.q: What is Extrapulmonary Tuberculosis in the spine called, and what are its features?
cards.a: Pott's Disease. Tuberculous osteomyelitis of the spine. Presents with chronic back pain, thoracic kyphosis (gibbus deformity), and cold paraspinal abscesses.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of toxic shock syndrome (TSS)?
cards.a:
Superantigen-mediated disease caused by TSS toxin-1 (TSST-1) from Staphylococcus aureus (tampons, nasal packing, wound infection) or exotoxins from Streptococcus pyogenes.

Presentation: High fever, hypotension, diffuse erythroderma (sunburn-like rash followed by desquamation of palms/soles), multi-organ failure.
Treatment: IV fluids, wound debridement, and IV antibiotics (Vancomycin + Clindamycin).

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Cryptococcal Meningitis in HIV, and the diagnostic test.
cards.a:
• Presentation: Subacute headache, fever, neck stiffness (often minimal). CD4 typically < 100.
• Diagnosis: Cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) in CSF or serum. CSF opening pressure is often very high. India ink shows encapsulated yeast.
• Treatment: Amphotericin B + Flucytosine, followed by long-term Fluconazole.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for pulmonary Nocardiosis vs. Actinomycosis?
cards.a:
• Nocardia (acid-fast, branching, filamentous): TMP-SMX. Mnemonic: Snap (Sulfonamides for Nocardia).
• Actinomyces (non-acid-fast, sulfur granules): Penicillin G. Mnemonic: Abandon (Actinomyces gets Penicillin).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for a patient with suspected Mucormycosis?
cards.a:
Angioinvasive fungal infection seen in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or neutropenia.

Presentation: Black eschar on nasal turbinates/palate, orbital swelling, cranial nerve palsies.
Treatment: Immediate surgical debridement + IV Liposomal Amphotericin B.

cards.q: What is the prophylaxis strategy for Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) in a patient with a severe sulfa allergy?
cards.a: Oral Dapsone or Atovaquone suspension (or monthly inhaled pentamidine).

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and diagnostic test for Histoplasmosis.
cards.a:
Endemic mycosis of Ohio/Mississippi River valleys (bat/bird droppings).

Presentation: Pneumonia, hepatosplenomegaly, palatal ulcers in immunocompromised.
Diagnosis: Histoplasma urinary antigen test (high sensitivity in disseminated disease). Histology shows small intracellular yeasts inside macrophages.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Coccidioidomycosis vs. Blastomycosis?
cards.a:
• Coccidioidomycosis (Southwest US/desert, spherules on biopsy): Fluconazole for mild; Amphotericin B for severe.
• Blastomycosis (Great Lakes/broad-based budding yeast): Itraconazole for mild; Amphotericin B for severe.

cards.q: What are the indications for prophylaxis against Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) in HIV?
cards.a: MAC prophylaxis with azithromycin is only recommended for CD4 < 50 who are not on effective ART. If ART is initiated immediately, MAC prophylaxis is not required because immune reconstitution occurs.

cards.q: Describe the presentation and diagnostic features of Brucellosis.
cards.a:
Exposure to unpasteurized dairy products or infected livestock.

Presentation: Undulant (rising and falling) fever, night sweats with moldy odor, arthralgias/osteomyelitis of spine.
Diagnosis: Blood cultures, Brucella serologies.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Brucellosis?
cards.a: Doxycycline + Rifampin (or Gentamicin) for ≥ 6 weeks.

cards.q: What are the clinical manifestations of leptospirosis, and what is its severe form called?
cards.a:
Exposure to water contaminated with animal urine (rodents, dogs).

Presentation: Flu-like symptoms, conjunctival suffusion (redness without exudate), muscle pain.
Weil's Disease: Severe form with renal failure, jaundice, and hemorrhage.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Leptospirosis?
cards.a: Oral Doxycycline for mild; IV Penicillin G for severe.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and diagnostic findings of Ehrlichiosis vs. Anaplasmosis?
cards.a:
Tick-borne diseases causing flu-like symptoms and cytopenias.
• Ehrlichiosis: Transmitted by Lone Star tick. Histology shows morulae inside monocytes.
• Anaplasmosis: Transmitted by Ixodes tick. Histology shows morulae inside granulocytes/neutrophils.
Treatment: Doxycycline.

cards.q: What is the presentation of primary, secondary, and tertiary Lyme disease?
cards.a:
• Primary: Erythema migrans.
• Secondary: Multiple erythema migrans lesions, AV blocks, carditis, unilateral/bilateral facial nerve palsy.
• Tertiary: Encephalopathy, polyneuropathy, chronic large joint arthritis (e.g., knee).

cards.q: What is the next best step for a patient presenting with suspected Lyme disease and erythema migrans?
cards.a: Immediate empiric treatment with oral Doxycycline. Do not perform Lyme serologies (ELISA/Western blot) in early localized disease, as antibodies have not yet formed and testing is insensitive.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of traveler's diarrhea, and what is the treatment of choice?
cards.a:
• Pathogen: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC).
• Treatment: Hydration. Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) or Azithromycin (preferred in pregnant women/children and travelers to Southeast Asia due to Campylobacter resistance) for severe/febrile cases.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and diagnostic findings of typhoid fever?
cards.a:
Caused by Salmonella typhi.

Presentation: Fever with bradycardia (Faget's sign), abdominal pain, rose spots (faint salmon-colored macules on chest/abdomen), splenomegaly, and leukopenia.
Treatment: Ceftriaxone or Fluoroquinolones.

cards.q: What is the drug of choice for empirical treatment of severe community-acquired sepsis of unknown origin?
cards.a: IV Piperacillin-Tazobactam or Cefepime + IV Vancomycin (covers MRSA and Pseudomonas).

cards.q: Empiric treatment for bacterial meningitis in adults < 50 years?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin

cards.q: Empiric treatment for bacterial meningitis in adults > 50 years or immunocompromised?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin + Ampicillin (to cover Listeria)

cards.q: Most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)?
cards.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae

cards.q: Empiric outpatient treatment for CAP in healthy adult with no comorbidities?
cards.a: Amoxicillin OR Doxycycline OR Macrolide (if local pneumococcal resistance is < 25%)

cards.q: Empiric inpatient (non-ICU) treatment for CAP?
cards.a: Fluoroquinolone (Respiratory) OR (Beta-lactam + Macrolide)

cards.q: CURB-65 criteria components?
cards.a: Confusion, Urea > 20 mg/dL, Respiratory rate ≥ 30, Blood pressure (SBP < 90 or DBP ≤ 60), Age ≥ 65

cards.q: Treatment for latent Tuberculosis infection (LTBI)?
cards.a: Isoniazid + Rifapentine weekly for 3 months OR Rifampin daily for 4 months OR Isoniazid + Rifampin daily for 3 months.

cards.q: Most specific test for diagnosing syphilis?
cards.a: FTA-ABS or TPPA (Treponemal tests)

cards.q: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction symptoms and management?
cards.a: Fever, myalgias, headache within 24 hours of starting syphilis treatment. Management is supportive (NSAIDs), continue antibiotics.

cards.q: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimen and duration?
cards.a: Tenofovir + Emtricitabine + (Raltegravir or Dolutegravir) for 28 days.

cards.q: CD4 count < 200/mm<sup>3</sup> prophylaxis in HIV?
cards.a: TMP-SMX for Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP)

cards.q: CD4 count < 100/mm<sup>3</sup> and positive Toxoplasma IgG prophylaxis in HIV?
cards.a: TMP-SMX for Toxoplasma gondii

cards.q: Diagnosis of HIV in adults?
cards.a: HIV-1/2 Antigen/Antibody combo immunoassay, followed by HIV-1/2 antibody differentiation immunoassay if positive.

cards.q: Primary syphilis presentation?
cards.a: Painless chancre (ulcer) with indurated borders and painless regional lymphadenopathy.

cards.q: Genital ulcer disease: Painful vesicles on erythematous base?
cards.a: Herpes simplex virus (HSV)

cards.q: Genital ulcer disease: Painful, purulent ulcer with ragged edges and painful lymphadenopathy (buboes)?
cards.a: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi)

cards.q: Genital ulcer disease: Painless, beefy-red ulcer with bleeding and no lymphadenopathy?
cards.a: Granuloma inguinale (Donovanosis, Klebsiella granulomatis)

cards.q: Treatment for uncomplicated cystitis in women?
cards.a: Nitrofurantoin (5 days), TMP-SMX (3 days), or Fosfomycin (single dose).

cards.q: Treatment for pyelonephritis?
cards.a: Ciprofloxacin or Levofloxacin (oral if stable), or IV Ceftriaxone/Ampicillin-Sulbactam (if hospitalized).

cards.q: Next best step in management for suspected infective endocarditis?
cards.a: Three sets of blood cultures drawn from different sites BEFORE initiating empiric antibiotics, followed by Echocardiogram.

cards.q: Empiric treatment for native valve infective endocarditis?
cards.a: Vancomycin (covers MRSA, Strep, and Enterococcus).

cards.q: Prophylaxis for infective endocarditis prior to dental procedures is indicated for whom?
cards.a: Prosthetic heart valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, completely repaired CHD within 6 months, repaired CHD with residual defects, cardiac transplant with valvulopathy.

cards.q: Tick-borne disease presenting with fever, headache, myalgias, and thrombocytopenia/leukopenia, without a rash?
cards.a: Ehrlichiosis or Anaplasmosis (Treat with Doxycycline)

cards.q: Classic triad of Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF)?
cards.a: Fever, headache, and petechial rash (starts on wrists/ankles and spreads centrally).

cards.q: Treatment for Lyme disease (early localized)?
cards.a: Doxycycline (Amoxicillin or Cefuroxime for children < 8 years or pregnant women).

cards.q: Malaria prophylaxis for Chloroquine-resistant areas?
cards.a: Atovaquone-proguanil, Doxycycline, or Mefloquine.

cards.q: Treatment for severe Clostridioides difficile infection (WBC > 15,000 or Cr > 1.5)?
cards.a: Oral Vancomycin or Oral Fidaxomicin.

cards.q: Diagnostic test for Osteomyelitis?
cards.a: MRI (most sensitive), followed by bone biopsy with culture (gold standard for targeted therapy).

cards.q: Common cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Salmonella species and Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: Patient with neutropenic fever (ANC < 500). Empiric therapy?
cards.a: Antipseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g., Cefepime, Meropenem, Piperacillin-Tazobactam).

cards.q: Treatment for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis?
cards.a: Penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM single dose.

cards.q: Presentation of babesiosis?
cards.a: Fever, hemolytic anemia (jaundice, dark urine), thrombocytopenia. Blood smear shows Maltese cross.

cards.q: Vector and tick species for Lyme disease?
cards.a: Ixodes scapularis (deer tick).

cards.q: Typical CSF findings in viral meningitis?
cards.a: Normal/mildly elevated opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, normal/mildly elevated protein.

cards.q: Typical CSF findings in bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Elevated opening pressure, PMN pleocytosis, low glucose (< 40 mg/dL), highly elevated protein.

cards.q: Patient from Southwestern US (e.g., Arizona) with pneumonia, erythema nodosum, and arthralgias. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Coccidioidomycosis.

cards.q: Ohio/Mississippi River valley exposure (bat/bird droppings, caves), presenting with pulmonary symptoms and hilar lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Histoplasmosis.

cards.q: Most common cause of prosthetic joint infection within the first 3 months of surgery?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

cards.q: Most common cause of delayed (3-12 months) prosthetic joint infection?
cards.a: Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase-negative Staph).

cards.q: Empiric treatment for septic arthritis (Gram stain pending or negative)?
cards.a: Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone.

cards.q: Animal bite (dog/cat) treatment?
cards.a: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (covers Pasteurella multocida and oral anaerobes).

cards.q: Human bite treatment?
cards.a: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (covers Eikenella corrodens and anaerobes).

cards.q: When to add steroids (dexamethasone) in suspected bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Administer with or just before the first dose of antibiotics (proven beneficial for S. pneumoniae).

cards.q: Painful, grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution. Diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Herpes Zoster (Shingles); treat with Valacyclovir or Acyclovir.

cards.q: Cutaneous anthrax presentation?
cards.a: Painless ulcer with a black eschar and significant surrounding edema.

cards.q: Empiric treatment for hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) or ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)?
cards.a: Antipseudomonal coverage (e.g., Cefepime) + MRSA coverage (e.g., Vancomycin).

cards.q: Bloody diarrhea with no fever, possible history of consuming undercooked ground beef. Diagnosis?
cards.a: EHEC (Enterohemorrhagic E. coli, O157:H7). Avoid antibiotics due to risk of HUS.

cards.q: Cause of "rice-water" diarrhea and severe dehydration?
cards.a: Vibrio cholerae.

cards.q: Classic presentation of Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) in HIV?
cards.a: CD4 < 50; systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), diarrhea, and elevated ALP.

cards.q: Secondary syphilis presentation?
cards.a: Diffuse maculopapular rash involving palms and soles, condyloma lata, generalized lymphadenopathy.

cards.q: What is the initial empirical antibiotic regimen for suspected acute bacterial meningitis in an immunocompetent adult aged <50?
cards.a: Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime). Add ampicillin if age ≥50, immunocompromised, or alcohol use disorder (to cover Listeria monocytogenes).

cards.q: What is the recommended post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for an unvaccinated patient exposed to a wild bat with unknown rabies status without visible bite marks?
cards.a: Rabies immune globulin (RIG) plus a 4-dose rabies vaccine series (administered on days 0, 3, 7, and 14).

cards.q: What CD4 count threshold triggers primary prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) in HIV-infected patients, and what is the 1st-line agent?
cards.a: CD4 count <200/mm3; 1st-line agent is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).

cards.q: What CD4 count threshold triggers primary prophylaxis for Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis in HIV-infected patients with positive IgG, and what is the preferred agent?
cards.a: CD4 count <100/mm3; 1st-line agent is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).

cards.q: How is an initial episode of non-severe or severe acute Clostridioides difficile infection managed according to current clinical guidelines?
cards.a: Oral fidaxomicin (200 mg BID for 10 days) or oral vancomycin (125 mg QID for 10 days). Oral metronidazole is no longer preferred 1st-line.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic workflow and treatment of choice for primary or secondary syphilis in a non-pregnant adult without penicillin allergy?
cards.a: Diagnosis: Serologic testing with a nontreponemal test (VDRL or RPR) confirmed by a treponemal test (FTA-ABS or TP-PA). Treatment: Single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G (2.4 million units).

cards.q: What is the essential initial diagnostic step for suspected infective endocarditis prior to starting antibiotics, and when is transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) indicated over transthoracic (TTE)?
cards.a: Obtain 3 sets of blood cultures from separate venipuncture sites. TEE is indicated if TTE is negative/inconclusive with high clinical suspicion, or in patients with prosthetic valves, intracardiac devices, or suspected complications (e.g., perivalvular abscess).

cards.q: What is the mandatory initial empiric antibiotic monotherapy for neutropenic fever (absolute neutrophil count <500/mm<sup>3</sup> with temperature ≥38.3°C)?
cards.a: An anti-pseudomonal β-lactam agent such as cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem.

cards.q: A patient presents with expanding erythema migrans after a tick bite in the northeastern US. What is the most appropriate management step?
cards.a: Immediately initiate oral doxycycline. Clinical diagnosis is sufficient; serologic testing is not recommended during early localized Lyme disease due to low sensitivity.

cards.q: What are the most common causative organisms of acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease vs the general adult population?
cards.a: Sickle cell disease: Salmonella species and Staphylococcus aureus. General adult population: Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: What lumbar puncture finding confirms Cryptococcal meningitis in an immunocompromised patient, and what is the standard induction regimen?
cards.a: LP finding: Opening pressure >200 mm H2O and positive Cryptococcal antigen assay (or India ink staining). Induction therapy: Liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine for ≥2 weeks.

cards.q: What is the diagnosis and preferred 1st-line treatment for uncomplicated chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum malaria?
cards.a: Diagnosis: Malaria (confirmed via thick/thin peripheral blood smears). Treatment: Artemether-lumefantrine or atovaquone-proguanil.

cards.q: An HIV patient with CD4 <50/mm<sup>3</sup> presents with severe odynophagia. EGD shows deep linear esophageal ulcers and biopsy demonstrates intranuclear inclusions ('owl's eye'). What is the diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Diagnosis: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) esophagitis. Treatment: IV ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir.

cards.q: What clinical triad and chest CT finding characterize invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in an immunocompromised host, and what is the preferred drug of choice?
cards.a: Triad: Fever, pleuritic chest pain, and hemoptysis. Chest CT: Halo sign (nodule with surrounding ground-glass opacity). Treatment: Voriconazole.

cards.q: What is the recommended antibiotic prophylaxis for clean-contaminated elective surgical procedures (e.g., cardiac, vascular, orthopedic procedures)?
cards.a: Cefazolin IV administered within 60 minutes prior to surgical incision (or vancomycin / clindamycin if severe penicillin allergy or high local MRSA rate).

cards.q: How is Latent Tuberculosis Infection (LTBI) confirmed, and what is a preferred short-course treatment regimen?
cards.a: Confirmation: Positive TST or IGRA with negative chest X-ray and absence of TB symptoms. Treatment: 4 months of daily rifampin OR 3 months of weekly isoniazid + rifapentine.

cards.q: What cardinal physical exam feature distinguishes necrotizing fasciitis from simple cellulitis, and what is the definitive management step?
cards.a: Feature: Severe pain out of proportion to skin findings, skin anesthesia, crepitus, or rapid tissue necrosis. Management: Emergent surgical debridement alongside broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

cards.q: A patient presenting with fever, headache, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, and intracytoplasmic morulae inside neutrophils/monocytes following a tick exposure has what disease, and how is it treated?
cards.a: Disease: Ehrlichiosis (monocytes) or Anaplasmosis (neutrophils). Treatment: Doxycycline.

cards.q: What is the preferred oral antibiotic regimen for acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant female when local fluoroquinolone resistance is <10%?
cards.a: Oral ciprofloxacin (500 mg BID for 7 days) or oral levofloxacin (750 mg daily for 5 days).

cards.q: What endemic dimorphic fungus is transmitted via bat or bird droppings in the Ohio and Mississippi River Valleys and appears on tissue biopsy as small intracellular yeasts within macrophages?
cards.a: Histoplasmosis (Histoplasma capsulatum). Moderate-to-severe disease is treated with liposomal amphotericin B followed by oral itraconazole.

cards.q: What is the immediate drug of choice and route of administration for Anaphylaxis?
cards.a:
Intramuscular Epinephrine (0.3 mg in adults, 0.15 mg in children; 1:1000 concentration) administered in the anterolateral thigh.
Note: IM administration achieves faster and more reliable plasma levels than subcutaneous injection. Antihistamines and steroids are secondary therapies and do not treat airway obstruction or hypotension.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect and clinical presentation of Bruton (X-linked) Agammaglobulinemia?
cards.a:
Mutation in the Bruton Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) gene, leading to block in B-cell maturation.

Presentation: Recurrent sinopulmonary and GI infections (e.g., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Giardia) starting after 6 months of age (after maternal IgG wanes). Lymph nodes and tonsils are absent/hypoplastic.
Labs: Absent/decreased B cells (CD19/CD20) and decreased all immunoglobulins.

cards.q: Compare Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) and Bruton Agammaglobulinemia by B-cell count and age of onset.
cards.a:
• CVID: Presents in late childhood / young adulthood (typically 20s–30s). Normal numbers of B cells, but they cannot differentiate into plasma cells. Decreased immunoglobulins.
• Bruton's: Presents in infancy (> 6 months). Absent B cells.

cards.q: What is Selective IgA Deficiency, and what critical transfusion risk is associated with it?
cards.a:
Most common primary immunodeficiency. Often asymptomatic; presents with recurrent sinopulmonary and GI infections, celiac disease, and allergies.

Transfusion Risk: Anaphylaxis during blood transfusions, caused by anti-IgA IgE antibodies reacting against IgA present in donor blood/plasma. Requires washed RBC transfusions.

cards.q: What are the key genetic defects, clinical presentation, and treatment of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)?
cards.a:
• Defects: X-linked IL-2 receptor gamma chain mutation (most common) or autosomal recessive adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.
• Presentation: Failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, thrush, and recurrent severe infections (viral, bacterial, fungal, opportunistic) in infancy.
• Labs: Absent T cells, absent/nonfunctional B cells, and absent thymic shadow.
• Treatment: Stem cell transplant (curative).

cards.q: What is the defect and presentation of Hyper-IgM Syndrome?
cards.a:
Defect in CD40 Ligand (CD40L) on T cells, preventing class-switch recombination in B cells.

Labs: Elevated/normal IgM with severely low IgG, IgA, and IgE.
Presentation: Recurrent bacterial infections + opportunistic infections (PCP pneumonia, Cryptosporidium diarrhea due to impaired macrophage activation).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect and classic triad of Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome?
cards.a:
Mutation in the WASP gene (impaired actin cytoskeleton reorganization in leukocytes and platelets).

Classic Triad (Mnemonic: WATER):
1. Wiskott-Aldrich
2. Thrombocytopenia (presents with microthrombocytes / small platelets and bleeding)
3. Eczema
4. Recurrent infections (progressive loss of T/B cells).

cards.q: What is the enzymatic defect, diagnostic test of choice, and common pathogens in Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)?
cards.a:
• Defect: NADPH Oxidase deficiency → inability of neutrophils to generate superoxide/reactive oxygen species (impaired respiratory burst).
• Pathogens: Recurrent infections/abscesses with catalase-positive organisms (which degrade their own \(H_2O_2\), leaving neutrophils without substrate; e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus, Nocardia, Serratia marcescens, Burkholderia cepacia).
• Diagnosis: Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry (preferred, shows absent green fluorescence) or Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) slide test.

cards.q: What is Hereditary Angioedema, and what is contraindicated?
cards.a:
Autosomal dominant deficiency of C1 Esterase Inhibitor, leading to unregulated activation of kallikrein-kinin system and accumulation of bradykinin.

Presentation: Recurrent episodes of painless, non-pruritic angioedema (face, limbs, larynx) without urticaria. Low C4 levels during episodes.
Contraindicated: ACE Inhibitors (which block bradykinin breakdown, triggering life-threatening attacks).

cards.q: Name the 4 types of Hypersensitivity Reactions and their mechanisms.
cards.a:
• Type I (Immediate): IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation (e.g., anaphylaxis, asthma).
• Type II (Cytotoxic): IgG/IgM antibodies binding cell-surface antigens → complement or macrophage phagocytosis (e.g., autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture's).
• Type III (Immune Complex): Antigen-antibody complexes depositing in tissues → complement/neutrophil activation (e.g., SLE, Serum Sickness, PSGN).
• Type IV (Delayed): T-cell mediated (helper or cytotoxic) tissue damage; takes 48–72 hours (e.g., contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test).

cards.q: What is Serum Sickness, and what is its hypersensitivity type and clinical presentation?
cards.a:
• Hypersensitivity: Type III (immune complex deposition). Occurs 1–2 weeks after administration of foreign protein/drug (e.g., penicillin, monoclonal antibodies).
• Presentation: Triad of fever, urticarial rash, and arthralgias, with lymphadenopathy and low complement (C3/C4) levels.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect and clinical triad of DiGeorge Syndrome?
cards.a:
Mnemonic: CATCH-22.
Microdeletion on chromosome 22q11.2 leading to failure of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches to develop.

Triad:
1. Hypocalcemic tetany/seizures (due to absent parathyroids)
2. Thymic hypoplasia (causing T-cell deficiency)
3. Conotruncal cardiac anomalies (Tetralogy of Fallot, truncated arteriosus). Abnormally low T-cell count.

cards.q: What is the defect and clinical features of Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 1 (LAD-1)?
cards.a:
Autosomal recessive defect in CD18 / LFA-1 integrin (integrin beta-2), preventing leukocyte adhesion and migration into tissues.

Clinical Features:
1. Delayed separation of the umbilical cord (> 30 days).
2. Recurrent skin/mucosal infections without pus formation (no neutrophils can reach the tissue).
3. Extreme leukocytosis / neutrophilia (neutrophils trapped in blood vessels).

cards.q: What is the defect and clinical features of Chediak-Higashi Syndrome?
cards.a:
Autosomal recessive mutation in the LYST gene (impaired lysosomal-trafficking regulator causing defective vesicle fusion).

Clinical Features:
1. Partial oculocutaneous albinism.
2. Recurrent pyogenic infections (neutrophils cannot kill bacteria).
3. Progressive peripheral neuropathy.
4. Giant lysosomal granules inside neutrophils on blood smear.

cards.q: What is Hyper-IgE Syndrome (Job Syndrome)?
cards.a:
Autosomal dominant mutation in the STAT3 gene, causing impaired Th17 differentiation and neutrophil recruitment.

FATED Mnemonic:
• Facies (coarse facial features)
• Abscesses (recurrent cold staphylococcal abscesses — lacking warmth/erythema due to no inflammatory response)
• Teeth (retained primary teeth)
• Elevated IgE (often > 2,000)
• Dermatitis (eczema).

cards.q: What immunodeficiency is characterized by cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and high risk of cancer?
cards.a:
Ataxia-Telangiectasia.

Defect: Mutation in the ATM gene (defective double-strand DNA repair).
Labs: IgA deficiency, lymphopenia, and elevated Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP).

cards.q: Compare the clinical presentation of early complement (C1, C2, C4) vs. late complement (C5-C9) deficiencies.
cards.a:
• Early Complement (C1, C2, C4) Deficiency: Impaired clearance of immune complexes. Strongly predisposes to developing SLE (systemic lupus).
• Late Complement (C5–C9) Deficiency: Inability to form the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC). Predisposes to recurrent, severe Neisseria infections (e.g., meningococcal meningitis, disseminated gonorrhea).

cards.q: What is the diagnosis of a patient presenting with high fever, hypotension, and a diffuse sunburn-like rash after using nasal packing?
cards.a:
Staphylococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS).

Pathophysiology: TSST-1 acts as a superantigen that binds directly to the MHC II and T-cell receptor (TCR) beta chain, causing massive activation of T cells and cytokine storm (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IFN-gamma). Treated with IV fluids and clindamycin + vancomycin.

cards.q: How do you differentiate a food-induced Type I hypersensitivity reaction from food intolerance?
cards.a:
• Type I Hypersensitivity: Mediated by IgE. Occurs within minutes to 2 hours of ingestion; involves pruritus, urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, vomiting, or anaphylaxis.
• Food Intolerance (e.g., lactose): Non-immune-mediated. Involves localized GI symptoms (cramping, bloating, diarrhea) without systemic or IgE-mediated signs.

cards.q: What is the first-line long-term controller therapy for moderate-to-severe Allergic Rhinitis?
cards.a: Intranasal Glucocorticoid Sprays (e.g., Fluticasone, Budesonide). They are more effective than oral antihistamines for treating nasal congestion.

cards.q: Define the immunology of allergic asthma.
cards.a: Exposure to allergens triggers a Th2-dominated response, producing IL-4 (stimulates IgE class switching), IL-5 (activates eosinophils), and IL-13 (stimulates mucus production and airway hyperresponsiveness).

cards.q: What is the utility of a C1 Esterase Inhibitor level and function test in suspected angioedema?
cards.a: A low C1 inhibitor level or function confirms Hereditary Angioedema. During an acute flare, C4 level is also invariably low and serves as an excellent screening test.

cards.q: What is the emergency management of laryngeal edema in a patient with hereditary angioedema?
cards.a: Give IV C1 Esterase Inhibitor concentrate, Ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor), or Icatibant (bradykinin receptor antagonist). Secure the airway. Epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids are ineffective.

cards.q: What is the drug of choice for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)?
cards.a:
Hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus in asthma/CF patients.

Treatment: Systemic Corticosteroids + oral Itraconazole (voriconazole).

cards.q: Describe the clinical features of an IgA-mediated anaphylactic transfusion reaction.
cards.a: Occurs within seconds of starting blood transfusion in an IgA-deficient patient. Presents with sudden hypotension, bronchospasm, urticaria, and respiratory distress. Stop transfusion immediately and administer epinephrine.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for chronic urticaria refractory to standard antihistamines?
cards.a: Add Omalizumab (monoclonal anti-IgE antibody) or increase H1-antihistamine dose up to 4-fold.

cards.q: What primary immunodeficiency presents with recurrent infections and is associated with thymus hypoplasia and midline defects?
cards.a: DiGeorge Syndrome (22q11.2 deletion).

cards.q: Explain the difference in immune response between live-attenuated and inactivated vaccines.
cards.a:
• Live-Attenuated (e.g., MMR, Varicella): Triggers both humoral (antibody) and cell-mediated (T-cell) immunity. Long-lasting protection. Contraindicated in immunocompromised and pregnancy.
• Inactivated/subunit: Triggers primarily humoral immunity. Often requires boosters and adjuvants.

cards.q: What immunodeficiency is characterized by recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated organisms, combined with autoimmune diseases and splenomegaly?
cards.a: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID).

cards.q: What is the immunology of poison ivy contact dermatitis?
cards.a: Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity. Urushiol from the plant acts as a hapten, binding to skin proteins. Langerhans cells present it to T cells, sensitizing them. Re-exposure triggers CD8+ T-cell-mediated epidermal cell apoptosis, causing vesicles/pruritus 48h later.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for moderate-to-severe contact dermatitis involving the face or hands?
cards.a: A 2–3 week taper of oral Prednisone. Short courses (< 2 weeks) often lead to rebound flares.

cards.q: What laboratory marker is elevated in systemic mastocytosis, and what is its role?
cards.a:
• Marker: Elevated serum tryptase (released by mast cell degranulation).
• Pathophysiology: Clonal mast cell proliferation (KIT D816V mutation) causing flushing, abdominal pain, diarrhea, pruritus, and anaphylaxis.

cards.q: What primary immunodeficiency is characterized by recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms?
cards.a: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD).

cards.q: What is the inheritance and screening recommendation for relatives of patients with CVID?
cards.a: Sporadic in most cases, but family members should be screened with quantitative immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM) as subclinical cases can exist.

cards.q: What is the primary treatment for patients with Bruton's Agammaglobulinemia or CVID?
cards.a: Regular lifelong administration of Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) or Subcutaneous Immunoglobulin (SCIG) to provide passive immunity against pathogens.

cards.q: Why is IVIG therapy ineffective for preventing infections in patients with SCID?
cards.a: While IVIG provides antibodies, it does not replace the missing T-cell cellular immunity, which is required to fight viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections. Patients with SCID still die of infections without a stem cell transplant.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of acute serum sickness-like reaction in a child?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Fever, urticaria, and polyarthralgias occurring 1–3 weeks after starting an antibiotic (commonly cefaclor, amoxicillin). Normal complement levels (unlike true serum sickness).
• Management: Discontinue the offending drug, administer antihistamines and oral steroids if severe; self-limiting.

cards.q: What complement factor deficiency is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus?
cards.a: Deficiency of C1q, C1r, C1s, C4, or C2 (leads to failed clearance of apoptotic cells, triggering autoantibody production).

cards.q: Explain the difference in immune mechanism between Hereditary Angioedema (HAE) and allergic angioedema.
cards.a:
• HAE: Mediated by bradykinin (no urticaria, no pruritus, no response to epinephrine/antihistamines).
• Allergic Angioedema: Mediated by histamine (accompanied by urticaria/hives, pruritus, responds well to antihistamines/epinephrine).

cards.q: What antibody is highly associated with idiopathic anaphylaxis or systemic mastocytosis?
cards.a: Not an antibody, but the KIT D816V mutation in mast cells. No specific IgE antibody is identified, but serum tryptase levels are elevated.

cards.q: What is the primary immunological defect in patients with Job Syndrome?
cards.a: Deficiency of Th17 helper T cells, leading to impaired recruitment of neutrophils to sites of infection.

cards.q: What immunodeficiency is characterized by giant granules inside neutrophils?
cards.a: Chediak-Higashi Syndrome.

cards.q: Explain the difference in inheritance between Bruton's Agammaglobulinemia and CVID.
cards.a:
• Bruton's: X-linked recessive (BTK gene). Affects males.
• CVID: Autosomal dominant or polygenic/sporadic. Affects both males and females.

cards.q: What is the drug of choice for allergic conjunctivitis?
cards.a: Topical antihistamines with mast cell stabilizing properties (e.g., Olopatadine or Ketotifen).

cards.q: What is the definition of cold urticaria, and how is it diagnosed?
cards.a:
Physical urticaria triggered by cold exposure.

Diagnosis: Ice Cube Test (placement of an ice cube on the forearm for 5 minutes triggers a localized hive/wheal upon rewarming).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for cold urticaria?
cards.a: Second-generation H1 antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine) at standard or high doses.

cards.q: What primary immunodeficiency presents with microthrombocytopenia?
cards.a: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome.

cards.q: What is the role of IgE antibodies in parasite defense?
cards.a: Parasitic antigens crosslink IgE bound to IgE receptors on eosinophils, triggering eosinophil degranulation and release of Major Basic Protein, which is toxic to helminths.

cards.q: What immunodeficiency is associated with delayed separation of the umbilical cord?
cards.a: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD-1).

cards.q: What is the primary treatment for severe IgA anaphylactic transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Immediate injection of IM Epinephrine (1:1000) + airway protection, followed by IV fluids and antihistamines. Discontinue transfusion.

cards.q: What is the immediate first-line treatment for acute anaphylaxis, including route, anatomical site, and physiological mechanism of action?
cards.a: Intramuscular (IM) epinephrine 1:1,000 (0.3–0.5 mg in adults) injected into the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis). Mechanism: α1 vasoconstriction (reverses hypotension and airway edema) and β2 bronchodilation (relieves bronchospasm and inhibits mast cell mediator release).

cards.q: How does Hereditary Angioedema (HAE) typically present, and what is the single best initial screening laboratory test?
cards.a: Presentation: Recurrent episodes of non-pruritic, non-pitting subcutaneous or submucosal swelling (laryngeal edema, intestinal wall colic) without urticaria or pruritus. Initial screening test: Low serum C4 level (consistently depressed even during asymptomatic remission).

cards.q: What is the underlying molecular defect in Hereditary Angioedema Types 1 and 2, and what key vasoactive plasma mediator drives clinical attacks?
cards.a: Defect: Deficiency (Type 1, ~85%) or dysfunction (Type 2, ~15%) of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH), causing uncontrolled activation of the kallikrein-kinin system. Pathogenic mediator: Bradykinin.

cards.q: How can Acquired C1 Inhibitor Deficiency be laboratory differentiated from Hereditary Angioedema (HAE)?
cards.a: Acquired C1-INH deficiency (seen in older adults with lymphoproliferative disorders or autoantibodies) presents with low C1q levels alongside low C4. Hereditary Angioedema has normal C1q levels.

cards.q: What acute targeted therapies are approved for severe attacks of Hereditary Angioedema, and which class of antihypertensive medications is strictly contraindicated?
cards.a: Acute targeted therapy: C1-INH concentrate, ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor), or icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist). Strictly contraindicated: ACE inhibitors (prevent bradykinin degradation and trigger severe angioedema attacks).

cards.q: What clinical and laboratory findings define Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) in young adults?
cards.a: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections (encapsulated bacteria), chronic diarrhea (Giardia lamblia), and autoimmune cytopenias in patients with markedly decreased serum IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM, accompanied by impaired vaccine antibody response.

cards.q: What are the key non-infectious complications of Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID), and what is the mainstay of long-term therapy?
cards.a: Complications: Autoimmune diseases (ITP, AIHA), non-caseating granulomatous organ disease, and a significantly increased risk of Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma. Mainstay treatment: Regular infusions of Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) or Subcutaneous Immunoglobulin (SCIG).

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of Selective IgA Deficiency during blood product transfusions?
cards.a: Patients with total IgA absence (<7 mg/dL) can form anti-IgA antibodies. Transfusion of standard IgA-containing blood products can trigger a severe or fatal anaphylactic transfusion reaction.

cards.q: How must blood components be prepared before administration to a patient with known Selective IgA Deficiency?
cards.a: Provide washed red blood cells or washed platelets (removes residual IgA-containing donor plasma), or use blood products obtained exclusively from IgA-deficient donors.

cards.q: What is the genetic mutation in X-linked Agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's), and what key physical examination finding distinguishes it from CVID?
cards.a: Mutation: BTK gene defect (Bruton tyrosine kinase), blocking pre-B cell maturation. Physical exam finding: Absence of tonsils and peripheral lymph nodes (due to failure of germinal center formation).

cards.q: At what age do male infants with X-linked Agammaglobulinemia typically present with recurrent bacterial infections, and why?
cards.a: At approximately 6 months of age, coinciding with the decay of transplacentally acquired maternal IgG antibodies.

cards.q: What specific immunophenotypic finding on flow cytometry confirms X-linked Agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's)?
cards.a: Markedly reduced or absent peripheral CD19+ and CD20+ B lymphocytes, along with pan-hypogammaglobulinemia (profound depression of IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE).

cards.q: What classic clinical triad defines Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), and what is its most frequent genetic cause?
cards.a: Triad: Severe failure to thrive, persistent opportunistic infections (fungal, viral, bacterial, Pneumocystis jirovecii), and chronic diarrhea. Most common cause: X-linked recessive IL-2RG gene mutation (common gamma chain deficiency).

cards.q: What metabolic enzyme defect accounts for ~15% of autosomal recessive SCID cases, and what toxicity occurs?
cards.a: Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency. Accumulation of toxic deoxyadenosine (dATP) induces lymphotoxicity, causing depletion of both T and B lymphocytes.

cards.q: What classic radiographic abnormality is present in infants with SCID, and what is the definitive curative treatment?
cards.a: Radiograph: Absence of a thymic shadow (thymic hypoplasia/aplasia). Curative treatment: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).

cards.q: What molecular screening test on dried blood spots enables universal newborn detection of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)?
cards.a: Quantitative PCR detection of T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs); absent or low TREC counts signal severe T-cell lymphopenia.

cards.q: What clinical triad and genetic mutation characterize Hyper-IgE Syndrome (Job Syndrome)?
cards.a: Triad: Severe eczema, recurrent "cold" (non-inflammatory) staphylococcal skin abscesses, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections with pneumatocele formation. Genetic mutation: Autosomal dominant STAT3 mutation, impairing Th17 differentiation.

cards.q: What facial, skeletal, and dental features are seen in patients with Hyper-IgE Syndrome (Job Syndrome)?
cards.a: Coarse facial features, deep-set eyes, broad nasal bridge, retained primary teeth (double rows of teeth), joint hyperextensibility, and osteopenia with recurrent minimal-trauma fractures.

cards.q: What genetic defect causes Hyper-IgM Syndrome, and what is the cellular mechanism behind the immunoglobulin pattern?
cards.a: Defect: X-linked mutation in CD40 ligand (CD40L / CD154) on helper T cells. Cellular mechanism: Failure of T-cell CD40L to engage B-cell CD40 prevents B-cell class-switch recombination, resulting in elevated/normal IgM with near-absent IgG, IgA, and IgE.

cards.q: Patients with Hyper-IgM Syndrome are uniquely vulnerable to opportunistic infections from which protozoan and fungal pathogens?
cards.a: Protozoan: Cryptosporidium parvum (causing chronic severe watery diarrhea and sclerosing cholangitis). Fungal: Pneumocystis jirovecii (pneumonia).

cards.q: What classic clinical triad defines Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, and what characteristic platelet abnormality is seen on peripheral blood smear?
cards.a: Triad: Severe eczema, microthrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections (bacterial, viral, fungal). Platelet feature: Microthrombocytes (significantly decreased platelet volume/size).

cards.q: What gene is mutated in Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, and what is the typical serum immunoglobulin profile?
cards.a: Gene: X-linked WAS gene defect (disrupting actin cytoskeleton organization in hematopoietic cells). Serum immunoglobulins: Low to normal IgM, elevated IgA and IgE, with variable IgG.

cards.q: What clinical triad defines Ataxia-Telangiectasia, and what lab biomarker is characteristically elevated?
cards.a: Triad: Progressive cerebellar ataxia (gait instability), oculocutaneous telangiectasias, and immunodeficiency (recurrent sinopulmonary infections). Lab biomarker: Elevated serum α-fetoprotein (AFP).

cards.q: What metabolic/cellular defect causes Ataxia-Telangiectasia, and what major long-term malignancy risk do affected individuals face?
cards.a: Defect: Autosomal recessive mutation in the ATM gene, leading to defective repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Malignancy risk: High incidence of lymphomas and leukemias.

cards.q: What enzymatic defect causes Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD), and what modern flow cytometry test confirms the diagnosis?
cards.a: Defect: Mutation in sub-units of NADPH oxidase (most common: X-linked gp91phox), impairing generation of superoxide radicals (O2−). Diagnostic test: Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) 123 flow cytometry (demonstrates loss of fluorescence upon oxidation).

cards.q: List 5 major catalase-positive organisms that cause recurrent tissue infections and abscesses in Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD).
cards.a:
1. Staphylococcus aureus
2. Aspergillus species
3. Serratia marcescens
4. Burkholderia cepacia
5. Nocardia species.

cards.q: What pathognomonic clinical feature occurs at birth in Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD) Type 1, and what leukocyte abnormality is present?
cards.a: Clinical feature: Delayed umbilical cord separation (>30 days) followed by recurrent necrotic infections without pus formation. Leukocyte abnormality: Marked neutrophilia / leukocytosis during active infection (neutrophils trapped in vasculature).

cards.q: What specific membrane protein is deficient in Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD) Type 1?
cards.a: CD18 (the β2 integrin subunit), which pairs with CD11 to form LFA-1, preventing firm adhesion and extravasation of leukocytes into inflamed tissues.

cards.q: What physical exam triad and microscopic blood smear finding characterize Chédiak-Higashi Syndrome?
cards.a: Exam triad: Partial oculocutaneous albinism, recurrent pyogenic skin/respiratory infections, and progressive peripheral neuropathy. Blood smear: Giant azurophilic granules within neutrophils and lymphocytes (due to LYST lysosomal trafficking gene defect).

cards.q: Patients with inherited deficiencies of terminal complement components (C5–C9) are predisposed to recurrent infections with which specific organism?
cards.a: Recurrent invasive infections with Neisseria species (Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae) due to inability to form the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC).

cards.q: Deficiencies in early classical complement components (C1q, C2, C4) strongly predispose patients to developing which autoimmune disorder?
cards.a: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and lupus-like glomerulonephritis, secondary to defective clearance of circulating immune complexes and apoptotic debris.

cards.q: What is Oral Allergy Syndrome (Pollen-Food Allergy Syndrome), and what classic plant-food cross-reactivity is seen with birch tree pollen?
cards.a: IgE-mediated contact urticaria of the lips, tongue, and throat after eating raw fruits/vegetables due to cross-reacting pollen antibodies. Birch pollen cross-reacts with apples, pears, peaches, plums, hazelnuts, and celery.

cards.q: How does Serum Sickness differ pathologically from Serum Sickness-Like Reactions (SSLR), and what antibiotic is the classic cause of SSLR in children?
cards.a: Serum Sickness is a true Type III immune-complex hypersensitivity with complement consumption (low C3/C4). SSLR does not involve immune-complex deposition or complement activation. Classic SSLR trigger: Cefaclor (also amoxicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).

cards.q: What is the classic clinical triad of Serum Sickness, and what is the typical timeframe between antigen exposure and symptom onset?
cards.a: Triad: Fever, urticarial or morbilliform rash, and polyarthralgias/polyarthritis. Onset timeframe: 1 to 2 weeks (7–14 days) after primary drug or foreign antigen exposure.

cards.q: What is the typical incubation period and clinical presentation of DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) syndrome?
cards.a: Incubation: 2 to 8 weeks post-drug exposure. Presentation: High fever, diffuse morbilliform rash progressing to facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia (with atypical lymphocytes), and internal organ damage (most commonly hepatitis).

cards.q: Which high-yield drug classes are most frequently implicated in triggering DRESS syndrome?
cards.a: Allopurinol, aromatic antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine), sulfonamides (Bactrim), and vancomycin.

cards.q: How are Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) categorized based on percentage of Body Surface Area (BSA) epidermal detachment?
cards.a:
SJS: <10% BSA detachment.
SJS/TEN overlap: 10%–30% BSA detachment.
TEN: >30% BSA detachment.

cards.q: What pathognomonic physical exam sign is elicited in SJS/TEN, and what is the primary cause of mortality in these patients?
cards.a: Physical exam sign: Positive Nikolsky sign (epidermal sloughing induced by gentle mechanical pressure). Primary cause of mortality: Sepsis / systemic bacteremia (due to total loss of cutaneous skin barrier) and acute hypovolemic shock.

cards.q: What is the recommended treatment step for Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria that fails standard-dose H1 antihistamines?
cards.a: First step: Increase the dosage of second-generation H1 antihistamines up to 4-fold. If refractory after 4 weeks: Add Omalizumab (anti-IgE monoclonal antibody).

cards.q: Which foods are classic components of Latex-Fruit Syndrome due to cross-reactive IgE epitopes?
cards.a: Avocado, banana, chestnut, and kiwi (the "ABC-K" latex cross-reactive foods).

cards.q: What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of radiocontrast media anaphylactoid reactions, and how are high-risk patients pretreated?
cards.a: Mechanism: Direct, non-IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation driven by hyperosmolality. Prevention: Pretreatment with oral corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) and H1 antihistamines, plus using low-osmolality contrast agents.

cards.q: What classic clinical triad defines Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD / Samter's Triad)?
cards.a:
1. Asthma
2. Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis
3. Acute broncho-nasal reactions following COX-1 inhibiting NSAIDs or aspirin.

cards.q: What biochemical alteration drives Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD), and what pharmacotherapy targets this pathomechanism?
cards.a: COX-1 inhibition blocks prostaglandin synthesis, shunting arachidonic acid into the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and causing massive overproduction of cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4). Treatment target: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (Montelukast) or 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor (Zileuton).

cards.q: In which two clinical scenarios is rapid Penicillin desensitization mandatory despite a history of documented IgE-mediated penicillin allergy?
cards.a:
1. Neurosyphilis (or congenital/tertiary syphilis).
2. Syphilis in a pregnant patient.
(Scenarios where penicillin is the only proven bactericidal therapy without acceptable alternatives).

cards.q: What endoscopic and histopathologic findings confirm the diagnosis of Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE)?
cards.a: Endoscopy: Stacked circular rings (trachealization), linear furrows, or microabscesses. Histopathology: ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field (hpf) on distal/proximal esophageal mucosal biopsy after a PPI trial.

cards.q: What pathognomonic somatic gene mutation is present in >90% of cases of Systemic Mastocytosis, and what lab test serves as the principal serum biomarker?
cards.a: Gene mutation: c-KIT D816V mutation (constitutive tyrosine kinase activation). Principal serum biomarker: Elevated baseline serum tryptase (>20 ng/mL).

cards.q: What is Alpha-Gal Syndrome, what vector transmits it, and why is the allergic reaction uniquely delayed?
cards.a: Definition: IgE-mediated allergy against galactose-α-1,3-galactose (carbohydrate on mammalian red meat). Vector: Lone Star tick (Amblyomma americanum) bite. Delay: IgE reaction occurs 3 to 6 hours post-ingestion due to the slow digestion and delayed release of lipid-bound alpha-gal antigens into systemic circulation.

cards.q: What type of hypersensitivity causes Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction, and what diagnostic blood test confirms donor red cell hemolysis?
cards.a: Hypersensitivity: Type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity (pre-existing anti-ABO IgM antibody-mediated intravascular complement lysis). Diagnostic test: Positive Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT / Direct Coombs test) showing antibody coating of recipient red cells.

cards.q: How can Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI) be clinically differentiated from Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO)?
cards.a:
TRALI: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema from donor anti-HLA antibodies; features normal PCWP, normal BNP, and transient leukopenia, often with hypotension.
TACO: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema from hypervolemia; features elevated BNP (>1.5x baseline), hypertension, neck vein distension, and prompt response to IV loop diuretics.

cards.q: What immunologic mechanisms undergo shift during successful Allergen-Specific Immunotherapy (SCIT/SLIT) to generate persistent clinical tolerance?
cards.a: Shift from Th2 to Th1 immune profile, expansion of regulatory T cells (Treg) secreting IL-10 and TGF-β, and generation of allergen-specific IgG4 blocking antibodies that neutralize allergen before it cross-links IgE on mast cells.

cards.q: What is the first-line emergency treatment for acute anaphylaxis, and what serum marker confirms the diagnosis retroactively?
cards.a: Intramuscular (IM) epinephrine (1:1,000 dilution, 0.3–0.5 mg in adults) injected into the anterolateral thigh. Serum tryptase (elevated within 1–2 hours of symptom onset) confirms mast cell degranulation.

cards.q: A patient presenting with recurrent episodes of non-pruritic, non-pitting angioedema without urticaria and recurrent abdominal pain has low C4. What is the underlying pathophysiology and diagnostic confirmation?
cards.a: Hereditary Angioedema caused by C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency or dysfunction, leading to unchecked kallikrein activity and excessive bradykinin accumulation. Confirmed by low C4 levels and decreased functional C1 inhibitor activity.

cards.q: How do you differentiate Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency from Hereditary Angioedema in an older adult presenting with angioedema?
cards.a: Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency is associated with underlying lymphoproliferative disorders (e.g., NHL) or autoimmunity and presents with low C1q levels, whereas Hereditary Angioedema has normal C1q levels.

cards.q: An individual with an asymptomatic immunodeficiency experiences severe hypotension, bronchospasm, and hives during a packed red blood cell transfusion. What is the diagnosis and prevention strategy?
cards.a: Selective IgA deficiency with pre-existing anti-IgA antibodies reacting to donor IgA. Prevent future reactions by administering washed red blood cells or products from IgA-deficient donors.

cards.q: A 25-year-old patient with recurrent sinus infections and bronchiectasis has normal total B cell counts but severely low serum IgG, IgA, and IgM. What is the diagnosis and primary long-term management?
cards.a: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID), characterized by defective B-cell differentiation into plasma cells. Managed with lifelong Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) replacement.

cards.q: A 9-month-old male infant presents with recurrent Streptococcus pneumoniae otitis media and pneumonia. Physical exam reveals absent tonsils. Lab work shows markedly decreased CD19+/CD20+ B cells and low immunoglobulins. What is the genetic defect?
cards.a: Mutation in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene on the X chromosome (X-linked Agammaglobulinemia), leading to failure of pre-B cell maturation.

cards.q: A 3-month-old infant with chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, persistent oral candidiasis, and an absent thymic shadow on chest X-ray is diagnosed with Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID). What are the two most common genetic causes?
cards.a: X-linked recessive IL-2Rγ chain subunit defect (most common) and autosomal recessive Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency, leading to toxic accumulation of dATP in lymphocytes.

cards.q: A child presents with severe eczema, retained primary teeth, high serum IgE, eosinophilia, and recurrent 'cold' (non-inflammatory) staphylococcal abscesses. What is the mutated gene and altered immunologic helper cell pathway?
cards.a: Mutation in STAT3 (Hyper-IgE Syndrome / Job Syndrome), leading to impaired Th17 differentiation and deficient IL-17 production, disrupting neutrophil recruitment.

cards.q: What classic clinical triad characterizes Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, and what cellular mechanism is defective?
cards.a: Triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia (with microthrombocytes/small platelets), and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Caused by WAS gene mutations disrupting actin cytoskeleton reorganization in leukocytes and platelets.

cards.q: A patient with recurrent granulomatous abscesses caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus is suspected of having Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD). What is the enzyme defect and diagnostic test of choice?
cards.a: Defect in NADPH oxidase (impaired production of reactive oxygen species like H2O2 and O2•–). Confirmed by abnormal dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry (decreased fluorescence) or negative nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test.

cards.q: An infant presents with delayed umbilical cord separation (>30 days after birth), marked leukocytosis (neutrophils > 50,000/μL), and skin infections devoid of pus formation. What is the underlying surface receptor deficiency?
cards.a: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency type 1 (LAD-1), caused by an autosomal recessive defect in the CD18 integrin (β2 integrin / LFA-1), preventing leukocyte adhesion and extravasation.
