cards.q: A patient with recurrent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia has elevated serum IgM but absent serum IgG, IgA, and IgE. What cell surface ligand interaction is defective?
cards.a: Defect in CD40 Ligand (CD40L / CD154) expressed on activated CD4+ T cells (Hyper-IgM Syndrome), which prevents interaction with CD40 on B cells, blocking class-switch recombination.

cards.q: Ten days after starting penicillin, a patient develops fever, urticarial rash, joint pain, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Lab tests show low serum C3 and C4 levels. What hypersensitivity type is responsible?
cards.a: Type III hypersensitivity (Serum Sickness), mediated by systemic immune complex (IgG-antigen) deposition that activates the classical complement cascade, lowering serum C3/C4.

cards.q: A patient on allopurinol develops fever, diffuse morbilliform eruption, facial swelling, peripheral eosinophilia (>1,500/μL), and elevated serum transaminases 4 weeks after drug initiation. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: DRESS Syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), a severe T-cell mediated drug reaction with multi-organ involvement (most commonly liver and kidney).

cards.q: What is the most effective single pharmacotherapy for long-term control of moderate-to-severe Allergic Rhinitis?
cards.a: Intranasal corticosteroid spray (e.g., fluticasone, mometasone), which inhibits local inflammatory cytokine release and inflammatory cell influx.

cards.q: A patient with birch pollen allergy experiences localized itching and tingling of the lips and soft palate after eating raw apples and peaches. What is the mechanism of this condition?
cards.a: Oral Allergy Syndrome (Pollen-Food Allergy Syndrome), caused by IgE cross-reactivity between airborne pollen proteins (e.g., Bet v 1 in birch) and homologous heat-labile proteins in raw fruits/vegetables.

cards.q: A young adult presents with recurrent, severe Neisseria meningitidis infections. Screening tests show decreased CH50 activity. Which complement components are most likely deficient?
cards.a: Deficient Terminal Complement Components (C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9), impairing the formation of the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC / C5b-9).

cards.q: A newborn with tetralogy of Fallot develops tetany. Labs show serum Ca2+ 6.2 mg/dL and elevated serum phosphate. What is the microdeletion and embryological structure failed in development?
cards.a: 22q11.2 microdeletion (DiGeorge Syndrome), due to failure of third and fourth pharyngeal pouches to develop, resulting in thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia.

cards.q: A runner experiences generalized pruritus, hives, and wheezing specifically when jogging within 2 hours after eating a meal containing wheat. What is the diagnosis and acute management strategy?
cards.a: Food-Dependent Exercise-Induced Anaphylaxis (FDEIA). Managed acutely with IM epinephrine, and prevented by refraining from exercise for 4 hours after consuming trigger foods (e.g., gliadin/wheat).

cards.q: A 42-year-old patient with severe asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis presents with peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex), skin nodules, and eosinophilia > 15%. Serology is positive for MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA). What vasculitis is this?
cards.a: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss syndrome), a small-to-medium vessel necrotizing vasculitis. Eosinophilic myocarditis is the primary cause of mortality.

cards.q: Compare Pemphigus Vulgaris and Bullous Pemphigoid by target antigen, blister description, and mucosal involvement.
cards.a:
• Pemphigus Vulgaris: Autoantibodies against desmoglein-1 / desmoglein-3 (desmosomes). Blisters are flaccid, easily ruptured, and mucosal involvement is common.
• Bullous Pemphigoid: Autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes (dystrophin BP180/BP230). Blisters are tense, pruritic, and mucosal involvement is rare.

cards.q: Compare Pemphigus Vulgaris and Bullous Pemphigoid by Nikolsky Sign and immunofluorescence pattern.
cards.a:
• Pemphigus Vulgaris: Nikolsky positive (gentle rubbing sloughs skin). Immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG/C3 in a 'net-like' / chicken-wire pattern.
• Bullous Pemphigoid: Nikolsky negative. Immunofluorescence shows IgG/C3 deposition in a linear band along the basement membrane zone.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology, body surface area threshold, and clinical management of SJS vs. TEN?
cards.a:
Severe, life-threatening drug reaction causing widespread keratinocyte apoptosis.

Thresholds:
• Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS): < 10% body surface area (BSA) epidermal detachment.
• SJS/TEN Overlap: 10–30% BSA.
• Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN): > 30% BSA.
Management: Immediate discontinuation of offending drug, admission to a burn unit, supportive fluid resuscitation; Nikolsky positive, mucosal involvement (mouth, eyes, genitals).

cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor for cutaneous Melanoma, and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• Prognostic Factor: Breslow Depth (thickness of the tumor in millimeters from the granular layer of the epidermis to the deepest tumor cell).
• Management: Wide local excision with surgical margins determined by Breslow depth. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is indicated for depth ≥ 0.8 mm.

cards.q: What are the ABCDE criteria for screening suspicious pigmented lesions for melanoma?
cards.a:
• A: Asymmetry.
• B: Border irregularity.
• C: Color variation (multiple shades).
• D: Diameter ≥ 6 mm.
• E: Evolving (changing in size, shape, color, or symptoms like itching/bleeding).

cards.q: What is Psoriasis Vulgaris, and what are the classic clinical signs on exam?
cards.a:
Chronic inflammatory skin disease mediated by Th17/IL-17.

Signs: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees).
• Koebner Phenomenon: New plaques forming at sites of skin trauma.
• Auspitz Sign: Pinpoint bleeding when silvery scales are scraped off.

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema) by age group.
cards.a:
Mnemonic: 'Itch that rashes.' Pruritic, erythematous, dry skin.
• Infants: Affects the face, scalp, and extensor surfaces of limbs.
• Children/Adults: Affects the flexural creases (antecubital and popliteal fossae), neck, and hands.

cards.q: What is Erythema Multiforme, and what are its most common etiologies?
cards.a:
Type IV hypersensitivity reaction presenting with classic targetoid lesions (three zones: dusky center, pale ring, erythematous halo) on extremities.

Etiologies: Most commonly triggered by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Mycoplasma pneumoniae; can also be drug-induced (sulfas, anticonvulsants).

cards.q: What clinical conditions are associated with Acanthosis Nigricans?
cards.a:
Hyperpigmented, velvety plaques in intertriginous areas (axilla, neck).

Associations: Insulin resistance (diabetes, obesity, PCOS). If sudden, severe, and eruptive, it indicates Gastric Adenocarcinoma (malignant acanthosis nigricans).

cards.q: What is Rosacea, and how do you differentiate it from Acne Vulgaris?
cards.a:
Inflammatory dermatosis presenting with facial flushing, telangiectasias, papules, and pustules on cheeks/nose. Chronic cases lead to rhinophyma (bulbous nose).

Differentiating Feature: Rosacea is characterized by the absence of comedones (blackheads/whiteheads), which are required for the diagnosis of acne.

cards.q: What is the enzyme defect, clinical presentation, and triggers of Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT)?
cards.a:
Deficiency of Uroporphyrinogen Decarboxylase (UROD).

Presentation: Painful, blistering, and fragile skin in sun-exposed areas (back of hands), leading to hyperpigmentation, scarring, and facial hypertrichosis (excessive hair). Urine glows coral-red under Wood's lamp.
Triggers: Alcohol, estrogen, iron overload, and strongly associated with Hepatitis C infection.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of Leser-Trélat Sign?
cards.a: Sudden eruption of multiple seborrheic keratoses (benign 'stuck-on' waxy lesions). Indicates an underlying internal malignancy (most commonly gastric adenocarcinoma) as a paraneoplastic syndrome.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and histologic description of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)?
cards.a:
Most common skin cancer. Slow-growing, rarely metastasizes.

Presentation: Pearly nodule with telangiectasias (prominent blood vessels) and central ulceration ('rodent ulcer') on sun-exposed head/neck.
Histology: Palisading nuclei at the periphery of tumor nests.

cards.q: What is Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) of the skin, its precursor lesion, and histology?
cards.a:
Second most common skin cancer. Has metastatic potential.

Precursor: Actinic Keratosis (rough, scaly, sand-paper feel plaque on sun-exposed skin).
Presentation: Ulcerated, scaling, or keratotic nodule/plaque. Histology shows keratin pearls.

cards.q: What is Dermatitis Herpetiformis, its autoantibody target, and treatment of choice?
cards.a:
Extremely pruritic vesicular eruption on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). Strongly associated with Celiac Disease.

Pathophysiology: IgA antibodies react against epidermal transglutaminase, depositing as granular IgA in dermal papillae.
Treatment: Gluten-free diet + oral Dapsone (provides rapid symptomatic relief).

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and etiologies of Erythema Nodosum.
cards.a:
Inflammatory panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat).

Presentation: Painful, erythematous, tender nodules on the anterior shins.
Etiologies: Idiopathic, Strep infection, Sarcoidosis (Löfgren syndrome), IBD, Coccidioidomycosis, and drugs (oral contraceptives, sulfonamides).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of Scabies?
cards.a:
Infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei mites.

Presentation: Intense nocturnal generalized pruritus with linear burrows in the web spaces of fingers/wrists, axillae, and groin.
Diagnosis: Skin scraping demonstrating mites, eggs, or scybala (feces) under microscopy.
Treatment: Topical Permethrin 5% cream (applied from neck down, washed off after 8–14 hours, repeated in 1 week) OR oral Ivermectin. Treat all close contacts.

cards.q: What is Pityriasis Rosea, and what is its typical course?
cards.a:
Self-limiting inflammatory dermatosis. Often associated with HHV-6 or HHV-7.

Presentation: Starts with a single, large 2-10 cm 'Herald Patch' on the trunk, followed 1-2 weeks later by a generalized eruption of smaller oval plaques along skin cleavage lines in a 'Christmas Tree' distribution.
Course: Self-limiting; resolves spontaneously in 4–8 weeks; symptomatic treatment.

cards.q: What are the 5 Ps of Lichen Planus, and what key clinical associations exist?
cards.a:
• 5 Ps: Purple, Pruritic, Polygonal, Planar Papules/Plaques, typically on flexor wrists and shins.
• Wickham Striae: Fine white reticular lines on the surface of papules or oral mucosa.
• Association: Strongly associated with Hepatitis C virus.

cards.q: What is Alopecia Areata, its pathophysiology, and diagnostic hair finding?
cards.a:
Autoimmune-mediated hair loss.

Presentation: Smooth, circular, well-demarcated patches of hair loss on the scalp.
Hair Finding: 'Exclamation point' hairs (short, broken hairs that are narrower near the scalp).
Treatment: Intralesional corticosteroids.

cards.q: What is Vitiligo, and how is it clinically evaluated?
cards.a:
Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes causing depigmented patches of skin.

Evaluation: Clinically or using Wood's lamp (depigmented patches show bright blue-white fluorescence). Associated with other autoimmune diseases (Hashimoto's, Type 1 DM, Addison's).

cards.q: Describe the clinical presentation of Seborrheic Dermatitis and its first-line treatment.
cards.a:
Inflammatory scaling dermatosis affecting areas with high sebaceous gland density (scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, external ear canal). Associated with Malassezia yeast and highly prevalent in Parkinson's disease and HIV.

Presentation: Erythematous plaques with greasy, yellowish scales ('cradle cap' in infants, dandruff in adults).
Treatment: Topical antifungals (ketoconazole shampoo/cream) or low-potency topical steroids.

cards.q: What is the diagnosis of a patient presenting with an expanding, painful, necrotic ulcer with a violaceous, ragged border, often associated with IBD?
cards.a:
Pyoderma Gangrenosum.

Pathophysiology: Neutrophilic dermatosis. Exhibits pathergy (worsens with trauma/biopsy). Associated with IBD, RA, and AML.
Treatment: Systemic Corticosteroids or cyclosporine. Do not perform surgical debridement (pathergy will cause rapid expansion of the ulcer).

cards.q: How is Acne Vulgaris managed in a stepwise manner?
cards.a:
• Mild (comedonal): Topical retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene) + benzoyl peroxide.
• Moderate (inflammatory papules): Add topical antibiotics (clindamycin) or oral antibiotics (doxycycline/sarecycline).
• Severe (nodulocystic / scarring): Oral Isotretinoin (Accutane).

cards.q: What are the critical monitoring and safety rules for initiating oral Isotretinoin (Accutane)?
cards.a:
• Toxicity: Highly teratogenic.
• Safety Rules (iPLEDGE): Requires 2 negative pregnancy tests prior to initiation, monthly pregnancy tests, and use of 2 forms of contraception.
• Monitoring: Baseline and periodic monitoring of fasting lipids and LFTs (causes hypertriglyceridemia and hepatotoxicity).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for Tinea Versicolor?
cards.a:
Caused by overgrowth of Malassezia furfur.

Presentation: Hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules on the chest/back that do not tan in summer. KOH prep shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance (short hyphae and yeast cells).
Treatment: Topical Selenium Sulfide lotion or topical ketoconazole.

cards.q: What is Erythema Toxicum Neonatorum, and what is the management?
cards.a:
Benign neonatal rash appearing within 24–72 hours of birth. Presents as erythematous macules with central yellow/white pustules on the trunk/extremities, sparing palms and soles. Smear of pustule shows eosinophils.

Management: Reassurance. Self-limiting, resolves in 1–2 weeks.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and treatment of choice for Impetigo?
cards.a:
Superficial bacterial skin infection (usually S. aureus or S. pyogenes).

Presentation: Erythematous macules progressing to vesicles/pustules that rupture, forming honey-colored crusts on the face/mouth.
Treatment: Topical Mupirocin for localized lesions; oral cephalexin for widespread (bullous) impetigo.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of Molluscum Contigiosum, and what pathogen causes it?
cards.a:
• Pathogen: Poxvirus.
• Presentation: Firm, dome-shaped, flesh-colored, umbilicated papules with a central dimple. Often self-limiting in children. Widespread facial lesions in adults suggest HIV infection.

cards.q: What is the next best step for a patient presenting with suspected venous stasis dermatitis?
cards.a: Compression therapy, leg elevation, and emollients. Stasis dermatitis is caused by venous hypertension and valve incompetence, presenting as bilateral lower extremity erythema, hyperpigmentation (hemosiderin deposition), and medial malleolus ulcers.

cards.q: Contrast the ulcers of Arterial Insufficiency vs. Venous Insufficiency vs. Neuropathic (Diabetic) disease.
cards.a:
• Arterial: Located on tips of toes / lateral malleolus. Punched-out appearance, pale/necrotic base, very painful, cold skin, absent pulses.
• Venous: Located on medial malleolus. Irregular borders, wet/exudative, hyperpigmentation of surrounding skin, minimally painful, warm skin.
• Neuropathic (Diabetic): Located on pressure points (soles of feet/plantar metatarsal heads). Deep, painless, surrounded by thick callus, warm skin.

cards.q: What is Hidradenitis Suppurativa, and what is its chronic management?
cards.a:
Chronic inflammatory occlusion of follicular infundibulum in apocrine gland-bearing areas (axillae, groin, perineum).

Presentation: Recurrent painful nodules, abscesses, draining sinus tracts, and double-comedones leading to severe scarring.
Management: Topical clindamycin for mild; oral tetracyclines for moderate; TNF inhibitors (adalimumab) or surgical excision of the entire gland-bearing area for severe.

cards.q: Describe the clinical features of Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease) and the causative pathogen.
cards.a:
• Pathogen: Parvovirus B19.
• Presentation: Low-grade fever followed by a bright-red 'slapped-cheek' rash on the face, which then spreads to the body as a reticular, lacy maculopapular eruption.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of roseola infantum (sixth disease), and what pathogen causes it?
cards.a:
• Pathogen: HHV-6 or HHV-7.
• Presentation: High fever (often > 104°F) for 3–5 days in an infant, which resolves abruptly, followed immediately by the onset of a rose-pink maculopapular rash on the trunk spreading to extremities.

cards.q: What is the next best step for a patient presenting with suspected toxic epidermal necrolysis?
cards.a: Discontinue all non-essential medications immediately and admit the patient to an intensive care or burn unit for supportive fluid and electrolyte management.

cards.q: Explain the difference in etiology between a cherry angioma and a strawberry (infantile) hemangioma.
cards.a:
• Cherry Angioma: Benign vascular proliferation in adults. Bright red, small papules, increase with age. Do not regress.
• Strawberry Hemangioma: Benign capillary hemangioma of infancy. Appears within weeks of birth, grows rapidly, and then regresses spontaneously by age 5–9. Treated with beta-blockers (propranolol) if obstructing vision/airway.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for a patient with tinea capitis?
cards.a: Oral Griseofulvin or oral Terbinafine. Topical antifungals are ineffective because they do not penetrate the hair shaft.

cards.q: Describe the diagnostic test and treatment of choice for Intertrigo.
cards.a:
Inflammation of skin folds caused by Candida albicans.

Presentation: Erythematous macerated plaques in groin/axillae/under breasts with satellite lesions (small pustules nearby).
Diagnosis: KOH prep showing pseudohyphae and budding yeast.
Treatment: Topical Nystatin or topical Clotrimazole.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of Actinic Keratosis, and why is it treated?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Small, rough, scaly, erythematous papule with a sandpaper-like feel on sun-exposed skin (face, scalp, forearms).
• Why: It is a premalignant lesion that can progress to Squamous Cell Carcinoma. Treated with cryotherapy or topical 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU).

cards.q: What is the diagnosis of an elderly patient presenting with multiple waxy, stuck-on, brown plaques on the trunk?
cards.a: Seborrheic Keratosis (benign, non-malignant, no treatment required unless irritated).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for a patient presenting with localized Shingles (Herpes Zoster) within 72 hours of symptom onset?
cards.a: Oral Valacyclovir or Famciclovir for 7 days (reduces duration of rash and severity of postherpetic neuralgia).

cards.q: What is the definition of postherpetic neuralgia, and what is the treatment of choice?
cards.a:
• Definition: Persistent pain lasting ≥ 4 months after the resolution of a shingles rash.
• Treatment: Gabapentin, Pregabalin, or Tricyclic Antidepressants (Amitriptyline).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and management of a keloid?
cards.a:
Hypertrophic scar that extends beyond the borders of the original wound, caused by overproduction of collagen (Type I and III). Common in patients with dark skin.

Management: Intralesional corticosteroid injections (triamcinolone). Surgical excision alone is contraindicated due to high recurrence rates.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of bullous impetigo, and what toxin causes it?
cards.a:
• Presentation: Large, flaccid, fluid-filled bullae that rupture, leaving scaly rim. Occurs in infants/young children.
• Pathogenesis: Caused by Staphylococcus aureus producing exfoliative toxin A, which targets desmoglein-1 (causing intraepidermal cleavage, similar to pemphigus).

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation and causative pathogen of Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease?
cards.a:
• Pathogen: Coxsackievirus A16.
• Presentation: Painful oral ulcers (herpangina) + vesicular lesions on the palms of hands, soles of feet, and buttocks, accompanied by fever.

cards.q: Describe the clinical features and management of Pityriasis Versicolor.
cards.a: Malassezia furfur overgrowth. Presents as hypo- or hyperpigmented macules on the upper chest/back that do not tan. Diagnosed by KOH prep showing short septate hyphae and spores. Treated with topical selenium sulfide.

cards.q: What is the definition of Erythroderma (Exfoliative Dermatitis)?
cards.a: Inflammatory skin condition involving ≥ 90% of the body surface area with diffuse erythema and scaling. Can be caused by psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, drug reactions, or cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sezary syndrome). Requires hospitalization for fluid/electrolyte management.

cards.q: Explain the difference in presentation between drug-induced urticaria and serum sickness-like reaction.
cards.a:
• Urticaria: Type I IgE-mediated. Occurs within minutes/hours of drug administration. Presents as transient pruritic wheals.
• Serum Sickness-like Reaction: Type III immune-complex-mediated. Occurs 1-3 weeks after drug administration. Presents with fever, hives/rash, and joint pain.

cards.q: What is the diagnosis of an infant presenting with scaling, yellow, greasy plaques on the scalp?
cards.a: Seborrheic Dermatitis (specifically 'cradle cap').

cards.q: What is the primary treatment for mild localized plaque psoriasis?
cards.a: Topical Corticosteroids (high-potency) + topical Vitamin D analogs (Calcipotriene).

cards.q: What is the primary purpose of a surgical drain?
cards.a: To evacuate fluid (blood, serous fluid, bile, pus, or pancreatic secretions), reduce dead space, and allow early detection of postoperative leaks.

cards.q: What is the difference between an open drain and a closed-suction drain?
cards.a: Open drains allow fluid to drain externally and carry a higher infection risk; closed-suction drains (e.g., Jackson-Pratt) reduce contamination by using a sealed system.

cards.q: Which drain is most commonly used after many abdominal operations?
cards.a: Jackson-Pratt (JP) drain.

cards.q: Which drain provides stronger negative pressure than a Jackson-Pratt drain?
cards.a: Hemovac drain.

cards.q: Which postoperative drain finding suggests a bile leak?
cards.a: Persistent bilious drainage.

cards.q: Which postoperative drain finding suggests a pancreatic leak?
cards.a: High-amylase drainage fluid.

cards.q: Should surgical drains be left in place longer than necessary?
cards.a: No. Remove them as soon as clinically appropriate to reduce infection risk. Nasogastric Tubes

cards.q: What are the major indications for nasogastric (NG) tube placement?
cards.a: Gastric decompression, bowel obstruction, postoperative ileus, gastric outlet obstruction, and prevention of aspiration in selected patients.

cards.q: Is routine postoperative NG tube placement recommended after uncomplicated abdominal surgery?
cards.a: No. Routine use delays recovery and is generally avoided.

cards.q: What should always be confirmed after NG tube placement?
cards.a: Correct gastric position before use, typically with radiographic confirmation when indicated. Ostomies

cards.q: What is an ileostomy?
cards.a: A surgically created opening of the ileum to the abdominal wall.

cards.q: What is a colostomy?
cards.a: A surgically created opening of the colon to the abdominal wall.

cards.q: Which ostomy usually produces liquid, enzyme-rich output?
cards.a: Ileostomy.

cards.q: Which ostomy has the greatest risk of dehydration and electrolyte loss?
cards.a: Ileostomy.

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality commonly develops with high-output ileostomy?
cards.a: Hyponatremia (often with volume depletion and other electrolyte losses).

cards.q: Which ostomy generally produces more formed stool?
cards.a: Descending or sigmoid colostomy.

cards.q: Which ostomy output is expected to be continuously liquid in the early postoperative period?
cards.a: Ileostomy output. Enterocutaneous Fistulas

cards.q: What is an enterocutaneous fistula?
cards.a: An abnormal connection between the gastrointestinal tract and the skin.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of enterocutaneous fistulas?
cards.a: Previous abdominal surgery.

cards.q: What are the priorities in managing an enterocutaneous fistula?
cards.a: Control sepsis, optimize nutrition, replace fluids/electrolytes, protect surrounding skin, and define fistula anatomy.

cards.q: Which nutritional approach is preferred if the gastrointestinal tract remains usable?
cards.a: Enteral nutrition.

cards.q: Which factors reduce the likelihood of spontaneous fistula closure? (FRIEND mnemonic)
cards.a: Foreign body, Radiation, Infection/Inflammation, Epithelialization, Neoplasm, Distal obstruction. Anastomotic Leak

cards.q: What is an anastomotic leak?
cards.a: Breakdown of a surgical bowel anastomosis resulting in leakage of intestinal contents.

cards.q: When do anastomotic leaks most commonly present?
cards.a: Usually within the first postoperative week (often postoperative days 3–7).

cards.q: What is the earliest clinical clue to an anastomotic leak?
cards.a: Persistent tachycardia with unexplained clinical deterioration.

cards.q: What other symptoms suggest an anastomotic leak?
cards.a: Fever, abdominal pain, ileus, peritonitis, leukocytosis, and sepsis.

cards.q: What imaging study is commonly used to evaluate a suspected anastomotic leak?
cards.a: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast and, when appropriate, oral or rectal contrast.

cards.q: What is the treatment for an anastomotic leak?
cards.a: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, source control (percutaneous drainage or surgery), fluid resuscitation, and supportive care. Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)

cards.q: What is the goal of ERAS protocols?
cards.a: Reduce surgical stress, shorten recovery, and decrease postoperative complications.

cards.q: Name key components of ERAS protocols.
cards.a: Patient education, multimodal analgesia, minimal fasting, early feeding, early ambulation, avoidance of unnecessary tubes/drains, and VTE prophylaxis.

cards.q: Why is early postoperative ambulation encouraged?
cards.a: It reduces venous thromboembolism, pulmonary complications, and ileus while improving functional recovery.

cards.q: Why is multimodal analgesia preferred over opioid-only pain control?
cards.a: It decreases opioid requirements and related adverse effects while improving recovery. Surgical Site Infection (SSI)

cards.q: When are prophylactic antibiotics most effective?
cards.a: When administered within 60 minutes before skin incision (timing varies for some antibiotics).

cards.q: Should prophylactic antibiotics routinely continue for several days after clean surgery?
cards.a: No. Prolonged prophylaxis generally provides no additional benefit and increases risks.

cards.q: What is the first step in treating a superficial surgical site infection with purulent drainage?
cards.a: Open the incision to allow drainage and manage according to the clinical situation. Postoperative Fever

cards.q: What is the most common cause of fever within the first 48 hours after surgery?
cards.a: The normal inflammatory response to surgery (after excluding serious complications).

cards.q: What should always be considered in postoperative fever with hypotension and abdominal pain?
cards.a: Anastomotic leak or intra-abdominal sepsis. Ileus

cards.q: What is postoperative ileus?
cards.a: Temporary impairment of bowel motility following surgery.

cards.q: What symptoms suggest postoperative ileus?
cards.a: Abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting, inability to tolerate oral intake, delayed flatus, and absent or hypoactive bowel sounds.

cards.q: What is the initial management of postoperative ileus?
cards.a: Supportive care: IV fluids, electrolyte correction, minimize opioids, early ambulation, and NG decompression if needed. Perioperative Anticoagulation

cards.q: Which postoperative complication is VTE prophylaxis designed to prevent?
cards.a: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE).

cards.q: Which patients often require both mechanical and pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis?
cards.a: High-risk surgical patients without contraindications to anticoagulation.

cards.q: What is the preferred pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis in many hospitalized surgical patients?
cards.a: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), unless contraindicated. Postoperative Urinary Retention

cards.q: What are common risk factors for postoperative urinary retention?
cards.a: Neuraxial anesthesia, opioids, older age, male sex, prolonged surgery, and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).

cards.q: How is postoperative urinary retention confirmed?
cards.a: Bladder ultrasound (bladder scan).

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for significant postoperative urinary retention?
cards.a: Bladder catheterization (intermittent or indwelling, depending on the clinical situation). High-Yield Review

cards.q: Which postoperative finding should always raise concern for an anastomotic leak?
cards.a: Persistent unexplained tachycardia, especially with fever or abdominal pain.

cards.q: Which ostomy has the greatest risk of dehydration?
cards.a: Ileostomy.

cards.q: Which postoperative measure most effectively reduces pulmonary and thromboembolic complications?
cards.a: Early ambulation.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for postoperative care?
cards.a: Persistent tachycardia after gastrointestinal surgery should prompt evaluation for an anastomotic leak. ERAS emphasizes early feeding, multimodal analgesia, and early mobilization. Ileostomies require careful fluid and electrolyte monitoring, and enterocutaneous fistulas are managed by controlling sepsis, optimizing nutrition, and achieving source control before definitive repair.

cards.q: A patient has sudden severe abdominal pain with involuntary guarding and rebound tenderness. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Begin resuscitation (IV fluids, analgesia, antibiotics if indicated), obtain urgent surgical consultation, and evaluate for perforation or other surgical emergencies.

cards.q: A chest X-ray shows free air beneath the diaphragm in a patient with severe abdominal pain. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Perforated hollow viscus until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What is the next best step after identifying pneumoperitoneum in a patient with generalized peritonitis?
cards.a: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, resuscitation, and urgent operative evaluation. Bowel Obstruction

cards.q: What is the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in developed countries?
cards.a: Postoperative adhesions.

cards.q: A patient with prior abdominal surgery presents with vomiting, abdominal distension, and high-pitched bowel sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Adhesive small bowel obstruction.

cards.q: Which CT finding suggests strangulated bowel requiring urgent surgery?
cards.a: Bowel wall ischemia (e.g., poor enhancement), pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, closed-loop obstruction, or free intraperitoneal air.

cards.q: Which symptoms suggest bowel ischemia rather than uncomplicated obstruction?
cards.a: Fever, leukocytosis, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis, localized peritonitis, or severe continuous pain. Appendicitis

cards.q: A young adult has periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant with fever and leukocytosis. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Acute appendicitis.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for suspected appendicitis in nonpregnant adults?
cards.a: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast (when appropriate).

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for suspected appendicitis in children and pregnant patients?
cards.a: Ultrasound first (MRI if ultrasound is nondiagnostic in pregnancy). Cholecystitis

cards.q: A patient has fever, right upper quadrant pain, leukocytosis, and a positive Murphy sign. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Acute cholecystitis.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial imaging study for suspected acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant ultrasound.

cards.q: Which imaging study is most sensitive if the ultrasound is equivocal but suspicion remains high?
cards.a: Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan. Cholangitis

cards.q: What is Charcot triad?
cards.a: Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain.

cards.q: What is Reynold pentad?
cards.a: Charcot triad plus hypotension and altered mental status.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for ascending cholangitis?
cards.a: Urgent biliary decompression (usually ERCP) after resuscitation and IV antibiotics. Pancreatitis

cards.q: Which laboratory test is most useful for diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Serum lipase.

cards.q: Which imaging study should not be routinely obtained early in uncomplicated acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT (unless diagnosis is uncertain or complications are suspected).

cards.q: What is the cornerstone of initial treatment for acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Aggressive IV fluids, analgesia, and early enteral nutrition when tolerated. Mesenteric Ischemia

cards.q: Which symptom is classically associated with acute mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the physical examination.

cards.q: What is the preferred diagnostic test in a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected acute mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: CT angiography. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm

cards.q: An older patient develops sudden abdominal pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile abdominal mass. What should be suspected?
cards.a: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).

cards.q: What is the next best step in an unstable patient with suspected ruptured AAA?
cards.a: Immediate vascular surgery consultation and operative management without delaying for CT imaging. Breast

cards.q: What is the next best step for a palpable breast mass in a woman ≥30 years old?
cards.a: Diagnostic mammography with targeted breast ultrasound, followed by biopsy if indicated.

cards.q: What is the preferred biopsy for a suspicious breast lesion?
cards.a: Core needle biopsy. Thyroid

cards.q: What is the first laboratory test in evaluating a thyroid nodule?
cards.a: Serum TSH.

cards.q: If TSH is suppressed, what is the next best diagnostic test?
cards.a: Radionuclide thyroid uptake scan.

cards.q: Which thyroid nodules generally require fine-needle aspiration (FNA)?
cards.a: Nodules meeting guideline-based size and ultrasound risk criteria. Hernias

cards.q: Which hernia is most prone to strangulation?
cards.a: Femoral hernia.

cards.q: Which clinical finding mandates emergency surgery in a patient with a hernia?
cards.a: Signs of strangulation (severe pain, erythema, peritonitis, bowel obstruction, or systemic toxicity). Testicular Emergencies

cards.q: What is the next best step for suspected testicular torsion?
cards.a: Immediate surgical exploration without delaying for imaging if clinical suspicion is high.

cards.q: What is the classic time window associated with the highest likelihood of testicular salvage?
cards.a: Within approximately 6 hours of symptom onset. Trauma

cards.q: What is the first priority in trauma management?
cards.a: Follow the ATLS primary survey (ABCDE).

cards.q: Which trauma patients should undergo FAST examination?
cards.a: Hemodynamically unstable patients with suspected torso trauma.

cards.q: Which imaging study is preferred for stable patients with blunt abdominal trauma?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis. Burns

cards.q: Which formula estimates initial fluid requirements for major burns?
cards.a: Parkland formula: 4 mL × body weight (kg) × %TBSA burned

cards.q: How is the Parkland formula administered?
cards.a: Half of the calculated volume in the first 8 hours from the time of burn injury and the remaining half over the next 16 hours. Vascular Surgery

cards.q: What is the first diagnostic test for suspected deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?
cards.a: Compression venous ultrasonography.

cards.q: What is the first diagnostic test for suspected pulmonary embolism in a stable patient?
cards.a: CT pulmonary angiography (if no contraindication). Urology

cards.q: What imaging study should precede catheterization if urethral injury is suspected?
cards.a: Retrograde urethrogram.

cards.q: What is the emergency treatment for an obstructed infected kidney?
cards.a: Urgent urinary decompression with a ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy plus antibiotics. Thoracic Surgery

cards.q: What is the first treatment for tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Immediate decompression followed by chest tube placement.

cards.q: Should imaging delay treatment of tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: No. ICU

cards.q: Which vasopressor is first-line for septic shock?
cards.a: Norepinephrine.

cards.q: Which nutritional route is preferred in critically ill patients with a functional GI tract?
cards.a: Enteral nutrition. Pediatric Surgery

cards.q: Bilious vomiting in a newborn should be considered what until proven otherwise?
cards.a: Midgut volvulus or another intestinal obstruction requiring urgent evaluation.

cards.q: Projectile nonbilious vomiting in a 4-week-old infant most likely indicates what diagnosis?
cards.a: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Surgical Principles

cards.q: Which postoperative vital sign abnormality should never be ignored after gastrointestinal surgery?
cards.a: Persistent unexplained tachycardia.

cards.q: What is the single most important principle of surgical infection management?
cards.a: Source control in addition to appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK comprehensive surgery principle?
cards.a: Know the "next best step." Stabilize first (ABCs), recognize surgical emergencies early (peritonitis, compartment syndrome, tension pneumothorax, ruptured AAA, testicular torsion, obstructed infected kidney, cholangitis), choose the correct first imaging study, and obtain definitive source control without unnecessary delays.

cards.q: What is the first priority in every trauma patient?
cards.a: ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) according to the ATLS primary survey.

cards.q: Which trauma patient should go directly to the operating room without CT imaging?
cards.a: Hemodynamically unstable patient with ongoing hemorrhage or peritonitis requiring emergent surgery.

cards.q: Which trauma imaging study is preferred in an unstable patient?
cards.a: FAST examination.

cards.q: Which trauma imaging study is preferred in a stable patient with blunt abdominal trauma?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis.

cards.q: What is the immediate treatment for tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Immediate decompression followed by chest tube placement.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for cardiac tamponade causing hemodynamic instability?
cards.a: Emergent operative intervention (pericardiocentesis may be a temporizing measure in selected situations).

cards.q: Which trauma patient should receive a massive transfusion protocol?
cards.a: Patient with life-threatening hemorrhagic shock requiring rapid blood product replacement. Acute Abdomen

cards.q: Free intraperitoneal air plus diffuse abdominal tenderness indicates what?
cards.a: Perforated hollow viscus requiring urgent surgical evaluation.

cards.q: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination should immediately suggest what?
cards.a: Acute mesenteric ischemia.

cards.q: Bilious vomiting in a newborn should always raise concern for what?
cards.a: Midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. Gastrointestinal Surgery

cards.q: What is the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults?
cards.a: Postoperative adhesions.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction in adults?
cards.a: Colorectal cancer.

cards.q: Which hernia has the highest risk of strangulation?
cards.a: Femoral hernia.

cards.q: What is the first-line imaging study for suspected acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant ultrasound.

cards.q: Which imaging study confirms acute cholecystitis when ultrasound is inconclusive?
cards.a: HIDA scan.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for ascending cholangitis?
cards.a: ERCP with biliary decompression after resuscitation and antibiotics.

cards.q: What is the hallmark laboratory test for acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Elevated serum lipase.

cards.q: What is the cornerstone of early treatment for acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation. Vascular Surgery

cards.q: What is the strongest modifiable risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
cards.a: Cigarette smoking.

cards.q: Hypotension plus back/abdominal pain plus a pulsatile abdominal mass suggests what?
cards.a: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for suspected DVT?
cards.a: Compression ultrasonography.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for stable suspected pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: CT pulmonary angiography. Endocrine Surgery

cards.q: What is the first laboratory test for evaluating a thyroid nodule?
cards.a: Serum TSH.

cards.q: Which thyroid cancer has the best prognosis?
cards.a: Papillary thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: Which thyroid cancer produces calcitonin?
cards.a: Medullary thyroid carcinoma. Breast Surgery

cards.q: What is the preferred biopsy for a suspicious breast lesion?
cards.a: Core needle biopsy.

cards.q: Which breast cancer is associated with HER2 overexpression?
cards.a: HER2-positive invasive breast carcinoma. Urology

cards.q: Sudden unilateral scrotal pain in an adolescent is what until proven otherwise?
cards.a: Testicular torsion.

cards.q: Blood at the urethral meatus indicates what until proven otherwise?
cards.a: Urethral injury.

cards.q: What imaging must be performed before catheterization in suspected urethral injury?
cards.a: Retrograde urethrogram. Thoracic Surgery

cards.q: Progressive dysphagia to solids followed by liquids suggests what diagnosis?
cards.a: Esophageal carcinoma.

cards.q: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the beginning suggests what diagnosis?
cards.a: Achalasia.

cards.q: Severe chest pain after forceful vomiting suggests what emergency?
cards.a: Boerhaave syndrome. Pediatric Surgery

cards.q: Projectile nonbilious vomiting in a 1-month-old infant suggests what?
cards.a: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

cards.q: Currant jelly stool most strongly suggests what?
cards.a: Intussusception.

cards.q: Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours should raise concern for what?
cards.a: Hirschsprung disease.

cards.q: Painless rectal bleeding in a young child most strongly suggests what?
cards.a: Meckel diverticulum. Surgical ICU

cards.q: Which vasopressor is first-line in septic shock?
cards.a: Norepinephrine.

cards.q: Which nutrition route is preferred in ICU patients with a functioning gastrointestinal tract?
cards.a: Enteral nutrition.

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality defines refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Hypophosphatemia.

cards.q: Which blood product contains the highest concentration of fibrinogen?
cards.a: Cryoprecipitate.

cards.q: What is the first treatment for hyperkalemia with ECG changes?
cards.a: IV calcium to stabilize the cardiac membrane. Postoperative Complications

cards.q: Persistent tachycardia after abdominal surgery should immediately raise concern for what?
cards.a: Anastomotic leak or intra-abdominal sepsis.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of postoperative oliguria?
cards.a: Hypovolemia causing prerenal acute kidney injury.

cards.q: What is the earliest symptom of compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Pain out of proportion to the injury, especially with passive stretch. Surgical Principles

cards.q: What is the single most important principle in managing surgical infections?
cards.a: Source control.

cards.q: What is the single most important intervention to reduce postoperative pulmonary complications?
cards.a: Early ambulation with pulmonary hygiene (including incentive spirometry when appropriate).

cards.q: What is the most common preventable postoperative complication in hospitalized surgical patients?
cards.a: Venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE).

cards.q: What is the single most common mistake tested on USMLE Step 2 CK surgery questions?
cards.a: Ordering unnecessary diagnostic tests before stabilizing or treating an obvious surgical emergency.

cards.q: What is the single highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK surgical principle?
cards.a: Recognize life-threatening surgical emergencies immediately, stabilize the patient first (ABCs), choose the correct initial imaging only when appropriate, and proceed rapidly to definitive source control or operative management when indicated.

cards.q: What are the four classes of surgical wounds?
cards.a: Clean Clean-contaminated Contaminated Dirty/infected

cards.q: What defines a clean surgical wound?
cards.a: An uninfected operative wound with no entry into respiratory, GI, genital, or urinary tracts. Examples: Hernia repair Thyroid surgery

cards.q: What defines a clean-contaminated wound?
cards.a: Controlled entry into respiratory, GI, genital, or urinary tract without unusual contamination. Examples: Elective bowel surgery

cards.q: What defines a contaminated wound?
cards.a: Open traumatic wounds, gross spillage from GI tract, or major breaks in sterile technique.

cards.q: What defines a dirty/infected wound?
cards.a: Existing infection, pus, perforated viscera, or old traumatic wounds. Wound Healing

cards.q: What are the three phases of wound healing?
cards.a: Inflammatory phase Proliferative phase Remodeling phase

cards.q: What occurs during the inflammatory phase of wound healing?
cards.a: Hemostasis, platelet activation, and inflammatory cell recruitment.

cards.q: What cells dominate the early inflammatory phase?
cards.a: Neutrophils followed by macrophages.

cards.q: What is the main function of macrophages in wound healing?
cards.a: Remove debris and release growth factors that stimulate repair.

cards.q: What occurs during the proliferative phase?
cards.a: Fibroblast proliferation Collagen deposition Angiogenesis Granulation tissue formation

cards.q: What collagen type is initially deposited during wound healing?
cards.a: Type III collagen.

cards.q: What collagen type predominates later in wound remodeling?
cards.a: Type I collagen.

cards.q: When does wound tensile strength reach approximately 80% of normal?
cards.a: Around 1 year.

cards.q: What is the maximum tensile strength a healed wound achieves?
cards.a: Approximately 80% of original tissue strength. Factors Affecting Wound Healing

cards.q: What systemic factors impair wound healing?
cards.a: Malnutrition Diabetes mellitus Smoking Immunosuppression Steroids Advanced age

cards.q: Why does smoking impair wound healing?
cards.a: Nicotine causes vasoconstriction and carbon monoxide reduces oxygen delivery.

cards.q: Why does diabetes impair wound healing?
cards.a: Poor perfusion, immune dysfunction, and impaired collagen synthesis.

cards.q: What nutritional marker may suggest poor healing capacity?
cards.a: Low albumin/prealbumin (although influenced by inflammation). Wound Dehiscence

cards.q: What is wound dehiscence?
cards.a: Separation of wound edges after closure.

cards.q: When does wound dehiscence most commonly occur?
cards.a: Approximately 5–8 days after surgery.

cards.q: What are risk factors for wound dehiscence?
cards.a: Infection Poor nutrition Smoking Steroids Increased intra-abdominal pressure

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of wound dehiscence?
cards.a: Sudden drainage of pink serosanguineous fluid from the incision. Evisceration

cards.q: What is wound evisceration?
cards.a: Protrusion of abdominal contents through a separated surgical incision.

cards.q: What is the immediate management of evisceration?
cards.a: Cover organs with sterile saline-moistened dressings Keep patient NPO Emergency surgical evaluation

cards.q: Why should exposed organs not be pushed back manually?
cards.a: Risk of injury and contamination. Surgical Site Infection (SSI)

cards.q: What is the most common organism causing surgical site infection?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: When do superficial surgical site infections typically appear?
cards.a: Usually within 30 days after surgery.

cards.q: What are signs of surgical site infection?
cards.a: Increasing pain Redness Warmth Purulent drainage Fever Leukocytosis

cards.q: What is the treatment of superficial incisional infection?
cards.a: Drainage of infected material and antibiotics when indicated. Anastomotic Leak

cards.q: What is an anastomotic leak?
cards.a: Breakdown of a surgical connection between two hollow organs.

cards.q: When do anastomotic leaks commonly occur?
cards.a: Usually within the first postoperative week.

cards.q: What findings suggest an anastomotic leak?
cards.a: Fever Tachycardia Abdominal pain Leukocytosis Peritonitis Sepsis

cards.q: What imaging study helps diagnose anastomotic leak?
cards.a: CT scan with contrast.

cards.q: What is the treatment for anastomotic leak?
cards.a: Depends on severity: Antibiotics Drainage Bowel rest Surgery if uncontrolled contamination or sepsis Enterocutaneous Fistula

cards.q: What is an enterocutaneous fistula?
cards.a: Abnormal connection between bowel and skin causing intestinal drainage.

cards.q: What are major causes of enterocutaneous fistula?
cards.a: Surgery Crohn disease Malignancy Radiation Trauma

cards.q: What are the priorities in managing enterocutaneous fistula?
cards.a: Control sepsis Maintain nutrition Protect skin Allow spontaneous closure if possible

cards.q: Which factors decrease spontaneous fistula closure?
cards.a: Foreign body Radiation Infection Distal obstruction Malignancy Seroma and Hematoma

cards.q: What is a seroma?
cards.a: Collection of clear serous fluid after surgery.

cards.q: Where are seromas commonly seen?
cards.a: After procedures involving large tissue dissection. Examples: Mastectomy Hernia repair

cards.q: What is a postoperative hematoma?
cards.a: Collection of blood within the surgical site.

cards.q: What is the main concern with expanding postoperative hematoma?
cards.a: Compression of nearby structures and infection risk. Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)

cards.q: Why are postoperative patients at increased risk for DVT?
cards.a: Surgery causes: Immobility Inflammation Hypercoagulability (Virchow triad)

cards.q: What is Virchow triad?
cards.a: Venous stasis Endothelial injury Hypercoagulability

cards.q: What is the most common location of postoperative DVT?
cards.a: Deep veins of the lower extremities. DVT Prophylaxis

cards.q: What methods reduce postoperative DVT risk?
cards.a: Early ambulation Mechanical compression devices Pharmacologic prophylaxis

cards.q: Which medication is commonly used for surgical DVT prophylaxis?
cards.a: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH).

cards.q: When should pharmacologic DVT prophylaxis be avoided?
cards.a: Active bleeding or very high bleeding risk. Pulmonary Embolism

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of postoperative pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and hypoxemia.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for postoperative complications?
cards.a: Recognize complications by timing and clinical pattern. Wound dehiscence occurs around days 5–8 and presents with serosanguineous drainage. Evisceration requires immediate protection of exposed organs and surgical evaluation. Anastomotic leaks cause fever, tachycardia, and sepsis in the first postoperative week. Prevent DVT using early ambulation and appropriate prophylaxis, while treating suspected PE promptly with anticoagulation when safe.

cards.q: Why is nutritional support important in surgical patients?
cards.a: Adequate nutrition improves wound healing, immune function, and recovery.

cards.q: What is the preferred route of nutritional support when the gastrointestinal tract is functional?
cards.a: Enteral nutrition.

cards.q: Why is enteral nutrition preferred over parenteral nutrition?
cards.a: Maintains gut mucosal integrity Reduces bacterial translocation Fewer infectious complications More physiologic

cards.q: When is parenteral nutrition indicated?
cards.a: When the GI tract cannot be used. Examples: Bowel obstruction Severe ileus Short bowel syndrome Severe malabsorption

cards.q: What is total parenteral nutrition (TPN)?
cards.a: Intravenous administration of complete nutritional requirements.

cards.q: What components are included in TPN?
cards.a: Dextrose Amino acids Lipids Electrolytes Vitamins Trace elements

cards.q: What is the major complication of TPN?
cards.a: Catheter-related bloodstream infection.

cards.q: What metabolic complication can occur after starting nutrition in severely malnourished patients?
cards.a: Refeeding syndrome. Refeeding Syndrome

cards.q: What is refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: A metabolic disturbance occurring after rapid nutritional replacement in severely malnourished patients.

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormality is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Hypophosphatemia.

cards.q: Why does phosphate decrease during refeeding?
cards.a: Insulin stimulation drives phosphate into cells for ATP production.

cards.q: What other abnormalities occur in refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Hypokalemia Hypomagnesemia Fluid retention Cardiac arrhythmias

cards.q: Who is at risk for refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Prolonged starvation Alcohol use disorder Eating disorders Severe malnutrition Enteral Feeding

cards.q: What are common methods of enteral feeding?
cards.a: Nasogastric tube Nasojejunal tube Gastrostomy tube Jejunostomy tube

cards.q: When is jejunal feeding preferred over gastric feeding?
cards.a: When gastric emptying is impaired or aspiration risk is high.

cards.q: What is the most common complication of feeding tubes?
cards.a: Aspiration. Surgical Fluid Management

cards.q: What are the major body fluid compartments?
cards.a: Intracellular fluid (ICF) Extracellular fluid (ECF)

cards.q: What percentage of body weight is total body water in adults?
cards.a: Approximately 60%. TBW≈0.6×body weight (kg)

cards.q: What is the most abundant extracellular cation?
cards.a: Sodium (Na⁺).

cards.q: What is the most abundant intracellular cation?
cards.a: Potassium (K⁺). IV Fluids

cards.q: What are the main types of IV fluids?
cards.a: Crystalloids Colloids Blood products

cards.q: What is the most commonly used initial resuscitation fluid?
cards.a: Isotonic crystalloid.

cards.q: Examples of isotonic crystalloids?
cards.a: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) Lactated Ringer solution

cards.q: What is the composition of normal saline?
cards.a: 0.9% NaCl Approximately: Na⁺ = 154 mEq/L Cl⁻ = 154 mEq/L

cards.q: What is lactated Ringer solution?
cards.a: Balanced crystalloid containing: Sodium Chloride Potassium Calcium Lactate buffer

cards.q: In which situation is lactated Ringer preferred?
cards.a: Many trauma and surgical resuscitation settings. Maintenance Fluid Calculation

cards.q: What is the 4-2-1 rule for maintenance fluids?
cards.a: First 10 kg: 4 mL/kg/hr Next 10 kg: 2 mL/kg/hr Each kg above 20 kg: 1 mL/kg/hr

cards.q: Calculate maintenance fluid rate for a 70 kg adult.
cards.a: First 10 kg: 10×4=40 Next 10 kg: 10×2=20 Remaining 50 kg: 50×1=50 Total: 40+20+50=110 mL/hr Electrolyte Disorders

cards.q: What is the normal serum sodium range?
What causes postoperative hyponatremia?
cards.a: Excess free water SIADH Hypotonic fluids Stress response

cards.q: What are symptoms of severe hyponatremia?
cards.a: Confusion Seizures Coma

cards.q: What is the safe correction rate for chronic hyponatremia?
cards.a: Usually no more than: 8−10 mEq/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination. Hypernatremia

cards.q: What causes hypernatremia?
cards.a: Water loss exceeding sodium loss.

cards.q: What are symptoms of hypernatremia?
cards.a: Thirst Confusion Neurologic dysfunction Potassium Disorders

cards.q: What is the normal potassium range?
What ECG changes occur in hyperkalemia?
cards.a: Tall peaked T waves Widened QRS Arrhythmias

cards.q: What is the immediate treatment for life-threatening hyperkalemia?
cards.a: IV calcium gluconate to stabilize cardiac membranes.

cards.q: How does insulin treat hyperkalemia?
cards.a: Insulin drives potassium into cells. Acid–Base Disorders in Surgery

cards.q: What is the normal arterial blood pH?
What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship?
What acid-base disorder occurs with prolonged vomiting?
cards.a: Metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: Why does vomiting cause metabolic alkalosis?
cards.a: Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl).

cards.q: What acid-base disorder occurs with severe diarrhea?
cards.a: Metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: Why does diarrhea cause metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: Loss of bicarbonate from the GI tract. Surgical Drains and Tubes

cards.q: Why are surgical drains placed?
cards.a: Remove fluid collections Prevent abscess formation Monitor postoperative leaks

cards.q: What is a Jackson-Pratt (JP) drain?
cards.a: Closed suction drain used to remove postoperative fluid.

cards.q: What does increasing drain output after surgery suggest?
cards.a: Possible bleeding or anastomotic leak depending on fluid characteristics. Surgical Antibiotics

cards.q: What is the purpose of prophylactic antibiotics before surgery?
cards.a: Reduce surgical site infections.

cards.q: When should surgical prophylactic antibiotics usually be administered?
cards.a: Within 60 minutes before incision.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for general surgery basics?
cards.a: Use enteral nutrition whenever possible, recognize TPN complications, correct fluid and electrolyte abnormalities carefully, understand acid-base disturbances from surgical conditions, give prophylactic antibiotics before incision, and always connect postoperative findings with the most likely complication based on timing and physiology.

cards.q: What are the major components of whole blood?
cards.a: Red blood cells (RBCs) Plasma Platelets White blood cells

cards.q: What is the main purpose of packed red blood cells (PRBCs)?
cards.a: Increase oxygen-carrying capacity.

cards.q: What is the main indication for PRBC transfusion?
cards.a: Significant anemia or acute blood loss causing inadequate oxygen delivery.

cards.q: What is the approximate hemoglobin threshold for transfusion in stable hospitalized patients?
cards.a: Generally: Hb<7 g/dL (Threshold may be higher in active cardiac ischemia or specific clinical situations.)

cards.q: What is the main purpose of fresh frozen plasma (FFP)?
cards.a: Replace clotting factors.

cards.q: What are indications for FFP transfusion?
cards.a: Active bleeding with coagulation factor deficiency Massive transfusion Warfarin reversal when urgent

cards.q: What is the main purpose of platelet transfusion?
cards.a: Treat thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction causing bleeding risk.

cards.q: At what platelet count is prophylactic platelet transfusion commonly considered before procedures?
cards.a: Often when: Platelets<50,000/μL for invasive procedures.

cards.q: What is cryoprecipitate?
cards.a: Blood product rich in: Fibrinogen Factor VIII Factor XIII von Willebrand factor

cards.q: When is cryoprecipitate used?
cards.a: Low fibrinogen states, such as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Blood Types & Compatibility

cards.q: What determines ABO blood type?
cards.a: Presence or absence of A and B antigens on RBCs.

cards.q: What blood type is the universal RBC donor?
cards.a: O negative.

cards.q: What blood type is the universal RBC recipient?
cards.a: AB positive.

cards.q: What blood type is the universal plasma donor?
cards.a: AB plasma.

cards.q: Why is O-negative blood used in emergencies?
cards.a: It lacks A, B, and Rh antigens, minimizing hemolytic reactions. Blood Transfusion Reactions

cards.q: What is the most severe immediate transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.

cards.q: What causes acute hemolytic transfusion reactions?
cards.a: ABO incompatibility causing antibody-mediated RBC destruction.

cards.q: What are symptoms of acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Fever Chills Flank pain Hypotension Hemoglobinuria DIC

cards.q: What is the first step if an acute hemolytic reaction is suspected?
cards.a: Stop transfusion immediately.

cards.q: What is the treatment after stopping a suspected hemolytic transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Maintain IV access with normal saline Evaluate blood compatibility Support renal function

cards.q: What causes febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reactions?
cards.a: Recipient antibodies reacting against donor leukocytes/cytokines.

cards.q: How do febrile nonhemolytic reactions present?
cards.a: Fever and chills without hemolysis.

cards.q: What causes allergic transfusion reactions?
cards.a: Recipient reaction to donor plasma proteins.

cards.q: How are mild allergic transfusion reactions treated?
cards.a: Antihistamines and supportive care.

cards.q: What is transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)?
cards.a: Acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema after transfusion.

cards.q: What are findings of TRALI?
cards.a: Hypoxemia Respiratory distress Bilateral infiltrates No evidence of heart failure

cards.q: How is TRALI treated?
cards.a: Supportive respiratory care.

cards.q: What is transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)?
cards.a: Pulmonary edema caused by excessive transfusion volume.

cards.q: How does TACO differ from TRALI?
cards.a: TACO: Volume overload Elevated BNP Hypertension Responds to diuretics TRALI: Inflammatory lung injury Normal cardiac function Coagulation Principles

cards.q: What are the three components of normal hemostasis?
cards.a: Platelet plug formation Coagulation cascade Fibrinolysis regulation

cards.q: What is primary hemostasis?
cards.a: Platelet adhesion and aggregation.

cards.q: What is secondary hemostasis?
cards.a: Activation of coagulation factors producing fibrin stabilization.

cards.q: Which laboratory test evaluates the intrinsic pathway?
cards.a: Partial thromboplastin time (PTT).

cards.q: Which laboratory test evaluates the extrinsic pathway?
cards.a: Prothrombin time (PT/INR).

cards.q: Which anticoagulant is monitored by PTT?
cards.a: Unfractionated heparin.

cards.q: Which anticoagulant is monitored by INR?
cards.a: Warfarin. Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)

cards.q: What is DIC?
cards.a: Systemic activation of coagulation causing widespread clot formation and consumption of clotting factors.

cards.q: What conditions trigger DIC?
cards.a: Sepsis Trauma Obstetric complications Malignancy Massive tissue injury

cards.q: What are laboratory findings in DIC?
cards.a: ↑ PT ↑ PTT ↓ Platelets ↓ Fibrinogen ↑ D-dimer

cards.q: Why does DIC cause both thrombosis and bleeding?
cards.a: Clot formation consumes platelets and coagulation factors.

cards.q: What is the treatment of DIC?
cards.a: Treat underlying cause first; replace blood products if significant bleeding occurs. Surgical Hemostasis

cards.q: What are methods of achieving surgical hemostasis?
cards.a: Pressure Electrocautery Suturing Hemostatic agents Clips

cards.q: What is electrocautery used for?
cards.a: Cutting tissue and controlling bleeding using electrical energy.

cards.q: What is the difference between monopolar and bipolar cautery?
cards.a: Monopolar: Current travels through patient **Bipolar: Current passes between instrument tips Sutures

cards.q: What are absorbable sutures?
cards.a: Sutures degraded by the body over time. Examples: Vicryl Chromic gut

cards.q: What are nonabsorbable sutures?
cards.a: Sutures that remain unless removed. Examples: Nylon Prolene Silk

cards.q: What factors determine suture selection?
cards.a: Tissue type Required strength Healing speed Infection risk Sterilization & Infection Control

cards.q: What is the standard method for sterilizing surgical instruments?
cards.a: Autoclaving with pressurized steam.

cards.q: What is the purpose of sterile technique in surgery?
cards.a: Prevent introduction of microorganisms into sterile tissues.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for transfusion and surgical principles?
cards.a: Know which blood product replaces which deficiency, recognize life-threatening transfusion reactions immediately, understand PT/PTT interpretation, recognize DIC as consumption of platelets and clotting factors, and remember that prevention of infection depends on strict sterile technique and appropriate perioperative practices.

cards.q: What is a hernia?
cards.a: Protrusion of an organ or tissue through an abnormal opening or weakness in the containing wall.

cards.q: What are the main components of a hernia?
cards.a: Hernia sac Hernia contents Hernia defect (neck)

cards.q: What are the most common types of abdominal wall hernias?
cards.a: Inguinal hernia Femoral hernia Umbilical hernia Incisional hernia Inguinal Hernia

cards.q: What is the most common type of abdominal wall hernia?
cards.a: Inguinal hernia.

cards.q: Where does an indirect inguinal hernia pass?
cards.a: Through the internal inguinal ring and travels within the spermatic cord.

cards.q: What causes indirect inguinal hernias?
cards.a: Persistence of the processus vaginalis.

cards.q: In indirect inguinal hernia, where is the defect located relative to the inferior epigastric vessels?
cards.a: Lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

cards.q: Who commonly develops indirect inguinal hernias?
cards.a: Young males, especially due to congenital persistence of processus vaginalis.

cards.q: What is a direct inguinal hernia?
cards.a: Herniation through weakness in the posterior inguinal wall.

cards.q: Where does a direct inguinal hernia occur relative to inferior epigastric vessels?
cards.a: Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

cards.q: What anatomical area contains direct inguinal hernias?
cards.a: Hesselbach triangle.

cards.q: What are the borders of Hesselbach triangle?
cards.a: Lateral border: Inferior epigastric vessels Medial border: Rectus abdominis muscle Inferior border: Inguinal ligament

cards.q: Which inguinal hernia type is more likely to occur in older men?
cards.a: Direct inguinal hernia. Direct vs Indirect Inguinal Hernia

cards.q: Which inguinal hernia is more likely to descend into the scrotum?
cards.a: Indirect inguinal hernia.

cards.q: Which inguinal hernia has a higher risk of incarceration?
cards.a: Indirect inguinal hernia.

cards.q: What is the key USMLE distinction between direct and indirect inguinal hernias?
cards.a: Indirect: Lateral to inferior epigastric vessels Through internal ring Congenital Direct: Medial to inferior epigastric vessels Through Hesselbach triangle Acquired weakness Femoral Hernia

cards.q: Where does a femoral hernia protrude?
cards.a: Through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament.

cards.q: Who is most commonly affected by femoral hernias?
cards.a: Older women.

cards.q: Why are femoral hernias clinically important?
cards.a: They have a high risk of incarceration and strangulation.

cards.q: How does a femoral hernia appear clinically?
cards.a: Mass below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Hernia Complications

cards.q: What is an incarcerated hernia?
cards.a: Hernia contents cannot be reduced back into the abdominal cavity.

cards.q: What is a strangulated hernia?
cards.a: Hernia with compromised blood supply causing ischemia.

cards.q: What findings suggest strangulated hernia?
cards.a: Severe pain Fever Tachycardia Leukocytosis Skin changes Peritonitis

cards.q: What is the treatment for strangulated hernia?
cards.a: Emergency surgical repair. Hernia Diagnosis & Management

cards.q: What is the diagnosis of most abdominal wall hernias based on?
cards.a: Clinical examination.

cards.q: What imaging is used if diagnosis is uncertain?
cards.a: Ultrasound or CT scan.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for symptomatic inguinal hernia?
cards.a: Surgical repair.

cards.q: What is commonly used in modern hernia repair?
cards.a: Mesh reinforcement.

cards.q: Why is mesh used in hernia repair?
cards.a: Reduces recurrence by strengthening weakened tissue. Umbilical Hernia

cards.q: What causes adult umbilical hernias?
cards.a: Increased intra-abdominal pressure.

cards.q: What conditions increase risk of umbilical hernia?
cards.a: Obesity Pregnancy Ascites Tumors causing increased pressure

cards.q: What is the management of small asymptomatic umbilical hernias?
cards.a: Observation may be appropriate. Incisional Hernia

cards.q: What is an incisional hernia?
cards.a: Herniation through a previous surgical incision.

cards.q: What are risk factors for incisional hernia?
cards.a: Wound infection Obesity Smoking Poor nutrition Steroid use

cards.q: How is an incisional hernia treated?
cards.a: Surgical repair, often with mesh. Abdominal Wall Mass Evaluation

cards.q: What features suggest a malignant soft tissue mass?
cards.a: Size >5 cm Deep location Rapid growth Pain Fixation to surrounding tissues

cards.q: What is the first step when evaluating a suspicious soft tissue mass?
cards.a: Imaging followed by biopsy when indicated.

cards.q: What imaging modality is commonly used for soft tissue masses?
cards.a: MRI.

cards.q: Why should biopsy planning be performed carefully for suspected sarcoma?
cards.a: The biopsy tract may need to be removed during definitive surgery. Biopsy Principles

cards.q: What are the major types of biopsy?
cards.a: Fine needle aspiration (FNA) Core needle biopsy Incisional biopsy Excisional biopsy

cards.q: What is fine needle aspiration (FNA)?
cards.a: Removal of cells using a thin needle.

cards.q: What is the limitation of FNA?
cards.a: Provides cells but not tissue architecture.

cards.q: What is a core needle biopsy?
cards.a: Removal of a cylindrical tissue sample preserving architecture.

cards.q: When is excisional biopsy preferred?
cards.a: Small, easily removable lesions where complete removal is reasonable.

cards.q: When is incisional biopsy preferred?
cards.a: Large lesions where complete removal would be inappropriate initially. Surgical Oncology Principles

cards.q: What are the main goals of cancer surgery?
cards.a: Remove primary tumor Achieve negative margins Stage disease when necessary

cards.q: What is a surgical margin?
cards.a: The rim of normal tissue removed around a tumor.

cards.q: What is a negative surgical margin?
cards.a: No tumor cells at the edge of the removed specimen.

cards.q: What is lymph node dissection used for?
cards.a: Diagnosis of spread and regional disease control.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for general surgery anatomy?
cards.a: Know the anatomical differences between hernias. Indirect inguinal hernias pass through the internal ring and are lateral to inferior epigastric vessels; direct hernias occur through Hesselbach triangle and are medial. Femoral hernias occur below the inguinal ligament and have high strangulation risk. Surgical oncology requires proper biopsy planning, negative margins, and appropriate staging.

cards.q: What is the most common symptom of breast cancer?
cards.a: A painless breast mass.

cards.q: What breast findings are concerning for malignancy?
cards.a: Hard irregular mass Fixed lesion Nipple retraction Skin dimpling Bloody nipple discharge Enlarged axillary lymph nodes

cards.q: What is the most common benign breast mass in young women?
cards.a: Fibroadenoma.

cards.q: What is the typical presentation of fibroadenoma?
cards.a: Young woman Mobile Firm Well-circumscribed Painless mass

cards.q: What is the classic description of a fibroadenoma?
cards.a: "Breast mouse" — a freely mobile breast mass. Breast Imaging

cards.q: What is the primary screening test for breast cancer?
cards.a: Mammography.

cards.q: What is the purpose of mammography?
cards.a: Detect early breast cancer, especially microcalcifications.

cards.q: What mammographic finding is suspicious for malignancy?
cards.a: Spiculated mass Clustered pleomorphic calcifications Architectural distortion

cards.q: What is the role of breast ultrasound?
cards.a: Differentiate cystic vs solid lesions Evaluate masses in younger patients Guide biopsy

cards.q: In which patients is ultrasound often preferred as initial breast imaging?
cards.a: Younger women with dense breast tissue. Breast Biopsy

cards.q: What is the definitive diagnosis of a suspicious breast lesion?
cards.a: Tissue biopsy.

cards.q: What is the preferred biopsy method for most suspicious breast masses?
cards.a: Core needle biopsy.

cards.q: Why is core needle biopsy preferred over FNA for breast masses?
cards.a: Provides tissue architecture and allows tumor classification.

cards.q: What is fine needle aspiration (FNA) useful for?
cards.a: Aspiration of simple cysts and cytologic evaluation. Breast Cancer Types

cards.q: What is the most common type of invasive breast cancer?
cards.a: Invasive ductal carcinoma.

cards.q: What is ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)?
cards.a: Malignant cells confined within breast ducts without basement membrane invasion.

cards.q: What mammographic finding is classic for DCIS?
cards.a: Microcalcifications.

cards.q: What is the significance of estrogen receptor (ER) positivity?
cards.a: Tumor growth is stimulated by estrogen; hormonal therapy may be effective.

cards.q: What medication is commonly used for ER-positive breast cancer?
cards.a: Tamoxifen (especially in premenopausal women).

cards.q: What is HER2-positive breast cancer?
cards.a: Breast cancer with overexpression of HER2 receptors.

cards.q: What targeted therapy is used for HER2-positive breast cancer?
cards.a: Trastuzumab. Breast Cancer Surgery

cards.q: What are the major surgical options for breast cancer?
cards.a: Breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) Mastectomy

cards.q: What is breast-conserving surgery?
cards.a: Removal of tumor with surrounding normal tissue while preserving the breast.

cards.q: What therapy usually follows lumpectomy?
cards.a: Radiation therapy.

cards.q: When is mastectomy preferred?
cards.a: Large tumor relative to breast size Multifocal disease Patient preference Contraindication to radiation Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy

cards.q: What is a sentinel lymph node?
cards.a: The first lymph node receiving drainage from the tumor area.

cards.q: Why is sentinel lymph node biopsy performed?
cards.a: To determine whether cancer has spread to lymph nodes.

cards.q: When is sentinel lymph node biopsy indicated?
cards.a: Clinically node-negative invasive breast cancer.

cards.q: What is avoided when sentinel nodes are negative?
cards.a: Complete axillary lymph node dissection. Breast Surgical Complications

cards.q: What is a common complication of axillary lymph node dissection?
cards.a: Lymphedema.

cards.q: Why does axillary dissection cause lymphedema?
cards.a: Disruption of lymphatic drainage.

cards.q: What nerve injury can occur during axillary surgery?
cards.a: Long thoracic nerve injury.

cards.q: What occurs with long thoracic nerve injury?
cards.a: Winged scapula due to serratus anterior paralysis. Thyroid Nodules

cards.q: What is the initial evaluation of a thyroid nodule?
cards.a: Measure serum TSH.

cards.q: Why is TSH measured first in thyroid nodules?
cards.a: Determines whether the nodule is functioning.

cards.q: What does a low TSH suggest?
cards.a: Hyperfunctioning ("hot") thyroid nodule.

cards.q: What is the next step after finding a low TSH?
cards.a: Radionuclide thyroid scan.

cards.q: Are hot thyroid nodules usually malignant?
cards.a: No, they are rarely malignant.

cards.q: What does a normal or elevated TSH suggest?
cards.a: Nonfunctioning ("cold") nodule requiring further evaluation. Thyroid Cancer Evaluation

cards.q: What is the most common thyroid cancer?
cards.a: Papillary thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the classic histologic finding of papillary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Orphan Annie eye nuclei and psammoma bodies.

cards.q: What is the major route of spread of papillary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Lymphatic spread.

cards.q: What thyroid cancer spreads hematogenously?
cards.a: Follicular thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the association of medullary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: MEN 2 syndrome and RET mutation.

cards.q: What tumor marker is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Calcitonin. Thyroid Surgery

cards.q: What are indications for thyroidectomy?
cards.a: Thyroid cancer Large compressive goiter Suspicious nodules Symptomatic hyperthyroidism not controlled otherwise

cards.q: What nerve injury is a major complication of thyroid surgery?
cards.a: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

cards.q: What happens with recurrent laryngeal nerve injury?
cards.a: Hoarseness due to vocal cord paralysis.

cards.q: What endocrine complication may occur after thyroidectomy?
cards.a: Hypocalcemia due to accidental parathyroid removal/damage.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for breast and thyroid surgery?
cards.a: Evaluate breast masses systematically with imaging followed by biopsy when suspicious. Core needle biopsy is preferred for diagnosis. Breast cancer surgery depends on stage and patient factors. Thyroid nodules are evaluated first with TSH; low TSH suggests a hot benign nodule, while normal/high TSH requires ultrasound and possible biopsy. Know surgical complications such as lymphedema, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, and hypocalcemia.

cards.q: What is the primary function of the parathyroid glands?
cards.a: Regulation of serum calcium through secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH).

cards.q: What is the effect of PTH on serum calcium?
cards.a: Increases serum calcium.

cards.q: How does PTH increase calcium levels?
cards.a: Increases bone resorption Increases renal calcium reabsorption Activates vitamin D Increases intestinal calcium absorption

cards.q: What is the relationship between PTH and phosphate?
cards.a: PTH decreases serum phosphate by increasing renal phosphate excretion. Hyperparathyroidism

cards.q: What is primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Excess PTH secretion due to abnormal parathyroid gland activity.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Parathyroid adenoma.

cards.q: What are other causes of primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Parathyroid hyperplasia Parathyroid carcinoma

cards.q: What are classic laboratory findings in primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: ↑ Calcium ↑ PTH ↓ Phosphate

cards.q: What are clinical manifestations of hypercalcemia?
cards.a: "Stones, bones, groans, psychiatric overtones" Kidney stones Bone pain Constipation Depression/confusion

cards.q: What is the common renal complication of hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Nephrolithiasis.

cards.q: What skeletal finding occurs in severe hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Osteitis fibrosa cystica. Secondary Hyperparathyroidism

cards.q: What is secondary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Increased PTH secretion due to chronic hypocalcemia.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Chronic kidney disease.

cards.q: What are laboratory findings in secondary hyperparathyroidism due to CKD?
cards.a: ↑ PTH ↓ Calcium ↑ Phosphate Hyperparathyroidism Surgical Management

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Parathyroidectomy.
