cards.q: What are indications for surgery in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Significant hypercalcemia Kidney stones Reduced bone density Young age Reduced kidney function

cards.q: What imaging is used to localize abnormal parathyroid glands before surgery?
cards.a: Sestamibi scan Neck ultrasound

cards.q: What is a major complication of parathyroidectomy?
cards.a: Hypocalcemia.

cards.q: Why can hypocalcemia occur after parathyroidectomy?
cards.a: Remaining bones rapidly absorb calcium ("hungry bone syndrome"). Adrenal Anatomy & Surgery

cards.q: What hormones are produced by the adrenal cortex?
cards.a: Cortisol Aldosterone Androgens

cards.q: What hormone is produced by the adrenal medulla?
cards.a: Catecholamines. Adrenal Incidentaloma

cards.q: What is an adrenal incidentaloma?
cards.a: Unexpected adrenal mass found on imaging performed for another reason.

cards.q: What are the two major questions when evaluating an adrenal mass?
cards.a: Is it hormonally active? Is it malignant?

cards.q: What hormone excess should be evaluated in adrenal masses?
cards.a: Cortisol Aldosterone (if hypertensive/hypokalemic) Catecholamines Pheochromocytoma

cards.q: What is pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Catecholamine-producing tumor of chromaffin cells.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Episodic headache Sweating Palpitations Hypertension

cards.q: What biochemical test is used to diagnose pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Plasma free metanephrines or urinary fractionated metanephrines.

cards.q: What syndrome is associated with pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: MEN 2 Von Hippel-Lindau disease Neurofibromatosis type 1

cards.q: What is the first medication given before surgery for pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Alpha blockade.

cards.q: Why must α blockade occur before β blockade in pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Prevents unopposed α stimulation causing severe hypertension.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Surgical adrenalectomy. Adrenal Cortical Tumors

cards.q: What syndrome results from excess cortisol production?
cards.a: Cushing syndrome.

cards.q: What are clinical features of Cushing syndrome?
cards.a: Central obesity Moon facies Purple striae Hypertension Diabetes Muscle weakness

cards.q: What syndrome results from excess aldosterone?
cards.a: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome).

cards.q: What are findings of hyperaldosteronism?
cards.a: Hypertension Hypokalemia Metabolic alkalosis

cards.q: What screening test is used for primary hyperaldosteronism?
cards.a: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Adrenal Surgery Principles

cards.q: What are indications for adrenalectomy?
cards.a: Functional tumors Suspicious malignancy Large adrenal masses

cards.q: What is the major concern before removing a cortisol-producing adrenal tumor?
cards.a: Risk of adrenal insufficiency after surgery. Skin Cancer Surgery

cards.q: What is the most common skin cancer?
cards.a: Basal cell carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the major risk factor for basal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Chronic UV exposure.

cards.q: What is the classic appearance of basal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Pearly papule with rolled borders and possible ulceration.

cards.q: Does basal cell carcinoma commonly metastasize?
cards.a: No, metastasis is rare.

cards.q: What is the treatment for basal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Surgical excision Mohs micrographic surgery in high-risk locations Squamous Cell Carcinoma

cards.q: What is a major risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of skin?
cards.a: UV exposure.

cards.q: What is the appearance of squamous cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Scaly, erythematous, ulcerated lesion.

cards.q: Compared with basal cell carcinoma, what is the metastatic risk of SCC?
cards.a: Higher. Melanoma

cards.q: What are the ABCDE criteria for melanoma?
cards.a: A – Asymmetry B – Border irregularity C – Color variation D – Diameter >6 mm E – Evolution/change

cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor in melanoma?
cards.a: Breslow depth (tumor thickness).

cards.q: What is the surgical treatment for melanoma?
cards.a: Wide local excision with margins based on tumor depth.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for endocrine and skin surgery?
cards.a: Primary hyperparathyroidism presents with high calcium and high PTH and is treated definitively with parathyroidectomy when indicated. Pheochromocytoma requires α blockade before surgery. Adrenal masses must be assessed for hormone secretion and malignancy risk. Skin cancers are managed according to type: basal cell carcinoma is locally destructive but rarely metastatic, while melanoma prognosis depends mainly on Breslow depth.

cards.q: What are the two major types of vascular disease?
cards.a: Arterial disease Venous disease

cards.q: What is the primary problem in arterial disease?
cards.a: Reduced blood flow causing tissue ischemia.

cards.q: What is the primary problem in venous disease?
cards.a: Impaired venous return causing blood pooling and edema.

cards.q: What are the major risk factors for peripheral arterial disease (PAD)?
cards.a: Smoking Diabetes mellitus Hypertension Hyperlipidemia Advanced age Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)

cards.q: What is peripheral arterial disease?
cards.a: Atherosclerotic narrowing of peripheral arteries causing reduced limb perfusion.

cards.q: What is the classic symptom of PAD?
cards.a: Intermittent claudication.

cards.q: What is intermittent claudication?
cards.a: Exercise-induced leg pain relieved by rest.

cards.q: Why does PAD cause pain during exercise?
cards.a: Muscle oxygen demand exceeds arterial supply.

cards.q: Where does claudication pain occur in aortoiliac disease?
cards.a: Buttocks, hips, and thighs.

cards.q: Where does claudication pain occur in femoropopliteal disease?
cards.a: Calf. Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)

cards.q: What is the ankle-brachial index (ABI)?
cards.a: Ratio comparing ankle systolic pressure to brachial systolic pressure. ABI= Brachial systolic pressure Ankle systolic pressure ​

cards.q: What ABI value indicates normal arterial flow?
What ABI value indicates peripheral arterial disease?
What ABI value indicates severe ischemia?
In which patients may ABI be falsely elevated?
cards.a: Patients with calcified arteries. Examples: Diabetes Chronic kidney disease PAD Physical Findings

cards.q: What physical findings suggest PAD?
cards.a: Diminished pulses Cool extremity Hair loss Shiny skin Delayed capillary refill

cards.q: What type of ulcers are associated with arterial insufficiency?
cards.a: Painful ulcers on distal toes or pressure points.

cards.q: Why are arterial ulcers painful?
cards.a: Poor tissue perfusion causes ischemic pain. PAD Management

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for intermittent claudication?
cards.a: Smoking cessation Exercise therapy Risk factor modification

cards.q: What medication improves cardiovascular outcomes in PAD?
cards.a: Antiplatelet therapy. Examples: Aspirin Clopidogrel

cards.q: Why are statins used in PAD?
cards.a: Reduce cardiovascular events by lowering atherosclerotic risk.

cards.q: What medication improves walking distance in PAD?
cards.a: Cilostazol.

cards.q: When is revascularization considered in PAD?
cards.a: Lifestyle-limiting symptoms despite medical therapy or critical limb ischemia. Critical Limb Ischemia

cards.q: What is critical limb ischemia?
cards.a: Severe arterial insufficiency causing rest pain, tissue loss, or gangrene.

cards.q: What is the classic symptom of critical limb ischemia?
cards.a: Rest pain, especially at night.

cards.q: Why does elevating the leg worsen ischemic pain?
cards.a: Reduces arterial perfusion pressure.

cards.q: Why do patients with severe PAD often hang their legs over the bed?
cards.a: Gravity improves blood flow. Acute Limb Ischemia

cards.q: What is acute limb ischemia?
cards.a: Sudden loss of arterial blood flow threatening limb viability.

cards.q: What are the "6 Ps" of acute limb ischemia?
cards.a: Pain Pallor Pulselessness Paresthesia Paralysis Poikilothermia

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acute limb ischemia?
cards.a: Embolism from cardiac sources (especially atrial fibrillation).

cards.q: What is the immediate treatment for acute limb ischemia?
cards.a: IV unfractionated heparin.

cards.q: Why is heparin given immediately in acute limb ischemia?
cards.a: Prevents propagation of thrombus while planning revascularization.

cards.q: What imaging evaluates arterial occlusion?
cards.a: CT angiography. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)

cards.q: What is an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
cards.a: Abnormal dilation of the abdominal aorta.

cards.q: What is the major risk factor for AAA?
cards.a: Smoking.

cards.q: Who should undergo AAA screening?
cards.a: Older men with a history of smoking.

cards.q: What imaging is used for AAA screening?
cards.a: Abdominal ultrasound.

cards.q: What is the most common location of AAA?
cards.a: Below the renal arteries (infrarenal aorta).

cards.q: What is the major complication of AAA?
cards.a: Rupture.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of ruptured AAA?
cards.a: Sudden abdominal/back pain Hypotension Pulsatile abdominal mass

cards.q: What is the immediate management of suspected ruptured AAA?
cards.a: Emergency surgical or endovascular repair. Carotid Artery Disease

cards.q: What is the main clinical concern in carotid artery stenosis?
cards.a: Ischemic stroke.

cards.q: What is the most common symptom of symptomatic carotid stenosis?
cards.a: Transient ischemic attack (TIA).

cards.q: What is a TIA?
cards.a: Temporary neurologic dysfunction due to transient cerebral ischemia without infarction.

cards.q: What imaging is used to evaluate carotid stenosis?
cards.a: Carotid duplex ultrasound.

cards.q: What procedure reduces stroke risk in severe carotid stenosis?
cards.a: Carotid endarterectomy. Venous Disease

cards.q: What causes chronic venous insufficiency?
cards.a: Failure of venous valves causing venous hypertension.

cards.q: What are findings of chronic venous insufficiency?
cards.a: Leg edema Skin discoloration Varicose veins Venous ulcers

cards.q: Where do venous ulcers usually occur?
cards.a: Medial malleolus.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for vascular surgery?
cards.a: Differentiate arterial from venous disease. PAD causes exertional pain and ischemic ulcers; acute limb ischemia requires immediate heparin and vascular evaluation. AAA is associated strongly with smoking and rupture presents with abdominal/back pain and shock. Chronic venous disease causes edema, skin changes, and medial malleolar ulcers. ------------------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery (Make Section if not exist)

cards.q: What are the five components of the preoperative assessment?
cards.a: History, physical examination, medication review, assessment of comorbidities (especially cardiac and pulmonary), and determination of operative risk (e.g., ASA classification).

cards.q: Which cardiac condition is the strongest predictor of perioperative major adverse cardiac events?
cards.a: Active cardiac disease (unstable angina, recent MI, decompensated heart failure, severe arrhythmia, or severe valvular disease).

cards.q: Which medication should generally be continued perioperatively?
cards.a: Chronic &β;-blockers should be continued to reduce the risk of perioperative cardiac events.

cards.q: Which antihypertensive medications are commonly held on the morning of surgery?
cards.a: ACE inhibitors and ARBs, due to the risk of intraoperative hypotension.

cards.q: What is the preferred laboratory test to evaluate renal function before surgery?
cards.a: Serum creatinine (with estimated GFR) and basic metabolic panel.

cards.q: What is the ASA Physical Status Classification used for?
cards.a: To estimate perioperative risk based on the patient's overall health status.

cards.q: What does ASA Class I represent?
cards.a: A healthy patient without systemic disease.

cards.q: What does ASA Class V represent?
cards.a: A moribund patient not expected to survive without surgery.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging test before elective surgery in an otherwise healthy patient?
cards.a: None. Routine imaging is not indicated unless clinically warranted.

cards.q: Which patients require preoperative ECG?
cards.a: Patients with known cardiovascular disease, significant risk factors, or those undergoing intermediate- or high-risk surgery.

cards.q: What is the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) used for?
cards.a: To estimate the risk of major cardiac complications after noncardiac surgery.

cards.q: Name the six predictors in the RCRI.
cards.a: High-risk surgery, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, and creatinine >2.0 mg/dL.

cards.q: Which surgery is considered high cardiac risk?
cards.a: Major vascular surgery.

cards.q: What functional capacity generally indicates acceptable operative risk?
cards.a: ≥4 METs.

cards.q: Give an example of a 4-MET activity.
cards.a: Climbing one flight of stairs or walking uphill.

cards.q: Which patients should receive perioperative stress-dose corticosteroids?
cards.a: Patients on chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy with suspected adrenal suppression.

cards.q: When should smoking cessation ideally occur before surgery?
cards.a: At least 4–8 weeks before surgery.

cards.q: What is the most effective intervention to reduce postoperative pulmonary complications?
cards.a: Smoking cessation.

cards.q: Which patients benefit most from incentive spirometry?
cards.a: Patients undergoing abdominal or thoracic surgery.

cards.q: What is the most common postoperative pulmonary complication?
cards.a: Atelectasis.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of fever within the first 24 hours after surgery?
cards.a: Normal inflammatory response; atelectasis is commonly tested but is not the primary cause of early postoperative fever.

cards.q: What is the first step in evaluating postoperative fever?
cards.a: Assess timing, vital signs, surgical site, and associated symptoms.

cards.q: What are the classic "5 Ws" of postoperative fever?
cards.a: Wind, Water, Wound, Walking, Wonder drugs.

cards.q: Which postoperative day is wound infection most likely to appear?
cards.a: Postoperative days 5–7.

cards.q: Which postoperative complication usually occurs after postoperative day 7?
cards.a: Deep surgical site infection or intra-abdominal abscess.

cards.q: What organism is the most common cause of surgical site infection?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: What is the most important measure to prevent surgical site infection?
cards.a: Appropriate prophylactic antibiotics administered within 60 minutes before incision.

cards.q: When should prophylactic antibiotics generally be discontinued?
cards.a: Within 24 hours after surgery.

cards.q: Which antibiotic is most commonly used for clean surgical procedures?
cards.a: Cefazolin.

cards.q: Which prophylactic antibiotic is preferred for colorectal surgery?
cards.a: Cefazolin plus metronidazole (or another regimen covering gram-negative and anaerobic organisms).

cards.q: What defines a clean surgical wound?
cards.a: No inflammation and no entry into the respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, or biliary tract.

cards.q: What defines a clean-contaminated wound?
cards.a: Controlled entry into the respiratory, gastrointestinal, biliary, or genitourinary tract without significant contamination.

cards.q: What defines a contaminated wound?
cards.a: Major break in sterile technique, gross spillage from the GI tract, or fresh traumatic wound.

cards.q: What defines a dirty wound?
cards.a: Existing infection, perforated viscus, abscess, or old traumatic wound with devitalized tissue.

cards.q: What is primary intention wound healing?
cards.a: Direct closure of wound edges with minimal tissue loss.

cards.q: What is secondary intention wound healing?
cards.a: Healing by granulation tissue without surgical closure.

cards.q: What is tertiary intention (delayed primary closure)?
cards.a: Leaving a contaminated wound open initially and closing it after infection risk decreases.

cards.q: Which phase of wound healing begins immediately after injury?
cards.a: Hemostasis.

cards.q: Which cells dominate the inflammatory phase of wound healing after the first 24–48 hours?
cards.a: Macrophages.

cards.q: Which cells are primarily responsible for collagen production?
cards.a: Fibroblasts.

cards.q: During which phase is type III collagen replaced by type I collagen?
cards.a: Remodeling (maturation) phase.

cards.q: Which vitamin deficiency impairs collagen synthesis and wound healing?
cards.a: Vitamin C deficiency.

cards.q: Which mineral is essential for wound healing?
cards.a: Zinc.

cards.q: What is the most important nutritional factor for wound healing?
cards.a: Adequate protein intake.

cards.q: Which chronic disease most impairs wound healing?
cards.a: Diabetes mellitus.

cards.q: How does diabetes impair wound healing?
cards.a: Through impaired leukocyte function, reduced perfusion, and decreased collagen synthesis.

cards.q: Which medications delay wound healing?
cards.a: Corticosteroids and cytotoxic chemotherapy.

cards.q: What is wound dehiscence?
cards.a: Partial or complete separation of a surgical incision after closure.

cards.q: On which postoperative days does wound dehiscence most commonly occur?
cards.a: Postoperative days 5–8.

cards.q: What is the immediate management of wound dehiscence with evisceration?
cards.a: Cover exposed bowel with sterile saline-moistened dressings, begin IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics as indicated, and take the patient urgently to the operating room for surgical repair. ------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: What are the four major classes of shock?
cards.a: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, and distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of shock in trauma patients?
cards.a: Hemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What is the earliest physiologic response to hypovolemia?
cards.a: Tachycardia due to sympathetic activation.

cards.q: Which vital sign change is a late finding in hypovolemic shock?
cards.a: Hypotension.

cards.q: Which laboratory marker is most useful for assessing tissue hypoperfusion?
cards.a: Serum lactate.

cards.q: What does an elevated lactate indicate?
cards.a: Tissue hypoxia with anaerobic metabolism.

cards.q: What is the initial fluid of choice for hypovolemic shock?
cards.a: Isotonic crystalloid (Lactated Ringer's or Normal Saline).

cards.q: Which crystalloid is generally preferred in trauma resuscitation?
cards.a: Lactated Ringer's solution.

cards.q: When should blood products be started instead of continued crystalloid?
cards.a: Ongoing significant hemorrhage or failure to respond to initial crystalloid resuscitation.

cards.q: What blood product ratio is recommended during massive transfusion?
cards.a: Approximately 1:1:1 (packed RBCs : fresh frozen plasma : platelets).

cards.q: Define massive transfusion.
cards.a: Transfusion of ≥10 units of packed RBCs within 24 hours or replacement of one blood volume.

cards.q: What complication results from citrate toxicity during massive transfusion?
cards.a: Hypocalcemia.

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality commonly develops with stored blood transfusion?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia.

cards.q: What acid-base disturbance is common early in hemorrhagic shock?
cards.a: High anion gap metabolic acidosis due to lactic acidosis.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for hemorrhagic shock?
cards.a: Control the source of bleeding. Septic Shock

cards.q: What is the most common cause of distributive shock?
cards.a: Sepsis.

cards.q: What are the hemodynamic features of early septic shock?
cards.a: High cardiac output with low systemic vascular resistance (warm shock).

cards.q: What is the first step in managing septic shock?
cards.a: Rapid administration of IV crystalloids and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

cards.q: How much crystalloid should initially be given in septic shock?
cards.a: Approximately 30 mL/kg.

cards.q: Which vasopressor is first-line if hypotension persists after fluids?
cards.a: Norepinephrine.

cards.q: What is the target mean arterial pressure (MAP) in septic shock?
cards.a: ≥65 mmHg.

cards.q: Besides antibiotics, what is the most important treatment principle in sepsis?
cards.a: Source control (e.g., drain abscess, remove infected catheter). Cardiogenic Shock

cards.q: What is the most common cause of cardiogenic shock?
cards.a: Acute myocardial infarction.

cards.q: How do pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) and cardiac output change in cardiogenic shock?
cards.a: Increased PCWP with decreased cardiac output.

cards.q: Why should large-volume fluid boluses generally be avoided in cardiogenic shock?
cards.a: They worsen pulmonary edema. Obstructive Shock

cards.q: Name three common causes of obstructive shock.
cards.a: Cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, and massive pulmonary embolism.

cards.q: What are Beck's triad findings in cardiac tamponade?
cards.a: Hypotension, jugular venous distention, and muffled heart sounds.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for cardiac tamponade?
cards.a: Pericardiocentesis.

cards.q: What is the immediate treatment for tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube placement.

cards.q: Which side should undergo needle decompression for a tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: The affected side. Fluids & Electrolytes

cards.q: Which IV fluid most closely resembles plasma electrolyte composition?
cards.a: Lactated Ringer's solution.

cards.q: Which IV fluid can worsen hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: Normal saline.

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality most commonly develops after prolonged nasogastric suction?
cards.a: Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality commonly occurs after prolonged vomiting?
cards.a: Hypokalemia.

cards.q: Why does hypokalemia often persist despite potassium replacement?
cards.a: Coexisting hypomagnesemia impairs potassium repletion.

cards.q: Which electrolyte should be corrected before potassium if both are low?
cards.a: Magnesium.

cards.q: Which ECG change is classically seen in hyperkalemia?
cards.a: Peaked T waves.

cards.q: What is the first medication given for life-threatening hyperkalemia with ECG changes?
cards.a: IV calcium gluconate (or calcium chloride in selected settings) to stabilize the cardiac membrane.

cards.q: Which medications shift potassium into cells?
cards.a: Insulin with dextrose, β₂-agonists (e.g., albuterol), and sodium bicarbonate (if severe metabolic acidosis).

cards.q: Which therapy removes potassium from the body most rapidly in severe or refractory hyperkalemia?
cards.a: Hemodialysis. Acid–Base Disorders

cards.q: What acid-base disorder is most commonly seen in septic shock?
cards.a: High anion gap metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: What acid-base disorder results from prolonged vomiting?
cards.a: Metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: What acid-base disorder is associated with severe diarrhea?
cards.a: Non-anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: Which formula estimates expected respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: Winter's formula: Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5(HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2.

cards.q: How is the anion gap calculated?
cards.a: AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). Blood Transfusion

cards.q: What is the usual hemoglobin threshold for transfusion in stable hospitalized adults?
cards.a: <7 g/dL, unless there are special clinical indications (e.g., active ischemia, ongoing hemorrhage).

cards.q: Which blood product is used to reverse warfarin-associated life-threatening bleeding?
cards.a: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) plus IV vitamin K.

cards.q: Which blood product is indicated for isolated fibrinogen deficiency?
cards.a: Cryoprecipitate.

cards.q: What is the most common acute complication of blood transfusion?
cards.a: Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction.

cards.q: What is the most dangerous acute transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction due to ABO incompatibility. Immediate management includes stopping the transfusion, maintaining IV access with normal saline, providing supportive care, and notifying the blood bank.

cards.q: What are the priorities of the ATLS primary survey?
cards.a: A-B-C-D-E: Airway with cervical spine protection, Breathing, Circulation with hemorrhage control, Disability (neurologic assessment), Exposure with prevention of hypothermia.

cards.q: What is the first priority in trauma management?
cards.a: Secure the airway while maintaining cervical spine immobilization.

cards.q: What does the "A" in the ATLS primary survey include?
cards.a: Airway assessment, cervical spine stabilization, suctioning, airway adjuncts, and definitive airway if indicated.

cards.q: Which trauma patients require cervical spine immobilization?
cards.a: Any patient with significant blunt trauma, altered mental status, neurologic deficits, neck pain/tenderness, or distracting injuries until the cervical spine is cleared.

cards.q: What finding suggests a patent airway?
cards.a: The patient can speak clearly in full sentences.

cards.q: What are indications for immediate endotracheal intubation in trauma?
cards.a: Airway obstruction, inability to protect the airway (GCS ≤8), respiratory failure, severe facial trauma, or impending airway compromise.

cards.q: What is the preferred airway technique in trauma patients with suspected cervical spine injury?
cards.a: Rapid sequence intubation with manual in-line cervical stabilization.

cards.q: When is a surgical airway indicated?
cards.a: Failed intubation with inability to oxygenate or severe upper airway obstruction preventing oral or nasal intubation.

cards.q: What is the preferred emergency surgical airway in adults?
cards.a: Cricothyrotomy.

cards.q: What is the most common preventable cause of death in trauma?
cards.a: Airway obstruction. Breathing

cards.q: What is assessed during the "B" portion of the primary survey?
cards.a: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, chest wall movement, breath sounds, tracheal position, and signs of thoracic injury.

cards.q: What are the six immediately life-threatening chest injuries identified during the primary survey?
cards.a: Airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, and cardiac tamponade.

cards.q: What clinical findings suggest tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Severe respiratory distress, hypotension, unilateral absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, tracheal deviation (late), and jugular venous distention.

cards.q: Should a chest x-ray be obtained before treating a suspected tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: No. Treat immediately based on clinical diagnosis.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Tube thoracostomy after immediate needle or finger decompression.

cards.q: What is an open pneumothorax?
cards.a: A chest wall defect that allows free communication between the pleural space and the atmosphere ("sucking chest wound").

cards.q: How should an open pneumothorax initially be managed?
cards.a: Apply a three-sided occlusive dressing and place a chest tube away from the wound.

cards.q: What defines a massive hemothorax?
cards.a: >1,500 mL of blood immediately after chest tube placement or continued drainage >200 mL/hour for 2–4 hours.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for massive hemothorax?
cards.a: Large-bore chest tube, aggressive resuscitation, and urgent thoracic surgical consultation.

cards.q: What injury causes paradoxical chest wall movement?
cards.a: Flail chest.

cards.q: What is the most common associated injury with flail chest?
cards.a: Pulmonary contusion.

cards.q: What is the primary treatment for pulmonary contusion?
cards.a: Supportive care with adequate oxygenation, pain control, and cautious fluid administration. Circulation

cards.q: What is the leading preventable cause of death after trauma?
cards.a: Uncontrolled hemorrhage.

cards.q: What is the first intervention for severe external bleeding?
cards.a: Direct pressure.

cards.q: When should a tourniquet be used?
cards.a: Life-threatening extremity hemorrhage not controlled with direct pressure.

cards.q: Which IV access is recommended in unstable trauma patients?
cards.a: Two large-bore peripheral IV lines (14–16 gauge) or intraosseous access if IV access cannot be rapidly obtained.

cards.q: Which crystalloid is preferred during initial trauma resuscitation?
cards.a: Lactated Ringer's solution.

cards.q: When should blood products replace crystalloid during trauma resuscitation?
cards.a: Persistent hypotension or suspected major hemorrhage.

cards.q: What blood pressure strategy is recommended in uncontrolled hemorrhage without traumatic brain injury?
cards.a: Permissive hypotension (target SBP ≈80–90 mmHg) until bleeding is controlled.

cards.q: Why is permissive hypotension avoided in traumatic brain injury?
cards.a: Because adequate cerebral perfusion pressure must be maintained. Disability

cards.q: What does the "D" in the primary survey assess?
cards.a: Neurologic status using GCS, pupil examination, and limb movement.

cards.q: What are the components of the Glasgow Coma Scale?
cards.a: Eye opening, verbal response, and motor response.

cards.q: What GCS score indicates severe traumatic brain injury?
What pupil finding suggests uncal herniation?
cards.a: Unilateral fixed, dilated pupil. Exposure

cards.q: Why is complete exposure necessary in trauma patients?
cards.a: To identify occult injuries while preventing missed diagnoses.

cards.q: What important complication must be prevented after exposing the patient?
cards.a: Hypothermia. FAST Examination

cards.q: What does FAST stand for?
cards.a: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the FAST examination?
cards.a: Rapid detection of free intraperitoneal or pericardial fluid.

cards.q: Which four areas are evaluated during a FAST examination?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant (Morison pouch), left upper quadrant, pelvis, and pericardium.

cards.q: In an unstable trauma patient with a positive FAST examination, what is the next step?
cards.a: Immediate exploratory laparotomy.

cards.q: What is the next step if the FAST examination is negative but the patient remains hemodynamically unstable?
cards.a: Continue evaluation for other bleeding sources (thorax, pelvis, retroperitoneum, long bones) and repeat FAST or proceed with further indicated interventions. Secondary Survey

cards.q: When is the secondary survey performed?
cards.a: After completion of the primary survey and stabilization of life-threatening conditions.

cards.q: What is included in the secondary survey?
cards.a: Complete head-to-toe examination, detailed history (AMPLE), and selective imaging/laboratory studies.

cards.q: What does the AMPLE history include?
cards.a: Allergies, Medications, Past medical history/Pregnancy, Last meal, Events surrounding injury. Imaging

cards.q: Which imaging study is preferred for hemodynamically stable blunt abdominal trauma?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis.

cards.q: Which imaging study is preferred for unstable blunt abdominal trauma?
cards.a: FAST examination.

cards.q: Is diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) commonly used today?
cards.a: No. It has largely been replaced by FAST but may be useful when FAST is unavailable or equivocal. Trauma Decision-Making

cards.q: Which factor is more important than CT findings when deciding trauma management?
cards.a: Hemodynamic stability.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for hemorrhagic shock in trauma?
cards.a: Surgical or procedural control of bleeding.

cards.q: What is the single most important principle in trauma care?
cards.a: Treat immediately life-threatening injuries as they are identified—do not delay life-saving interventions for diagnostic testing. Blunt Abdominal Trauma

cards.q: What is the most commonly injured intra-abdominal organ in blunt abdominal trauma?
cards.a: Spleen.

cards.q: What is the second most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma?
cards.a: Liver.

cards.q: What is the most commonly injured abdominal organ in penetrating trauma?
cards.a: Small intestine.

cards.q: What is the most commonly injured solid organ in penetrating abdominal trauma?
cards.a: Liver.

cards.q: Which patients with blunt abdominal trauma require immediate laparotomy?
cards.a: Hemodynamically unstable patients with evidence of intra-abdominal bleeding (e.g., positive FAST) or signs of peritonitis.

cards.q: What physical finding strongly suggests hollow viscus perforation?
cards.a: Diffuse peritonitis with rebound tenderness and guarding.

cards.q: Which imaging modality is preferred for stable blunt abdominal trauma?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis.

cards.q: What does free intraperitoneal air on imaging indicate?
cards.a: Perforated hollow viscus until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for bowel perforation?
cards.a: Exploratory laparotomy with repair or resection of the injured bowel.

cards.q: What antibiotic coverage is required for bowel perforation?
cards.a: Broad-spectrum antibiotics covering gram-negative organisms and anaerobes. Splenic Trauma

cards.q: Which organ is most frequently managed nonoperatively after blunt injury?
cards.a: Spleen.

cards.q: Which patients with splenic injury are candidates for nonoperative management?
cards.a: Hemodynamically stable patients without diffuse peritonitis.

cards.q: When is splenectomy indicated?
cards.a: Hemodynamic instability, ongoing hemorrhage, or failure of nonoperative management.

cards.q: What is Kehr's sign?
cards.a: Left shoulder pain caused by diaphragmatic irritation from splenic bleeding.

cards.q: Which vaccines should be administered after splenectomy?
cards.a: Pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccines.

cards.q: Why are asplenic patients at increased risk for overwhelming infection?
cards.a: Loss of splenic function impairs clearance of encapsulated bacteria. Liver Trauma

cards.q: What is the most commonly injured solid organ overall?
cards.a: Liver.

cards.q: How are most liver injuries managed?
cards.a: Nonoperatively if the patient is hemodynamically stable.

cards.q: What maneuver temporarily controls hepatic bleeding during surgery?
cards.a: Pringle maneuver (temporary occlusion of the portal triad).

cards.q: What structures are compressed during the Pringle maneuver?
cards.a: Hepatic artery, portal vein, and common bile duct. Renal Trauma

cards.q: What is the most common sign of renal trauma?
cards.a: Hematuria.

cards.q: Which imaging study evaluates suspected renal injury in stable patients?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT scan with delayed urographic images.

cards.q: Which renal injuries usually require surgery?
cards.a: Hemodynamically unstable patients or those with major vascular injury. Bladder Trauma

cards.q: Which pelvic injury is commonly associated with bladder rupture?
cards.a: Pelvic fracture.

cards.q: What is the gold standard test for suspected bladder rupture?
cards.a: Retrograde cystography (CT cystography is commonly used).

cards.q: Which type of bladder rupture usually requires surgical repair?
cards.a: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture.

cards.q: How is uncomplicated extraperitoneal bladder rupture usually managed?
cards.a: Foley catheter drainage. Urethral Trauma

cards.q: What findings suggest urethral injury?
cards.a: Blood at the urethral meatus, inability to void, perineal hematoma, or a high-riding prostate (historically described).

cards.q: What study should be obtained before Foley catheter placement if urethral injury is suspected?
cards.a: Retrograde urethrogram.

cards.q: What should be avoided in suspected urethral injury until evaluation is complete?
cards.a: Blind urethral catheterization. Pelvic Trauma

cards.q: Why are pelvic fractures potentially life-threatening?
cards.a: They can cause massive venous and arterial hemorrhage.

cards.q: What is the first stabilization maneuver for an unstable pelvic fracture?
cards.a: Apply a pelvic binder.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for ongoing pelvic hemorrhage despite resuscitation?
cards.a: Angioembolization and/or preperitoneal pelvic packing, depending on the clinical scenario and available resources.

cards.q: Which pelvic fracture pattern has the highest risk of major hemorrhage?
cards.a: Open-book (anteroposterior compression) pelvic fracture. Thoracic Trauma

cards.q: What is the most common cause of hemothorax?
cards.a: Blunt or penetrating chest trauma causing injury to the lung or intercostal vessels.

cards.q: What is the initial management of most hemothoraces?
cards.a: Tube thoracostomy.

cards.q: Which injury causes persistent large air leak after chest tube placement?
cards.a: Major tracheobronchial injury.

cards.q: What symptom is classic for esophageal rupture after trauma?
cards.a: Severe chest pain with subcutaneous emphysema and systemic toxicity.

cards.q: What imaging study best confirms suspected traumatic esophageal perforation?
cards.a: Water-soluble contrast esophagography (often followed by CT if needed). Cardiac Trauma

cards.q: What is the most common blunt cardiac injury?
cards.a: Myocardial contusion.

cards.q: Which tests are used to evaluate suspected blunt cardiac injury?
cards.a: ECG and cardiac troponin; echocardiography if clinically indicated.

cards.q: What is the most common ECG finding in myocardial contusion?
cards.a: Sinus tachycardia or nonspecific ST-T wave abnormalities. Damage Control Surgery

cards.q: What is the goal of damage-control surgery?
cards.a: Rapid control of hemorrhage and contamination, followed by physiologic stabilization before definitive repair.

cards.q: Which "lethal triad" indicates the need for damage-control surgery?
cards.a: Hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy.

cards.q: Why is hypothermia dangerous in trauma patients?
cards.a: It worsens coagulopathy and increases mortality. Trauma Pearls

cards.q: What is the most important determinant of trauma management?
cards.a: Hemodynamic stability.

cards.q: Which trauma patients require immediate surgery without CT imaging?
cards.a: Hemodynamically unstable patients with evidence of surgically correctable hemorrhage or diffuse peritonitis.

cards.q: What is the leading cause of preventable trauma death after hospital arrival?
cards.a: Uncontrolled hemorrhage.

cards.q: What is the cornerstone of successful trauma resuscitation?
cards.a: Early hemorrhage control, balanced blood product resuscitation, and correction of coagulopathy.

cards.q: What is the single highest-yield ATLS principle for the USMLE Step 2 CK?
cards.a: Always prioritize life-threatening injuries using the ABCDE approach. Hemodynamic instability takes precedence over diagnostic imaging, and definitive hemorrhage control is the key to survival. ------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: How are burns classified?
cards.a: By depth: superficial (first-degree), superficial partial-thickness, deep partial-thickness, and full-thickness (third-degree). Fourth-degree burns extend into muscle, tendon, or bone.

cards.q: Which skin layers are involved in a superficial (first-degree) burn?
cards.a: Epidermis only.

cards.q: What are the clinical features of a superficial burn?
cards.a: Erythema, pain, dry skin, no blisters, and blanching.

cards.q: What is the classic example of a superficial burn?
cards.a: Sunburn.

cards.q: Which skin layers are involved in a superficial partial-thickness burn?
cards.a: Epidermis and superficial dermis.

cards.q: What are the clinical features of a superficial partial-thickness burn?
cards.a: Blisters, moist appearance, severe pain, and brisk capillary refill.

cards.q: Which skin layers are involved in a deep partial-thickness burn?
cards.a: Epidermis and deep dermis.

cards.q: What are the clinical features of a deep partial-thickness burn?
cards.a: Pale or mottled appearance, decreased sensation, delayed capillary refill, and reduced spontaneous healing.

cards.q: Which skin layers are involved in a full-thickness burn?
cards.a: Entire epidermis and dermis are destroyed.

cards.q: What are the clinical features of a full-thickness burn?
cards.a: White, brown, or charred skin; leathery texture; absent sensation within the burn; and absent capillary refill. Burn Assessment

cards.q: Which method estimates burn size in adults?
cards.a: Rule of Nines.

cards.q: According to the Rule of Nines, what percentage of TBSA does each arm represent in adults?
cards.a: 9% (4.5% anterior + 4.5% posterior).

cards.q: According to the Rule of Nines, what percentage of TBSA does each leg represent?
cards.a: 18% (9% anterior + 9% posterior).

cards.q: What percentage of TBSA does the anterior trunk represent?
What percentage of TBSA does the posterior trunk represent?
What percentage of TBSA does the head represent in adults?
What percentage of TBSA does the perineum represent?
Which burn assessment tool is more accurate in children?
cards.a: Lund–Browder chart.

cards.q: Which burns are included when calculating TBSA for fluid resuscitation?
cards.a: Partial-thickness and full-thickness burns only.

cards.q: Are first-degree burns included in TBSA calculations?
cards.a: No. Initial Burn Management

cards.q: What is the first priority in major burn management?
cards.a: Airway assessment and stabilization (ABCs).

cards.q: Which burn patients should receive high-flow oxygen immediately?
cards.a: Any patient with suspected inhalation injury or smoke exposure.

cards.q: Which findings suggest inhalation injury?
cards.a: Facial burns, singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth or sputum, hoarseness, stridor, carbonaceous sputum, or burns sustained in an enclosed space.

cards.q: When should early endotracheal intubation be strongly considered in burn patients?
cards.a: Progressive facial/airway edema, stridor, respiratory distress, or significant inhalation injury.

cards.q: Why is early intubation preferred in severe inhalation injury?
cards.a: Airway edema can rapidly progress, making later intubation difficult or impossible. Fluid Resuscitation

cards.q: Which formula is used for initial fluid resuscitation in major burns?
cards.a: Parkland formula.

cards.q: What is the Parkland formula?
cards.a: 4 mL × body weight (kg) × %TBSA burned using Lactated Ringer's solution.

cards.q: Over what time period is the Parkland formula applied?
cards.a: The first 24 hours after the burn.

cards.q: How should the calculated Parkland fluid be administered?
cards.a: 50% in the first 8 hours from the time of injury, and the remaining 50% over the next 16 hours.

cards.q: Which IV fluid is preferred for burn resuscitation?
cards.a: Lactated Ringer's solution.

cards.q: What is the best endpoint of adequate burn resuscitation in adults?
cards.a: Urine output of ≥0.5 mL/kg/hour.

cards.q: What is the urine output goal in children with major burns?
cards.a: Approximately 1 mL/kg/hour.

cards.q: Why should fluid administration be adjusted rather than relying solely on the Parkland calculation?
cards.a: The formula provides an initial estimate; fluids should be titrated based on clinical response, especially urine output and perfusion. Burn Center Referral

cards.q: Which adult burn patients generally require burn center referral?
cards.a: Partial-thickness burns >10% TBSA, burns involving the face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum, major joints, full-thickness burns, inhalation injury, electrical burns, chemical burns, or significant comorbidities.

cards.q: Which burn location is particularly important because of cosmetic and functional outcomes?
cards.a: Face and hands. Burn Wound Care

cards.q: What is the first step in local burn wound management?
cards.a: Cool the burn with cool (not ice) running water if done shortly after injury, then gently clean the wound.

cards.q: Why should ice not be applied directly to burns?
cards.a: It may worsen tissue injury through vasoconstriction and cold-induced damage.

cards.q: What should be done with intact burn blisters?
cards.a: Management depends on size and location; large, tense, or function-limiting blisters are often debrided, whereas small intact blisters may be left intact.

cards.q: Which topical antimicrobial is commonly used for partial-thickness burns?
cards.a: Bacitracin is commonly used for superficial partial-thickness burns; topical therapy varies by burn depth and location.

cards.q: Which topical burn agent is avoided on the face due to cosmetic concerns and delayed healing?
cards.a: Silver sulfadiazine is generally avoided on the face and is no longer preferred for many superficial burns because it may delay wound healing. Burn Complications

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death during the first 24 hours after a major burn?
cards.a: Burn shock (hypovolemic shock from plasma loss).

cards.q: What is the major cause of death after the first several days in severe burns?
cards.a: Sepsis and multiorgan dysfunction.

cards.q: Why are burn patients at high risk for infection?
cards.a: Loss of the skin barrier and burn-induced immune dysfunction.

cards.q: When are prophylactic systemic antibiotics indicated for uncomplicated burns?
cards.a: They are not routinely indicated; antibiotics are reserved for documented infection or specific indications. Escharotomy & Fasciotomy

cards.q: What is an escharotomy?
cards.a: Surgical incision through constricting burn eschar to relieve pressure and restore circulation or ventilation.

cards.q: When is escharotomy indicated?
cards.a: Circumferential full-thickness burns causing vascular compromise or impaired chest wall expansion.

cards.q: How does escharotomy differ from fasciotomy?
cards.a: Escharotomy releases the burned skin (eschar); fasciotomy releases the deep fascia to treat compartment syndrome. Electrical & Chemical Burns

cards.q: What cardiac evaluation is recommended after a significant electrical injury?
cards.a: ECG for all significant electrical injuries, with cardiac monitoring if there are ECG abnormalities, loss of consciousness, high-voltage exposure, or concerning symptoms.

cards.q: What is the major muscle complication of high-voltage electrical burns?
cards.a: Rhabdomyolysis, which can lead to acute kidney injury.

cards.q: What is the first step in managing a chemical burn?
cards.a: Remove contaminated clothing and immediately irrigate the affected area with copious amounts of water (except for a few specific chemicals that require special management). -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

topic: Surgical Infections, Soft Tissue Infections & Wound Care

cards.q: What is the mechanism of carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning?
cards.a: CO binds hemoglobin with an affinity approximately 200–250 times greater than oxygen, reducing oxygen delivery and impairing tissue oxygenation.

cards.q: Why can pulse oximetry appear normal in carbon monoxide poisoning?
cards.a: Standard pulse oximeters cannot distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin.

cards.q: What is the best diagnostic test for carbon monoxide poisoning?
cards.a: Arterial or venous blood gas with co-oximetry to measure carboxyhemoglobin.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for carbon monoxide poisoning?
cards.a: 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask.

cards.q: When should hyperbaric oxygen therapy be considered in carbon monoxide poisoning?
cards.a: Severe neurologic symptoms, myocardial ischemia, significant metabolic acidosis, pregnancy with significant exposure, or markedly elevated carboxyhemoglobin levels (clinical judgment and local protocols apply).

cards.q: Which poison is commonly associated with smoke inhalation from enclosed-space fires?
cards.a: Cyanide.

cards.q: What is the antidote for suspected cyanide poisoning?
cards.a: Hydroxocobalamin is first-line in most settings.

cards.q: What laboratory finding suggests cyanide poisoning?
cards.a: Severe lactic acidosis with markedly elevated serum lactate. Compartment Syndrome

cards.q: What is compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment causing reduced tissue perfusion and ischemia.

cards.q: What is the earliest and most sensitive symptom of compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Severe pain out of proportion to the injury, especially pain with passive stretch.

cards.q: What are the classic "6 Ps" of compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Pain, paresthesia, pallor, paralysis, pulselessness, and poikilothermia (pulselessness is a late finding).

cards.q: Which finding is usually present before pulselessness develops?
cards.a: Pain with passive stretch.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Emergent fasciotomy.

cards.q: Should treatment be delayed while awaiting imaging if compartment syndrome is strongly suspected?
cards.a: No. It is a surgical emergency. Necrotizing Soft Tissue Infection

cards.q: What is necrotizing fasciitis?
cards.a: A rapidly progressive infection of the fascia with secondary necrosis of subcutaneous tissue.

cards.q: What is the hallmark clinical feature of necrotizing fasciitis?
cards.a: Severe pain out of proportion to physical examination findings.

cards.q: What skin findings may develop as necrotizing fasciitis progresses?
cards.a: Bullae, ecchymosis, skin discoloration, crepitus, anesthesia, and tissue necrosis.

cards.q: Which imaging finding may support the diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis?
cards.a: Gas within the soft tissues (although imaging should not delay surgery).

cards.q: What is the definitive management of necrotizing fasciitis?
cards.a: Immediate surgical exploration and aggressive debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

cards.q: Which antibiotic regimen provides broad empiric coverage for necrotizing fasciitis?
cards.a: Broad-spectrum therapy (e.g., vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem) plus clindamycin to inhibit toxin production when streptococcal infection is suspected.

cards.q: Why is clindamycin useful in necrotizing fasciitis?
cards.a: It suppresses bacterial toxin production, particularly in streptococcal infections. Fournier Gangrene

cards.q: What is Fournier gangrene?
cards.a: Necrotizing fasciitis involving the perineum, genitalia, or perianal region.

cards.q: Which patients are at highest risk for Fournier gangrene?
cards.a: Patients with diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, alcoholism, obesity, or chronic kidney disease.

cards.q: What is the treatment of Fournier gangrene?
cards.a: Immediate aggressive surgical debridement, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and hemodynamic support. Cellulitis & Abscess

cards.q: What is cellulitis?
cards.a: A diffuse bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue without a localized pus collection.

cards.q: Which organisms most commonly cause cellulitis?
cards.a: Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: What is the hallmark of an abscess?
cards.a: A localized, fluctuant collection of pus.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for a simple cutaneous abscess?
cards.a: Incision and drainage (I&D).

cards.q: Are antibiotics always required after I&D of an uncomplicated abscess?
cards.a: No. Antibiotics are reserved for selected patients (e.g., extensive cellulitis, systemic illness, immunocompromise, or high-risk features).

cards.q: Which pathogen should be considered in recurrent skin abscesses?
cards.a: Community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA). Bite Wounds

cards.q: Which animal bite has the highest infection rate?
cards.a: Cat bites.

cards.q: Which organism is classically associated with dog and cat bites?
cards.a: Pasteurella multocida.

cards.q: What is the preferred prophylactic antibiotic for most dog and cat bites?
cards.a: Amoxicillin-clavulanate.

cards.q: Which human bite injury is particularly high risk for infection?
cards.a: Closed-fist ("fight bite") injuries over the metacarpophalangeal joints.

cards.q: Which organism is classically associated with human bites?
cards.a: Eikenella corrodens.

cards.q: Why should fight-bite injuries receive careful surgical evaluation?
cards.a: They may involve tendons, joints, or deep spaces of the hand and have a high risk of serious infection. Tetanus

cards.q: Which organism causes tetanus?
cards.a: Clostridium tetani.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of tetanus toxin?
cards.a: It blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA and glycine), causing muscle rigidity and spasms.

cards.q: Which wound characteristics increase tetanus risk?
cards.a: Dirty, contaminated, puncture, crush, devitalized, or necrotic wounds.

cards.q: When is tetanus immune globulin (TIG) indicated?
cards.a: In patients with high-risk wounds who are inadequately immunized or have an unknown vaccination history, in addition to tetanus vaccination when indicated. Surgical Site Infection (SSI)

cards.q: What are the cardinal signs of a surgical site infection?
cards.a: Increasing pain, erythema, warmth, swelling, purulent drainage, and fever.

cards.q: What is the first step in managing a superficial incisional SSI?
cards.a: Open the incision if needed to allow drainage, assess the wound, and provide appropriate local care; antibiotics are used when clinically indicated.

cards.q: What is the most common pathogen causing postoperative wound infections?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus. Surgical Drains

cards.q: Why are surgical drains used?
cards.a: To evacuate fluid, blood, bile, or pus and reduce fluid accumulation.

cards.q: What is the difference between an open and a closed surgical drain?
cards.a: Open drains empty onto dressings; closed drains collect fluid in a sealed system and generally have a lower infection risk.

cards.q: Name two commonly used closed suction drains.
cards.a: Jackson-Pratt (JP) drain and Hemovac drain.

cards.q: What does bilious output from a postoperative drain suggest?
cards.a: A possible bile leak or enteric injury, depending on the surgical procedure.

cards.q: What does feculent drain output suggest?
cards.a: An enteric leak or bowel injury. Wound Healing Pearls

cards.q: Which patients are at increased risk of postoperative wound infection?
cards.a: Patients with diabetes, obesity, smoking history, malnutrition, immunosuppression, prolonged operations, or contaminated wounds.

cards.q: What is the single most effective measure to reduce surgical site infections?
cards.a: Meticulous surgical technique with appropriate perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis, strict sterile practice, and good perioperative glycemic control when indicated. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: What is a hernia?
cards.a: Protrusion of an organ or tissue through a weakness or defect in the surrounding fascia or muscle.

cards.q: What is the most common abdominal wall hernia?
cards.a: Inguinal hernia.

cards.q: Which sex is more commonly affected by inguinal hernias?
cards.a: Males.

cards.q: What is the most common type of groin hernia?
cards.a: Indirect inguinal hernia.

cards.q: Which groin hernia has the highest risk of strangulation?
cards.a: Femoral hernia. Inguinal Anatomy

cards.q: What forms the deep (internal) inguinal ring?
cards.a: An opening in the transversalis fascia located lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

cards.q: What forms the superficial (external) inguinal ring?
cards.a: An opening in the external oblique aponeurosis.

cards.q: Which ligament forms the floor of the inguinal canal?
cards.a: Inguinal ligament.

cards.q: Which structure forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal?
cards.a: Transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon).

cards.q: What structures pass through the inguinal canal in males?
cards.a: Spermatic cord and the ilioinguinal nerve. Indirect Inguinal Hernia

cards.q: Where does an indirect inguinal hernia pass in relation to the inferior epigastric vessels?
cards.a: Lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

cards.q: Through which ring does an indirect inguinal hernia enter?
cards.a: Deep inguinal ring.

cards.q: What is the embryologic cause of an indirect inguinal hernia?
cards.a: Failure of the processus vaginalis to close.

cards.q: Can an indirect inguinal hernia extend into the scrotum?
cards.a: Yes.

cards.q: Which age group most commonly develops indirect inguinal hernias?
cards.a: Infants, children, and young adults, although they can occur at any age. Direct Inguinal Hernia

cards.q: Where does a direct inguinal hernia occur in relation to the inferior epigastric vessels?
cards.a: Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

cards.q: Through which anatomical area does a direct inguinal hernia protrude?
cards.a: Hesselbach triangle.

cards.q: What are the boundaries of Hesselbach triangle?
cards.a: Inferior epigastric vessels (lateral), lateral border of the rectus abdominis (medial), and inguinal ligament (inferior).

cards.q: Does a direct inguinal hernia usually pass through the deep inguinal ring?
cards.a: No.

cards.q: Does a direct inguinal hernia commonly enter the scrotum?
cards.a: No, although very large hernias occasionally may. Femoral Hernia

cards.q: Where is a femoral hernia located relative to the inguinal ligament?
cards.a: Inferior to the inguinal ligament.

cards.q: Which patients most commonly develop femoral hernias?
cards.a: Women, especially older women and those with multiple pregnancies.

cards.q: Why are femoral hernias surgically important?
cards.a: They have a high risk of incarceration and strangulation.

cards.q: What is the recommended treatment for a femoral hernia?
cards.a: Elective surgical repair, even if asymptomatic in most patients, because of the high risk of complications. Clinical Presentation

cards.q: What is the most common symptom of an uncomplicated inguinal hernia?
cards.a: Groin bulge that enlarges with standing, lifting, or coughing and decreases when supine.

cards.q: What physical examination maneuver helps identify a groin hernia?
cards.a: Ask the patient to cough or perform a Valsalva maneuver while palpating the groin.

cards.q: What is a reducible hernia?
cards.a: A hernia whose contents can be returned to the abdominal cavity manually or spontaneously.

cards.q: What is an incarcerated hernia?
cards.a: A nonreducible hernia without evidence of compromised blood supply.

cards.q: What is a strangulated hernia?
cards.a: An incarcerated hernia with compromised blood flow, resulting in ischemia.

cards.q: What symptoms suggest strangulation?
cards.a: Severe pain, erythema, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and signs of bowel obstruction or peritonitis. Hernia Complications

cards.q: What is the most dangerous complication of any hernia?
cards.a: Strangulation.

cards.q: What complication results from prolonged strangulation?
cards.a: Bowel ischemia, necrosis, perforation, and sepsis.

cards.q: What are symptoms of bowel obstruction from a hernia?
cards.a: Abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distention, and inability to pass stool or flatus.

cards.q: What is the treatment for a strangulated hernia?
cards.a: Emergency surgical exploration and repair. Diagnosis

cards.q: How is an inguinal hernia usually diagnosed?
cards.a: Clinical history and physical examination.

cards.q: Which imaging modality is preferred if the diagnosis is uncertain?
cards.a: Groin ultrasound; CT or MRI may be used in selected cases.

cards.q: Which imaging modality is most useful for occult or recurrent groin hernias?
cards.a: MRI has the highest sensitivity in difficult cases. Surgical Management

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for symptomatic inguinal hernias?
cards.a: Surgical repair.

cards.q: Which repair technique is the standard for most adult inguinal hernias?
cards.a: Tension-free mesh repair.

cards.q: When is tissue repair preferred over mesh repair?
cards.a: When mesh is contraindicated, such as in contaminated or infected surgical fields.

cards.q: What are the two major surgical approaches for inguinal hernia repair?
cards.a: Open repair and laparoscopic repair.

cards.q: Which patients particularly benefit from laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair?
cards.a: Patients with bilateral or recurrent inguinal hernias and selected patients desiring faster recovery.

cards.q: What is the major advantage of laparoscopic repair?
cards.a: Less postoperative pain and earlier return to normal activities in appropriately selected patients. Special Hernias

cards.q: What is a Richter hernia?
cards.a: Herniation of only part of the bowel wall (antimesenteric border), which may strangulate without causing complete bowel obstruction.

cards.q: Why is a Richter hernia clinically important?
cards.a: Patients may develop bowel ischemia without classic signs of intestinal obstruction.

cards.q: What is a sliding hernia?
cards.a: A hernia in which part of the hernia sac wall is formed by a retroperitoneal organ, commonly the colon or bladder.

cards.q: What is an incisional hernia?
cards.a: Herniation through a previous surgical incision due to fascial weakness or failure of healing.

cards.q: Which factors increase the risk of incisional hernia?
cards.a: Wound infection, obesity, smoking, malnutrition, diabetes, chronic cough, ascites, and poor surgical healing.

cards.q: What is an umbilical hernia?
cards.a: Herniation through the umbilical ring.

cards.q: When should an adult umbilical hernia be repaired?
cards.a: Symptomatic hernias, enlarging hernias, incarcerated or strangulated hernias, and many elective cases because spontaneous closure is uncommon in adults. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: What is the most common cause of dysphagia in adults?
cards.a: Mechanical obstruction (e.g., peptic stricture, esophageal cancer) or a motility disorder (e.g., achalasia); the differential depends on whether dysphagia is for solids only or solids and liquids.

cards.q: What pattern of dysphagia suggests a mechanical obstruction?
cards.a: Progressive dysphagia for solids first, later progressing to liquids.

cards.q: What pattern of dysphagia suggests a motility disorder?
cards.a: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the onset.

cards.q: What is the initial diagnostic test for esophageal dysphagia with alarm features (e.g., weight loss, anemia, progressive symptoms)?
cards.a: Upper endoscopy (EGD).

cards.q: What is the gold standard diagnostic test for achalasia?
cards.a: Esophageal manometry.

cards.q: What are the classic manometric findings in achalasia?
cards.a: Incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and absent normal esophageal peristalsis.

cards.q: What is the classic barium swallow finding in achalasia?
cards.a: Bird's-beak appearance.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for achalasia in a good surgical candidate?
cards.a: Laparoscopic Heller myotomy (often combined with a partial fundoplication) or peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM), depending on patient factors and expertise.

cards.q: Which temporary treatment may be used in poor surgical candidates with achalasia?
cards.a: Botulinum toxin injection into the LES or pneumatic dilation in selected patients.

cards.q: What malignancy is associated with long-standing achalasia?
cards.a: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)

cards.q: What is the most common cause of GERD?
cards.a: Incompetent lower esophageal sphincter.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for uncomplicated GERD?
cards.a: Lifestyle modification and proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy.

cards.q: Which patients with GERD should undergo upper endoscopy?
cards.a: Patients with alarm symptoms (dysphagia, GI bleeding, anemia, weight loss, recurrent vomiting) or persistent symptoms despite appropriate therapy.

cards.q: What is Barrett esophagus?
cards.a: Replacement of normal squamous epithelium by specialized intestinal-type columnar epithelium due to chronic GERD.

cards.q: Why is Barrett esophagus clinically important?
cards.a: It increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Which type of esophageal cancer is associated with Barrett esophagus?
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Which operation is the classic surgical treatment for refractory GERD?
cards.a: Nissen fundoplication. Hiatal Hernias

cards.q: What are the two major types of hiatal hernia?
cards.a: Sliding hiatal hernia and paraesophageal (rolling) hiatal hernia.

cards.q: Which type of hiatal hernia is most common?
cards.a: Sliding hiatal hernia.

cards.q: Which hiatal hernia is most strongly associated with GERD?
cards.a: Sliding hiatal hernia.

cards.q: Which hiatal hernia has the greatest risk of volvulus and strangulation?
cards.a: Paraesophageal (rolling) hiatal hernia.

cards.q: What is the treatment for symptomatic paraesophageal hernia?
cards.a: Surgical repair. Esophageal Perforation

cards.q: What is Boerhaave syndrome?
cards.a: Spontaneous transmural esophageal rupture, usually after forceful vomiting.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Boerhaave syndrome?
cards.a: Severe chest pain after vomiting, subcutaneous emphysema, and systemic toxicity (Mackler triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema).

cards.q: What is the preferred initial imaging study for suspected esophageal perforation?
cards.a: Water-soluble contrast esophagram (often followed by CT if needed).

cards.q: What is the treatment for esophageal perforation?
cards.a: Urgent broad-spectrum antibiotics, NPO status, IV fluids, and prompt surgical or endoscopic management depending on the location, size, timing, and patient stability. Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)

cards.q: What are the two most common causes of peptic ulcer disease?
cards.a: Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID use.

cards.q: Which organism causes most duodenal ulcers?
cards.a: Helicobacter pylori.

cards.q: What is the preferred diagnostic test for H. pylori in patients without alarm features?
cards.a: Urea breath test or stool antigen test (off PPIs for an appropriate interval before testing).

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for H. pylori infection?
cards.a: Guideline-recommended eradication therapy (commonly bismuth quadruple therapy in areas with high macrolide resistance, with confirmation of eradication after treatment). Perforated Peptic Ulcer

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a perforated peptic ulcer?
cards.a: Sudden severe epigastric pain with a rigid, board-like abdomen and signs of peritonitis.

cards.q: Which imaging finding suggests perforated peptic ulcer?
cards.a: Free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum).

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for perforated peptic ulcer?
cards.a: Urgent surgical repair (often with an omental/Graham patch), IV fluids, antibiotics, acid suppression, and treatment of H. pylori if present. Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding

cards.q: What is the most common cause of upper GI bleeding?
cards.a: Peptic ulcer disease.

cards.q: What is the first step in managing acute upper GI bleeding?
cards.a: Assess airway if needed, stabilize with IV access and fluid/blood resuscitation, then perform risk assessment.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic and therapeutic procedure of choice for upper GI bleeding?
cards.a: Upper endoscopy (EGD).

cards.q: Which endoscopic therapies are commonly used for bleeding peptic ulcers?
cards.a: Combination therapy such as epinephrine injection plus thermal coagulation and/or endoscopic clips.

cards.q: When is surgery considered for peptic ulcer bleeding?
cards.a: Persistent or recurrent bleeding despite appropriate endoscopic and interventional radiology therapy, or when those options are unavailable or unsuitable. Gastric Outlet Obstruction

cards.q: What are common causes of gastric outlet obstruction?
cards.a: Chronic peptic ulcer disease (less common today) and malignancy (e.g., gastric or pancreatic cancer).

cards.q: What are the classic symptoms of gastric outlet obstruction?
cards.a: Early satiety, postprandial vomiting of undigested food, abdominal distention, and weight loss.

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormality is classically associated with prolonged gastric outlet obstruction?
cards.a: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: What is the initial management of gastric outlet obstruction?
cards.a: NPO, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, electrolyte correction, and evaluation of the underlying cause. Gastric Cancer

cards.q: What is the most common histologic type of gastric cancer?
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Which bacterium is an important risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: Helicobacter pylori.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial diagnostic test for suspected gastric cancer?
cards.a: Upper endoscopy with biopsy.

cards.q: Which imaging modality is commonly used for staging gastric cancer?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis (often with endoscopic ultrasound for local staging when appropriate). Bariatric Surgery

cards.q: Which bariatric procedure is considered the most commonly performed worldwide?
cards.a: Sleeve gastrectomy.

cards.q: Which bariatric procedure provides substantial weight loss and metabolic benefit but carries a risk of nutritional deficiencies?
cards.a: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass.

cards.q: What is a common long-term nutritional deficiency after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass?
cards.a: Iron deficiency, vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, folate deficiency, calcium deficiency, and vitamin D deficiency.

cards.q: What is the most important principle in managing upper gastrointestinal surgical disease on the USMLE Step 2 CK?
cards.a: Stabilize the patient first, recognize surgical emergencies (perforation, obstruction, ischemia, uncontrolled bleeding), and choose the next best diagnostic or therapeutic step based on hemodynamic stability. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: What is the most common cause of small bowel obstruction (SBO) in developed countries?
cards.a: Postoperative intra-abdominal adhesions.

cards.q: What are the next most common causes of SBO after adhesions?
cards.a: Hernias and malignancy.

cards.q: What are the classic symptoms of SBO?
cards.a: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distention, and obstipation (failure to pass stool or flatus).

cards.q: What are the classic physical examination findings in early SBO?
cards.a: Abdominal distention, high-pitched or "tinkling" bowel sounds, and diffuse tenderness.

cards.q: What bowel sound finding is more typical of late SBO with bowel ischemia or perforation?
cards.a: Hypoactive or absent bowel sounds.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial imaging study for suspected SBO?
cards.a: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (when not contraindicated).

cards.q: What are classic imaging findings of SBO on CT?
cards.a: Dilated proximal small bowel, collapsed distal bowel, and a transition point.

cards.q: What small bowel diameter suggests obstruction?
cards.a: Greater than 3 cm.

cards.q: What is the initial management of uncomplicated SBO?
cards.a: NPO, IV fluids, electrolyte correction, and nasogastric tube decompression if significant vomiting or distention is present.

cards.q: Which patients with SBO require urgent surgery?
cards.a: Patients with bowel ischemia, perforation, peritonitis, strangulation, closed-loop obstruction, or failure of nonoperative management.

cards.q: Which CT findings suggest bowel ischemia?
cards.a: Reduced bowel wall enhancement, pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, mesenteric edema, or free intraperitoneal air (with perforation).

cards.q: What laboratory finding raises concern for bowel ischemia?
cards.a: Elevated serum lactate. Ileus

cards.q: What is ileus?
cards.a: Functional paralysis of the intestine without a mechanical obstruction.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of postoperative ileus?
cards.a: Recent abdominal surgery.

cards.q: Which medications commonly contribute to ileus?
cards.a: Opioids and anticholinergic medications.

cards.q: How does ileus differ from SBO on imaging?
cards.a: Ileus shows diffuse dilation of both the small bowel and colon without a discrete transition point.

cards.q: What is the treatment of postoperative ileus?
cards.a: Supportive care with early ambulation, minimizing opioids, correcting electrolyte abnormalities, IV fluids, and NG decompression if needed. Volvulus

cards.q: What is volvulus?
cards.a: Twisting of the bowel around its mesentery, causing obstruction and possible ischemia.

cards.q: Which is the most common site of volvulus in adults?
cards.a: Sigmoid colon.

cards.q: Which patients are at highest risk for sigmoid volvulus?
cards.a: Elderly, institutionalized patients and those with chronic constipation or neuropsychiatric disease.

cards.q: What is the classic abdominal x-ray finding in sigmoid volvulus?
cards.a: Coffee-bean sign.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus?
cards.a: Endoscopic detorsion (flexible sigmoidoscopy) with rectal tube placement.

cards.q: When is surgery indicated for sigmoid volvulus?
cards.a: Peritonitis, bowel ischemia, perforation, or failed endoscopic decompression.

cards.q: Which volvulus commonly affects younger patients?
cards.a: Cecal volvulus.

cards.q: What is the treatment of cecal volvulus?
cards.a: Surgical resection or fixation; endoscopic decompression is generally ineffective. Intussusception

cards.q: What is intussusception?
cards.a: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of pediatric intussusception?
cards.a: Intermittent colicky abdominal pain, currant jelly stools, and a palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of intussusception in children?
cards.a: Idiopathic, often associated with hypertrophied Peyer patches after a viral illness.

cards.q: What is the preferred diagnostic study in children with suspected intussusception?
cards.a: Abdominal ultrasound showing the "target" or "doughnut" sign.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial treatment for stable pediatric intussusception?
cards.a: Air (or contrast) enema reduction.

cards.q: When is surgery indicated for intussusception?
cards.a: Perforation, peritonitis, shock, failed enema reduction, or suspicion of a pathologic lead point. Meckel Diverticulum

cards.q: What is Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: A true congenital diverticulum resulting from persistence of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct.

cards.q: What is the "Rule of 2s" for Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: Occurs in ~2% of the population, ~2 inches long, within ~2 feet of the ileocecal valve, often presents before age 2, and may contain two types of ectopic tissue (gastric and pancreatic).

cards.q: What is the most common presentation of Meckel diverticulum in children?
cards.a: Painless lower GI bleeding.

cards.q: Which nuclear medicine study diagnoses Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan (Meckel scan).

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for symptomatic Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: Surgical resection. Acute Appendicitis

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acute appendicitis?
cards.a: Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen (commonly by a fecalith or lymphoid hyperplasia).

cards.q: What is the classic progression of pain in appendicitis?
cards.a: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant.

cards.q: Why does appendicitis initially cause periumbilical pain?
cards.a: Visceral afferent pain from the midgut is referred to the T10 dermatome.

cards.q: What causes the pain to localize to the right lower quadrant?
cards.a: Inflammation of the parietal peritoneum.

cards.q: What is McBurney point?
cards.a: A point located approximately one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, corresponding to the typical location of maximal tenderness.

cards.q: What is Rovsing sign?
cards.a: Right lower quadrant pain elicited by palpation of the left lower quadrant.

cards.q: What is the psoas sign?
cards.a: Right lower quadrant pain with passive extension of the right hip, suggesting irritation of the psoas muscle.

cards.q: What is the obturator sign?
cards.a: Right lower quadrant pain with internal rotation of the flexed right hip, suggesting a pelvic appendix.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for suspected appendicitis in nonpregnant adults?
cards.a: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial imaging study for children and pregnant patients with suspected appendicitis?
cards.a: Ultrasound (MRI if ultrasound is nondiagnostic in pregnancy).

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for uncomplicated appendicitis?
cards.a: Laparoscopic appendectomy is standard; selected uncomplicated cases may be managed initially with antibiotics in carefully chosen patients.

cards.q: What antibiotics should be administered before appendectomy?
cards.a: Broad-spectrum antibiotics covering gram-negative organisms and anaerobes.

cards.q: What complication should be suspected if fever persists several days after appendectomy?
cards.a: Intra-abdominal abscess.

cards.q: What is the single highest-yield USMLE principle for appendicitis?
cards.a: Migratory periumbilical-to-right lower quadrant pain with localized tenderness strongly suggests appendicitis; prompt diagnosis and treatment reduce the risk of perforation.

cards.q: What is diverticulosis?
cards.a: The presence of acquired mucosal and submucosal outpouchings (false diverticula) through the colonic muscular wall, most commonly in the sigmoid colon.

cards.q: What is the most common risk factor for diverticulosis?
cards.a: Increasing age.

cards.q: What is the most common presentation of diverticulosis?
cards.a: Asymptomatic; it is often discovered incidentally during colonoscopy or imaging.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of significant lower gastrointestinal bleeding in adults?
cards.a: Diverticular bleeding.

cards.q: How does diverticular bleeding typically present?
cards.a: Sudden, painless hematochezia.

cards.q: What is diverticulitis?
cards.a: Inflammation and microperforation of a colonic diverticulum.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute diverticulitis?
cards.a: Left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and leukocytosis.

cards.q: Which patients are more likely to have right-sided diverticulitis?
cards.a: Patients of Asian ancestry, although left-sided disease remains most common overall.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for suspected diverticulitis?
cards.a: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast.

cards.q: What CT findings suggest acute diverticulitis?
cards.a: Colonic wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, and inflamed diverticula; abscess or perforation may also be seen in complicated disease.

cards.q: Should colonoscopy be performed during acute diverticulitis?
cards.a: No. It is avoided during the acute episode because of perforation risk and is typically performed after recovery if indicated.

cards.q: How is uncomplicated diverticulitis treated?
cards.a: Selected patients may be managed as outpatients with supportive care; antibiotics are used selectively based on severity, comorbidities, and current guidelines.
