cards.q: Which patients with diverticulitis require hospitalization?
cards.a: Patients with sepsis, peritonitis, inability to tolerate oral intake, significant comorbidities, immunosuppression, or complicated disease.

cards.q: What is the treatment for diverticular abscess >3 cm?
cards.a: Percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics when feasible.

cards.q: What is the treatment for perforated diverticulitis with generalized peritonitis?
cards.a: Emergency surgical intervention. Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding

cards.q: What is the first priority in acute lower GI bleeding?
cards.a: Assess hemodynamic stability and begin resuscitation with IV access, fluids, and blood products as needed.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial diagnostic test for hemodynamically stable patients with significant lower GI bleeding?
cards.a: Colonoscopy after appropriate bowel preparation.

cards.q: What is the preferred evaluation for ongoing brisk lower GI bleeding in an unstable patient?
cards.a: CT angiography is commonly the initial imaging study if the patient can undergo scanning; catheter angiography allows diagnosis and embolization when appropriate.

cards.q: What intervention can be performed during catheter angiography for active GI bleeding?
cards.a: Transcatheter arterial embolization.

cards.q: Which upper GI condition can present with hematochezia?
cards.a: Massive upper GI bleeding. Colorectal Cancer

cards.q: What is the most common histologic type of colorectal cancer?
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: What are the most important risk factors for colorectal cancer?
cards.a: Increasing age, adenomatous polyps, hereditary syndromes (e.g., Lynch syndrome, FAP), inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, smoking, and diets high in processed/red meat.

cards.q: What symptoms suggest left-sided colon cancer?
cards.a: Change in bowel habits, pencil-thin stools, constipation, and obstructive symptoms.

cards.q: What symptoms suggest right-sided colon cancer?
cards.a: Occult bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, fatigue, and weight loss.

cards.q: Which laboratory abnormality commonly occurs with right-sided colon cancer?
cards.a: Iron deficiency anemia.

cards.q: What is the preferred diagnostic test for suspected colorectal cancer?
cards.a: Colonoscopy with biopsy.

cards.q: Which imaging study is used for staging colorectal cancer?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.

cards.q: Which tumor marker is commonly used for postoperative surveillance rather than screening?
cards.a: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA).

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for localized colon cancer?
cards.a: Surgical resection with regional lymph node evaluation.

cards.q: Which syndrome should be suspected in a young patient with colorectal cancer and endometrial cancer in the family?
cards.a: Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer). Mesenteric Ischemia

cards.q: What is acute mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Sudden interruption of intestinal blood flow causing bowel ischemia.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings.

cards.q: Which patients are at highest risk for embolic mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Patients with atrial fibrillation or other cardiac embolic sources.

cards.q: Which laboratory abnormality commonly develops in mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Elevated serum lactate due to tissue hypoperfusion.

cards.q: What is the preferred diagnostic test in a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected acute mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: CT angiography.

cards.q: What is the initial management of acute mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Aggressive IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, bowel rest, anticoagulation when appropriate (e.g., arterial thrombosis or embolism without contraindication), and urgent vascular/surgical consultation.

cards.q: Which patients require emergency laparotomy for mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Patients with peritonitis, bowel perforation, bowel necrosis, or clinical deterioration. Colonic Emergencies

cards.q: What is toxic megacolon?
cards.a: Acute, severe colonic dilation with systemic toxicity, usually complicating inflammatory bowel disease or infectious colitis (especially Clostridioides difficile).

cards.q: Which imaging finding is characteristic of toxic megacolon?
cards.a: Marked colonic dilation (commonly transverse colon >6 cm) on abdominal imaging.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment of toxic megacolon?
cards.a: Bowel rest, IV fluids, correction of electrolytes, treatment of the underlying cause, close monitoring, and urgent surgical consultation.

cards.q: When is surgery indicated for toxic megacolon?
cards.a: Perforation, uncontrolled bleeding, worsening sepsis, or failure of medical therapy.

cards.q: What is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)?
cards.a: Massive colonic dilation without a mechanical obstruction.

cards.q: Which hospitalized patients are at greatest risk for Ogilvie syndrome?
cards.a: Elderly, severely ill, postoperative, trauma, neurologic, or immobilized patients.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment of uncomplicated Ogilvie syndrome?
cards.a: Supportive care, correction of reversible causes, bowel rest, and discontinuation of contributing medications.

cards.q: Which medication is used when conservative therapy fails in Ogilvie syndrome without contraindications?
cards.a: Neostigmine.

cards.q: When is colonoscopic decompression considered in Ogilvie syndrome?
cards.a: If neostigmine is contraindicated or unsuccessful and there is no perforation. Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Surgical Pearls)

cards.q: Which inflammatory bowel disease is cured by total proctocolectomy?
cards.a: Ulcerative colitis.

cards.q: Is surgery curative for Crohn disease?
cards.a: No. Surgery treats complications but disease recurrence is common.

cards.q: What is the most common indication for surgery in Crohn disease?
cards.a: Complications such as obstruction from fibrostenotic disease, fistulas, abscesses, perforation, or medically refractory disease.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for colorectal surgical emergencies?
cards.a: Differentiate mechanical obstruction, ischemia, perforation, and inflammatory disease early. Hemodynamic instability, peritonitis, bowel ischemia, or perforation generally require urgent surgical evaluation and intervention. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: What are the major types of gallstones?
cards.a: Cholesterol stones (most common in developed countries), black pigment stones (associated with chronic hemolysis/cirrhosis), and brown pigment stones (associated with biliary infection).

cards.q: What are the classic risk factors for cholesterol gallstones?
cards.a: Female sex, increasing age, obesity, pregnancy, rapid weight loss, diabetes, and estrogen exposure.

cards.q: What is biliary colic?
cards.a: Episodic right upper quadrant (RUQ) or epigastric pain caused by transient cystic duct obstruction, often after a fatty meal, without gallbladder inflammation.

cards.q: How does biliary colic differ from acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Biliary colic is transient, typically lasts <6 hours, and lacks fever or significant inflammatory markers; acute cholecystitis involves persistent pain, inflammation, and often fever/leukocytosis.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial imaging study for suspected gallstones?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant ultrasound.

cards.q: What ultrasound findings indicate cholelithiasis?
cards.a: Echogenic stones with posterior acoustic shadowing and mobility.

cards.q: Should asymptomatic gallstones routinely be treated with cholecystectomy?
cards.a: No. Most asymptomatic gallstones are managed expectantly, with selected exceptions (e.g., certain high-risk conditions). Acute Cholecystitis

cards.q: What causes acute calculous cholecystitis?
cards.a: Persistent obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone leading to gallbladder inflammation.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Persistent RUQ pain, fever, nausea/vomiting, leukocytosis, and Murphy sign.

cards.q: What is Murphy sign?
cards.a: Inspiratory arrest due to pain when palpating the RUQ beneath the costal margin.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial imaging study for acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant ultrasound.

cards.q: Which ultrasound findings support acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), pericholecystic fluid, and a sonographic Murphy sign.

cards.q: Which imaging study is most sensitive when ultrasound is equivocal?
cards.a: Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan.

cards.q: What HIDA scan finding confirms acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Nonvisualization of the gallbladder due to cystic duct obstruction.

cards.q: What is the initial management of acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: NPO, IV fluids, analgesia, and antibiotics when indicated (especially moderate/severe disease), followed by surgical evaluation.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for acute calculous cholecystitis?
cards.a: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the index hospitalization for most suitable patients.

cards.q: Which patients may require percutaneous cholecystostomy instead of immediate surgery?
cards.a: Critically ill or poor surgical candidates with acute cholecystitis. Acalculous Cholecystitis

cards.q: What is acalculous cholecystitis?
cards.a: Gallbladder inflammation without gallstones.

cards.q: Which patients are at greatest risk for acalculous cholecystitis?
cards.a: Critically ill patients, those with sepsis, trauma, burns, prolonged fasting, or total parenteral nutrition.

cards.q: Why is acalculous cholecystitis associated with higher mortality?
cards.a: Diagnosis is often delayed, increasing the risk of gangrene and perforation. Choledocholithiasis

cards.q: What is choledocholithiasis?
cards.a: Presence of gallstones in the common bile duct (CBD).

cards.q: What laboratory abnormalities suggest choledocholithiasis?
cards.a: Elevated bilirubin and cholestatic liver enzymes (especially alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyl transferase), often with elevated AST/ALT.

cards.q: Which imaging finding suggests common bile duct obstruction?
cards.a: Dilated common bile duct on ultrasound.

cards.q: Which imaging study is commonly used to evaluate suspected choledocholithiasis in stable patients?
cards.a: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) or endoscopic ultrasound (EUS), depending on the probability of CBD stones.

cards.q: What is the preferred therapeutic procedure for confirmed choledocholithiasis?
cards.a: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with stone extraction, followed by cholecystectomy when appropriate. Acute Cholangitis

cards.q: What causes ascending cholangitis?
cards.a: Biliary obstruction with superimposed bacterial infection.

cards.q: What is Charcot triad?
cards.a: Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain.

cards.q: What is Reynolds pentad?
cards.a: Charcot triad plus hypotension and altered mental status.

cards.q: What is the initial management of acute cholangitis?
cards.a: IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and urgent biliary decompression when indicated.

cards.q: What is the preferred method of biliary decompression in most patients with acute cholangitis?
cards.a: ERCP. Gallstone Pancreatitis

cards.q: What causes gallstone pancreatitis?
cards.a: Transient obstruction of the ampulla of Vater by a gallstone.

cards.q: Which laboratory finding supports gallstone pancreatitis?
cards.a: Elevated serum lipase (or amylase) with elevated ALT suggesting a biliary source.

cards.q: When is urgent ERCP indicated in gallstone pancreatitis?
cards.a: If there is concomitant acute cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction.

cards.q: When should cholecystectomy be performed after mild gallstone pancreatitis?
cards.a: During the same hospitalization after the pancreatitis has clinically improved. Gallbladder Polyps & Cancer

cards.q: Which gallbladder polyp size is generally considered an indication for cholecystectomy due to increased malignancy risk?
cards.a: Polyps ≥10 mm, or smaller polyps with high-risk features.

cards.q: What is the most common histologic type of gallbladder cancer?
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: What is the strongest risk factor for gallbladder carcinoma?
cards.a: Chronic gallstones (cholelithiasis).

cards.q: What imaging modality is typically used first to evaluate suspected gallbladder carcinoma?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant ultrasound, followed by cross-sectional imaging for staging. Liver Lesions

cards.q: What is the most common benign liver tumor?
cards.a: Cavernous hemangioma.

cards.q: Which benign liver tumor is associated with oral contraceptive use and carries a risk of hemorrhage?
cards.a: Hepatocellular adenoma.

cards.q: Which benign liver lesion characteristically contains a central stellate scar?
cards.a: Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH). Liver Abscess

cards.q: What is the classic triad of pyogenic liver abscess?
cards.a: Fever, right upper quadrant pain, and leukocytosis (jaundice is less common).

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for suspected liver abscess?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT scan (ultrasound is also useful).

cards.q: What is the treatment for most pyogenic liver abscesses?
cards.a: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage for drainable collections. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)

cards.q: Which patients are at greatest risk for hepatocellular carcinoma?
cards.a: Patients with cirrhosis (from hepatitis B, hepatitis C, alcohol-associated liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, etc.).

cards.q: Which serum tumor marker is commonly associated with HCC?
cards.a: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), although it is not sufficiently sensitive or specific for diagnosis alone.

cards.q: What imaging feature is characteristic of HCC on multiphasic CT or MRI?
cards.a: Arterial phase hyperenhancement with portal venous or delayed washout. Portal Hypertension

cards.q: What is the most common cause of portal hypertension?
cards.a: Cirrhosis.

cards.q: What are the major complications of portal hypertension?
cards.a: Esophageal/gastric varices, ascites, splenomegaly, hepatic encephalopathy, and hypersplenism.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle in hepatobiliary surgery?
cards.a: Use RUQ ultrasound as the first test for suspected gallbladder disease, recognize cholangitis as a medical emergency requiring antibiotics and biliary drainage, and distinguish biliary colic from acute cholecystitis by the presence of persistent pain and inflammation.

cards.q: What are the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Gallstones and alcohol use.

cards.q: What are other important causes of acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, ERCP, medications (e.g., azathioprine, valproate, thiazides in rare cases), trauma, infections, and pancreatic tumors.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea and vomiting.

cards.q: Which serum enzyme is most specific for acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Serum lipase.

cards.q: What diagnostic criteria are used for acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: Characteristic abdominal pain Lipase or amylase ≥3× the upper limit of normal Imaging findings consistent with pancreatitis.

cards.q: Is CT required to diagnose acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: No. CT is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, severe disease, or suspected complications.

cards.q: What imaging study should be obtained in most patients with acute pancreatitis to evaluate the cause?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant ultrasound to assess for gallstones.

cards.q: What is the cornerstone of initial treatment for acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, adequate analgesia, and early enteral nutrition when tolerated.

cards.q: Which IV fluid is generally preferred for initial resuscitation in acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Lactated Ringer's solution.

cards.q: Are prophylactic antibiotics recommended in uncomplicated acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: No. Severity Assessment

cards.q: Which scoring system is commonly used to predict the severity of acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: BISAP score (also APACHE II and revised Atlanta classification are used).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death during the first week of severe acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) leading to multiorgan failure.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death after the first week of severe pancreatitis?
cards.a: Infected pancreatic necrosis and its complications.

cards.q: What laboratory abnormality is associated with severe pancreatitis?
cards.a: Elevated hematocrit (hemoconcentration), elevated BUN, and elevated CRP may indicate more severe disease. Pancreatic Necrosis

cards.q: When should pancreatic necrosis be suspected?
cards.a: Persistent fever, leukocytosis, organ failure, or clinical deterioration despite supportive treatment.

cards.q: Which imaging study best evaluates pancreatic necrosis?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT scan.

cards.q: When should CT generally be performed to evaluate suspected necrosis?
cards.a: Usually after 72 hours from symptom onset if the diagnosis is uncertain or complications are suspected.

cards.q: When are antibiotics indicated in pancreatic necrosis?
cards.a: Only for infected pancreatic necrosis or another documented infection—not for sterile necrosis.

cards.q: What is the preferred treatment for infected pancreatic necrosis?
cards.a: A step-up approach: antibiotics plus image-guided drainage, with minimally invasive or surgical necrosectomy if needed. Pancreatic Pseudocyst

cards.q: What is a pancreatic pseudocyst?
cards.a: A mature, encapsulated collection of pancreatic fluid surrounded by a fibrous wall without an epithelial lining, typically developing ≥4 weeks after pancreatitis.

cards.q: Which imaging modality is most useful for diagnosing a pancreatic pseudocyst?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT scan.

cards.q: Which pancreatic pseudocysts require intervention?
cards.a: Symptomatic, infected, enlarging, bleeding, obstructing, or persistent pseudocysts with clinically significant complications.

cards.q: What is the preferred treatment for symptomatic pancreatic pseudocysts?
cards.a: Endoscopic drainage when anatomically appropriate; percutaneous or surgical drainage in selected cases. Chronic Pancreatitis

cards.q: What is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in adults?
cards.a: Chronic alcohol use (although other causes such as genetic disorders and obstructive disease also occur).

cards.q: What are the classic symptoms of chronic pancreatitis?
cards.a: Chronic epigastric pain, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (steatorrhea), weight loss, and diabetes mellitus.

cards.q: Which imaging finding is characteristic of chronic pancreatitis?
cards.a: Pancreatic calcifications.

cards.q: Why do patients with chronic pancreatitis develop steatorrhea?
cards.a: Loss of pancreatic exocrine enzyme production causes fat malabsorption.

cards.q: How is pancreatic exocrine insufficiency treated?
cards.a: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy. Pancreatic Cancer

cards.q: What is the most common type of pancreatic cancer?
cards.a: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: What is the strongest modifiable risk factor for pancreatic adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: Cigarette smoking.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of pancreatic head cancer?
cards.a: Painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss.

cards.q: What is Courvoisier sign?
cards.a: A palpable, nontender enlarged gallbladder in a jaundiced patient, suggesting malignant biliary obstruction.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial imaging study for suspected pancreatic cancer?
cards.a: Pancreatic protocol contrast-enhanced CT scan.

cards.q: Which tumor marker is commonly elevated in pancreatic adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: CA 19-9 (used mainly for prognosis and monitoring, not screening).

cards.q: What operation is performed for resectable pancreatic head cancer?
cards.a: Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure).

cards.q: Which structures are typically removed during a Whipple procedure?
cards.a: Pancreatic head, duodenum, distal common bile duct, gallbladder, and usually the gastric antrum or pylorus (depending on the technique). Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors

cards.q: Which pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor causes recurrent fasting hypoglycemia?
cards.a: Insulinoma.

cards.q: Which pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?
cards.a: Gastrinoma.

cards.q: What laboratory finding supports the diagnosis of gastrinoma?
cards.a: Markedly elevated fasting serum gastrin with gastric acid hypersecretion (after appropriate evaluation). Splenic Disorders

cards.q: What is the most common indication for splenectomy after trauma?
cards.a: Hemodynamic instability due to splenic injury.

cards.q: Which patients with splenic trauma can usually be managed nonoperatively?
cards.a: Hemodynamically stable patients without peritonitis.

cards.q: What is the most common complication after splenectomy?
cards.a: Increased lifelong susceptibility to overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria.

cards.q: Which organisms are classically associated with overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI)?
cards.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis.

cards.q: Which vaccines should be administered before elective splenectomy when possible?
cards.a: Pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Hib vaccines (ideally at least 2 weeks before surgery).

cards.q: If an emergency splenectomy is performed, when should these vaccines generally be given?
cards.a: As soon as the patient has recovered adequately, typically about 2 weeks after surgery, according to current guidelines.

cards.q: Which blood cell abnormality commonly develops after splenectomy?
cards.a: Reactive thrombocytosis.

cards.q: Which peripheral blood smear finding is characteristic after splenectomy?
cards.a: Howell-Jolly bodies.

cards.q: Why do Howell-Jolly bodies appear after splenectomy?
cards.a: The spleen normally removes nuclear remnants from erythrocytes; without splenic function, these persist.

cards.q: Which patients should be educated to seek urgent medical care for fever after splenectomy?
cards.a: All asplenic patients, because fever may indicate overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle regarding pancreatic and splenic disease?
cards.a: Treat acute pancreatitis with supportive care first, reserve antibiotics for infected necrosis (not sterile disease), recognize painless jaundice as pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise, and always protect asplenic patients against encapsulated organisms with appropriate vaccination. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: Which lymph nodes receive most lymphatic drainage from the breast?
cards.a: Axillary lymph nodes (especially the anterior/pectoral group).

cards.q: Which quadrant of the breast is the most common site of breast cancer?
cards.a: Upper outer quadrant.

cards.q: Which ligament provides structural support to the breast?
cards.a: Cooper (suspensory) ligaments.

cards.q: Why does advanced breast cancer cause skin dimpling?
cards.a: Tumor invasion and shortening of Cooper ligaments. Breast Mass Evaluation

cards.q: What are the three components of the "triple assessment" of a breast mass?
cards.a: Clinical breast examination, breast imaging, and tissue diagnosis (biopsy when indicated).

cards.q: What is the preferred initial imaging study for a palpable breast mass in women <30 years?
cards.a: Breast ultrasound.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial imaging study for a palpable breast mass in women ≥30 years?
cards.a: Diagnostic mammography (usually with targeted ultrasound).

cards.q: What is the preferred biopsy method for most suspicious breast lesions?
cards.a: Core needle biopsy.

cards.q: Why is core needle biopsy preferred over fine-needle aspiration for suspicious breast masses?
cards.a: It preserves tissue architecture, allowing histologic diagnosis and receptor testing (ER, PR, HER2). Fibroadenoma

cards.q: What is the most common benign breast tumor in young women?
cards.a: Fibroadenoma.

cards.q: How does a fibroadenoma typically feel on examination?
cards.a: Firm, rubbery, smooth, mobile, and well-circumscribed.

cards.q: Which imaging finding is typical of fibroadenoma on ultrasound?
cards.a: Oval, well-circumscribed, homogeneous hypoechoic mass with parallel orientation.

cards.q: How are small, biopsy-proven fibroadenomas usually managed?
cards.a: Observation with periodic clinical or imaging follow-up if asymptomatic. Fibrocystic Breast Changes

cards.q: What is the most common cause of cyclic breast pain in premenopausal women?
cards.a: Fibrocystic breast changes.

cards.q: How do fibrocystic breast changes typically present?
cards.a: Bilateral breast pain, nodularity, and tenderness that fluctuate with the menstrual cycle.

cards.q: Do fibrocystic breast changes increase the risk of breast cancer?
cards.a: Simple nonproliferative fibrocystic changes do not significantly increase breast cancer risk. Mastitis & Breast Abscess

cards.q: Which organism most commonly causes lactational mastitis?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: What is the typical presentation of lactational mastitis?
cards.a: Localized painful erythematous breast with fever in a breastfeeding woman.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for lactational mastitis?
cards.a: Anti-staphylococcal antibiotics, continued breastfeeding or milk expression, and supportive care.

cards.q: When should a breast abscess be suspected?
cards.a: Persistent fluctuance or failure of mastitis to improve with appropriate antibiotics.

cards.q: What is the preferred treatment for a breast abscess?
cards.a: Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics. Nipple Discharge

cards.q: Which type of nipple discharge is most concerning for malignancy?
cards.a: Spontaneous, unilateral, bloody, or serous discharge from a single duct.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge?
cards.a: Intraductal papilloma.

cards.q: What is an intraductal papilloma?
cards.a: A benign papillary tumor arising within a lactiferous duct. Fat Necrosis

cards.q: What commonly causes fat necrosis of the breast?
cards.a: Trauma, surgery, radiation, or previous breast procedures.

cards.q: Why is fat necrosis clinically important?
cards.a: It may mimic breast cancer on physical examination and imaging. Mammography

cards.q: Which mammographic finding is highly suspicious for malignancy?
cards.a: Fine pleomorphic or linear branching microcalcifications, especially in clustered distributions.

cards.q: What does a BI-RADS 1 result indicate?
cards.a: Negative examination.

cards.q: What does BI-RADS 2 indicate?
cards.a: Benign finding.

cards.q: What does BI-RADS 3 indicate?
cards.a: Probably benign lesion (<2% risk of malignancy); short-interval imaging follow-up is recommended.

cards.q: What does BI-RADS 4 indicate?
cards.a: Suspicious abnormality requiring tissue diagnosis (biopsy).

cards.q: What does BI-RADS 5 indicate?
cards.a: Highly suggestive of malignancy (>95% likelihood); biopsy is indicated. Breast Cancer

cards.q: What is the most common histologic type of breast cancer?
cards.a: Invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type).

cards.q: What is the second most common invasive breast cancer?
cards.a: Invasive lobular carcinoma.

cards.q: Which breast cancer is often bilateral and multifocal?
cards.a: Invasive lobular carcinoma.

cards.q: Which receptor status predicts response to endocrine therapy?
cards.a: Estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) positivity.

cards.q: Which receptor predicts response to trastuzumab?
cards.a: HER2 overexpression or amplification.

cards.q: Which subtype generally has the poorest prognosis and lacks targeted endocrine or HER2 therapy?
cards.a: Triple-negative breast cancer (ER−, PR−, HER2−). Clinical Signs

cards.q: What is peau d'orange?
cards.a: Edematous skin with an orange-peel appearance caused by lymphatic obstruction from breast cancer.

cards.q: Which breast cancer presents with diffuse erythema, edema, warmth, and peau d'orange?
cards.a: Inflammatory breast cancer.

cards.q: Does inflammatory breast cancer usually present as a discrete palpable mass?
cards.a: No. It often presents with diffuse skin changes rather than a distinct mass. Paget Disease

cards.q: What is Paget disease of the breast?
cards.a: Malignant involvement of the nipple-areolar complex, usually associated with underlying ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or invasive carcinoma.

cards.q: How does Paget disease typically present?
cards.a: Chronic unilateral eczematous, scaly, or ulcerative nipple changes that do not resolve with topical therapy. Surgical Management

cards.q: What is the preferred axillary staging procedure for clinically node-negative invasive breast cancer?
cards.a: Sentinel lymph node biopsy.

cards.q: When is axillary lymph node dissection generally performed?
cards.a: In selected patients with proven axillary nodal involvement or based on surgical and oncologic indications.

cards.q: What is the major complication of axillary lymph node dissection?
cards.a: Lymphedema of the ipsilateral upper extremity. Genetics

cards.q: Which genes are most commonly associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome?
cards.a: BRCA1 and BRCA2.

cards.q: Which patients should be referred for genetic risk assessment and possible BRCA testing?
cards.a: Patients with strong family histories, early-onset breast cancer, male breast cancer, ovarian cancer, multiple affected relatives, or other features suggesting hereditary cancer syndromes. Treatment Principles

cards.q: What is breast-conserving therapy?
cards.a: Lumpectomy followed by whole-breast radiation therapy in appropriate candidates.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for breast surgery?
cards.a: Every suspicious breast mass requires triple assessment (clinical examination, appropriate imaging, and tissue diagnosis). Core needle biopsy is the standard diagnostic method, and treatment is guided by stage and receptor status (ER, PR, and HER2). -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: What is the first laboratory test in the evaluation of a thyroid nodule?
cards.a: Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).

cards.q: What is the next step if TSH is suppressed in a patient with a thyroid nodule?
cards.a: Perform a radionuclide thyroid uptake scan to determine whether the nodule is hyperfunctioning ("hot").

cards.q: Why are hyperfunctioning ("hot") thyroid nodules rarely biopsied?
cards.a: They have a very low risk of malignancy.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating thyroid nodules?
cards.a: High-resolution thyroid ultrasound.

cards.q: Which ultrasound features increase suspicion for thyroid malignancy?
cards.a: Hypoechogenicity, irregular margins, microcalcifications, taller-than-wide shape, extrathyroidal extension, and suspicious cervical lymph nodes.

cards.q: What is the preferred biopsy method for suspicious thyroid nodules?
cards.a: Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA). Thyroid Cancer

cards.q: What is the most common type of thyroid cancer?
cards.a: Papillary thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: Which thyroid cancer has the best prognosis?
cards.a: Papillary thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: Which environmental exposure is a major risk factor for papillary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Childhood exposure to ionizing radiation.

cards.q: Which histologic feature is characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Orphan Annie eye nuclei (optically clear nuclei), often with nuclear grooves and psammoma bodies.

cards.q: Which thyroid cancer spreads primarily via lymphatics?
cards.a: Papillary thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: Which thyroid cancer spreads primarily via the bloodstream?
cards.a: Follicular thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: Which thyroid cancer arises from parafollicular (C) cells?
cards.a: Medullary thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: Which tumor marker is elevated in medullary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Calcitonin (CEA may also be elevated).

cards.q: Which hereditary syndrome is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN2).

cards.q: Which thyroid cancer is the most aggressive?
cards.a: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Hyperthyroidism

cards.q: What is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism?
cards.a: Graves disease.

cards.q: Which antibody is responsible for Graves disease?
cards.a: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), also called TSH receptor antibody.

cards.q: What are the classic clinical findings of Graves disease?
cards.a: Diffuse goiter, hyperthyroidism, ophthalmopathy, and pretibial myxedema.

cards.q: What is the first-line medication for symptomatic hyperthyroidism?
cards.a: &β;-blockers for symptomatic control (along with antithyroid therapy when indicated).

cards.q: Which antithyroid drugs are commonly used?
cards.a: Methimazole and propylthiouracil (PTU).

cards.q: Which antithyroid drug is preferred during the first trimester of pregnancy?
cards.a: Propylthiouracil (PTU).

cards.q: Which antithyroid drug is generally preferred outside the first trimester?
cards.a: Methimazole. Thyroid Storm

cards.q: What is thyroid storm?
cards.a: A life-threatening exacerbation of severe thyrotoxicosis causing multisystem dysfunction.

cards.q: What are common clinical features of thyroid storm?
cards.a: High fever, severe tachycardia, agitation, delirium, vomiting, diarrhea, and heart failure.

cards.q: What is the correct treatment sequence for thyroid storm?
cards.a: &β;-blocker → PTU (or methimazole) → iodine (after antithyroid drug) → glucocorticoids, along with aggressive supportive care.

cards.q: Why should iodine be administered only after antithyroid medication?
cards.a: To prevent new thyroid hormone synthesis before blocking hormone release. Hypothyroidism

cards.q: What is the treatment for primary hypothyroidism?
cards.a: Levothyroxine.

cards.q: What is myxedema coma?
cards.a: Severe decompensated hypothyroidism causing altered mental status, hypothermia, hypotension, and hypoventilation.

cards.q: How is myxedema coma treated?
cards.a: IV levothyroxine, stress-dose glucocorticoids until adrenal insufficiency is excluded, supportive care, and treatment of precipitating factors. Hyperparathyroidism

cards.q: What is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Solitary parathyroid adenoma.

cards.q: What are the classic manifestations of hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: "Bones, stones, abdominal groans, psychic overtones."

cards.q: What laboratory pattern is typical of primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: ↑PTH, ↑calcium, ↓phosphate.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Parathyroidectomy. Hypoparathyroidism

cards.q: What is the most common cause of hypoparathyroidism?
cards.a: Accidental injury or removal during thyroid surgery.

cards.q: What laboratory abnormalities occur in hypoparathyroidism?
cards.a: ↓PTH, ↓calcium, ↑phosphate.

cards.q: What physical examination signs indicate hypocalcemia?
cards.a: Chvostek sign and Trousseau sign. MEN Syndromes

cards.q: What tumors are associated with MEN1?
cards.a: Parathyroid tumors, Pituitary tumors, and Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors ("3 Ps").

cards.q: What tumors are associated with MEN2A?
cards.a: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism.

cards.q: What tumors are associated with MEN2B?
cards.a: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus, and intestinal ganglioneuromatosis. Pheochromocytoma

cards.q: What is pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: A catecholamine-secreting tumor arising from adrenal medullary chromaffin cells.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Episodic headache, diaphoresis, and palpitations.

cards.q: What is the preferred biochemical test for pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Plasma free metanephrines (or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines).

cards.q: Which imaging study is commonly used to localize pheochromocytoma after biochemical confirmation?
cards.a: CT or MRI of the adrenal glands.

cards.q: What medication must always be started before &β;-blockers in pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Alpha-blockade (e.g., phenoxybenzamine or selective α₁-blockers).

cards.q: Why must α-blockade precede β-blockade?
cards.a: Beta-blockade alone can cause unopposed α-adrenergic stimulation, leading to severe hypertension. Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome)

cards.q: What laboratory abnormalities suggest primary hyperaldosteronism?
cards.a: Hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, low plasma renin, and elevated aldosterone.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma?
cards.a: Laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Adrenal Incidentaloma

cards.q: What is the first step after discovering an adrenal incidentaloma?
cards.a: Evaluate for hormonal activity (e.g., cortisol, catecholamines, aldosterone when indicated) and assess imaging features suggesting malignancy.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle in endocrine surgery?
cards.a: Always determine whether an endocrine lesion is functioning before surgery. For pheochromocytoma, α-blockade must always precede β-blockade. Evaluate thyroid nodules with TSH followed by ultrasound, and biopsy appropriate nodules with ultrasound-guided FNA. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

topic: Vascular Surgery (Arterial Disease, Venous Disease & Aortic Disorders)

cards.q: What is the most common cause of peripheral arterial disease (PAD)?
cards.a: Atherosclerosis.

cards.q: What is the strongest modifiable risk factor for PAD?
cards.a: Cigarette smoking.

cards.q: What is the classic symptom of PAD?
cards.a: Intermittent claudication (reproducible muscle pain with exertion that resolves with rest).

cards.q: Which muscle group is affected in femoropopliteal PAD?
cards.a: Calf muscles.

cards.q: Which muscle group is affected in aortoiliac occlusive disease?
cards.a: Buttocks and thighs.

cards.q: What is Leriche syndrome?
cards.a: Aortoiliac occlusive disease causing buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, and diminished femoral pulses.

cards.q: What physical examination findings suggest PAD?
cards.a: Diminished or absent peripheral pulses, cool extremity, delayed capillary refill, trophic skin changes, and hair loss.

cards.q: What is the best initial diagnostic test for suspected PAD?
cards.a: Ankle-brachial index (ABI).

cards.q: How is the ankle-brachial index (ABI) calculated?
cards.a: ABI = Highest ankle systolic pressure ÷ Highest brachial systolic pressure

cards.q: What ABI value is considered normal?
What ABI suggests peripheral arterial disease?
What ABI suggests critical limb ischemia?
cards.a: Approximately ≤0.40.

cards.q: What is the first-line medical treatment for symptomatic PAD?
cards.a: Smoking cessation, supervised exercise therapy, statin therapy, and antiplatelet therapy.

cards.q: Which antiplatelet medications are commonly used in PAD?
cards.a: Aspirin or clopidogrel.

cards.q: Which medication can improve walking distance in patients with lifestyle-limiting claudication who do not have heart failure?
cards.a: Cilostazol. Critical Limb Ischemia (Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia)

cards.q: What defines chronic limb-threatening ischemia?
cards.a: Ischemic rest pain, nonhealing ulcers, or gangrene due to advanced PAD.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for chronic limb-threatening ischemia when feasible?
cards.a: Revascularization (endovascular or surgical bypass). Acute Limb Ischemia

cards.q: What is acute limb ischemia?
cards.a: Sudden reduction in arterial blood flow threatening limb viability.

cards.q: What are the classic "6 Ps" of acute limb ischemia?
cards.a: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and poikilothermia.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acute limb ischemia?
cards.a: Arterial embolism (commonly from atrial fibrillation) or acute thrombosis of preexisting PAD.

cards.q: What is the first treatment after recognizing acute limb ischemia (unless contraindicated)?
cards.a: Immediate IV unfractionated heparin.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for a threatened limb in acute limb ischemia?
cards.a: Urgent revascularization (catheter-directed therapy or surgery, depending on the clinical scenario).

cards.q: Which finding indicates irreversible limb ischemia?
cards.a: Profound anesthesia, paralysis with fixed rigor, and nonviable tissue. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)

cards.q: What is an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)?
cards.a: Permanent dilation of the abdominal aorta to ≥3.0 cm.

cards.q: What is the most common location of an AAA?
cards.a: Infrarenal abdominal aorta.

cards.q: What are the major risk factors for AAA?
cards.a: Older age, male sex, smoking, atherosclerosis, and family history.

cards.q: What is the preferred screening test for AAA?
cards.a: Abdominal ultrasound.

cards.q: Which population is routinely recommended for one-time AAA screening in many guidelines?
cards.a: Men aged 65–75 years who have ever smoked.

cards.q: What symptom strongly suggests rupture of an AAA?
cards.a: Sudden abdominal or back pain with hypotension.

cards.q: What classic triad is associated with ruptured AAA?
cards.a: Hypotension, abdominal/back pain, and a pulsatile abdominal mass (not always present).

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for ruptured AAA?
cards.a: Emergency surgical or endovascular repair.

cards.q: At approximately what aneurysm diameter is elective repair generally recommended in men?
cards.a: ≥5.5 cm, rapid expansion, or symptomatic aneurysm. Thoracic Aortic Disease

cards.q: Which connective tissue disorder is strongly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysm?
cards.a: Marfan syndrome.

cards.q: What imaging modality is commonly used to evaluate thoracic aortic aneurysm?
cards.a: CT angiography (or MR angiography in selected patients). Aortic Dissection

cards.q: What is the most common risk factor for aortic dissection?
cards.a: Chronic hypertension.

cards.q: What is the classic symptom of acute aortic dissection?
cards.a: Sudden severe tearing chest or back pain.

cards.q: What imaging study is preferred for diagnosing aortic dissection in a hemodynamically stable patient?
cards.a: CT angiography.

cards.q: Which medication should be administered first in acute aortic dissection?
cards.a: IV &β;-blocker (e.g., esmolol) to reduce heart rate and shear stress.

cards.q: Which Stanford type of aortic dissection requires emergency surgery?
cards.a: Stanford Type A (ascending aorta involved).

cards.q: How is uncomplicated Stanford Type B dissection generally managed initially?
cards.a: Aggressive medical therapy with blood pressure and heart rate control; intervention is reserved for complications. Carotid Artery Disease

cards.q: What is the major complication of carotid artery stenosis?
cards.a: Ischemic stroke.

cards.q: Which imaging test is used first to evaluate carotid stenosis?
cards.a: Carotid duplex ultrasound.

cards.q: Which patients benefit most from carotid endarterectomy?
cards.a: Selected patients with symptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis. Venous Disease

cards.q: What is the most common cause of chronic venous insufficiency?
cards.a: Venous valvular incompetence, often following prior DVT or due to primary valve failure.

cards.q: What are typical clinical features of chronic venous insufficiency?
cards.a: Leg edema, varicose veins, hyperpigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis, and venous ulcers.

cards.q: Where do venous stasis ulcers most commonly occur?
cards.a: Near the medial malleolus.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for chronic venous insufficiency?
cards.a: Compression therapy (if there is no significant arterial insufficiency). Varicose Veins

cards.q: What causes varicose veins?
cards.a: Superficial venous valve incompetence leading to venous reflux.

cards.q: What is the preferred diagnostic test for symptomatic varicose veins?
cards.a: Duplex venous ultrasound.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for vascular surgery?
cards.a: Differentiate acute from chronic vascular disease. Acute limb ischemia requires immediate anticoagulation and urgent revascularization. Suspected ruptured AAA or Stanford Type A aortic dissection requires emergent surgical management. ABI is the initial test for PAD, and compression therapy is first-line for chronic venous insufficiency after excluding significant arterial disease.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?
cards.a: Venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability (Virchow triad).

cards.q: What are the components of Virchow triad?
cards.a: Venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability.

cards.q: What are the most important risk factors for DVT?
cards.a: Recent surgery, trauma, malignancy, prolonged immobility, pregnancy/postpartum, estrogen therapy, obesity, prior DVT, inherited thrombophilias, and increasing age.

cards.q: What are the classic symptoms of DVT?
cards.a: Unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, and erythema.

cards.q: Is Homan sign reliable for diagnosing DVT?
cards.a: No. It has poor sensitivity and specificity and is not recommended for diagnosis.

cards.q: What clinical prediction rule is commonly used to estimate the probability of DVT?
cards.a: Wells score for DVT.

cards.q: In a patient with low clinical probability of DVT, what is the appropriate initial test?
cards.a: High-sensitivity D-dimer (if negative, DVT is effectively excluded in most patients).

cards.q: What is the preferred diagnostic test for suspected lower-extremity DVT?
cards.a: Compression duplex ultrasonography.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for proximal DVT in a hemodynamically stable patient?
cards.a: Anticoagulation (e.g., a DOAC in appropriate patients, or LMWH followed by another anticoagulant depending on the clinical scenario).

cards.q: When is catheter-directed thrombolysis considered for DVT?
cards.a: Selected patients with extensive iliofemoral DVT, severe symptoms, low bleeding risk, and good functional status. Pulmonary Embolism (PE)

cards.q: What is the most common source of pulmonary emboli?
cards.a: Proximal deep veins of the lower extremities.

cards.q: What are the classic symptoms of pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, and tachycardia.

cards.q: What ECG finding is classically associated with pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: Sinus tachycardia is most common; the S₁Q₃T₃ pattern is classic but uncommon.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for diagnosing PE in a hemodynamically stable patient?
cards.a: CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA).

cards.q: Which imaging test is preferred when CTPA is contraindicated (e.g., severe contrast allergy or selected patients)?
cards.a: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan, when appropriate.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for hemodynamically stable pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: Anticoagulation.

cards.q: Which patients with PE should receive systemic thrombolytic therapy?
cards.a: Patients with high-risk (massive) PE causing hemodynamic instability, if there are no major contraindications.

cards.q: Which patients with PE may require surgical embolectomy or catheter-based intervention?
cards.a: Selected patients with massive PE who cannot receive thrombolysis or who fail thrombolytic therapy. Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) Filters

cards.q: What is the primary indication for placement of an IVC filter?
cards.a: Acute VTE with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation.

cards.q: Should retrievable IVC filters be removed?
cards.a: Yes. They should generally be removed once anticoagulation can be safely initiated and the indication has resolved. Superficial Thrombophlebitis

cards.q: What is superficial thrombophlebitis?
cards.a: Thrombosis and inflammation of a superficial vein.

cards.q: How is uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis treated?
cards.a: NSAIDs, warm compresses, ambulation, and compression therapy when appropriate; anticoagulation is considered for extensive or high-risk disease. Dialysis Access

cards.q: What is the preferred long-term vascular access for hemodialysis?
cards.a: Native arteriovenous (AV) fistula.

cards.q: Why are AV fistulas preferred over AV grafts?
cards.a: They have lower infection and thrombosis rates and better long-term patency.

cards.q: Which AV fistula is most commonly created first?
cards.a: Radiocephalic (Brescia-Cimino) fistula at the wrist, when feasible.

cards.q: What physical examination finding confirms a functioning AV fistula?
cards.a: A palpable thrill and an audible bruit. Vascular Graft Complications

cards.q: What is the most common early complication of a vascular graft?
cards.a: Graft thrombosis.

cards.q: What is the most serious complication of a prosthetic vascular graft?
cards.a: Graft infection. Organ Donation

cards.q: What is brain death?
cards.a: Irreversible cessation of all functions of the entire brain, including the brainstem.

cards.q: Is brain death legally recognized as death?
cards.a: Yes.

cards.q: Can organs be donated after brain death?
cards.a: Yes, with appropriate consent and according to applicable laws and protocols. Kidney Transplantation

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for eligible patients with end-stage kidney disease?
cards.a: Kidney transplantation.

cards.q: Which donor generally provides the best long-term graft survival?
cards.a: Living donor.

cards.q: What vascular anastomosis is commonly performed during kidney transplantation?
cards.a: Donor renal vessels are anastomosed to the recipient's external iliac vessels. Immunosuppressive Therapy

cards.q: Which calcineurin inhibitors are commonly used after organ transplantation?
cards.a: Tacrolimus and cyclosporine.

cards.q: What is a major adverse effect of calcineurin inhibitors?
cards.a: Nephrotoxicity.

cards.q: Which antiproliferative agents are commonly used in transplant immunosuppression?
cards.a: Mycophenolate mofetil and azathioprine.

cards.q: Which mTOR inhibitors are used in transplant recipients?
cards.a: Sirolimus and everolimus.

cards.q: What is the role of corticosteroids after transplantation?
cards.a: Prevention and treatment of acute rejection as part of immunosuppressive regimens. Transplant Rejection

cards.q: When does hyperacute rejection occur?
cards.a: Minutes to hours after transplantation.

cards.q: What causes hyperacute rejection?
cards.a: Preformed recipient antibodies against donor antigens.

cards.q: How is hyperacute rejection treated?
cards.a: It is generally not reversible; graft removal is usually required.

cards.q: When does acute rejection usually occur?
cards.a: Days to months after transplantation (and can occur later).

cards.q: What causes acute rejection?
cards.a: Primarily T-cell-mediated immune responses, with or without antibody-mediated mechanisms.

cards.q: How is acute rejection treated?
cards.a: Increased immunosuppression (e.g., high-dose corticosteroids; additional therapies based on rejection type).

cards.q: When does chronic rejection occur?
cards.a: Months to years after transplantation.

cards.q: Is chronic rejection generally reversible?
cards.a: No. It usually progresses despite treatment. Post-Transplant Complications

cards.q: What is the leading cause of death after successful organ transplantation?
cards.a: Cardiovascular disease overall; infection is a major cause early after transplantation due to immunosuppression.

cards.q: Which malignancies occur more frequently after transplantation?
cards.a: Skin cancers, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (often EBV-associated), and several other malignancies.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for vascular and transplant surgery?
cards.a: Use compression ultrasound to diagnose DVT, CT pulmonary angiography for stable PE, anticoagulate unless contraindicated, reserve IVC filters for patients who cannot receive anticoagulation, and recognize hyperacute rejection as antibody-mediated and generally irreversible. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: How is microscopic hematuria defined?
cards.a: ≥3 red blood cells (RBCs) per high-power field (HPF) on microscopic examination of a properly collected urine specimen.

cards.q: What is the first step in evaluating hematuria?
cards.a: Confirm hematuria with urinalysis, assess for infection or glomerular disease, and obtain a focused history and physical examination.

cards.q: Which painless presentation should be considered bladder cancer until proven otherwise?
cards.a: Painless gross hematuria in an adult.

cards.q: What are common nonglomerular causes of hematuria?
cards.a: Urolithiasis, urinary tract infection, bladder cancer, renal cell carcinoma, trauma, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and anticoagulation (which does not exclude underlying pathology).

cards.q: Which urinalysis findings suggest a glomerular source of hematuria?
cards.a: Dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, and significant proteinuria.

cards.q: What is the preferred evaluation for visible (gross) hematuria in adults at risk for urinary tract malignancy?
cards.a: Cystoscopy plus upper urinary tract imaging (typically CT urography if appropriate).

cards.q: Which imaging study is preferred for evaluation of the upper urinary tract in many patients with hematuria?
cards.a: CT urography.

cards.q: What is the gold standard for evaluating the bladder in patients with suspected bladder cancer?
cards.a: Cystoscopy. Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)

cards.q: What is the most common cause of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in older men?
cards.a: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).

cards.q: Which symptoms are characteristic of BPH?
cards.a: Hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, incomplete emptying, urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, and postvoid dribbling.

cards.q: Which symptom is usually the earliest complaint in BPH?
cards.a: Nocturia.

cards.q: Which examination should be performed in all men with suspected BPH?
cards.a: Digital rectal examination (DRE).

cards.q: How does the prostate typically feel on DRE in BPH?
cards.a: Smooth, enlarged, rubbery, and symmetric.

cards.q: Which DRE finding raises concern for prostate cancer rather than BPH?
cards.a: Hard, irregular, asymmetric nodules or induration.

cards.q: Which symptom score is commonly used to assess BPH severity?
cards.a: International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS).

cards.q: What is the first-line medication for symptomatic BPH?
cards.a: An α₁-adrenergic blocker (e.g., tamsulosin) for rapid symptom relief.

cards.q: Which medications shrink the prostate over time?
cards.a: 5-α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride or dutasteride).

cards.q: How do 5-α-reductase inhibitors work?
cards.a: They inhibit conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT).

cards.q: Which medication class improves BPH symptoms most rapidly?
cards.a: α₁-blockers.

cards.q: Which patients benefit most from adding a 5-α-reductase inhibitor?
cards.a: Men with enlarged prostates and moderate to severe symptoms. Acute Urinary Retention

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acute urinary retention in older men?
cards.a: Benign prostatic hyperplasia.

cards.q: What is the immediate management of acute urinary retention?
cards.a: Prompt bladder decompression with a urethral Foley catheter (or suprapubic catheter if urethral catheterization is contraindicated or unsuccessful).

cards.q: Which medications can precipitate urinary retention?
cards.a: Anticholinergics, sympathomimetics, opioids, and some antihistamines.

cards.q: What is post-obstructive diuresis?
cards.a: Marked polyuria after relief of urinary obstruction that may require careful monitoring of volume status and electrolytes. Prostate Cancer

cards.q: What is the most common noncutaneous cancer in men?
cards.a: Prostate adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: What are the major risk factors for prostate cancer?
cards.a: Increasing age, family history, African ancestry, and certain inherited genetic mutations (e.g., BRCA2).

cards.q: Which laboratory test is commonly used with DRE to evaluate for prostate cancer?
cards.a: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA).

cards.q: Is an elevated PSA diagnostic of prostate cancer?
cards.a: No. PSA can also be elevated in BPH, prostatitis, urinary retention, and after certain urologic procedures.

cards.q: What is the definitive diagnostic test for prostate cancer?
cards.a: Prostate biopsy (usually image-guided after appropriate evaluation).

cards.q: Where does prostate cancer most commonly arise?
cards.a: Peripheral zone of the prostate.

cards.q: Where does BPH most commonly occur?
cards.a: Transitional zone.

cards.q: What is the most common site of distant metastasis from prostate cancer?
cards.a: Bone, particularly the axial skeleton.

cards.q: What type of bone lesions are classically seen in metastatic prostate cancer?
cards.a: Osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions. Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC)

cards.q: What is the most common type of kidney cancer in adults?
cards.a: Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell subtype is most common).

cards.q: What are the major risk factors for RCC?
cards.a: Smoking, obesity, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and certain hereditary syndromes (e.g., von Hippel-Lindau).

cards.q: What is the classic triad of RCC?
cards.a: Hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable flank mass.

cards.q: Is the classic triad of RCC common at presentation?
cards.a: No. Most patients present before all three findings develop.

cards.q: Which paraneoplastic syndromes are associated with RCC?
cards.a: Polycythemia (↑EPO), hypercalcemia, hypertension, hepatic dysfunction (Stauffer syndrome), and others.

cards.q: Which imaging study is preferred for evaluating a suspected renal mass?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen (renal mass protocol when appropriate).

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for localized RCC?
cards.a: Partial nephrectomy when feasible, or radical nephrectomy depending on tumor characteristics. Renal Trauma

cards.q: Which imaging study is preferred for evaluating renal trauma in a hemodynamically stable patient?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis.

cards.q: Which patients with renal trauma generally require surgery?
cards.a: Hemodynamically unstable patients or those with certain severe injuries not amenable to nonoperative management. Obstructive Uropathy

cards.q: What is hydronephrosis?
cards.a: Dilation of the renal collecting system due to urinary tract obstruction.

cards.q: Which imaging study is commonly used first to detect hydronephrosis?
cards.a: Renal ultrasound.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment of obstructive uropathy?
cards.a: Relief of the obstruction (e.g., catheterization, ureteral stent, or percutaneous nephrostomy depending on the cause and level of obstruction). Postrenal Acute Kidney Injury

cards.q: What is the most common postrenal cause of acute kidney injury in older men?
cards.a: Benign prostatic hyperplasia causing bladder outlet obstruction.

cards.q: What bedside study rapidly detects urinary retention?
cards.a: Bladder ultrasound (bladder scan). Surgical Pearls

cards.q: Which urologic emergency requires immediate bladder decompression?
cards.a: Acute urinary retention.

cards.q: Which adult patient with hematuria requires urgent evaluation for malignancy?
cards.a: Any adult with painless gross hematuria, particularly those with smoking history or other urothelial cancer risk factors.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for common urologic surgical disease?
cards.a: Painless gross hematuria is bladder cancer until proven otherwise. Treat acute urinary retention with immediate catheterization, evaluate BPH with DRE and symptom assessment, and recognize that RCC often presents with incidental imaging findings rather than the classic triad.

cards.q: What is the most common type of kidney stone?
cards.a: Calcium oxalate stone.

cards.q: What are the four major types of kidney stones?
cards.a: Calcium oxalate/calcium phosphate, uric acid, struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate), and cystine.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of nephrolithiasis?
cards.a: Sudden, severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with hematuria, nausea, and vomiting.

cards.q: Which imaging study is the preferred initial test for suspected nephrolithiasis in most nonpregnant adults?
cards.a: Noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (CT KUB).

cards.q: Which imaging modality is preferred in pregnancy for suspected nephrolithiasis?
cards.a: Renal and bladder ultrasound.

cards.q: Which laboratory test should be obtained in all patients with suspected nephrolithiasis?
cards.a: Urinalysis (with urine culture if infection is suspected).

cards.q: Which stone is radiolucent on plain abdominal radiographs?
cards.a: Uric acid stone.

cards.q: Which stone is classically associated with urease-producing bacteria?
cards.a: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stone.

cards.q: Which organisms commonly produce struvite stones?
cards.a: Proteus, Klebsiella, and some other urease-producing organisms.

cards.q: Which stone forms staghorn calculi?
cards.a: Struvite stone.

cards.q: Which inherited disorder is associated with cystine stones?
cards.a: Cystinuria.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for a stable patient with a small ureteral stone (<10 mm)?
cards.a: Hydration, analgesia (NSAIDs when appropriate), and medical expulsive therapy in selected distal ureteral stones (e.g., tamsulosin).

cards.q: Which medication may facilitate passage of distal ureteral stones?
cards.a: Tamsulosin.

cards.q: Which patients with nephrolithiasis require urgent urologic decompression?
cards.a: Patients with obstructing stones plus infection (infected obstructed system), sepsis, solitary kidney with obstruction, bilateral obstruction, or worsening renal failure.

cards.q: What are the methods of urgent urinary decompression?
cards.a: Ureteral stent placement or percutaneous nephrostomy. Testicular Torsion

cards.q: What causes testicular torsion?
cards.a: Twisting of the spermatic cord, causing acute interruption of testicular blood flow.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of testicular torsion?
cards.a: Sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain with nausea and vomiting.

cards.q: Which physical examination finding strongly suggests testicular torsion?
cards.a: High-riding, horizontally oriented testis.

cards.q: Which reflex is typically absent in testicular torsion?
cards.a: Cremasteric reflex.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for testicular torsion?
cards.a: Immediate surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy.

cards.q: Should surgery be delayed for imaging when torsion is strongly suspected?
cards.a: No. Immediate surgery is indicated.

cards.q: What imaging study is used if the diagnosis is uncertain and torsion is less likely?
cards.a: Color Doppler scrotal ultrasound.

cards.q: Why is rapid treatment of testicular torsion essential?
cards.a: Testicular salvage rates decrease rapidly as ischemia duration increases. Epididymitis

cards.q: What is the most common cause of epididymitis in sexually active men <35 years?
cards.a: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of epididymitis in older men?
cards.a: Enteric gram-negative bacteria (e.g., Escherichia coli), often associated with urinary tract pathology.

cards.q: How does epididymitis differ clinically from testicular torsion?
cards.a: Epididymitis usually has gradual onset, preserved cremasteric reflex, epididymal tenderness, and often urinary symptoms.

cards.q: What is the treatment for epididymitis?
cards.a: Appropriate antibiotics based on likely pathogens, scrotal elevation, NSAIDs, and supportive care. Hydrocele & Varicocele

cards.q: What is a hydrocele?
cards.a: Collection of serous fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testicle.

cards.q: How does a hydrocele appear on transillumination?
cards.a: It transilluminates.

cards.q: What is a varicocele?
cards.a: Dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus.

cards.q: On which side do varicoceles occur most commonly?
cards.a: Left side.

cards.q: What physical examination finding is characteristic of a varicocele?
cards.a: "Bag of worms" appearance or feel.

cards.q: When should an isolated right-sided varicocele raise concern?
cards.a: It may suggest retroperitoneal pathology (e.g., renal or inferior vena cava obstruction) and warrants further evaluation. Fournier Gangrene

cards.q: What is Fournier gangrene?
cards.a: Necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and external genitalia.

cards.q: Which patients are at greatest risk for Fournier gangrene?
cards.a: Patients with diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, alcohol use disorder, obesity, or chronic kidney disease.

cards.q: What is the treatment for Fournier gangrene?
cards.a: Immediate surgical debridement, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, aggressive resuscitation, and repeated debridement as needed. Priapism

cards.q: What is ischemic (low-flow) priapism?
cards.a: Painful penile erection lasting >4 hours due to impaired venous outflow; it is a urologic emergency.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for ischemic priapism?
cards.a: Aspiration of corporal blood with intracavernosal phenylephrine.

cards.q: Which condition is classically associated with ischemic priapism?
cards.a: Sickle cell disease. Paraphimosis

cards.q: What is paraphimosis?
cards.a: Entrapment of a retracted foreskin behind the glans penis, causing venous congestion and possible ischemia.

cards.q: What is the treatment for paraphimosis?
cards.a: Immediate manual reduction after edema reduction; dorsal slit or circumcision if reduction fails. Bladder Cancer

cards.q: What is the most common histologic type of bladder cancer in the United States?
cards.a: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the strongest risk factor for bladder cancer?
cards.a: Cigarette smoking.

cards.q: What is the most common presentation of bladder cancer?
cards.a: Painless gross hematuria.

cards.q: What is the definitive diagnostic procedure for bladder cancer?
cards.a: Cystoscopy with transurethral resection/biopsy (TURBT). Urethral Injury

cards.q: Which pelvic injury is commonly associated with posterior urethral injury?
cards.a: Pelvic fracture.

cards.q: What clinical finding suggests urethral injury?
cards.a: Blood at the urethral meatus (often with inability to void and/or a high-riding prostate on DRE in posterior injury, though DRE is not highly sensitive).

cards.q: Which imaging study should be performed before urethral catheterization if urethral injury is suspected?
cards.a: Retrograde urethrogram (RUG). Urologic Trauma

cards.q: What is the most common injury to the urinary bladder?
cards.a: Extraperitoneal bladder rupture, usually associated with pelvic fracture.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for urologic surgery?
cards.a: Never miss testicular torsion—operate immediately if clinically suspected. Painless gross hematuria suggests bladder cancer until proven otherwise. An obstructed infected kidney requires urgent decompression, and suspected urethral injury requires a retrograde urethrogram before catheterization. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: What is a pneumothorax?
cards.a: Air within the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse.

cards.q: What is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
cards.a: A pneumothorax occurring without underlying lung disease, typically due to rupture of apical subpleural blebs in tall, thin young adults.

cards.q: What is a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax?
cards.a: A pneumothorax occurring in patients with underlying lung disease (e.g., COPD, cystic fibrosis, interstitial lung disease).

cards.q: What is the most common symptom of spontaneous pneumothorax?
cards.a: Sudden onset pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea.

cards.q: What physical examination findings suggest pneumothorax?
cards.a: Decreased breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion, and reduced chest expansion on the affected side.

cards.q: What is the initial imaging study for a stable patient with suspected pneumothorax?
cards.a: Upright chest radiograph (chest X-ray).

cards.q: What is the most life-threatening type of pneumothorax?
cards.a: Tension pneumothorax.

cards.q: What causes tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: A one-way valve mechanism allowing air into but not out of the pleural space, increasing intrathoracic pressure.

cards.q: What are the classic clinical features of tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Severe respiratory distress, hypotension, tachycardia, distended neck veins, unilateral absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side (a late sign).

cards.q: Should imaging be obtained before treating suspected tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: No. It is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate treatment.

cards.q: What is the immediate treatment for tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Immediate needle decompression (or finger thoracostomy where appropriate) followed by tube thoracostomy.

cards.q: Where is needle decompression commonly performed?
cards.a: Second intercostal space, midclavicular line, or fourth/fifth intercostal space at the anterior to mid-axillary line (based on current trauma practice and equipment).

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Tube thoracostomy (chest tube placement). Chest Tubes

cards.q: What is the preferred location for chest tube insertion?
cards.a: The "safe triangle" (approximately the 4th–5th intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line).

cards.q: Why is the superior border of the rib used for chest tube insertion?
cards.a: To avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle located along the inferior border of the rib.

cards.q: What are the major indications for chest tube placement?
cards.a: Pneumothorax, hemothorax, empyema, and selected pleural effusions.

cards.q: When can a chest tube usually be removed?
cards.a: After lung re-expansion, resolution of the air leak, and minimal appropriate drainage. Hemothorax

cards.q: What is a hemothorax?
cards.a: Blood within the pleural space.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of traumatic hemothorax?
cards.a: Blunt or penetrating chest trauma.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment of traumatic hemothorax?
cards.a: Tube thoracostomy.

cards.q: Which chest tube output generally indicates the need for urgent thoracic surgical evaluation?
cards.a: Initial drainage >1,500 mL or persistent bleeding >200 mL/hour for 2–4 hours (clinical judgment required). Massive Hemothorax

cards.q: What are the major clinical consequences of massive hemothorax?
cards.a: Hypovolemic shock and respiratory compromise.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for ongoing massive hemothorax?
cards.a: Surgical exploration (typically thoracotomy) when indicated. Rib Fractures

cards.q: What is the most common complication of rib fractures in older adults?
cards.a: Pneumonia due to inadequate ventilation from pain.

cards.q: What is the cornerstone of rib fracture management?
cards.a: Adequate multimodal pain control and pulmonary hygiene (e.g., incentive spirometry).

cards.q: Why should rib fracture pain be treated aggressively?
cards.a: To prevent atelectasis and pneumonia by allowing effective deep breathing and coughing. Flail Chest

cards.q: What is flail chest?
cards.a: Fractures of ≥3 consecutive ribs, each fractured in 2 or more places, creating a free-floating chest wall segment.

cards.q: What physical examination finding characterizes flail chest?
cards.a: Paradoxical chest wall movement during respiration.

cards.q: What injury commonly accompanies flail chest?
cards.a: Pulmonary contusion.

cards.q: What is the main treatment for flail chest?
cards.a: Adequate analgesia, respiratory support, pulmonary hygiene, and mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure develops. Pulmonary Contusion

cards.q: What is a pulmonary contusion?
cards.a: Bruising of the lung parenchyma causing alveolar hemorrhage and edema.

cards.q: What imaging study best identifies pulmonary contusion?
cards.a: CT chest (though chest X-ray findings may evolve over time).

cards.q: What is the primary treatment for pulmonary contusion?
cards.a: Supportive care with oxygen, pain control, and ventilatory support as needed while avoiding unnecessary fluid overload. Pleural Effusion

cards.q: What is a pleural effusion?
cards.a: Accumulation of fluid within the pleural space.

cards.q: What are the two major categories of pleural effusion?
cards.a: Transudative and exudative.

cards.q: Which criteria are used to differentiate transudative from exudative pleural effusions?
cards.a: Light's criteria.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of transudative pleural effusion?
cards.a: Congestive heart failure.

cards.q: What are common causes of exudative pleural effusions?
cards.a: Pneumonia, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, tuberculosis, pancreatitis, and inflammatory diseases. Empyema

cards.q: What is an empyema?
cards.a: Collection of pus within the pleural space.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of empyema?
cards.a: Complicated bacterial pneumonia.

cards.q: What is the treatment for empyema?
cards.a: Antibiotics plus pleural drainage (tube thoracostomy; surgery may be required if loculated or persistent). Thoracic Trauma

cards.q: Which imaging study is typically obtained first in a stable trauma patient with chest injury?
cards.a: Portable chest X-ray (with CT used for further evaluation when indicated).

cards.q: Which injury should be suspected after high-speed deceleration trauma with a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray?
cards.a: Traumatic aortic injury.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for suspected blunt thoracic aortic injury in a stable patient?
cards.a: CT angiography of the chest.

cards.q: What is Beck triad?
cards.a: Hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds.

cards.q: Which life-threatening condition is associated with Beck triad?
cards.a: Cardiac tamponade.

cards.q: What is the initial bedside imaging study for suspected cardiac tamponade in trauma?
cards.a: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) or focused cardiac ultrasound.

cards.q: What is the emergency treatment for traumatic cardiac tamponade?
cards.a: Immediate operative management in unstable trauma patients (pericardiocentesis may be a temporizing measure in selected settings).

cards.q: Which thoracic injuries are immediately life-threatening and must be recognized during the ATLS primary survey?
cards.a: Tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, cardiac tamponade, flail chest with pulmonary contusion, and major airway injury.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for thoracic trauma?
cards.a: Never delay treatment of tension pneumothorax for imaging. Insert chest tubes through the safe triangle, treat rib fractures with aggressive pain control to prevent pulmonary complications, and recognize massive hemothorax and cardiac tamponade as surgical emergencies.

cards.q: What is an esophageal perforation?
cards.a: A full-thickness tear of the esophageal wall causing leakage of esophageal contents into the mediastinum.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of esophageal perforation?
cards.a: Iatrogenic injury during endoscopy.

cards.q: What is Boerhaave syndrome?
cards.a: Spontaneous transmural esophageal rupture caused by forceful vomiting.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Boerhaave syndrome?
cards.a: Severe chest pain after repeated vomiting with subcutaneous emphysema and systemic toxicity.

cards.q: What is Mackler triad?
cards.a: Vomiting, chest pain, and subcutaneous emphysema.

cards.q: What imaging study is commonly used first in suspected esophageal perforation?
cards.a: CT chest with oral water-soluble contrast (or water-soluble contrast esophagram depending on the clinical situation).

cards.q: Why should barium generally be avoided initially if esophageal perforation is strongly suspected?
cards.a: Leakage of barium into the mediastinum can provoke significant inflammatory reactions.

cards.q: What is the initial management of esophageal perforation?
cards.a: NPO, IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, proton pump inhibitor, and urgent thoracic surgical consultation.

cards.q: Which patients usually require operative or endoscopic intervention for esophageal perforation?
cards.a: Patients with large leaks, sepsis, mediastinal contamination, or unstable clinical status. Achalasia

cards.q: What is achalasia?
cards.a: Failure of lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation with absent normal esophageal peristalsis.

cards.q: What are the classic symptoms of achalasia?
cards.a: Progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation, and weight loss.

cards.q: Which imaging finding is characteristic of achalasia on barium esophagram?
cards.a: Bird-beak narrowing of the distal esophagus.

cards.q: What is the gold standard diagnostic test for achalasia?
cards.a: High-resolution esophageal manometry.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for achalasia in appropriate surgical candidates?
cards.a: Laparoscopic Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication or peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) in selected patients. Esophageal Cancer

cards.q: What are the two major histologic types of esophageal cancer?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Which risk factors are most strongly associated with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Tobacco use, alcohol use, achalasia, caustic injury, and prior head and neck cancer.

cards.q: Which condition is the strongest precursor for esophageal adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: Barrett esophagus.

cards.q: What is the most common symptom of esophageal cancer?
cards.a: Progressive dysphagia, initially to solids and later to liquids.

cards.q: What is the preferred diagnostic test for suspected esophageal cancer?
cards.a: Upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy) with biopsy.

cards.q: Which imaging modality is commonly used for staging esophageal cancer?
cards.a: CT chest/abdomen with contrast and endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) for local staging; PET/CT may be used for metastatic evaluation. Lung Cancer

cards.q: What is the strongest risk factor for lung cancer?
cards.a: Cigarette smoking.

cards.q: What is the most common type of lung cancer?
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Which lung cancer is most commonly found in the peripheral lung?
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Which lung cancer is classically associated with central cavitary lesions and hypercalcemia?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma.
