cards.q: Which lung cancer is strongly associated with ectopic ACTH production and SIADH?
cards.a: Small cell lung carcinoma.

cards.q: Which lung cancer is usually treated primarily with chemotherapy and radiation rather than surgery?
cards.a: Small cell lung carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for evaluating a suspicious lung mass?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest.

cards.q: What is the definitive diagnostic test for lung cancer?
cards.a: Tissue biopsy (bronchoscopy, CT-guided biopsy, or surgical biopsy depending on lesion location). Solitary Pulmonary Nodule

cards.q: Which features increase the likelihood that a pulmonary nodule is malignant?
cards.a: Larger size, irregular or spiculated borders, upper lobe location, interval growth, older age, and smoking history.

cards.q: Which imaging modality helps assess metabolic activity of an indeterminate pulmonary nodule?
cards.a: FDG-PET/CT. Mediastinal Masses

cards.q: What are the classic "4 Ts" of anterior mediastinal masses?
cards.a: Thymoma, Teratoma (and other germ cell tumors), Thyroid mass, and "Terrible" lymphoma.

cards.q: Which mediastinal tumor is strongly associated with myasthenia gravis?
cards.a: Thymoma. Thoracic Outlet Syndrome

cards.q: What causes thoracic outlet syndrome?
cards.a: Compression of the brachial plexus and/or subclavian vessels at the thoracic outlet.

cards.q: What are common symptoms of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome?
cards.a: Arm pain, paresthesias, weakness, and hand fatigue, especially with overhead activity.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for most patients with neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome?
cards.a: Physical therapy and postural rehabilitation. Diaphragmatic Injury

cards.q: Which mechanism commonly causes traumatic diaphragmatic rupture?
cards.a: High-energy blunt trauma (especially motor vehicle collisions) or penetrating trauma.

cards.q: Which side is more commonly affected in blunt diaphragmatic rupture?
cards.a: Left side.

cards.q: Which imaging study is preferred in a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected diaphragmatic injury?
cards.a: CT scan of the chest and abdomen.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for traumatic diaphragmatic rupture?
cards.a: Surgical repair. Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS)

cards.q: What is VATS?
cards.a: A minimally invasive thoracic surgical technique using small incisions and a thoracoscope.

cards.q: What are common indications for VATS?
cards.a: Lung biopsy, wedge resection, treatment of spontaneous pneumothorax, empyema management, and selected lung cancer resections. Postoperative Thoracic Complications

cards.q: What is the most common pulmonary complication after thoracic or upper abdominal surgery?
cards.a: Atelectasis.

cards.q: How can postoperative atelectasis be prevented?
cards.a: Early ambulation, incentive spirometry, effective pain control, and pulmonary hygiene. Lung Resection

cards.q: What is the standard surgical treatment for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in appropriate candidates?
cards.a: Anatomic lobectomy with lymph node evaluation.

cards.q: Which preoperative pulmonary function parameter is important before major lung resection?
cards.a: Predicted postoperative pulmonary function (e.g., FEV₁ and DLCO). Thoracic Surgical Emergencies

cards.q: Which esophageal condition is a surgical emergency because of rapidly developing mediastinitis?
cards.a: Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophageal rupture).

cards.q: Which thoracic malignancy is considered an oncologic emergency when causing facial swelling and venous congestion?
cards.a: Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome, often due to lung cancer (especially small cell) or lymphoma.

cards.q: What is the initial management of suspected SVC syndrome?
cards.a: Confirm the diagnosis with imaging and obtain tissue diagnosis when feasible; manage airway compromise urgently and treat the underlying malignancy. High-Yield Review

cards.q: What is the key difference between achalasia and esophageal cancer?
cards.a: Achalasia typically causes dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the onset, whereas esophageal cancer usually causes progressive dysphagia beginning with solids.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for thoracic surgery?
cards.a: Never miss Boerhaave syndrome after forceful vomiting. Progressive dysphagia requires endoscopy with biopsy to exclude malignancy. Remember the "4 Ts" of anterior mediastinal masses, and treat early-stage NSCLC with surgical resection when appropriate, while small cell lung cancer is usually managed primarily with systemic therapy. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: What is hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction in young infants.

cards.q: At what age does hypertrophic pyloric stenosis most commonly present?
cards.a: 2–8 weeks of age (classically 3–6 weeks).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: Progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting after feeding in a hungry infant.

cards.q: Why is vomiting nonbilious in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: The obstruction is proximal to the duodenum, before bile enters the gastrointestinal tract.

cards.q: What classic abdominal examination finding is associated with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: A palpable "olive-like" mass in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium.

cards.q: Which visible physical examination finding may be seen after feeding?
cards.a: Visible gastric peristaltic waves moving from left to right.

cards.q: What is the preferred diagnostic test for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: Abdominal ultrasound.

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormality is classically associated with prolonged pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: Why does metabolic alkalosis occur in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) from repeated vomiting.

cards.q: What is the first step in management of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: Correct dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities before surgery.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy. Intussusception

cards.q: What is intussusception?
cards.a: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, causing intestinal obstruction and possible ischemia.

cards.q: What is the most common age for intussusception?
cards.a: 6–36 months, with a peak around 6–18 months.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of intussusception?
cards.a: Intermittent colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and currant jelly stool.

cards.q: Is the classic triad present in all patients with intussusception?
cards.a: No. Many children do not present with all three findings.

cards.q: What is the characteristic physical examination finding?
cards.a: Sausage-shaped abdominal mass.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial imaging study?
cards.a: Abdominal ultrasound.

cards.q: What ultrasound finding is characteristic of intussusception?
cards.a: Target sign (donut sign).

cards.q: What is both the diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for stable intussusception without perforation?
cards.a: Air (or contrast) enema reduction.

cards.q: When is surgery indicated for intussusception?
cards.a: Failed enema reduction, perforation, peritonitis, bowel ischemia, or hemodynamic instability. Meckel Diverticulum

cards.q: What is Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: A congenital true diverticulum resulting from persistence of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct.

cards.q: What is the "Rule of 2s" for Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: 2% of the population, ~2 inches long, within ~2 feet of the ileocecal valve, may contain 2 types of ectopic mucosa (gastric and pancreatic), often presents before age 2 (mnemonic only; not exact).

cards.q: What is the most common presentation of Meckel diverticulum in children?
cards.a: Painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding.

cards.q: Why does Meckel diverticulum bleed?
cards.a: Ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid, causing adjacent ileal ulceration.

cards.q: What is the preferred diagnostic test?
cards.a: Technetium-99m pertechnetate (Meckel) scan.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for symptomatic Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: Surgical resection. Malrotation & Midgut Volvulus

cards.q: What causes intestinal malrotation?
cards.a: Abnormal embryologic rotation and fixation of the midgut.

cards.q: What life-threatening complication can occur with malrotation?
cards.a: Midgut volvulus.

cards.q: What is the hallmark symptom of midgut volvulus?
cards.a: Bilious vomiting in a neonate.

cards.q: Why is bilious vomiting in a neonate considered a surgical emergency?
cards.a: It suggests intestinal obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Which imaging study is the gold standard for diagnosing malrotation?
cards.a: Upper gastrointestinal contrast series.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for malrotation with volvulus?
cards.a: Emergent Ladd procedure. Hirschsprung Disease

cards.q: What causes Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a: Congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in the distal bowel.

cards.q: Which portion of the colon is most commonly affected?
cards.a: Rectosigmoid colon.

cards.q: What is the classic neonatal presentation?
cards.a: Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life.

cards.q: What other symptoms are common in Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a: Abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, chronic constipation, and poor feeding.

cards.q: Which imaging finding is characteristic on contrast enema?
cards.a: Transition zone between dilated proximal bowel and narrow aganglionic distal bowel.

cards.q: What is the definitive diagnostic test?
cards.a: Rectal suction biopsy demonstrating absence of ganglion cells.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment?
cards.a: Surgical pull-through procedure. Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC)

cards.q: Which infants are at highest risk for necrotizing enterocolitis?
cards.a: Premature, low-birth-weight infants.

cards.q: What are the classic symptoms of NEC?
cards.a: Feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, bloody stools, lethargy, and temperature instability.

cards.q: What abdominal X-ray finding is pathognomonic for NEC?
cards.a: Pneumatosis intestinalis.

cards.q: What additional radiographic finding suggests bowel perforation?
cards.a: Free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum).

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for NEC?
cards.a: NPO, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and supportive care.

cards.q: When is surgery indicated in NEC?
cards.a: Perforation, intestinal necrosis, clinical deterioration despite medical management, or fixed bowel loop concerning for necrosis. Pediatric Surgical Principles

cards.q: What is the most important diagnosis to exclude in any neonate with bilious vomiting?
cards.a: Midgut volvulus.

cards.q: Which pediatric abdominal emergency is treated with air enema rather than immediate surgery?
cards.a: Intussusception (if stable and without perforation/peritonitis).

cards.q: Which congenital GI disorder classically presents with painless rectal bleeding?
cards.a: Meckel diverticulum.

cards.q: Which neonatal disorder classically causes failure to pass meconium within 48 hours?
cards.a: Hirschsprung disease.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for neonatal gastrointestinal emergencies?
cards.a: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise. Projectile nonbilious vomiting suggests pyloric stenosis, currant jelly stool suggests intussusception, painless GI bleeding suggests Meckel diverticulum, and delayed meconium passage suggests Hirschsprung disease.

cards.q: What is esophageal atresia?
cards.a: Congenital interruption of the esophagus, preventing continuity between the proximal and distal esophagus.

cards.q: What is the most common type of esophageal atresia?
cards.a: Proximal esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula (EA with distal TEF).

cards.q: What are the classic neonatal findings of esophageal atresia?
cards.a: Excessive salivation, choking, coughing, cyanosis during feeding, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube.

cards.q: Which prenatal finding commonly suggests esophageal atresia?
cards.a: Polyhydramnios.

cards.q: What radiographic finding supports the diagnosis of EA with distal TEF?
cards.a: A nasogastric tube coiled in the proximal esophageal pouch with air in the stomach and intestines.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for EA/TEF?
cards.a: Surgical repair after stabilization.

cards.q: Which congenital anomaly association should always be considered in infants with EA/TEF?
cards.a: VACTERL association (Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, Tracheoesophageal, Renal, Limb anomalies). Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH)

cards.q: What causes congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
cards.a: Failure of complete diaphragm formation, allowing abdominal organs to herniate into the thoracic cavity.

cards.q: Which side is most commonly affected in CDH?
cards.a: Left posterolateral side (Bochdalek hernia).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
cards.a: Severe respiratory distress immediately after birth with a scaphoid abdomen.

cards.q: Why do infants with CDH develop severe respiratory failure?
cards.a: Pulmonary hypoplasia and persistent pulmonary hypertension.

cards.q: What is the first priority in managing CDH?
cards.a: Immediate endotracheal intubation and gastric decompression with a nasogastric tube.

cards.q: Should bag-mask ventilation be used in congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
cards.a: No. It can worsen respiratory compromise by insufflating bowel within the thorax.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for CDH?
cards.a: Surgical repair after cardiopulmonary stabilization. Omphalocele

cards.q: What is an omphalocele?
cards.a: Herniation of abdominal contents through the umbilical ring covered by a membranous sac.

cards.q: Which congenital abnormalities are commonly associated with omphalocele?
cards.a: Cardiac defects, chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., trisomy 13 and 18), and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

cards.q: What is the initial management of omphalocele?
cards.a: Protect the sac, prevent heat and fluid loss, stabilize the infant, and plan surgical repair. Gastroschisis

cards.q: What is gastroschisis?
cards.a: Full-thickness abdominal wall defect, usually to the right of the umbilicus, with exposed bowel and no protective sac.

cards.q: How does gastroschisis differ from omphalocele?
cards.a: Gastroschisis has no covering membrane and fewer associated congenital anomalies.

cards.q: What is the initial management of gastroschisis?
cards.a: Cover exposed bowel with sterile saline-moistened dressings and plastic wrap, provide IV fluids, gastric decompression, temperature control, and urgent surgical consultation.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for gastroschisis?
cards.a: Surgical reduction and abdominal wall closure (primary or staged using a silo). Anorectal Malformations

cards.q: What is imperforate anus?
cards.a: Congenital absence or abnormal location of the anal opening.

cards.q: What is the typical neonatal presentation of imperforate anus?
cards.a: Failure to pass meconium with absent or abnormal anal opening.

cards.q: Which congenital association should be considered in imperforate anus?
cards.a: VACTERL association.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for imperforate anus?
cards.a: Surgical correction, often after evaluation for associated anomalies. Pediatric Inguinal Hernia

cards.q: What causes indirect inguinal hernias in children?
cards.a: Persistence of the processus vaginalis.

cards.q: Which children are at greatest risk for incarcerated inguinal hernia?
cards.a: Premature infants and young infants.

cards.q: What is the treatment for pediatric inguinal hernia?
cards.a: Elective surgical repair after diagnosis; urgent surgery if incarcerated or strangulated. Hydrocele

cards.q: What causes a communicating hydrocele?
cards.a: Persistent processus vaginalis allowing peritoneal fluid to enter the scrotum.

cards.q: When is surgery indicated for pediatric hydrocele?
cards.a: Persistent communicating hydrocele (or one that does not resolve appropriately with observation), symptomatic hydrocele, or associated hernia. Cryptorchidism (Undescended Testis)

cards.q: What is cryptorchidism?
cards.a: Failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum.

cards.q: What are the long-term complications of untreated cryptorchidism?
cards.a: Infertility, testicular cancer, inguinal hernia, and testicular torsion.

cards.q: At what age should orchiopexy ideally be performed?
cards.a: Between 6–18 months of age (commonly by 12–18 months).

cards.q: Does orchiopexy eliminate the future risk of testicular cancer?
cards.a: No, but it reduces risk and improves surveillance. Pediatric Testicular Disorders

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acute scrotal pain requiring emergency surgery in children?
cards.a: Testicular torsion.

cards.q: What is the first imaging study if torsion is uncertain?
cards.a: Color Doppler scrotal ultrasound.

cards.q: If clinical suspicion for torsion is high, should surgery await imaging?
cards.a: No. Immediate surgical exploration is indicated. Necrotizing Soft Tissue Infection

cards.q: Which rapidly progressive pediatric soft tissue infection requires emergency surgery?
cards.a: Necrotizing fasciitis.

cards.q: What is the treatment for necrotizing fasciitis?
cards.a: Immediate surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and aggressive supportive care. Pediatric Trauma

cards.q: Which solid abdominal organ is most commonly injured after blunt abdominal trauma in children?
cards.a: Spleen.

cards.q: What is the preferred management of most hemodynamically stable pediatric splenic injuries?
cards.a: Nonoperative management with close monitoring.

cards.q: Which imaging study is preferred for evaluating stable pediatric abdominal trauma?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis. Pediatric Surgical Oncology

cards.q: What is the most common renal malignancy in children?
cards.a: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma).

cards.q: Which syndrome is classically associated with Wilms tumor?
cards.a: WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability).

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for localized Wilms tumor?
cards.a: Radical nephrectomy with multimodal therapy based on staging. Pediatric Surgical Principles

cards.q: Which congenital abdominal wall defect is covered by a membrane?
cards.a: Omphalocele.

cards.q: Which congenital abdominal wall defect has exposed bowel without a membrane?
cards.a: Gastroschisis.

cards.q: Which neonatal respiratory emergency requires immediate intubation and avoidance of bag-mask ventilation?
cards.a: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

cards.q: Which congenital anomaly is frequently associated with multiple organ-system defects requiring systematic evaluation?
cards.a: Esophageal atresia/tracheoesophageal fistula and imperforate anus (consider VACTERL association).

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for pediatric surgery?
cards.a: Membrane present = omphalocele; membrane absent = gastroschisis. Bilious vomiting is volvulus until proven otherwise, failure to pass an NG tube suggests esophageal atresia, avoid bag-mask ventilation in congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and perform early orchiopexy for undescended testes. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

topic: Plastic, Reconstructive, Skin & Soft Tissue Surgery

cards.q: What is the most common skin cancer?
cards.a: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC).

cards.q: What is the strongest risk factor for BCC?
cards.a: Chronic ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure.

cards.q: What is the classic appearance of basal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Pearly papule with rolled borders and surface telangiectasias; ulceration may occur ("rodent ulcer").

cards.q: Which areas are most commonly affected by BCC?
cards.a: Sun-exposed areas, especially the head and neck.

cards.q: Does basal cell carcinoma commonly metastasize?
cards.a: No. Metastasis is extremely rare, but local tissue destruction can be significant.

cards.q: What is the definitive diagnosis of BCC?
cards.a: Skin biopsy.

cards.q: What is the preferred treatment for most localized BCCs?
cards.a: Surgical excision with histologically clear margins.

cards.q: When is Mohs micrographic surgery preferred for BCC?
cards.a: High-risk lesions (e.g., cosmetically sensitive areas, recurrent tumors, or lesions with ill-defined borders). Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)

cards.q: What is the second most common skin cancer?
cards.a: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).

cards.q: What are major risk factors for SCC?
cards.a: Chronic UV exposure, immunosuppression, chronic wounds/scars (Marjolin ulcer), radiation exposure, and HPV for some anatomic sites.

cards.q: How does SCC typically appear?
cards.a: Firm, hyperkeratotic, scaly plaque or nodule that may ulcerate.

cards.q: Does SCC have metastatic potential?
cards.a: Yes, particularly for larger, deeper, high-risk, or immunosuppression-associated tumors.

cards.q: What is the preferred treatment for localized SCC?
cards.a: Surgical excision; Mohs surgery is used for selected high-risk lesions. Melanoma

cards.q: What is the most dangerous common skin cancer?
cards.a: Melanoma.

cards.q: Which mnemonic is used to evaluate suspicious pigmented lesions?
cards.a: ABCDE: Asymmetry Border irregularity Color variation Diameter ≥6 mm (or enlarging lesion) Evolving lesion

cards.q: What is the strongest environmental risk factor for melanoma?
cards.a: Intermittent intense UV exposure causing blistering sunburns.

cards.q: Which patients have increased melanoma risk?
cards.a: Fair skin, numerous or atypical nevi, family history, prior melanoma, and immunosuppression.

cards.q: What is the preferred biopsy for suspected melanoma?
cards.a: Excisional biopsy with narrow margins whenever feasible.

cards.q: Which histologic measurement is the most important prognostic factor for localized melanoma?
cards.a: Breslow thickness.

cards.q: When is sentinel lymph node biopsy generally considered?
cards.a: For melanomas with sufficient Breslow thickness and/or other high-risk features according to current guidelines.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for localized melanoma?
cards.a: Wide local excision with margins based on Breslow thickness. Pressure Injuries (Pressure Ulcers)

cards.q: What causes pressure injuries?
cards.a: Prolonged pressure causing tissue ischemia, often over bony prominences.

cards.q: Which patients are at greatest risk for pressure injuries?
cards.a: Immobile, elderly, malnourished, spinal cord–injured, and critically ill patients.

cards.q: Which area is most commonly affected?
cards.a: Sacrum.

cards.q: How is a Stage I pressure injury defined?
cards.a: Intact skin with nonblanchable erythema.

cards.q: How is a Stage II pressure injury defined?
cards.a: Partial-thickness skin loss involving epidermis and/or dermis.

cards.q: How is a Stage III pressure injury defined?
cards.a: Full-thickness skin loss extending into subcutaneous tissue.

cards.q: How is a Stage IV pressure injury defined?
cards.a: Full-thickness tissue loss with exposed muscle, tendon, fascia, cartilage, or bone.

cards.q: What is the cornerstone of pressure injury prevention?
cards.a: Frequent repositioning and pressure redistribution.

cards.q: What is the cornerstone of pressure injury treatment?
cards.a: Pressure relief, wound care, nutritional optimization, and debridement of necrotic tissue when indicated. Keloids & Hypertrophic Scars

cards.q: What is a hypertrophic scar?
cards.a: Excess scar tissue confined to the original wound boundaries.

cards.q: What is a keloid?
cards.a: Excess scar tissue extending beyond the original wound margins.

cards.q: Which patients are more prone to keloid formation?
cards.a: Individuals with darker skin pigmentation and a positive family history.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for symptomatic keloids?
cards.a: Intralesional corticosteroid injections (often combined with other therapies as needed). Skin Grafts

cards.q: What is a split-thickness skin graft (STSG)?
cards.a: Graft containing the epidermis and part of the dermis.

cards.q: What is a full-thickness skin graft (FTSG)?
cards.a: Graft containing the epidermis and the entire dermis.

cards.q: Which type of graft generally has better cosmetic results?
cards.a: Full-thickness skin graft.

cards.q: Which graft generally has higher take rates on less ideal wound beds?
cards.a: Split-thickness skin graft. Flaps

cards.q: What is the difference between a flap and a graft?
cards.a: A flap retains or receives its own blood supply, whereas a graft relies on revascularization from the recipient bed.

cards.q: When are flaps preferred over grafts?
cards.a: When vascularized tissue is needed to cover exposed bone, tendon, hardware, or poorly vascularized wounds. Bite Wounds

cards.q: Which animal causes the most bite injuries?
cards.a: Dogs.

cards.q: Which animal bite carries the highest infection risk?
cards.a: Cat bites.

cards.q: Which organism is classically associated with cat and dog bites?
cards.a: Pasteurella multocida.

cards.q: What is the first-line antibiotic for prophylaxis or treatment of many dog and cat bites?
cards.a: Amoxicillin-clavulanate.

cards.q: Which organism is classically associated with human bites?
cards.a: Eikenella corrodens.

cards.q: Which human bite injury is considered particularly high risk?
cards.a: Closed-fist ("fight bite") injury over the metacarpophalangeal joint. Soft Tissue Masses

cards.q: What is the most common benign soft tissue tumor?
cards.a: Lipoma.

cards.q: Which features of a soft tissue mass raise concern for sarcoma?
cards.a: Size >5 cm, deep location, rapid growth, firmness, fixation, or recurrence.

cards.q: Which imaging study is preferred before biopsy of a suspected soft tissue sarcoma?
cards.a: MRI with contrast (for extremity lesions).

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for skin and soft tissue surgery?
cards.a: BCC rarely metastasizes but can be locally destructive. Melanoma prognosis depends largely on Breslow thickness. Cat bites have a high infection risk, human bites require aggressive management, pressure injuries are best prevented with frequent repositioning, and suspicious soft tissue masses should be evaluated for sarcoma before definitive treatment. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: How is sepsis defined?
cards.a: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.

cards.q: What bedside score is commonly used to rapidly identify patients at risk for poor outcomes from sepsis?
cards.a: qSOFA (Quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment).

cards.q: What are the components of qSOFA?
cards.a: Respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mental status, and systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg.

cards.q: What is septic shock?
cards.a: A subset of sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg despite adequate fluid resuscitation, with elevated serum lactate indicating significant circulatory/metabolic dysfunction.

cards.q: What are the three priorities during the initial management of sepsis?
cards.a: Early recognition, rapid IV fluid resuscitation, and prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics.

cards.q: How soon should broad-spectrum antibiotics ideally be administered after sepsis is recognized?
cards.a: As soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour in septic shock or high suspicion.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial crystalloid for fluid resuscitation in septic shock?
cards.a: Balanced crystalloids (e.g., lactated Ringer's) are often preferred; normal saline is also acceptable.

cards.q: What initial crystalloid volume is commonly recommended for septic shock?
cards.a: Approximately 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid for patients with hypoperfusion, while individualizing based on clinical status.

cards.q: What laboratory marker is commonly followed to assess tissue hypoperfusion in sepsis?
cards.a: Serum lactate.

cards.q: What is source control in sepsis?
cards.a: Elimination of the infection source (e.g., abscess drainage, debridement, removal of infected devices, surgery). Vasopressors

cards.q: Which vasopressor is first-line for septic shock?
cards.a: Norepinephrine.

cards.q: What is the target mean arterial pressure (MAP) in most patients with septic shock?
cards.a: ≥65 mmHg.

cards.q: Which vasopressor is commonly added if norepinephrine alone is insufficient?
cards.a: Vasopressin (typically as an adjunct).

cards.q: Which catecholamine is often used when there is persistent hypoperfusion with reduced cardiac output despite adequate MAP?
cards.a: Dobutamine (when appropriate for myocardial dysfunction).

cards.q: When should vasopressors be started?
cards.a: After or during adequate fluid resuscitation if hypotension persists. Mechanical Ventilation

cards.q: What is the most common indication for endotracheal intubation in the ICU?
cards.a: Acute respiratory failure with inability to maintain oxygenation, ventilation, or airway protection.

cards.q: What are the two major categories of respiratory failure?
cards.a: Hypoxemic (Type I) and hypercapnic (Type II).

cards.q: Which ventilator strategy is recommended for ARDS?
cards.a: Lung-protective ventilation using low tidal volumes.

cards.q: What tidal volume is recommended in ARDS?
cards.a: Approximately 6 mL/kg predicted body weight.

cards.q: Why are low tidal volumes used in ARDS?
cards.a: To reduce ventilator-induced lung injury.

cards.q: What is positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP)?
cards.a: Pressure maintained in the lungs at end expiration to prevent alveolar collapse.

cards.q: What is a potential complication of excessive PEEP?
cards.a: Reduced venous return leading to hypotension and possible barotrauma. Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)

cards.q: What is ARDS?
cards.a: Acute inflammatory lung injury causing diffuse alveolar damage and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.

cards.q: What are common causes of ARDS?
cards.a: Sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, major trauma, pancreatitis, massive transfusion, and severe burns.

cards.q: What are the characteristic chest X-ray findings in ARDS?
cards.a: Bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates not fully explained by heart failure or volume overload.

cards.q: What is the hallmark physiologic abnormality in ARDS?
cards.a: Severe hypoxemia due to intrapulmonary shunting.

cards.q: What is the primary treatment for ARDS?
cards.a: Treat the underlying cause and provide lung-protective mechanical ventilation.

cards.q: Which positioning strategy improves oxygenation in severe ARDS?
cards.a: Prone positioning.

cards.q: Should routine corticosteroids be given to every patient with ARDS?
cards.a: No. Use depends on the underlying cause and current evidence/guidelines. Sedation & Analgesia

cards.q: Which medication is commonly used for ICU sedation?
cards.a: Propofol (among several acceptable options).

cards.q: What is a major adverse effect of propofol?
cards.a: Hypotension.

cards.q: Which sedative provides anxiolysis with minimal respiratory depression and may facilitate lighter sedation?
cards.a: Dexmedetomidine.

cards.q: Which medications are commonly used for analgesia in mechanically ventilated ICU patients?
cards.a: Opioids such as fentanyl or hydromorphone, tailored to the clinical situation.

cards.q: Why are daily spontaneous awakening trials often performed?
cards.a: To minimize oversedation, shorten ventilation duration, and facilitate neurologic assessment when appropriate. ICU Delirium

cards.q: Which ICU complication is associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation and worse outcomes?
cards.a: Delirium.

cards.q: What are important nonpharmacologic measures to reduce ICU delirium?
cards.a: Early mobilization, sleep promotion, reorientation, minimizing unnecessary sedation, and ensuring use of hearing aids/glasses when needed. Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis

cards.q: Which ICU patients generally require stress ulcer prophylaxis?
cards.a: Selected high-risk patients (e.g., prolonged mechanical ventilation, coagulopathy, major burns, traumatic brain injury).

cards.q: Which medications are commonly used for stress ulcer prophylaxis?
cards.a: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) or H₂ receptor blockers. Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) Prophylaxis

cards.q: Why do ICU patients require VTE prophylaxis?
cards.a: They are at high risk for DVT and pulmonary embolism due to immobility and critical illness.

cards.q: What pharmacologic agents are commonly used for VTE prophylaxis?
cards.a: Low-molecular-weight heparin or low-dose unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated. Hemodynamic Monitoring

cards.q: What is the purpose of an arterial line?
cards.a: Continuous blood pressure monitoring and frequent arterial blood gas sampling.

cards.q: What is the primary use of a central venous catheter in the ICU?
cards.a: Administration of vasopressors, central venous access, and selected hemodynamic monitoring. Oxygen Delivery

cards.q: What determines oxygen delivery (DO₂) to tissues?
cards.a: Cardiac output × arterial oxygen content.

cards.q: What are the major components of arterial oxygen content?
cards.a: Hemoglobin concentration and arterial oxygen saturation (with a small dissolved oxygen component). ICU Infections

cards.q: What is the best method for preventing catheter-associated bloodstream infections?
cards.a: Strict aseptic insertion technique and prompt removal when no longer needed.

cards.q: What is the most effective strategy for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)?
cards.a: Ventilator care bundles (e.g., head-of-bed elevation, oral hygiene, minimizing sedation, and daily assessment for extubation readiness). High-Yield Review

cards.q: Which vasopressor is first-line for septic shock?
cards.a: Norepinephrine.

cards.q: Which ventilator strategy reduces mortality in ARDS?
cards.a: Low tidal volume (lung-protective) ventilation.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for septic shock beyond antibiotics and vasopressors?
cards.a: Source control (e.g., drainage, debridement, or surgery when indicated).

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for surgical critical care?
cards.a: Recognize sepsis early, administer prompt antibiotics, aggressively resuscitate with crystalloids, use norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor if hypotension persists, perform source control, and ventilate ARDS patients with low tidal volumes and appropriate PEEP.

cards.q: What is the preferred route of nutritional support in critically ill patients with a functional gastrointestinal tract?
cards.a: Enteral nutrition (EN).

cards.q: Why is enteral nutrition preferred over total parenteral nutrition (TPN)?
cards.a: It maintains gut mucosal integrity, reduces bacterial translocation, lowers infectious complications, and is generally less costly.

cards.q: When should enteral nutrition generally be initiated in hemodynamically stable ICU patients?
cards.a: Within 24–48 hours of ICU admission if feasible.

cards.q: When is total parenteral nutrition (TPN) indicated?
cards.a: When the gastrointestinal tract cannot be used or enteral feeding is contraindicated or insufficient.

cards.q: What are common complications of TPN?
cards.a: Catheter-related bloodstream infection, hyperglycemia, electrolyte abnormalities, hepatic dysfunction, and thrombosis. Refeeding Syndrome

cards.q: What is refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Potentially life-threatening electrolyte and fluid shifts that occur after restarting nutrition in severely malnourished patients.

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Hypophosphatemia.

cards.q: Which other electrolyte abnormalities commonly occur in refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia.

cards.q: Which patients are at highest risk for refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Patients with prolonged starvation, anorexia nervosa, chronic alcohol use disorder, severe malnutrition, or significant recent weight loss.

cards.q: How can refeeding syndrome be prevented?
cards.a: Begin nutrition slowly, replace electrolytes (especially phosphate, potassium, and magnesium), and administer thiamine before or with refeeding in high-risk patients. Blood Transfusion

cards.q: What blood component is used to increase oxygen-carrying capacity?
cards.a: Packed red blood cells (PRBCs).

cards.q: What blood component is used for thrombocytopenia with bleeding or before invasive procedures when indicated?
cards.a: Platelets.

cards.q: What blood component is used to replace multiple clotting factors?
cards.a: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP).

cards.q: Which blood product is rich in fibrinogen?
cards.a: Cryoprecipitate.

cards.q: Which blood type is considered the universal donor for packed red blood cells?
cards.a: O Rh-negative.

cards.q: Which blood type is the universal recipient for packed red blood cells?
cards.a: AB Rh-positive. Transfusion Reactions

cards.q: What is the most serious acute transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction due to ABO incompatibility.

cards.q: What are common symptoms of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Fever, chills, flank pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, and possible disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

cards.q: What is the first step in managing any suspected transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Immediately stop the transfusion while maintaining IV access with normal saline and begin evaluation.

cards.q: What is transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)?
cards.a: Acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema occurring during or within 6 hours of transfusion. Massive Transfusion

cards.q: What is massive transfusion?
cards.a: Commonly defined as transfusion of ≥10 units of PRBCs within 24 hours or equivalent replacement of blood volume.

cards.q: What is the goal of a massive transfusion protocol (MTP)?
cards.a: Rapid balanced replacement of blood components while correcting coagulopathy and maintaining perfusion.

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality commonly develops during massive transfusion because of citrate?
cards.a: Hypocalcemia.

cards.q: Why should calcium levels be monitored during massive transfusion?
cards.a: Citrate in stored blood binds ionized calcium, which may impair myocardial function and coagulation. Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)

cards.q: What is DIC?
cards.a: Widespread activation of coagulation leading to simultaneous thrombosis and bleeding.

cards.q: What are common causes of DIC?
cards.a: Sepsis, severe trauma, obstetric emergencies, and malignancy.

cards.q: What laboratory abnormalities are typical of DIC?
cards.a: ↓ Platelets, ↑ PT/INR, ↑ aPTT, ↓ fibrinogen, and ↑ D-dimer.

cards.q: What is the cornerstone of DIC treatment?
cards.a: Treat the underlying cause and provide supportive transfusion therapy when clinically indicated. Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)

cards.q: What is the most common cause of AKI in postoperative patients?
cards.a: Prerenal azotemia due to hypovolemia or decreased renal perfusion.

cards.q: What is the first step in evaluating postoperative oliguria?
cards.a: Assess volume status, hemodynamics, urine output trends, medications, and exclude urinary tract obstruction.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial treatment for prerenal AKI?
cards.a: Restore adequate intravascular volume and improve renal perfusion.

cards.q: Which urinary electrolyte finding suggests prerenal AKI?
cards.a: Low urine sodium (typically <20 mEq/L) and low fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa <1%) in appropriate clinical settings. Compartment Syndrome

cards.q: What causes compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment causing impaired tissue perfusion.

cards.q: What is the earliest and most important symptom of compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Severe pain out of proportion to the injury, especially with passive stretch.

cards.q: Which "6 Ps" are associated with compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Pain, pallor, paresthesia, paralysis, pulselessness, and poikilothermia (pulselessness is a late finding).

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Emergent fasciotomy. Rhabdomyolysis

cards.q: What is rhabdomyolysis?
cards.a: Skeletal muscle breakdown causing release of intracellular contents, including myoglobin.

cards.q: Which laboratory value is most sensitive for rhabdomyolysis?
cards.a: Markedly elevated creatine kinase (CK).

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality commonly occurs early in rhabdomyolysis?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia.

cards.q: What is the primary treatment for rhabdomyolysis?
cards.a: Aggressive IV isotonic fluid resuscitation while treating the underlying cause. ICU Electrolytes

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely to cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia.

cards.q: What ECG changes are classically seen in hyperkalemia?
cards.a: Peaked T waves, PR prolongation, QRS widening, and, in severe cases, a sine-wave pattern.

cards.q: What is the first medication given for hyperkalemia with ECG changes?
cards.a: IV calcium (calcium gluconate or calcium chloride, depending on the clinical setting) to stabilize the cardiac membrane.

cards.q: Which therapies shift potassium into cells?
cards.a: IV insulin with glucose, β₂-agonists (e.g., albuterol), and sodium bicarbonate in selected patients with metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: Which treatment removes potassium from the body most rapidly in severe or refractory cases?
cards.a: Hemodialysis. Acid–Base Disorders

cards.q: Which acid–base disorder is commonly seen in septic shock?
cards.a: High anion gap metabolic acidosis due to lactic acidosis.

cards.q: Which acid–base disorder is classically associated with prolonged vomiting?
cards.a: Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: Which acid–base disorder commonly occurs with severe diarrhea?
cards.a: Non–anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. High-Yield ICU Review

cards.q: What is the preferred nutritional route in critically ill patients with a functioning gastrointestinal tract?
cards.a: Enteral nutrition.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK principle for surgical critical care?
cards.a: Feed the gut when possible, recognize hypophosphatemia as the hallmark of refeeding syndrome, stop any transfusion immediately if a reaction is suspected, treat compartment syndrome with emergent fasciotomy, aggressively hydrate rhabdomyolysis, and stabilize the myocardium first with IV calcium in hyperkalemia with ECG changes. -------------------------------------- -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: What are the goals of the pre-anesthetic evaluation?
cards.a: Assess perioperative risk, optimize medical conditions, identify difficult airway, review medications/allergies, determine anesthesia plan, and obtain informed consent.

cards.q: Which patient history is most important before anesthesia?
cards.a: Previous anesthesia complications, difficult intubation, malignant hyperthermia, allergies, medications, cardiopulmonary disease, and obstructive sleep apnea.

cards.q: Why should previous anesthesia records be reviewed?
cards.a: They may reveal difficult airway, adverse drug reactions, or prior anesthetic complications.

cards.q: Which inherited anesthetic complication should always be asked about during the preoperative assessment?
cards.a: Malignant hyperthermia.

cards.q: Which medications require special perioperative planning?
cards.a: Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, insulin, oral hypoglycemics, corticosteroids, antihypertensives, and immunosuppressants. ASA Physical Status Classification

cards.q: What is the ASA Physical Status Classification used for?
cards.a: Estimating perioperative anesthetic risk based on overall systemic health.

cards.q: What is ASA Class I?
cards.a: Healthy patient with no systemic disease.

cards.q: What is ASA Class II?
cards.a: Mild systemic disease without functional limitation (e.g., well-controlled hypertension or diabetes).

cards.q: What is ASA Class III?
cards.a: Severe systemic disease with functional limitation (e.g., stable angina, poorly controlled diabetes).

cards.q: What is ASA Class IV?
cards.a: Severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life (e.g., decompensated heart failure).

cards.q: What is ASA Class V?
cards.a: Moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation.

cards.q: What is ASA Class VI?
cards.a: Brain-dead organ donor.

cards.q: What does the suffix "E" indicate in ASA classification?
cards.a: Emergency surgery. Airway Assessment

cards.q: Why is airway assessment essential before anesthesia?
cards.a: To predict difficult ventilation or intubation and prepare appropriate airway management.

cards.q: Which bedside airway classification is most commonly used?
cards.a: Mallampati classification.

cards.q: How is Mallampati Class I defined?
cards.a: Soft palate, uvula, fauces, and tonsillar pillars are fully visible.

cards.q: How is Mallampati Class II defined?
cards.a: Uvula is partially obscured but mostly visible.

cards.q: How is Mallampati Class III defined?
cards.a: Only the base of the uvula and soft palate are visible.

cards.q: How is Mallampati Class IV defined?
cards.a: Only the hard palate is visible.

cards.q: Which Mallampati classes predict the greatest likelihood of difficult intubation?
cards.a: Class III and Class IV. Thyromental Distance

cards.q: What is the thyromental distance?
cards.a: Distance from the thyroid notch to the mentum (chin).

cards.q: Which thyromental distance suggests difficult intubation?
cards.a: Less than approximately 6 cm (or fewer than 3 fingerbreadths). Mouth Opening

cards.q: What minimum mouth opening is generally needed for conventional laryngoscopy?
cards.a: Approximately 3 fingerbreadths.

cards.q: Which conditions reduce mouth opening?
cards.a: TMJ disorders, facial trauma, radiation fibrosis, and trismus. Neck Mobility

cards.q: Why is neck extension important during intubation?
cards.a: It aligns the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes for improved visualization.

cards.q: Which patients commonly have limited neck mobility?
cards.a: Cervical spine injury, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and severe cervical spondylosis. Difficult Airway Predictors

cards.q: Name common predictors of a difficult airway.
cards.a: Mallampati III/IV, obesity, OSA, short neck, limited mouth opening, reduced neck mobility, facial trauma, and prior difficult intubation.

cards.q: Which historical factor is the strongest predictor of future difficult intubation?
cards.a: Previous documented difficult intubation. STOP-BANG

cards.q: What is STOP-BANG used for?
cards.a: Screening for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).

cards.q: What does STOP stand for?
cards.a: Snoring, Tiredness, Observed apnea, high blood Pressure.

cards.q: What does BANG stand for?
cards.a: BMI >35 kg/m², Age >50 years, Neck circumference >40 cm, Gender male.

cards.q: Why is OSA important before surgery?
cards.a: It increases the risk of difficult airway and postoperative respiratory depression. Laboratory Evaluation

cards.q: Should routine preoperative laboratory testing be ordered for every patient?
cards.a: No. Testing should be guided by the patient's history, physical examination, and planned procedure.

cards.q: Which laboratory test is commonly indicated before major surgery with anticipated blood loss?
cards.a: CBC and type & screen (or type & crossmatch if transfusion is likely).

cards.q: When should coagulation studies be obtained preoperatively?
cards.a: In patients with bleeding disorders, liver disease, anticoagulant use, or suspected coagulopathy. Cardiac Evaluation

cards.q: Which active cardiac conditions generally require evaluation before elective surgery?
cards.a: Unstable angina, decompensated heart failure, significant arrhythmias, and severe symptomatic valvular disease.

cards.q: Is a resting ECG indicated for every surgical patient?
cards.a: No. It is obtained selectively based on age, cardiovascular risk factors, symptoms, and surgical risk. Pulmonary Evaluation

cards.q: Which patients are at highest risk for postoperative pulmonary complications?
cards.a: Smokers, patients with COPD, advanced age, obesity, OSA, and those undergoing thoracic or upper abdominal surgery.

cards.q: What is the most effective preoperative intervention for smokers?
cards.a: Smoking cessation as early as possible before surgery. Medication Management

cards.q: Should chronic corticosteroids be stopped abruptly before surgery?
cards.a: No. Patients may require perioperative glucocorticoid supplementation depending on adrenal suppression risk.

cards.q: Which diabetic medication is commonly withheld on the day of surgery to reduce hypoglycemia risk?
cards.a: Short-acting insulin doses are adjusted, and many oral hypoglycemic agents are withheld; management depends on the regimen.

cards.q: Why are anticoagulants reviewed carefully before surgery?
cards.a: To balance bleeding risk against thromboembolic risk and determine if interruption or bridging is needed. Informed Consent

cards.q: What are the four essential elements of informed consent?
cards.a: Decision-making capacity, adequate information, voluntary choice, and patient understanding.

cards.q: Who should obtain informed consent for surgery?
cards.a: The physician performing (or responsible for) the procedure. Pregnancy

cards.q: Why should pregnancy status be considered before anesthesia?
cards.a: Pregnancy affects anesthetic management and fetal safety, and may alter surgical planning. Obesity

cards.q: Why are obese patients at higher anesthetic risk?
cards.a: Increased risk of difficult airway, hypoventilation, aspiration, OSA, and postoperative pulmonary complications. Aspiration Risk

cards.q: Which patients are at increased risk for aspiration during anesthesia?
cards.a: Full stomach, bowel obstruction, pregnancy, obesity, gastroparesis, GERD, and emergency surgery.

cards.q: Which airway technique is commonly used in patients at high aspiration risk?
cards.a: Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI). High-Yield Review

cards.q: What is the most important predictor of difficult intubation?
cards.a: Previous difficult intubation.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK anesthesia principle?
cards.a: A thorough pre-anesthetic evaluation—including ASA classification, airway assessment (Mallampati, mouth opening, neck mobility), medication review, and aspiration risk assessment—is essential to anticipate complications and guide safe anesthetic management.

cards.q: Why are preoperative fasting (NPO) guidelines important?
cards.a: To reduce the risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction of anesthesia.

cards.q: How long before elective anesthesia may healthy patients drink clear liquids?
cards.a: 2 hours.

cards.q: Which fluids are considered clear liquids?
cards.a: Water, pulp-free juice, black coffee, clear tea, and carbohydrate-rich clear beverages.

cards.q: How long before anesthesia may infants receive breast milk?
cards.a: 4 hours.

cards.q: How long before anesthesia should infant formula be stopped?
cards.a: 6 hours.

cards.q: How long before anesthesia should a light meal be stopped?
cards.a: 6 hours.

cards.q: How long before anesthesia should a fatty meal be stopped?
cards.a: 8 hours or longer.

cards.q: Does emergency surgery wait until NPO guidelines are met?
cards.a: No. Emergencies proceed with aspiration precautions, usually using Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI). Types of Anesthesia

cards.q: What are the four major categories of anesthesia?
cards.a: General anesthesia, regional anesthesia, local anesthesia, and monitored anesthesia care (MAC).

cards.q: What is general anesthesia?
cards.a: Drug-induced unconsciousness with loss of protective airway reflexes, requiring airway management.

cards.q: What is regional anesthesia?
cards.a: Temporary blockade of nerve transmission to a specific region while the patient may remain awake or lightly sedated.

cards.q: What is local anesthesia?
cards.a: Local infiltration of anesthetic to numb a small area without affecting consciousness.

cards.q: What is monitored anesthesia care (MAC)?
cards.a: Sedation with continuous monitoring while maintaining spontaneous ventilation, with readiness to convert to general anesthesia if needed. General Anesthesia

cards.q: What are the three major components of balanced general anesthesia?
cards.a: Hypnosis (unconsciousness), analgesia, and muscle relaxation.

cards.q: Which airway reflexes are lost during general anesthesia?
cards.a: Protective reflexes such as coughing and gagging.

cards.q: Why do patients receiving general anesthesia often require endotracheal intubation?
cards.a: To secure the airway, facilitate ventilation, and reduce aspiration risk. Regional Anesthesia

cards.q: What is spinal anesthesia?
cards.a: Injection of local anesthetic into the cerebrospinal fluid in the subarachnoid space.

cards.q: Where is spinal anesthesia administered?
cards.a: Into the lumbar subarachnoid space, usually below the termination of the spinal cord (e.g., L3–L4 or L4–L5).

cards.q: What is epidural anesthesia?
cards.a: Injection of local anesthetic into the epidural space outside the dura.

cards.q: What is a major advantage of epidural anesthesia over spinal anesthesia?
cards.a: A catheter can provide continuous dosing and prolonged analgesia.

cards.q: Which surgeries commonly use spinal anesthesia?
cards.a: Lower abdominal, pelvic, perineal, and lower-extremity procedures.

cards.q: Which complication is more common after spinal anesthesia than epidural anesthesia?
cards.a: Post-dural puncture headache. Peripheral Nerve Blocks

cards.q: What is the purpose of a peripheral nerve block?
cards.a: To provide targeted anesthesia and analgesia to a specific limb or body region.

cards.q: What is a major advantage of peripheral nerve blocks?
cards.a: Reduced systemic opioid requirements and excellent postoperative pain control. Airway Devices

cards.q: What is the simplest airway maneuver to relieve upper airway obstruction?
cards.a: Head tilt–chin lift (or jaw thrust if cervical spine injury is suspected).

cards.q: When is the jaw-thrust maneuver preferred?
cards.a: In patients with possible cervical spine injury.

cards.q: What is an oropharyngeal airway (OPA)?
cards.a: An airway adjunct used in unconscious patients without an intact gag reflex.

cards.q: When is an oropharyngeal airway contraindicated?
cards.a: In awake or semiconscious patients with an intact gag reflex.

cards.q: What is a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA)?
cards.a: A soft airway inserted through the nose to help maintain airway patency in selected patients.

cards.q: When should a nasopharyngeal airway generally be avoided?
cards.a: Suspected basilar skull fracture or severe facial trauma. Laryngeal Mask Airway (LMA)

cards.q: What is a laryngeal mask airway (LMA)?
cards.a: A supraglottic airway device positioned over the laryngeal inlet.

cards.q: What is the major advantage of an LMA?
cards.a: Easier insertion than endotracheal intubation with less airway stimulation.

cards.q: What is a major limitation of the LMA?
cards.a: It does not reliably protect against aspiration. Endotracheal Intubation

cards.q: What is the gold standard for airway protection during general anesthesia?
cards.a: Cuffed endotracheal intubation.

cards.q: How is correct endotracheal tube placement confirmed?
cards.a: Continuous waveform capnography is the most reliable confirmation after intubation.

cards.q: Which bedside finding alone is insufficient to confirm proper endotracheal tube placement?
cards.a: Bilateral breath sounds. Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI)

cards.q: What is the primary indication for Rapid Sequence Intubation?
cards.a: Patients at high risk of aspiration.

cards.q: Which patients commonly require RSI?
cards.a: Emergency surgery, bowel obstruction, trauma, pregnancy, obesity, gastroparesis, and full stomach.

cards.q: What are the basic steps of RSI?
cards.a: Preoxygenation → induction agent → neuromuscular blocker → intubation without bag-mask ventilation (unless necessary) → confirmation with capnography.

cards.q: Why is positive-pressure bag-mask ventilation minimized during RSI?
cards.a: To reduce gastric insufflation and aspiration risk. Difficult Airway

cards.q: What is the first priority in difficult airway management?
cards.a: Maintain oxygenation.

cards.q: What is the most dangerous difficult airway scenario?
cards.a: Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate (CICO).

cards.q: What is the definitive emergency treatment for a CICO airway?
cards.a: Emergency cricothyrotomy.

cards.q: When should a surgical airway be considered?
cards.a: When oxygenation cannot be maintained despite noninvasive airway attempts.

cards.q: Which device is commonly used for anticipated difficult intubation while maintaining spontaneous breathing?
cards.a: Flexible fiberoptic bronchoscope (awake fiberoptic intubation in appropriate patients). Airway Confirmation

cards.q: What is the most reliable bedside method for confirming tracheal intubation?
cards.a: Continuous waveform capnography.

cards.q: What finding strongly suggests esophageal intubation?
cards.a: Absence of persistent end-tidal CO₂ after several ventilations. High-Yield Review

cards.q: Which airway device provides the best protection against aspiration?
cards.a: Cuffed endotracheal tube.

cards.q: What is the emergency airway procedure for a "cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate" situation?
cards.a: Cricothyrotomy.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK anesthesia principle?
cards.a: Know the fasting guidelines, recognize aspiration risk, understand when to perform Rapid Sequence Intubation, confirm endotracheal tube placement with continuous waveform capnography, and remember that oxygenation takes priority over intubation—perform an emergency cricothyrotomy in a cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate scenario.

cards.q: What are the three major classes of drugs used to induce general anesthesia?
cards.a: Induction agents (hypnotics), analgesics (usually opioids), and neuromuscular blocking agents.

cards.q: Does any induction agent provide all three components of balanced anesthesia?
cards.a: No. Multiple agents are typically combined to provide hypnosis, analgesia, and muscle relaxation. Propofol

cards.q: What is propofol?
cards.a: A rapid-onset, short-acting IV hypnotic used for induction and maintenance of anesthesia and procedural sedation.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of propofol?
cards.a: Potentiates GABA-A receptor activity, increasing inhibitory neurotransmission.

cards.q: What are the advantages of propofol?
cards.a: Rapid onset, rapid recovery, antiemetic properties, and decreased intracranial pressure (ICP).

cards.q: What is the most common hemodynamic adverse effect of propofol?
cards.a: Hypotension due to vasodilation and myocardial depression.

cards.q: Which respiratory adverse effect is commonly seen with propofol?
cards.a: Respiratory depression and apnea.

cards.q: In which patients should propofol be used cautiously?
cards.a: Patients with hypovolemia, severe hypotension, or hemodynamic instability. Etomidate

cards.q: Why is etomidate commonly chosen for induction in critically ill patients?
cards.a: It has minimal cardiovascular depression and maintains hemodynamic stability.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of etomidate?
cards.a: Potentiates GABA-A receptor activity.

cards.q: What is the major adverse effect of etomidate?
cards.a: Transient adrenal suppression (via inhibition of 11β-hydroxylase).

cards.q: Which patient is an ideal candidate for etomidate induction?
cards.a: A hypotensive patient requiring emergency intubation. Ketamine

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of ketamine?
cards.a: NMDA receptor antagonism.

cards.q: What type of anesthesia does ketamine produce?
cards.a: Dissociative anesthesia.

cards.q: What cardiovascular effect distinguishes ketamine from most other induction agents?
cards.a: It increases heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac output through sympathetic stimulation.

cards.q: Which patients particularly benefit from ketamine induction?
cards.a: Patients with hypotension, asthma, or severe bronchospasm.

cards.q: Why is ketamine useful in patients with asthma?
cards.a: It has bronchodilatory properties.

cards.q: What are common adverse effects of ketamine?
cards.a: Emergence reactions (hallucinations), hypersalivation, nausea, and vomiting.

cards.q: Which medication may reduce ketamine-associated emergence reactions?
cards.a: A benzodiazepine (e.g., midazolam) in selected patients. Benzodiazepines

cards.q: Which benzodiazepine is most commonly used perioperatively?
cards.a: Midazolam.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of benzodiazepines?
cards.a: They enhance GABA-A receptor activity by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening.

cards.q: What are the major clinical effects of midazolam?
cards.a: Anxiolysis, sedation, anterograde amnesia, and anticonvulsant activity.

cards.q: What is the major adverse effect of benzodiazepines?
cards.a: Respiratory depression, especially when combined with opioids. Dexmedetomidine

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of dexmedetomidine?
cards.a: Selective α₂-adrenergic agonist.

cards.q: What is a major advantage of dexmedetomidine?
cards.a: Sedation with minimal respiratory depression.

cards.q: What are common adverse effects of dexmedetomidine?
cards.a: Bradycardia and hypotension. Opioids

cards.q: Which opioid is most commonly used during anesthesia?
cards.a: Fentanyl.

cards.q: Why is fentanyl favored intraoperatively?
cards.a: Rapid onset, potent analgesia, and relatively short duration of action.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of fentanyl?
cards.a: μ-opioid receptor agonist.

cards.q: What are common adverse effects of fentanyl?
cards.a: Respiratory depression, bradycardia, nausea, constipation, and chest wall rigidity with rapid high-dose administration.

cards.q: Which opioid is commonly used for postoperative pain control?
cards.a: Morphine.

cards.q: What are common adverse effects of morphine?
cards.a: Respiratory depression, constipation, urinary retention, pruritus, nausea, vomiting, and histamine-mediated hypotension. Succinylcholine

cards.q: What type of neuromuscular blocker is succinylcholine?
cards.a: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of succinylcholine?
cards.a: Persistent depolarization of the neuromuscular junction by acting as an acetylcholine receptor agonist.

cards.q: What is the onset and duration of succinylcholine?
cards.a: Rapid onset (30–60 seconds) with short duration (approximately 5–10 minutes).

cards.q: Why is succinylcholine commonly used during RSI?
cards.a: It provides rapid paralysis with a short duration.

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality can succinylcholine cause?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia.

cards.q: In which patients is succinylcholine contraindicated because of severe hyperkalemia risk?
cards.a: Major burns (>24–48 hours after injury), crush injuries, prolonged immobilization, denervation injuries, neuromuscular diseases, and known hyperkalemia.

cards.q: Which inherited enzyme deficiency prolongs succinylcholine paralysis?
cards.a: Pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) deficiency. Nondepolarizing Neuromuscular Blockers

cards.q: Name two commonly used nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers.
cards.a: Rocuronium and vecuronium.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers?
cards.a: Competitive antagonism of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

cards.q: Which nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker is commonly used as an alternative to succinylcholine for RSI?
cards.a: Rocuronium.

cards.q: Which neuromuscular blocker undergoes Hofmann elimination and is useful in severe renal or hepatic dysfunction?
cards.a: Cisatracurium. Reversal Agents

cards.q: Which medication rapidly reverses rocuronium and vecuronium?
cards.a: Suγdex.

cards.q: How does suγdex work?
cards.a: It encapsulates steroidal neuromuscular blockers (especially rocuronium and vecuronium), rendering them inactive.

cards.q: Which medication reverses many nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers by increasing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction?
cards.a: Neostigmine.

cards.q: Why is glycopyrrolate or atropine commonly administered with neostigmine?
cards.a: To reduce muscarinic side effects such as bradycardia and excessive secretions. Drug Reversal

cards.q: Which medication reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression?
cards.a: Naloxone.

cards.q: Which medication reverses benzodiazepine-induced sedation?
cards.a: Flumazenil.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK anesthesia pharmacology principle?
cards.a: Choose the induction agent based on the patient's physiology: propofol for routine induction (but avoid in severe hypotension), etomidate for hemodynamic instability, ketamine for hypotension or bronchospasm. Remember succinylcholine causes hyperkalemia and is contraindicated in burns, denervation, and neuromuscular disease; rocuronium is a common alternative. Know the reversal agents: naloxone (opioids), flumazenil (benzodiazepines), suγdex (rocuronium/vecuronium), and neostigmine (nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers).

cards.q: What is the primary role of inhalational anesthetics?
cards.a: Maintenance of general anesthesia after induction.

cards.q: Which inhalational anesthetics are commonly used in modern practice?
cards.a: Sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane, and nitrous oxide.

cards.q: What does MAC (Minimum Alveolar Concentration) represent?
cards.a: The alveolar concentration of an inhaled anesthetic that prevents movement in response to a surgical stimulus in 50% of patients.

cards.q: How does MAC relate to anesthetic potency?
cards.a: Lower MAC = greater anesthetic potency.

cards.q: Which inhalational anesthetic has the fastest induction and emergence?
cards.a: Desflurane.

cards.q: Which inhalational anesthetic is commonly preferred for inhalational induction, especially in children?
cards.a: Sevoflurane.

cards.q: Why is sevoflurane preferred over desflurane for mask induction?
cards.a: It is less irritating to the airway.

cards.q: Which inhalational anesthetic may irritate the airway and provoke coughing or laryngospasm?
cards.a: Desflurane.

cards.q: Which inhalational anesthetic has significant analgesic properties?
cards.a: Nitrous oxide.

cards.q: Why is nitrous oxide rarely used as the sole anesthetic?
cards.a: It is a weak anesthetic and cannot reliably produce surgical anesthesia alone.

cards.q: Why should nitrous oxide be avoided in patients with pneumothorax or bowel obstruction?
cards.a: It diffuses into air-filled spaces and expands trapped gas.

cards.q: What is diffusion hypoxia?
cards.a: Rapid diffusion of nitrous oxide from blood into alveoli after discontinuation, transiently diluting alveolar oxygen.

cards.q: How is diffusion hypoxia prevented?
cards.a: Administer 100% oxygen for several minutes after discontinuing nitrous oxide. Local Anesthetics

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of local anesthetics?
cards.a: Reversible blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing nerve impulse conduction.

cards.q: Which nerve fibers are blocked first by local anesthetics?
cards.a: Small, myelinated pain fibers (Aδ) and unmyelinated C fibers.

cards.q: Name two commonly used local anesthetics.
cards.a: Lidocaine and bupivacaine.

cards.q: Which local anesthetic has the fastest onset?
cards.a: Lidocaine.

cards.q: Which local anesthetic has the longest duration?
cards.a: Bupivacaine.

cards.q: Why is epinephrine sometimes added to local anesthetics?
cards.a: It causes vasoconstriction, prolonging anesthetic duration and reducing systemic absorption.

cards.q: In which body areas should epinephrine-containing local anesthetics generally be avoided?
cards.a: Areas with end-arterial blood supply (e.g., digits, penis, nose, and ears), although practice is evolving and may vary by clinical context. Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST)

cards.q: What causes Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST)?
cards.a: Accidental intravascular injection or excessive systemic absorption of a local anesthetic.

cards.q: What are the earliest neurologic symptoms of LAST?
cards.a: Perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, dizziness, agitation, and circumoral paresthesias.

cards.q: What severe neurologic complication may occur in LAST?
cards.a: Generalized seizures.

cards.q: What cardiovascular complications occur in severe LAST?
cards.a: Hypotension, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiac depression, and cardiac arrest.

cards.q: Which local anesthetic carries the greatest risk of severe cardiotoxicity?
cards.a: Bupivacaine.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for severe LAST?
cards.a: Intravenous lipid emulsion therapy plus standard advanced resuscitation.

cards.q: How does lipid emulsion therapy work?
cards.a: It acts as a "lipid sink," reducing the free concentration of lipophilic local anesthetic in target tissues. Malignant Hyperthermia (MH)

cards.q: What is malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: A life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder causing uncontrolled skeletal muscle calcium release after exposure to certain anesthetic agents.

cards.q: Which receptor is abnormal in most cases of malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Ryanodine receptor (RYR1).

cards.q: Which anesthetic agents trigger malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Volatile inhalational anesthetics (e.g., sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane) and succinylcholine.

cards.q: Which commonly used anesthetic agents do not trigger malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Propofol, ketamine, etomidate, opioids, benzodiazepines, dexmedetomidine, nitrous oxide, and nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers.

cards.q: What is usually the earliest sign of malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Rapid rise in end-tidal CO₂ (hypercapnia) despite increased ventilation.

cards.q: What is the classic muscle finding in malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Generalized muscle rigidity, often including masseter muscle rigidity.

cards.q: Is hyperthermia the earliest manifestation of malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: No. Hypercapnia and muscle rigidity usually occur first.

cards.q: What metabolic abnormalities are common in malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, elevated CK, myoglobinuria, and hyperthermia.

cards.q: Which medication is the definitive treatment for malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Dantrolene.

cards.q: How does dantrolene work?
cards.a: It inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum by blocking the ryanodine receptor.

cards.q: Besides dantrolene, what supportive measures are essential?
cards.a: Discontinue triggering agents, provide 100% oxygen, active cooling, correct hyperkalemia and acidosis, treat arrhythmias, and monitor for renal injury.

cards.q: Why is CK markedly elevated in malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Massive skeletal muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis).

cards.q: Which inherited muscle disease is strongly associated with malignant hyperthermia susceptibility?
cards.a: Central core disease. Post-Anesthesia Care

cards.q: What is the most common cause of hypoxemia immediately after surgery?
cards.a: Upper airway obstruction or hypoventilation due to residual anesthetic or opioid effects.

cards.q: What is the first step in managing postoperative hypoxemia?
cards.a: Ensure airway patency and administer supplemental oxygen while assessing ventilation.

cards.q: Which patients are at highest risk for postoperative respiratory depression?
cards.a: Patients receiving opioids, those with OSA, obesity, advanced age, or significant pulmonary disease.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of delayed emergence from anesthesia?
cards.a: Residual anesthetic or sedative medications.

cards.q: What should always be considered in a patient who fails to awaken appropriately after surgery?
cards.a: Residual drugs, hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbances, hypoxia, hypercapnia, stroke, and other neurologic causes. Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting (PONV)

cards.q: Which patients are at highest risk for postoperative nausea and vomiting?
cards.a: Female sex, nonsmoking status, prior history of PONV or motion sickness, and postoperative opioid use.

cards.q: Which antiemetic is commonly used for PONV prophylaxis?
cards.a: Ondansetron (5-HT₃ receptor antagonist). High-Yield Review

cards.q: What is the antidote for malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Dantrolene.

cards.q: What is the antidote for Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST)?
cards.a: Intravenous lipid emulsion.

cards.q: What is the highest-yield USMLE Step 2 CK anesthesia emergency principle?
cards.a: Think malignant hyperthermia in any patient who develops rapidly rising end-tidal CO₂, muscle rigidity, hyperkalemia, and hyperthermia after exposure to volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine—stop triggering agents immediately and administer dantrolene. Think LAST when neurologic symptoms (e.g., tinnitus, perioral numbness, seizures) or cardiovascular collapse follows local anesthetic administration—treat promptly with intravenous lipid emulsion. -------------------------------------- For FlashCards USMLE 2 Section: Surgery

cards.q: What is the first priority in any patient with a suspected surgical emergency?
cards.a: Assess and stabilize Airway, Breathing, and Circulation (ABCs) before pursuing diagnostic testing.

cards.q: What are the first three simultaneous interventions in an unstable patient with an acute abdomen?
cards.a: Large-bore IV access, isotonic IV fluids, and continuous monitoring (plus supplemental oxygen as needed).

cards.q: Which laboratory studies are commonly obtained in patients with an acute surgical abdomen?
cards.a: CBC, CMP, coagulation profile (if indicated), serum lactate, lipase (if pancreatitis suspected), urinalysis, &β;-hCG in women of reproductive age, and type & screen/crossmatch if significant bleeding is possible.

cards.q: Why is serum lactate measured in suspected surgical emergencies?
cards.a: It may indicate tissue hypoperfusion or ischemia, although a normal lactate does not exclude early mesenteric ischemia.

cards.q: Which imaging study is preferred for most stable adults with an undifferentiated acute abdomen?
cards.a: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast (when appropriate and not contraindicated).

cards.q: Which imaging modality is preferred first for suspected biliary disease?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant ultrasound.

cards.q: Which imaging modality is preferred first for unstable trauma patients?
cards.a: FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma).

cards.q: When should imaging not delay surgery?
cards.a: When there is clear evidence of a life-threatening surgical emergency (e.g., diffuse peritonitis, ruptured AAA with instability, tension pneumothorax). Acute Abdomen

cards.q: What is meant by an "acute abdomen"?
cards.a: Sudden severe abdominal pain that may require urgent surgical intervention.

cards.q: Which physical examination finding most strongly suggests peritoneal irritation?
cards.a: Involuntary guarding (rigidity).

cards.q: What is rebound tenderness?
cards.a: Increased pain when pressure is suddenly released from the abdomen, suggesting peritoneal inflammation.

cards.q: Which finding is more specific for peritonitis: voluntary guarding or involuntary guarding?
cards.a: Involuntary guarding.

cards.q: Which patients may have minimal abdominal findings despite severe intra-abdominal disease?
cards.a: Elderly patients, immunocompromised patients, and those receiving corticosteroids. Peritonitis

cards.q: What is peritonitis?
cards.a: Inflammation of the peritoneal lining, usually due to infection or chemical irritation from gastrointestinal contents.

cards.q: What are the classic clinical features of generalized peritonitis?
cards.a: Severe abdominal pain, rigidity, rebound tenderness, fever, tachycardia, and absent or markedly decreased bowel sounds.

cards.q: Which bowel sound abnormality is commonly present in generalized peritonitis?
cards.a: Hypoactive or absent bowel sounds due to paralytic ileus.

cards.q: Why do patients with peritonitis often lie still?
cards.a: Movement worsens pain because of peritoneal irritation.

cards.q: What are the major causes of secondary peritonitis?
cards.a: Perforated peptic ulcer, perforated diverticulitis, perforated appendicitis, bowel ischemia with perforation, traumatic bowel injury, and anastomotic leak.

cards.q: What are the four initial management priorities for generalized peritonitis?
cards.a: IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, analgesia, and urgent surgical consultation.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for most cases of secondary peritonitis?
cards.a: Source control, usually through surgery or image-guided drainage when appropriate. Hollow Viscus Perforation

cards.q: What is meant by a hollow viscus perforation?
cards.a: A full-thickness perforation of a gastrointestinal organ, allowing air and/or contents to enter the peritoneal cavity.

cards.q: Which radiographic finding strongly suggests perforation of a hollow viscus?
cards.a: Free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum).

cards.q: Which upright radiograph may demonstrate free intraperitoneal air?
cards.a: Upright chest X-ray showing subdiaphragmatic free air.

cards.q: Which CT finding is most sensitive for detecting bowel perforation?
cards.a: Extraluminal free air adjacent to the gastrointestinal tract.

cards.q: What are common causes of hollow viscus perforation?
cards.a: Perforated peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, ischemic bowel, colorectal cancer, trauma, and inflammatory bowel disease.

cards.q: Which antibiotics are appropriate empirically for suspected bowel perforation?
cards.a: Broad-spectrum agents covering gram-negative organisms and anaerobes (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime plus metronidazole, depending on local practice).

cards.q: Is a normal white blood cell count sufficient to exclude bowel perforation?
cards.a: No. Sepsis from Intra-abdominal Infection

cards.q: Which patients with an acute abdomen require early sepsis recognition and treatment?
cards.a: Patients with hypotension, fever, tachycardia, altered mental status, elevated lactate, or evidence of organ dysfunction.

cards.q: Besides antibiotics, what intervention is critical for survival in intra-abdominal sepsis?
cards.a: Early source control.

cards.q: Why are antibiotics alone usually insufficient in perforated bowel?
cards.a: Because infected material remains in the abdomen until source control is achieved. Analgesia

cards.q: Should opioid analgesia be withheld until the diagnosis is established?
cards.a: No. Adequate pain control should be provided while evaluation proceeds.

cards.q: Does opioid administration significantly reduce diagnostic accuracy for acute abdominal pain?
cards.a: No. Appropriate analgesia does not preclude accurate diagnosis. Nasogastric Tube
